en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
This immeasurable [work] has issued from the lips of Dvaipāyana.
For one who listens to the *Bhārata* as it is being recited— [which is] meritorious, pure, a remover of sins,
and auspicious— what need is there for him to perform ablutions with the waters of Puṣkara?
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, four-armed,
and has a serene countenance, for the pacification of all obstacles.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having offered water libations for King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, with his senses overwhelmed by agitation, led the way and ascended [the funeral pyre]. Having emerged from the water, the protector of the earth, his eyes clouded with tears, [proceeded].
He fell upon the bank of the Gaṅgā like an elephant pierced by a hunter. As he was sinking, Bhīma seized him at the urging of Kṛṣṇa;
and Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of enemy forces, said to him, "Do not do this!"

O King, the Pāṇḍavas beheld the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira fallen upon the ground, distressed and sighing again and again. Seeing that lord of men with a dejected mind and his vital strength departed, they were overcome with grief.
Overcome once more by grief, the Pāṇḍavas sat down together;
and the mighty-armed King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, sitting beside him,
spoke these words to that highly wise one who was tormented by great sorrow.
"Arise, O tiger among the Kurus! Perform what must be done immediately. O descendant of Kuru, this earth has been conquered by you according to the duty of a Kṣatriya;
enjoy it together with your brothers and your friends, O lord of men."
"O best among the upholders of dharma, I see no reason for you to grieve; rather,
O lord of the people, it is I and Gāndhārī who ought to grieve, for we are deprived of our sons and our kingdom, like one who has lost wealth gained in a dream."

"Having failed to listen to the words of great significance spoken by the high-souled Vidura, who desires my welfare, I, a man of evil intellect, now suffer deeply. This righteous one, possessed of divine vision, spoke to me previously."
"Because of Duryodhana’s transgression, your lineage will perish. O King, if you desire the welfare of your own family as well as yourself,
let this evil-minded and foolish King Suyodhana be slain."
"Let neither Karṇa nor Śakuni ever behold him;
vigilantly prevent even a meeting with them for the purpose of gambling. Consecrate the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira as king."
That self-controlled one shall rule this earth according to dharma. If you do not desire Kuntī’s son Yudhiṣṭhira as king,
your sons will undoubtedly meet their destruction.
"O King, become yourself the central pillar and accept the sovereignty;
O lord of men, conduct yourself with impartiality toward all beings,
and let all your kinsmen live under you, O increaser of your kin."
While the far-sighted Vidura was speaking thus, O son of Kuntī,
I, of vain intellect, followed after the wicked Duryodhana;
for I did not listen to the sweet words of this hero.
Having obtained this great suffering as its fruit, you are submerged in an ocean of grief.
For your parents have grown old, O King; behold us two who are likewise distressed. You should not grieve, O lord of men; so I see it here.
14,002.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having been thus addressed by the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the intelligent Keśava remained silent and then spoke to him.
O lord of men, grief being indulged in excessively by the mind causes distress even to one’s deceased ancestors and grandfathers. Therefore, perform various sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.
"Satisfy the gods with Soma and the ancestors with the Svadhā offering;
satisfy guests with food and drink, and those who possess nothing with other desired objects.
For one of great intelligence such as yourself, this [present state] is not fitting today."
That which was to be known has been known by you, and that which was to be done has been done by you. You have heard the duties of kings from Bhīṣma, the son of Bhāgīrathī,
as well as from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, Nārada, and Vidura.
"You ought not to follow this way of life of the foolish;
instead, uphold the burden by adhering to the conduct of your fathers and grandfathers.
For it is fitting that the warrior class, through its glory, should undoubtedly attain heaven."
"Indeed, not a single one among these heroes was slain here with his back turned.
Abandon your grief, O Great King, for it was destined to be so. For those who were killed in this battle cannot be seen by you again."
Having said this much to the King of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, Govinda, the one of great splendor, became silent; then Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to him:
"O Govinda, that affection which you have for me is well known to me."
14,002.010c Out of friendship and likewise out of love, you always show compassion toward me. 14,002.011a But a very great favor would be done for me, O wielder of the discus and mace;
14,002.011c O glorious one, with a pleased mind, grant me everything, O Aniruddha.
"If you would grant me permission to go to the forest of asceticism, I shall have accomplished my purpose; this is my firm resolve. For I see no peace in having caused the death of my grandfather."
And regarding Karṇa, that tiger among men who never retreats in battles— O subduer of foes,
perform for me here such an act by which I may be liberated from this cruelty and my mind may be purified.
To him who was speaking thus, Vyāsa, the knower of dharma and possessed of great splendor, then spoke these auspicious and meaningful words in a consoling manner:
"O dear one, your mind is not yet matured; you are being deluded once again by childishness."
"Why do we all prattle thus again and again in the empty air?
You are well-acquainted with the duties of the Kṣatriyas, for whom livelihood is sustained by battle;
just as a king who has set out on his path is not bound by emotional attachment."
You have heard all the teachings on liberation (*mokṣadharma*) exactly as they are;
indeed, you ought to abandon this illusion born of desire. Furthermore, those doubts arising from desire have been severed by me for you more than once.
"You are surely lacking in faith, dull-witted, and devoid of mindfulness.
Do not be thus; such ignorance is not fitting for you, O sinless one, for you know all the rites of expiation."

"You have heard all the duties of war and all the duties of charity; how is it, O Bhārata, that you who know all dharmas and are proficient in all the scriptures, are once again bewildered as if out of ignorance?"
Vyāsa said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is my opinion that your understanding is not complete;
for no mortal whatsoever performs actions by his own will or under his own control."
"14,003.002a This man performs action, whether good or evil, impelled by the Lord; what lamentation can there be in that?
14,003.003a And yet, in the end, you consider yourself a doer of evil deeds."
Listen, O Bhārata, to how sin may be removed in that regard:
through austerities, sacrifices, and indeed through gifts, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Men are purified, O King; therefore, sacrifices are the supreme refuge.

O lord of men, those men who have committed sins always cross over [their transgressions] through sacrifice, austerity, and charity; O tiger among kings, such men who have performed evil deeds are purified.
Both the Asuras and the Suras, those great-souled ones, strive toward the performance of sacrifice for the sake of merit; therefore, sacrifices are the supreme goal.
It was through sacrifices alone that the great-souled Suras became superior.
14,003.007c Thereupon, the gods, being observant of their duties, overcame the Dānavas.
14,003.008a O Bhārata, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, you must perform the Rājasūya, the Aśvamedha, the Sarvamedha, and the Naramedha sacrifices.
"Perform the horse sacrifice according to the rules, with abundant sacrificial fees,
food, and wealth, just as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, did,
and as King Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta and lord of the earth, did."
"Śākuntala, of great prowess, was your ancestor.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Without doubt, the horse sacrifice would purify even the entire earth."
"However, O best of the twice-born, you ought to hear a certain intention of mine regarding this: having committed this very great slaughter of kinsmen,
I am unable to give even a small gift, for I possess no wealth."

"O best of the twice-born, having myself destroyed the earth for the sake of a sacrifice, I cannot bring myself to beg wealth from these wretched fools— the sons of kings who are suffering in hardship with their wounds still raw."

O best of sages, how shall I exact tribute from those who are now devoted to grief? Through the fault of Duryodhana, the lords of the earth have perished, and we ourselves have been joined with infamy.
The earth was exhausted by Duryodhana for the sake of wealth, and the treasury of that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was utterly depleted.
In this matter, the primary rule is that the earth itself constitutes the sacrificial fee.
"This reversal of the prescribed rule has been observed by the learned and remains sanctioned by the virtuous.
O one whose wealth is asceticism, I do not wish to perform a substitution;
therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to provide me with proper assistance in this matter."
14,003.019 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by Pārtha, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana then reflected for a moment and spoke to Dharmarāja.
This treasury, though now shattered, shall once again be filled;
O Pārtha, there exists wealth situated on the Himavat mountain,
which was left behind by the brahmins at the sacrifice of King Marutta.
"O son of Kuntī, bring that; it will be sufficient.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How was that wealth accumulated at the sacrifice of Marutta?"
14,003.021c "And at what time did that king live, O best of speakers?
14,003.022 Vyāsa said:
14,003.022a "If you wish to hear it, O Pārtha, listen to the story of King Kāraṃdhama."
14,003.022c At the time when that king of great heroism and vast wealth lived,
14,004.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
14,004.001a "O knower of dharma, I wish to hear the glorification of that royal sage."
"O sinless Dvaipāyana, tell me the story of Marutta.
Vyāsa said:
"In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a lord named Manu who held the rod of punishment."
His son was the great archer renowned as Prajāti. From Prajāti was born a son widely celebrated as Kṣupa.
And the son of Kṣupa was the lord Ikṣvāku, who became a protector of the earth.
O King, he had one hundred sons who were supremely righteous;
the lord Ikṣvāku made them all rulers of the earth.
Among them, Viṃśa was the eldest, a model for all archers.
O Bhārata, the son of Viṃśa was the auspicious one named Viviṃśa.
O King, Viviṃśa had fifteen sons,
all of whom were valiant in archery, devoted to Brahman, and speakers of truth.
Being devoted to the duty of charity and always speaking kindly, they were [virtuous];
yet their eldest brother, Khanīnetra, oppressed them all. Khanīnetra, however, being powerful, having conquered the kingdom, made it free of thorns.

He was unable to protect the kingdom, and the subjects did not take affection for him. Having cast him aside, O Indra among kings, that kingdom then consecrated his son Suvarcas, and it became joyful at that time.
Having witnessed his father’s transformation as well as his expulsion from the kingdom,
he lived with self-restraint, desiring to act for the welfare of his subjects.
Devoted to the Brahmins, truthful, pure, and endowed with tranquility and self-control, he remained steadfast.
The subjects were devoted to that wise king, who was ever constant in righteousness. However, as he remained devoted to dharma, his treasury and transport were exhausted;
and with his treasury depleted, his neighbors oppressed him from every side.
Oppressed by many, his treasury exhausted and his mounts gone,
the king, along with his servants and the city, fell into extreme distress; yet,
as their resources were utterly depleted, they were unable to avoid him.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, that king was indeed of right conduct and ever devoted to dharma;
yet when that monarch, along with his city, fell into supreme distress,
he blew upon his hand, and from that, an army appeared."
Then he conquered all those neighboring lords of men;
for this reason, O King, he became renowned as Karaṃdhama.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, he had a son named Kāraṃdhama.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, there was a son known as Āvikṣita;
he became the lord of the earth celebrated as Kāraṃdhama. Glorious and not inferior to Indra, he was exceedingly difficult even for the gods to conquer.
At that time, all the rulers of the earth remained under his control;
for he became their sovereign both by virtue of his conduct and his might. The righteous-souled one named Avikṣit was equal to Indra in heroism.
Devoted to sacrifice, delighting in ritual action, steadfast, and with senses restrained;
equal to the sun in splendor, like the earth in forbearance,
equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence, and as immovable as the Himavat mountains.
Through action, mind, and speech, as well as through self-restraint and tranquility, that lord of the earth gratified the hearts of his subjects; he,
the sovereign, duly performed a hundred horse-sacrifices.
The learned lord Aṅgiras himself officiated at his sacrifice;
his son, named Marutta— a knower of dharma, a highly illustrious universal monarch— surpassed his father in virtue.
Possessing strength equal to ten thousand elephants, like a second Viṣṇu in person,
that righteous-souled king,
intending to perform a sacrifice, had thousands of bright vessels made of gold.
Having reached Mount Meru on the northern side of the Himavat,
he performed his rites there upon a vast golden foothill.
Then [he prepared] sacrificial pits, vessels, cooking pots, and seats.
Goldsmiths whose number was beyond reckoning fashioned [the ornaments];
and right near him, that sacrificial enclosure was established. There, that righteous lord of the earth performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.
14,004.027e Marutta, that lord of men, together with all the protectors of the subjects—
14,005.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
14,005.001a Of what prowess was that king, the best among speakers?
"How did that twice-born one come to be endowed with gold?
O Blessed One, where does that substance reside at present?
And how, O rich in asceticism, is it possible for us to obtain it?"
Vyāsa said:
"O dear one, the Asuras and the Devas were the numerous offspring of the patriarch Dakṣa; they vied with one another."
In the same way, the two sons of Aṅgiras became equal in their vows:
Bṛhaspati, of great splendor, and Saṃvarta, whose wealth was asceticism.
O King, those two also lived separately, competing with one another.
Bṛhaspati repeatedly harassed Saṃvarta. Being constantly oppressed by his elder brother, O Bhārata,
he abandoned all worldly concerns and, clad in the directions as his garment, resolved to dwell in the forest.
Vāsava, too, having conquered and slain all the Asuras and attained the position of Indra among the worlds,
then chose as his domestic priest Bṛhaspati, the eldest son of Aṅgiras and the best of Brahmins.
In former times, King Karaṃdhama was the patron of the Aṅgirasas; he was peerless in the world in heroism, conduct, and strength—
powerful like Śatakratu, righteous-souled, and firm in his vows.
O King, his vehicles, warriors, and various kinds of goods, as well as his principal and most precious beds of every sort,
all came into being through meditation alone, by the mere breath from his mouth.
That lord of men brought all the kings under his control through his virtues;
having lived for his desired time, he ascended to heaven in his own body. His son, however, was a knower of dharma, just like Yayāti.
Named Avikṣit, that slayer of enemies brought the earth under his control;
through his prowess and virtues, that king was like a father to his subjects. To him was born a heroic son named Marutta, who was equal to Vāsava.
The earth, clothed by the oceans, was devoted to that son;
that king constantly vied with the king of the gods,
O descendant of Pāṇḍu, and Vāsava also vied with Marutta.
That lord of the earth, Marutta, was pure and possessed of every virtue;
though Śakra strove against him, he could not surpass him. Being unable to gain any advantage over him, Śakra summoned Bṛhaspati.
Accompanied by the gods, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, spoke these words:
"O Bṛhaspati, do not perform for Marutta any rite whatsoever—
whether it be a divine or ancestral ceremony— if you wish to do what is pleasing to me."

"O Bṛhaspati, I alone among the gods in the three worlds have attained the status of Indra; yet King Marutta has surpassed me. For how is it, O Brahmin, that you, having officiated for the immortal Lord of the Gods, [have now done so for him]?"
"Without hesitation, perform a sacrifice for Marutta, who is already joined with death;
choose either me—blessings be upon you—or Marutta, the lord of the earth.
Or, having abandoned Marutta, enjoy my company as you please."
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, O descendant of Kuru, Bṛhaspati reflected for a moment and then spoke to the king of the gods:
"You are the lord of all beings; in you the worlds are established."
You are the slayer of Namuci, of Viśvarūpa, and of Bala.
O Hero, you alone have secured the supreme glory of the gods. O destroyer of Bala, you always sustain both the earth and the heavens.

"O Lord of the hosts of gods, O Subduer of Pāka, how can I, having accepted the office of domestic priest for you, perform a sacrifice for a mortal such as Marutta? Take heart, O Lord of the gods; I shall never [serve] a mortal."
"I shall take up the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) in the sacrifice; listen to these words of mine:
the waters of the Fire-god might turn back, the earth might overturn, and the sun might cease to give light, if my truth should waver."
Having heard the words of Bṛhaspati, Śakra, freed from his envy, praised him and then entered his own abode. Vyāsa said:
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Bṛhaspati and Marutta,
concerning the agreement made with the King of the Gods by the son of Aṅgiras.
Upon hearing this, King Marutta then summoned his wrath.
Having mentally resolved to perform a sacrifice, the son of Karaṃdhama’s grandson,
eloquent in speech, approached Bṛhaspati and spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, O Teacher rich in asceticism, that intention which I previously formed after approaching you for the sake of a sacrifice at your word—
desiring to perform that very sacrifice, I have now gathered all the necessary materials."
"O virtuous one, I am worthy of being sacrificed for by you; therefore, accept that and perform the rite.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O lord of the earth, I do not desire to officiate as your priest."
"I have been chosen by the king of the gods, and he has made a promise to me.
Marutta said:
"I am your ancestral field, and I hold you in very high regard."
"I have not fallen into a state where I am unfit to officiate at sacrifices; therefore, accept me as one who seeks your favor.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Having performed a sacrifice for an immortal, I shall not perform one for a mortal."
"O Marutta, go or do not go; I have withdrawn today from officiating at your sacrifice.
I will not perform the sacrifice for you today; choose instead whomever you wish here as your preceptor, O mighty-armed one, who shall perform your sacrifice."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, King Marutta was filled with shame;
returning in agitation, he beheld Nārada on the road.
Having met with the celestial sage Nārada, that king stood before him in due form with palms joined in reverence; then Nārada said to him:
"O royal sage, you do not appear particularly joyful; is all well with you, O sinless one?"
"Where have you come from, and why have you arrived at this place of displeasure?
O King, bull among monarchs, if it is something I may hear, tell me;
O lord of men, I shall dispel your grief with every effort."
Thus addressed by the great seer Nārada,
Marutta reported everything regarding his deception by the preceptor:
"I went to Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras and the teacher of the gods."
He went to see the officiating priest for the sake of the sacrifice, but he did not welcome me;
having been rejected by him, I no longer desire to live today.
Abandoned by my preceptor and defamed, O Nārada, I am ruined.
Thus addressed by the king, Nārada replied to the son of Avikṣita,
O great king, as if reviving him with his words:
"O King, there is a righteous son of Aṅgiras named Saṃvarta."
"Wandering through all directions, naked and deluding all creatures,
go to him if Bṛhaspati does not desire you as his sacrificer. O Great King, if he is pleased with you, Saṃvarta will perform the sacrifice for you."
Marutta said:
"O Nārada, best among speakers, I have been restored to life by these words of yours;
tell me, where might I see Saṃvarta?"
"How should I conduct myself toward him so that he does not abandon me? Having been rejected by him as well, I have no desire to live.
Nārada said:
Bearing the garb of a madman, he wanders about as he pleases;
he frequents the city of Vārāṇasī constantly,
where the Supreme Lord Mahādeva himself resides at the end of one's bodily existence.
He explains the knowledge of the stars that grants liberation to living beings:
"Having reached its gate, you should place a corpse somewhere. O Lord of the Earth, he who turns back upon seeing it is Saṃvarta."
You should follow behind that heroic one wherever he goes;
having approached him in a secluded place, you should take refuge with him with palms joined in reverence.
And if he should ask you, "By whom was I told of you? you must speak.
"O slayer of enemies, as if distressed, you should say, 'Nārada told me so. If he should question you out of a desire to visit me,
you should report without hesitation that I have ascended the fire."
Vyāsa said:
Having promised "So be it," and having honored Nārada,
the royal sage took his leave and departed for the city of Vārāṇasī.
Having gone there, that highly illustrious one placed a corpse at the gate of the city as instructed, remembering the words of Nārada;
and at that very same moment, the brahmin entered the city gate.
Then, seeing that corpse, he suddenly turned back.
Observing that he had retreated, the king Āvikṣita followed behind him with palms joined in reverence,
desiring to learn from Saṃvarta.
Seeing him in a secluded place, he covered the king with dust, mud, phlegm, and spittle. Although the lord of the earth was thus tormented by Saṃvarta, [he remained steadfast].
With palms joined in reverence, he followed after that rishi, seeking to appease him.
Then, turning back, Saṃvarta sat down, exhausted,
having reached a banyan tree with many branches that offered cool shade.
Saṃvarta said:
"How have I been recognized by you, or by whom was I described to you?
Tell me this truth, if you desire to do what is pleasing to me."
"If you speak the truth, all your heart's desires shall be fulfilled;
but if you speak falsely, your head shall split into seven pieces.
Marutta said:
"14,007.003a While wandering on the road, Nārada indeed told me of you: 'He is my preceptor’s son. 14,007.003c Therefore, I feel the highest affection for you. 14,007.004 Saṃvarta said:
"What you have said is true; he knows me as one who performs the *sattra* sacrifice.
Tell me this one thing: where indeed is Nārada now?
Marutta replied:
"O best of divine sages, having spoken to you,
he then took leave of me and entered the sacrificial fire. O best of munis, I must now be joined by you."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this from the king, Saṃvarta, with supreme joy,
then said, "I too shall do as much for him."
Then, O King, that mad brahmin, as if reproaching Marutta with harsh words, spoke to him again and again:
"By me, who am dominated by wind and subject to the power of my own mind..."
"How can you wish to have the sacrifice performed by one of such deformed appearance? My brother is capable and honored by Vāsava;
he is currently engaged in officiating at sacrifices—have him perform the rites."
My own home, my patrons, all my household deities,
and even this body have been cast off by my elder brother;
O son of Avikṣita, I shall never, at any time, [approach you] without his permission.
"How could I possibly officiate as your priest? For he is most worthy of my worship.
"Therefore, go to Bṛhaspati; having obtained his permission, return.
Then I shall officiate for you, if you desire to sacrifice here."
Marutta said:
"O Saṃvarta, listen to this: I previously approached Bṛhaspati, but he did not desire me as his patron for the sacrifice, having been forbidden by Vāsava."
"O Sage, having obtained me as an immortal sacrificer, do not perform a sacrifice for Marutta, who is a mortal man afflicted by human frailty.
I have been forbidden by Śakra: 'Do not officiate at the sacrifice for Marutta.'"
"Kingship does not please me, for I am unrighteous and superhuman;
moreover, O Brahmin, that king always vies with me. Having been told by your brother, "So be it," the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra [departed].

"O bull among sages, know this: having taken refuge with the King of the Gods, he does not wish to honor me with his affection as he once did when I was his patron. Therefore, I desire to have him sacrificed for you, even at the cost of all my possessions."
"O Vāsava, I desire to surpass you by means of the virtues produced by you;
for my mind does not turn toward going to Bṛhaspati, O Brahmin,
since I was rejected by him even though I had done him no wrong."
Saṃvarta said:
"O King, all this that you desire to do shall certainly be accomplished by you, provided that you fulfill all my intentions."

"While you are being sacrificed by me, Bṛhaspati and Purandara will both hate you in their great wrath; accomplish this one task alone. How can you maintain stability in this matter? Therefore, act with absolute certainty."
"Otherwise, in my anger, I would now reduce you to ashes along with your kinsmen.
Marutta said:
"As long as the thousand-rayed sun shall burn, and as long as the mountains shall stand,"
"May I not attain those worlds for so long if I should ever abandon my association [with you]; nor may I ever here obtain a virtuous intellect,
if I should abandon my association with you, whether in perfect knowledge or in worldly affairs."
Saṃvarta said:
"O son of Avikṣita, let your auspicious mind be fixed upon your duties;
for, O King, my role as officiating priest likewise rests with you."

"O King, I shall provide for you an excellent and inexhaustible wealth, by which you will surpass the gods along with the Gandharvas and even Śakra himself. However, my mind is not inclined toward wealth, nor indeed toward those who are to be sacrificed for."
"I desire to do what is disagreeable to both my brother and Indra;
yet I shall certainly cause you to attain equality even with Indra. I shall do what is pleasing to you; I tell you this truly."
Saṃvarta said:
On the ridge of the Himavat mountain is a peak named Muñjavat,
where the Blessed Lord, the husband of Umā, constantly performs austerities.
At the roots, on the ridges, and upon the peaks of the trees,
as well as in the caves of the king of mountains, the Blessed Lord Maheśvara dwells eternally together with Umā, according to his desire and at his pleasure.
There sits the wielder of the trident, possessed of great splendor, surrounded by various hosts of beings;
there also dwell the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Vasus,
as well as Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera with his followers.
The elemental spirits and the piśācas, the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins,
as well as the gandharvas and apsarases, the yakṣas and the celestial rishis,
the Ādityas and the Maruts, and all the yātudhānas;
Brahmā and the other gods, the Maruts, and the sages who contemplate the inner self,
worship the Great-Souled Lord of Umā, who possesses many forms. There, the Blessed One delights together with the followers of Kubera.
O Lord of the Earth, he was seen blazing with splendor, possessing a radiance like that of the rising sun, playing with deformed beings of hideous forms;
yet his true form or configuration could not be perceived in any way whatsoever.
It cannot be described by any ordinary beings with fleshy eyes.
There, O King, there is neither heat nor cold, neither wind nor sun;
there is neither old age, hunger, nor thirst, nor death, nor fear.
O best among victors, on all the slopes of that mountain,
the ores of gold shine like the rays of the sun;
they are guarded by the companions of Kubera, who stand with weapons raised.
O King, by those desiring to do what is pleasing to the high-souled Kubera,
you should go there and, having approached Śiva, the great Lord of Yoga,
offer salutations endowed with supreme devotion, O royal sage.
Having paid homage to that Blessed One, Śarva, the Creator,
praise the God, the Lord of all sciences, with these names:
"To Rudra, the blue-throated one, the fair-formed, the radiant."
To Kapardin, to Karāla, to Haryakṣa, and to the Giver of Boons; to the Three-eyed One, to the Breaker of Pūṣan’s Teeth, to Vāmana, and to Śiva;
to Yāmya, to Avyaktakeśa, to Sadvṛtta, and to Śaṅkara.
To the one who brings security, the tawny-eyed, to Sthāṇu and to Puruṣa;
to the golden-haired, the shaven-headed, the emaciated, and the deliverer;
to the sun-like, the excellent ford, the god of gods, and to impetuous speed.
To the one of many forms, to Śarva, to the beloved, to the one who wears lovely garments;
to the turbaned one, to the fair-faced, to the thousand-eyed, to the bountiful;
to Giriśa, to the tranquil, to the ascetic, to the one clothed in bark.
To the one with the *bilva* staff, to the perfected one (*siddha*), and to the wielder of all staffs;
to the great hunter of deer, to the archer, and then to Bhava;
to the excellent one with a gentle face, who holds a sacrificial animal in his hand and bestows boons.
To him with golden arms, O King, the fierce lord of the quarters;
to the one who licks [the world], the protector of the earth, the one for whom mantras have been perfected, the bull-like one;
and likewise to the lord of cattle and the lord of all beings.
To Vṛṣa, to Mātṛbhakta, to Senānī, and to Madhyama; to Sruvahasta, to Pati, to Dhanvin, and to Bhārgava;
to Aja, to Kṛṣṇanetra, and indeed to Virūpākṣa.
To the one with sharp fangs, to the sharp one, to the one whose mouth is like Vaiśvānara;
to the one of great splendor, to the bodiless one, to the one possessing all limbs, to the progenitor;
to the deep red one, to the blazing one, to the one with blazing eyes, to the one of great power.
Likewise, [salutations] to the lord of Śukra, to Pṛthu, to the one clad in animal skins (kṛttivāsas), to the one who constantly wears a garland of skulls, and to the one with a golden crown;
to Mahādeva, to Kṛṣṇa, to Tryambaka, and to the sinless one.
To the wrathful, the cruel, the mild, and the mighty-armed; to the wielder of the staff, the one of heated asceticism, and likewise the one of fierce deeds;
and to the one with a thousand heads and a thousand feet.
Salutations to the one whose nature is *svadhā*, who possesses many forms, and who has fangs;
to Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the great yogin, the imperishable;
to the trident-bearer, the giver of boons, the three-eyed Lord of the world.
The destroyer of Tripura, the three-eyed one, the lord of the three worlds, possessed of great splendor;
the source of all beings, the sustainer, the upholder of the earth;
the sovereign, the benefactor, the all, the auspicious one, the lord of the universe, Bhava.
[He praised] Umāpati, Paśupati, Viśvarūpa, Maheśvara,
Virūpākṣa, the ten-armed one, whose banner bears Tiṣya and the bull;
the infinite, eternal God, the three-peaked one with the eyes of a bull.
The fierce Sthāṇu, Śiva, the terrible Śarva, the Lord of Gaurī, the Sovereign; the blue-throated, the unborn, the pure, the broad, the wide-ranging destroyer, Hara;
the one whose form is the universe, the odd-eyed, the multiformed, the Lord of Umā.
Having bowed your head to the god Hara, the destroyer of the limbs of Ananga,
seek refuge in Mahādeva, the four-faced one, who is worthy of seeking refuge,
whose body shines brilliantly, and who is adorned with divine ornaments.

Having bowed with palms joined in reverence to Śarva, the Lord Hara— who is without beginning or end, unborn, auspicious, all-pervading, free from the three qualities (*guṇas*), undisturbed, stainless, and a treasury of splendors— I go for refuge.

Having attained the inner Veda— which is universal, immovable, eternal, causeless, and untainted— I repeatedly go for refuge to that whose state is eternally known as liberation by those who contemplate the inner self.

I take refuge in Him— the source of the universe, unborn, whose nature is beyond the *guṇas*— whom the yogis established on the path of reality know as the imperishable state of liberation (*kaivalya*), who are free from attachment, and who perceive the universal equality.
I take refuge in that eternal Sthāṇu, who created the seven eternal worlds beginning with Bhūtādi, who stands upon Truth,
and who is easily attained by devotees but difficult for those who wander far away to reach.
I bow to the unborn God who stands not far away, situated beyond primordial nature; I go for refuge to Śiva, who dwells in all worlds.
Having thus offered salutation to that Mahādeva, the impetuous one—
"O lord of the earth, you shall obtain that gold for the sake of the Great-Souled One.
For men who are single-mindedly devoted to Him attain the status of leaders of the Gaṇas;
how much more so, then, golden vessels? Therefore, go without delay."
"Indeed, let those men go there to bring back gold along with great gains consisting of elephants, horses, camels, and other such things.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, that son of Kāraṇdhama carried out his word;
having paid homage to Gaṅgādhara, he obtained supreme wealth,
just as Kubera did upon receiving the grace of Mahādeva.
Then he made all the preparations for the sacrifice superhuman; and there the artisans fashioned golden vessels,
and the halls and all the requisites for the rite were prepared by the command of Saṃvarta.
But Bṛhaspati, having heard of that prosperity of King Marutta which surpassed even that of the gods, was deeply distressed. As he suffered, he became extremely pale and emaciated.
"Indeed, Saṃvarta Vasumān will become my enemy.
Hearing this, the King of the Gods, surrounded by the immortals, approached Bṛhaspati, who was deeply distressed, and then spoke these words.
Indra said:
"O Bṛhaspati, do you sleep in comfort?
Are your attendants pleasing to you?"
"O Brahmin, do you desire the welfare of the gods?
Do the gods protect you?
Bṛhaspati said:
"I sleep happily on my bed, O Mahendra,
and likewise my attendants are pleasing to me;
thus, O Śakra, I am one who desires the happiness of the gods."
"And the gods protect me most thoroughly.
Indra said:
"Whence comes this suffering—whether mental or born of the body?"
"You are pale and discolored; why are you thus today?
Tell me that, O twice-born one, so that I may slay all these who have caused you grief."
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Maghavan, they say that Marutta is about to sacrifice with a great sacrifice accompanied by the most excellent sacrificial fees."
"I have heard that Saṃvarta will perform the sacrifice for him;
I desire that he not perform it for him.
Indra said:
O Brahmin, you have attained all desires,
for you serve as the priest who counsels the gods;
both birth and death have transcended you.
"O Brahmin, what service can I perform for you today?
Bṛhaspati said:
"Having driven away the Asuras together with the gods..."
Even now you seek to destroy them along with their followers;
wherever you see someone prosperous, there you find only sorrow, for prosperity among rivals is a cause of pain.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, my appearance has become discolored;
having heard that my rival is prospering,
restrain him by every possible means, O Maghavan.
To Saṃvarta, Pārthiva, or Marutta,
Indra said:
"Come, go, O Jātavedas, sent by me!"
"To bestow Bṛhaspati upon Marutta, [Indra said]:
'This Bṛhaspati shall indeed officiate as your priest;
he will thus make you immortal.'"
Agni said:
"O Śakra, today I go as your messenger to deliver Bṛhaspati to Marutta."
Desiring to make the word of Indra true and wishing to pay honor to Bṛhaspati,
Vyāsa said:
Then the high-souled Dhūmaketu set forth,
crushing trees and creepers as he moved at will at the end of winter.
Roaring like the wind that transcends the quarters, Marutta said:
"Today I behold a marvel: the Fire-god has arrived in embodied form."
"O sage, please bring a seat, water for the feet, and a cow.
Agni said:
"O sinless one, I accept your seat, water, and water for the feet."
"Know that I have come as a messenger commissioned by Indra.
Marutta said:
"Is the glorious King of the Gods well?"
O Dhūmaketu, do you hold us in affection?
And are the gods properly under his control?
Tell me all this in full, O god.
Agni said:
"O lord of kings, Śakra is exceedingly well-disposed toward you;
he indeed desires an undecaying affection with you."
"O King, all the gods are under his command;
now hear from me the message of the king of the gods regarding the purpose for which he has sent me to you."
To bestow Bṛhaspati upon Marutta—
O King, this preceptor shall perform the sacrifice for you;
though you are mortal, he shall make you immortal.
Marutta said:
"This twice-born Saṃvarta shall be my officiating priest; this is my salutation with joined palms to Bṛhaspati."
"Having officiated for the god Mahendra, he would not look well today if he were to officiate for a mortal.
Agni said:
"Those great worlds that exist in the realm of the gods,
you shall attain them through the grace of the King of the Gods,
provided that Bṛhaspati performs the sacrifice for you."
Surely you, endowed with fame, shall conquer heaven,
as well as the human worlds and those that are divine,
and even the great realms of Prajāpati.
"By you, O lord of men, the entire kingdom of the gods has been conquered. If Bṛhaspati were to officiate as your priest,
Saṃvarta said."
"Do not come here again by any means to hand Bṛhaspati over to Marutta;
otherwise, I shall consume you with my terrible eye."
"O Fire, understand this, for I am enraged.
Vyāsa said:
Thereupon, he whose banner is smoke went to the gods.
Terrified by the burning and distressed like an *aśvattha* leaf,
the bearer of oblations (Agni) was seen by the high-souled Śakra, who spoke to him in the presence of Bṛhaspati.
"O Jātavedas, since you have been sent and have gone to deliver Bṛhaspati to Marutta,
what did that king, who is about to perform a sacrifice, say?"
"Does he accept those words?
Agni replied,
"Marutta does not find your speech pleasing."
He extended his joined palms toward Bṛhaspati,
saying repeatedly, "Saṃvarta will officiate as my priest," even though he was told by me again and again [not to do so].
He said this: "Whatever humans there are, and whatever divine beings,
and those great worlds of Prajāpati—
if I might obtain them by making an agreement with him;"
"Nevertheless, I do not wish for it," [he] replied. Indra, being thus understood, said:
"You must go again and meet that king."
"Deliver my words, which are consistent with his own interests:
'If, when addressed again, he does not act upon these words, then I shall hurl the thunderbolt at him.'"
Agni said:
"O Vāsava, let this king of the Gandharvas go there as a messenger; I am afraid to go there myself."
Enraged and filled with sharp fury, Saṃvarta, who had observed the vow of celibacy, spoke these words to me:
"If you should ever come here again in such a manner..."
"I shall consume you with my terrible eye when I am enraged, O Śakra; know this as I prepare to hand Bṛhaspati over to Marutta."
Indra said:
"O Jātavedas, you alone consume others; for indeed, there is no one other than you who can reduce things to ashes."
"O bearer of oblations, because of contact with you, the entire world is afraid; what you say is not to be believed. Agni replied:
O Śakra, Lord of the Gods, you could indeed envelop the entire heaven and earth with your own power alone; yet,
even for one such as you who exist here—
"How did Vṛtra formerly seize the triple heaven?
Indra said:
"Neither Caṇḍikā nor a female elephant is mobile; [she is not within my reach]."
O Fire, I do not drink the Soma water,
nor do I discharge the thunderbolt against one who is weak;
what man could strike me so as to cause me unhappiness?
I banished the Kālakeyas from the earth;
I drove the Dānavas out from the intermediate region;
I brought Prahrāda down from heaven to his end.
"What mortal would strike me for my own misfortune?
Agni said:
"Where Cyavana was about to perform a sacrifice for Śaryāti..."
In the past, a certain one offered Soma together with the Aśvins; you, O Mahendra, being enraged, forbade him— remember that sacrifice of Śaryāti.
O Purandara, having seized the thunderbolt,
you struck Cyavana most fiercely;
that brahmin [severed] your arm along with the thunderbolt.
Having suppressed his rising wrath through asceticism,
he then, out of anger, produced from all sides another adversary even more terrible in form than you.
The asura named Mada, who possesses universal forms—
the one you beheld and closed your eyes upon—
has one jaw situated in the earth and likewise one in heaven.
Having gone to heaven, the thousand teeth of that great Dānava, each a hundred yojanas long and extremely sharp,
assumed a terrible form.
His four tusks were rounded, thick, and the color of silver pillars, measuring two hundred yojanas each;
he rushed toward you, gnashing his teeth.
Raising a terrible trident with the intent to strike,
you then beheld him of fearsome form;
but all the others saw him as beautiful to behold.
"O slayer of Dānavas, since you, being afraid of him, have come with joined palms to seek refuge with the great ṛṣi,
it is clear that the power of the Brahman is more formidable than that of the Kṣatriya."
There is nothing more venerable than Brahman.
Knowing the power of Brahman as it truly is,
O Śakra, I do not wish to go to Saṃvarta.
Indra said:
"It is even so; the power of Brahman is most weighty;
there is nothing whatsoever more weighty than Brahman."
"I cannot endure the power of the son of Avikṣita;
I shall hurl my terrible thunderbolt at him.
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, go forth, sent by me, to Marutta."
Speak with him who is accompanied by Saṃvarta;
O King, learn from Bṛhaspati,
or else I shall hurl my terrible thunderbolt at you.
Vyāsa said:
Then, having gone to the lord of men, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words of Vāsava.
"Know me to be the Gandharva Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
O lord of men, who has come to you desiring to speak. Listen to my words, which concern Indra, O lion among kings."
That which the high-souled Lord of the World said to Bṛhaspati the officiating priest: "Choose me as your priest,
or I shall hurl my terrible thunderbolt at you."
"If you do not do this word of mine,
he of inconceivable deeds has already said as much:
he will not permit Bṛhaspati to perform the sacrifice."
"I shall strike him with a terrible thunderbolt.
Marutta said:
"Both you and Purandara know this very well."
The Viśvedevas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins—
there is always this saying in the worlds that there is indeed no atonement for betraying a friend.
Bṛhaspati was the officiating priest for Mahendra,
the best of gods and the most excellent among the wielders of the thunderbolt; O King, Saṃvarta shall officiate as my priest today.
"I do not approve of his words.
The Gandharva said:
"The terrible roar of Vāsava is being heard."
O lion among kings, as Mahendra thunders in the vault of heaven, it is evident that he will release his thunderbolt upon you;
O King, consider your safety, for this is the moment.
14,010.008 Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the king heard the roar of Vasava as he thundered.
He informed Saṃvarta— that foremost among those who know dharma and who was constantly devoted to asceticism— of the matter at hand.
Marutta said:
"This stone is floating nearby;
because of it, the road is not seen from afar today.
O best of Brahmins, I seek refuge with you for protection."
Therefore, O foremost of Brahmins, grant him freedom from fear;
for here comes the wielder of the thunderbolt, illuminating the ten directions with his superhuman and terrible radiance, and our sacrificial assistants have indeed been terrified.
14,010.011 Saṃvarta said: "O lion among kings, let your fear of Śakra depart;
I shall dispel this most terrible fear."
"By means of this paralyzing spell (*saṃstambhinī-vidyā*), he will be paralyzed immediately; do not fear him, and be confident.
O King, I shall paralyze Śakra for you—do not be afraid."
The weapons of all the gods have been exhausted by me.
Let the wind go toward the quarters of the sky carrying the thunderbolt;
having become rain, let it fall upon the forests.
"Let the waters flow freely in the atmosphere, and let lightning be seen at will; do not be afraid. Furthermore, may the fire protect you from all sides."
Let Vāsava rain down rain at will,
let the wind hurl the thunderbolt,
and let the most terrible flood of waters surge forth.
Marutta said:
"A terrible sound is indeed heard, a great roar; this is the thunderbolt accompanied by the wind."
"O Brahmin, my very self is indeed distressed again and again; no composure arises within me today.
Saṃvarta said:
"O lord of men, let your fear of the fierce thunderbolt depart today;
becoming the wind, I shall strike down the thunderbolt.
Casting aside your fear, choose another boon."
"What desire of yours shall I fulfill through my ascetic power?
Marutta replied,
"O Brahmin, let Indra himself come here in person."
May the gods accept the sacrificial oblation in the sacrifice, may they take pleasure in their respective seats,
and may they accept the pressed Soma.
14,010.018 Saṃvarta said: 14,010.018a "O King, here comes Indra with his bay horses, accompanied by all the gods, the drinker of Soma."
"Summoned by my mantras, behold today this sacrifice, its body disintegrated by the power of the mantras.
Vyāsa said:
Then the king of the gods, accompanied by the deities,
having yoked those foremost of horses, the bay steeds, to his chariot,
came toward the sacrifice of the king, desiring to drink.
Marutta, together with his family priest, went out to meet that immeasurable son of Avikṣita as he approached accompanied by hosts of gods.
Delighted, he performed the highest worship for the King of the Gods according to the scriptures and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Saṃvarta said:
"Welcome to you here, O wise Puruhūta!
Since you, O Indra, are present today, this sacrifice shines forth even more brightly, O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra."
"Drink the pressed Soma offered by me.
Marutta said:
"Behold me with auspicious eyes, and let there be salutation to you."
The sacrifice has been attained; my life has become fruitful.
O Lord of the Gods, this one who is junior to Bṛhaspati by birth performs my sacrifice.
Indra said:
"I know this preceptor of yours, rich in asceticism,
the younger brother of Bṛhaspati, who possesses fierce splendor."
"O lord of men, because of your summons I have come; today my joy is restored to me, and my anger has vanished.
Saṃvarta said:
14,010.024a "O King of the Gods, if you are indeed pleased,
then instruct the ritual procedure yourself for this sacrifice. 14,010.024c O Lord of the Suras, prepare all the paths yourself."
"Let this entire world and the gods know it.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the son of Aṅgiras, Śakra—
He himself commanded the gods:
"Let assembly halls and principal residences be constructed— thousands of them, with variegated floors and full of prosperity."
"Quickly construct stairways with well-arranged pillars for the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
upon which thousands of Apsarases may dance."
"Let a sacrificial ground be prepared for the purpose of attaining heaven," he said;
O king, having been thus addressed, those gods, being well-pleased, quickly did so at the word of Śakra.
Then Indra, being pleased and honoring Marutta, O King, spoke these words to the monarch:
"O King, having met with you here, I— "
And let those other kings who were your predecessors, O monarch,
and all other deities who are well-pleased, accept this oblation from you.
Let them indeed sacrifice a red animal to Agni;
let them sacrifice a multicolored, radiant one to the Viśvedevas; and let them sacrifice a dark-blue ox as a pure offering.
"O best of the twice-born, move your penis as directed by me.
Thereupon, the sacrifice of that king prospered,
wherein the gods themselves brought the sacrificial foods.
In that sacrifice, Śakra, the king of the gods, endowed with splendor, was honored by the brahmins as a member of the assembly; thereafter,
the high-souled Saṃvarta ascended the sacrificial altar.
Like a second blazing fire,
calling aloud to the hosts of gods, he, full of confidence, offered oblations into the fire according to the sacred mantras.
Then, having drunk the foremost soma, the slayer of Bala and all other soma-drinking denizens of heaven,
being permitted by the king, departed.
Having been gratified according to their desire and filled with joy,
the king, being delighted, then caused heaps of gold to be made at every step.
Bestowing abundant wealth upon the twice-born,
that slayer of enemies shone like the Lord of Wealth himself;
then, having gathered various kinds of riches together, he—
Having caused [the treasury] to be filled according to his resolve,
and having been permitted by his preceptor, he returned and ruled the entire earth as far as the ocean's edge.
Such was the king who flourished here,
at whose sacrifice that abundant gold was produced;
O lord of men, take that wealth with you.
"Sacrifice to the gods, gratifying them with the prescribed rites.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thereupon, the Pāṇḍava king appeared joyful in countenance.
Having heard the words of Satyavatī’s son,
he set his mind on performing a sacrifice with that wealth;
then he consulted again with his ministers.
14,011.001 Vaiśampāyana said: When King [Janamejaya] had been addressed thus by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds,
the immensely radiant Vāsudeva then spoke these words.

Knowing that King Pārtha was dejected in mind, having had his kinsmen and relatives slain— resembling the sun eclipsed by Rāhu or a fire enveloped in smoke— the scion of the Vṛṣṇi clan [approached] him whose heart was filled with despair.
Consoling the son of Dharma, he began to speak.
Vāsudeva said:
"All crookedness is the path of death; straightforwardness is the path of Brahman."
This much is the scope of knowledge; what will mere talk accomplish?
Your task is not yet finished, nor have your enemies been conquered.
How is it that you do not perceive the enemy residing within your own body?
14,011.006a Here I shall relate to you, according to the dharma and as it was heard by me, 14,011.006c how the battle between Indra and Vṛtra took place.
14,011.007a In former times, O lord of men, the earth was indeed pervaded by Vṛtra.
Seeing the earth pervaded [by the demon] while his own domain of smell was taken away,
the domain of smell became foul-smelling due to the seizure of the earth. Then Śatakratu became enraged because his domain of smell had been seized.
Then, enraged, he hurled his terrible thunderbolt at Vṛtra. Being struck by that thunderbolt of immense power, he suddenly entered the waters; thereupon, he seized their domain.
When the waters had been pervaded by Vṛtra and their essence— their very substance—
had been stolen away, Śatakratu, filled with rage, hurled his thunderbolt at them.
Being struck by that thunderbolt of immense power within the water, [Vṛtra...]
Suddenly, light entered [Vṛtra], and he then seized that object.
When the light was pervaded by Vṛtra and the object— form— was thus taken away,
Śatakratu, filled with rage, released his thunderbolt there.
Being struck most violently by the thunderbolt of immense splendor,
he suddenly entered the wind and seized its domain. When the wind was thus pervaded by Vṛtra, the sense-object of touch was then taken away.
Enraged, Śatakratu discharged his thunderbolt there;
being struck by that thunderbolt of immeasurable splendor,
he fled toward the sky and then seized its domain.
When the sky had become Vṛtra and the object of sound was seized,
Śatakratu, filled with rage, hurled his thunderbolt there. Being struck by that thunderbolt of immeasurable splendor, he—
Suddenly it entered Śakra and seized his sensory domain;
as he was thus possessed by Vṛtra, a great delusion arose within him.
O dear one, Vasiṣṭha then awakened him with the Rathaṃtara hymn.

Then, O bull of the Bharatas, Śatakratu struck Vṛtra while he was still within his body with an invisible thunderbolt; thus have we heard it told here. And this secret of dharma was spoken by Śakra to the great seers.
"O lord of men, learn from me that which was declared by the seers.
Vāsudeva said:
Disease arises in two ways: namely, physical and mental."
The origin of these two in relation to one another is not found to be free from duality.
A disease that arises in the body is bodily; of this there is no doubt. A disease that arises in the mind is mental; this is the certainty.
O King, cold, heat, and wind are the qualities born of the body. When these qualities are in equilibrium, they say that is the characteristic of health.
Cold is countered by heat, and heat is countered by cold.
The wind is bound by both; this is called the regulation [of breath].
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these three are known as the qualities of the self (ātman). When there is equilibrium among these qualities, they call that the characteristic of health.
14,012.004e When one or another of these predominates, a remedy is taught:
14,012.005a Sorrow is suppressed by joy; joy is suppressed by sorrow.
14,012.005b Delusion is slain by both; this is called the remedy.
Someone dwelling in suffering desires to remember happiness;
someone dwelling in happiness desires to remember suffering.
But you are neither a sufferer of suffering nor a partaker of great happiness.
"O Kaunteya, you wish to remember [the past], for destiny is indeed most powerful. Or rather, this is your very nature by which you are dragged away, O Pārtha,
having seen Kṛṣṇā brought into the assembly hall, clad in a single garment and in her courses."
While the sons of Pāṇḍu were looking on, you do not wish to remember that exile from the city, the banishment in deerskins,
and the dwelling in the great forest; you do not wish to remember it.
The suffering caused by Jaṭāsura, the battle with Citrasena, and the distress caused by the King of Sindhu— you do not wish to remember those. Furthermore,
during our life in concealment, there was the beating with his foot by Kīcaka.
O Pārtha, you do not wish to remember that [suffering] of Yājñasenī at that time;
O subduer of enemies, that battle which you had with Droṇa and Bhīṣma—
that battle of yours which must be fought with the mind alone has now arrived.
Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, you must resolve to fight;
for there is no higher goal than this for one whose true nature is unmanifest, except through the performance of one's own duties— a path where arrows are of no use, nor are servants or kinsmen.
"You must fight alone with yourself; that battle has now arrived before you. If you do not conquer it in that battle, what state will you reach?
Knowing this, O son of Kuntī, you will have accomplished your purpose."
Having firmly resolved upon this understanding regarding the coming and going of living beings,
rule the kingdom as is fitting, following the conduct of your fathers and grandfathers.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Bhārata, success does not come about by abandoning external objects;
nor does success come about, or perhaps it does not, by abandoning bodily objects.
For one who is liberated from external objects yet still covets bodily ones,"

Whatever dharma and whatever happiness belongs to my enemies, may that be theirs as well. Death consists of two syllables, while the eternal Brahman consists of three. "Mine" is the two-syllable death; "not mine" is the eternal.

"O King, both Brahman and Death are established within the Self itself; remaining invisible, they undoubtedly cause all beings to fight one another. O Bhārata, if the indestructibility of this Being were not fixed,"
Having pierced through the bodies of living beings, one attains non-violence;
even having obtained the entire earth together with its moving and stationary beings,
what will he do with it who has no sense of "mine-ness"?
Or rather, O Pārtha, even for one dwelling in the forest and subsisting on forest produce,
if he possesses a sense of "mine" regarding material things, he dwells in the very jaws of death.
Behold, O Bhārata, the true nature of external and internal enemies.
He who does not perceive that which has become real is liberated from great fear. People do not praise one whose soul is possessed by desire;
nor is there any activity whatsoever that exists without desire.
All desires have issued from a member of the mind;
the wise man restrains them by reflecting upon them through the repeated practice of cultivation throughout successive births.
The yogin, having contemplated yoga as the essential path—
namely, generosity, the study of the Vedas, austerity,
and Vedic rituals performed with desire— [attains his goal].
He who, having understood this, does not undertake vows, sacrifices, restraints, or the yoga of meditation out of desire— for whatever he desires, that is indeed *dharma*.
That which is not a fixed dharma is its root.
In this regard, those who know the past recite verses known as the *Kāmagītā*. Listen, O Yudhiṣṭhira, as they are proclaimed in their entirety.
I cannot be slain by any being through improper means.
If anyone, knowing the power of my weapon, strives to slay me,
I shall manifest myself once again within that very weapon of his.
14.013.013 "Whoever strives to slay me through sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees,
I manifest myself again among moving beings, like the soul of action (karmātmā).
14.013.014 Whoever strives to slay me through the Vedas and the means of the Vedānta,"
Just as I appear within immobile things, I manifest myself to him whose soul is tranquil;
to him who strives with fortitude and true valor to slay me,
I become his very being, and he does not perceive me.
"Whoever, firm in his vows through asceticism, strives to slay me,
I then manifest myself once more within his very asceticism.
And whoever, being wise, strives to slay me by resorting to liberation,"

While he remains established in his delight for liberation, I dance and I laugh; I alone am the eternal one, incapable of being slain by any living beings. Therefore, you too [should seek] that desire through sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees.
"O Great King, practice righteousness; therein you shall find success.
Perform the horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*) according to the rules, accompanied by generous sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and other various abundant sacrifices provided with ample fees."
Let there be no distress in you from seeing your kinsmen slain again and again;
those who have been killed on this field of battle cannot be seen by you once more.
Therefore, having performed great sacrifices, prosperous and accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, you shall attain [your goal].
"Having attained supreme fame in the world, you shall go to the highest state.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus, with these various words, those sages whose wealth is asceticism [spoke]."
"Take heart, O royal seer Yudhiṣṭhira, whose kinsmen have been slain! That lord was consoled by the Blessed One Viṣṭaraśravas himself,
as well as by Dvaipāyana Kṛṣṇa and Devasthāna."
Then the king was addressed by Nārada, Bhīma, Nakula,
Kṛṣṇā, Sahadeva, and the wise Vijaya,
as well as by other tigers among men and by brahmins whose vision was grounded in the scriptures.
He cast off the sorrow born of grief as well as his mental anguish.
Yudhiṣṭhira then honored the gods and the brahmins;
having performed the funeral rites for his kinsmen, that king once again—
Having regained his entire kingdom, the righteous-souled Kauravya, with a tranquil mind, ruled over the earth girt by the oceans; and having attained his sovereignty,
the king spoke to Vyāsa, Nārada, and those others.
"I have been comforted previously by you elders, the bulls among sages;
not even the slightest offense exists here on my part.
Furthermore, a very great wealth has been obtained, with which I shall sacrifice to the deities."
"Placing you at our head, we shall perform the sacrifice here;
O Grandfather, protected by you, we shall go to the Himavat.
Act accordingly, O brahmin-sage; that sacrifice of mine depends entirely upon you."
"O best of the twice-born, that land is indeed heard to be full of many wonders; likewise, much wonderful and auspicious speech has been spoken by the Blessed One,
as well as by the celestial sage Nārada and Devasthāna."
"No man lacking good fortune, having encountered calamity, ever obtains such teachers as these, who are esteemed by the virtuous as true friends.
Thus addressed by the king, all those great seers [responded].
Having taken leave of the king as well as both Kṛṣṇa and Phalguna,
they vanished right there while everyone was looking on. Then the lordly King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, sat down in that very place.
In this way, not a very long time passed for them as they performed the rites of purification following Bhīṣma’s death,
while bestowing great gifts upon the Brahmins for his funeral ceremonies.
O descendant of Kuru, together with Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he performed the funeral rites for the Kurus led by Bhīṣma and Karṇa. Then, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas gave abundant wealth to the Brahmins.
Placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at the forefront, he entered Hastināpura. Having comforted his father, the lord who possessed the eye of wisdom,
that righteous-souled one ruled the earth together with his brothers.
Just as Manu, O Great King, and as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, so too did that lion among the Bharatas protect the earth. There was nothing unrighteous there; every person delighted in dharma.
O tiger among men, it became as if the Kṛta age had returned; having warded off the approaching Kali age that had taken hold,
the wise son of the king shone together with his brothers, uplifted by the power of dharma.
The Blessed Lord, the God, rained down at the proper time and in the proper place, exactly as desired.
The world became free from disease; there was no hunger or thirst whatsoever. Men had no mental anguish, nor did their minds turn toward calamity.

The social classes, headed by the Brāhmaṇas, were auspicious and preeminent in their own respective duties; Dharma was characterized primarily by truth, and truth was endowed with a focus on what is real.
Seated upon the throne of Dharma, he [the king], together with the virtuous, [protected] women, children, the sick, and the elderly.
Because of the sequence of his merits performed in the past, he is not one who strives to protect [himself] at the wrong time;
even by means of providing good livelihoods, granting sustenance, and performing sacrifices,
there is no fear regarding the next world, for that which pertains to this world has already been accomplished.
While he ruled, the world became like the heavenly realm; there was nothing but supreme and most excellent happiness here. All the women were devoted to their husbands, beautiful, and well-adorned.
Conducting themselves as prescribed, they became causes of delight through their own virtues; those men, rich in meritorious character, were devoted to their respective duties and,
being happy, never committed even the slightest transgression.
All men and women were constantly speaking kindly;
they became straightforward in mind, pure, and free from fatigue.
They were adorned with earrings, necklaces, bracelets, and waist-bands.
On the surface of the earth, they were for the most part well-clothed and richly perfumed;
all were knowers of Brahman, tranquil, and firmly established in every way; free from wrinkles and grey hair, they were happy and possessed far-sighted vision.
No desire arose for anything other [than their own kind], and there was no intermixture among the castes.
O Great King, humans remained firmly established within their respective boundaries while that lord of kings ruled. Even wild beasts, predators, and reptiles [behaved accordingly].
Furthermore, birds do not harm one another, nor do they prey upon others;
the cattle are preeminent in their qualities, possessing beautiful tails, faces, and bellies.
They are free from the distress of plowing and other labors, and they have calves that are neither stolen nor diseased.
Human beings have no fixed lifespan, and they gradually progress through the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha).
They are diligent regarding objects that are not forbidden and devoted to the Vedic scriptures.
Their oxen are well-behaved, robust, capable of bearing heavy loads, and bringers of happiness.
The sound was exceedingly sweet, the touch most pleasant, and the taste delightful;
the form appeared beautiful, pleasing to the sight, and charming, while the fragrance wafted forth.
It was endowed with the aims of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma, and served as a means for both worldly prosperity and liberation.
Then there arose from his mind the meritorious Prahlāda-janana lake.
There were immobile beings (trees) rich in many flowers, providing fruit and shade; they were pleasant to the touch, free from poison, and possessed excellent leaves, bark, and shoots.
All their actions were agreeable to the minds of everyone, yet they remained free from worldly attachments;
such was the conduct of that royal sage upon the earth.
The Pāṇḍavas, endowed with all auspicious marks, were practitioners of righteousness.
All were pleasant to behold and followed their eldest brother;
they possessed lion-like chests, had conquered anger, and were endowed with splendor and strength.
All had arms reaching down to their knees, were of a generous disposition, and had mastered their senses.
While they were ruling the earth, the seasons shone forth with their own natural qualities;
the planets, together with the hosts of stars, moved for the arising of happiness;
and the earth was abundant with crops and the source of all precious gems.
Like a wish-fulfilling cow, she yielded enjoyments in a thousand ways.
Without transgressing any of the boundaries established for human beings by Manu and others in the past, as well as the traditional conventions within families, he governed.
Doing what was pleasing to the Son of Dharma, they constantly governed;
especially increasing the great families that were most devoted to righteousness,
they ruled the earth according to the conduct established by Manu.
For that conduct of kings was ever most righteous upon the earth;
generally, O dear one, the mind of the world follows the conduct of the king.
Thus did the king [rule] his own Bhāratavarṣa, like the lord of the gods in heaven.
Protected by Viṣṇu and guarded by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, he ruled.
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, when the kingdom had been conquered by the sons of Pāṇḍu and was at peace..."
"What did the two heroes, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, do in the kingdom?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lord of the people, when [the earth] had been conquered by the sons of Pāṇḍu and was at peace..."
In the kingdom, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya were filled with joy;
endowed with delight, they sported like the two lords of the gods in heaven,
amidst the diverse forests and upon the mountain peaks.
Wandering joyfully among delightful mountains, ponds, and rivers like the two Aśvins in the Nandana grove,
the high-souled Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava took their pleasure in Indraprastha.
Having entered that beautiful assembly hall, O Bhārata, they both took their pleasure there;
and in the course of their conversation, O King, they recounted various tales of war and their past sufferings.
They spoke by means of yoga, speaking in due order;
then those two great-souled ones, the ancient and most excellent of sages, being well-pleased, recounted the lineages of the ṛṣis and the deities.
Keśava, who knew the definitive conclusions, recounted to the son of Pṛthā various sweet stories with diverse meanings and well-determined words,
[addressing him] who was tormented by grief for his son and for his kinsmen by the thousands.
Śauri Janārdana pacified Pārtha with various stories.
Having comforted him according to the prescribed rites, that great ascetic Sātvata, who knew the proper methods,
felt as though he had rested after laying down his own burden.
Then, at the conclusion of their conversation, Govinda spoke these words, reasoned and full of consolation, in a gentle voice to Guḍākeśa:
"O Savyasācin, scorcher of enemies, this entire earth has been conquered."
Relying on the strength of your arms,
O best of men, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and lord of justice, enjoys the earth without rivals through the power of Bhīmasena and the twins.
O knower of dharma, the kingdom has been obtained without thorns by the king through righteousness;
and that King Suyodhana too was slain in battle through righteousness—
[he who was] greedy, delighting in unrighteousness, and always speaking unpleasant words.

The evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been struck down along with their followers. O Pārtha, best of the Kurus, protected by you, the King, the son of Dharma, now enjoys the entire earth in peace as its sovereign.
"I shall take delight even in the forests with you, O Pāṇḍava;
how much more so where these people are, and where Pṛthā is, O crusher of foes—
where the King, the son of Dharma, is, and where the mighty Bhīma is."
"O descendant of Bharata, wherever the two sons of Mādravatī are, there my supreme delight lies; likewise, O sinless one, in those assembly halls resembling heaven,
which are delightful and holy, when I am together with you."
"A great deal of time has passed for me without seeing the son of Śūra,
Baladeva, and the other bulls among the Vṛṣṇis, O Kauravya. Therefore, I desire to go toward the city of Dvāravatī."
"O bull among men, let my departure be pleasing to you as well.
Thus was King Yudhiṣṭhira addressed in various ways on those occasions by Bhīṣma, who spoke what we have related regarding the cause of his grief.
"Yudhiṣṭhira, though he is our teacher and a Pāṇḍava, has been instructed by us. That speech was properly grasped by that great-souled one,
for the son of Dharma is a knower of dharma, grateful, and truthful."
Truth, righteousness, preeminent intelligence, and a constant, firm stability—
[these are yours]. Therefore, O Arjuna, if it pleases you, go to that high-souled one and speak words concerning our visit to the lord of men.
"Indeed, I would not do anything displeasing to him even if the loss of my life were imminent; how much less, O mighty-armed one, would I go toward the city of Dvāravatī?
All this, O Pārtha, I have said out of a desire for your pleasure and welfare."
"I tell you the truth, O Kauravya; this is not false in any way.
My purpose for dwelling here has been accomplished, O Arjuna:
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son has been slain, along with his army and his followers."
O dear one, O Pāṇḍava, the entire earth— clothed by the oceans and filled with mountains, forests, and groves— stands under the control of the wise son of Dharma,
the Kuru king, who is strewn with various kinds of jewels.
O bull of the Bharatas, let the king, who knows the dharma, protect the entire earth through righteousness, while being attended by many high-souled *siddhas* and constantly praised by bards.

Therefore, O tiger among the Kurus, go with me today to the king, the enhancer of the Kuru lineage, and ask his permission for my departure toward Dvārakā. [I leave behind] this body and whatever wealth is in my house.
O Pārtha, this has always been reported to Yudhiṣṭhira:
for Yudhiṣṭhira is dear to me and worthy of my respect;
he is the high-minded lord of the Kurus at all times.
"O mighty-armed one, there is no purpose for my dwelling here other than you;
for the earth stands under your command, O Pārtha."
Thus was this spoken at that time by the high-souled Janārdana to Arjuna of immeasurable prowess, concerning his preceptor Yudhiṣṭhira of virtuous conduct.
"‘So be it,’ the king said, uttering these words with great difficulty,
after having honored Janārdana.
Janamejaya said:"
"O twice-born one, while those two high-souled ones, Keśava and Arjuna, were staying in that assembly hall after having slain their enemies, what conversation did they have? Vaiśampāyana said:
Having regained his own kingdom entirely, Pārtha, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa,
sported with great joy in that beautiful assembly hall. Then,
O King, he went to a certain part of the hall that was equal to a region of heaven.
14,016.003c Joyful, they departed together with their kinsmen, as chance would have it. 14,016.004a Then the Pāṇḍava Arjuna, filled with satisfaction and accompanied by Kṛṣṇa,
14,016.004c gazed upon that beautiful assembly hall and spoke these words.
"O mighty-armed one, when the battle was at hand, your greatness and that divine form of yours, O son of Devakī, were known to me;
yet that which was spoken by you then, O Keśava, out of friendship— "
"O tiger among men, all of that has been lost to me, whose mind is now distracted.
Yet, O Lord, I still have a great curiosity regarding those matters. And you, O Mādhava, will surely go to Dvārakā before long."
Thus addressed, the immensely radiant Kṛṣṇa, the best among speakers, embraced Phalguna and replied:
"I have made you hear the secret and have instructed you in the eternal truth."
"O Pārtha, that you did not perceive Dharma in its true form nor the eternal worlds, and therefore did not accept it, is deeply displeasing to me. Furthermore,
from this day forward, such memory shall no longer arise within me."
"O Pāṇḍava, you are surely lacking in faith and you are dull-witted;
O Dhanañjaya, it is not possible to speak of this again in its entirety.
For that Dharma is sufficient for the realization of the state of Brahman."
It is not possible for me to speak that further in its entirety;
for I have already described the Supreme Brahman through my union with yoga. However, I shall relate an ancient history concerning that same subject.
"O best among the upholders of dharma, listen as I tell you everything so that, by relying on that wisdom, you shall attain the highest state.
O subduer of enemies, once there was a certain brahmin who came from the heavenly world."
That invincible one was honored by us as he came from the world of Brahmā;
and when that best of the twice-born was questioned by us,
O bull of the Bharatas, he spoke what he said in response to our inquiry.
"O Pārtha, listen without hesitation to that which was told according to the divine method.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
'O Kṛṣṇa, regarding the dharma of liberation upon which you question me...'"
O Lord, O Madhusūdana, I shall duly declare to you that which is for the sake of compassion toward all beings and which cuts through delusion;
listen with an attentive mind as I speak, O Mādhava.
A certain brahmin, Kāśyapa, endowed with ascetic power and most knowledgeable in dharma,
approached another twice-born man who had mastered the traditional scriptures of dharma and had reached the further shore of knowledge and realization regarding the cycle of coming and going.
Skilled in the true meaning of the world’s principles, a knower of pleasure and pain;
one who understands the reality of birth and death, an expert in merit and demerit; a seer of the high and low destinies of embodied beings according to their actions.

Having heard the truth concerning him who moved like one liberated, perfected, tranquil, with senses restrained, blazing with Brahmic splendor, traversing everywhere, and knowing the power of invisibility— Kāśyapa [approached].
Likewise, he saw him conversing in private with invisible Siddhas who possess the power of the discus,
and sitting together with them;
and he saw him moving at will, unattached like the wind.
Having approached him at that time, that wise and best of brahmins,
a practitioner of austerity who desired righteousness and was perfectly composed, paid homage to his feet with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rule.

Filled with wonder at seeing that marvel, Kāśyapa gratified his teacher, that best of the twice-born, with great service; and being pleased in spirit, well-endowed, and possessed of both learning and virtuous conduct, he [served him].
Pleasing him with his disposition and through service toward his teacher, that scorcher of foes [Arjuna] satisfied him;
then the preceptor, pleased and gratified with that disciple, spoke to him while foreseeing supreme success: "Listen to that from me, O Janārdana."
O dear one, through various actions and solely through the application of merit,
mortals attain their respective destinies here and even a station in the world of the gods;
yet, there is no absolute happiness anywhere, nor is there any eternal station anywhere.
Again and again, I have fallen from great stations that were hard-won, and through the practice of evil, I have reached miserable and painful states of existence,
being overcome by desire and anger and deluded by craving.
Again and again there is death and birth; again and again various foods have been eaten and various breasts have been sucked. Various mothers have been seen, and fathers of diverse kinds.
O sinless one, I have experienced various kinds of pleasures and pains; I have frequently been separated from loved ones and lived together with those who are not dear;
and I have encountered the loss of wealth after having acquired that wealth with great difficulty.
14,016.034a Insults, both from strangers and from one's own kin,
as well as physical and mental agonies that are exceedingly cruel;
14,016.035a And severe humiliations, along with terrible executions and imprisonments, have been endured.
I have experienced falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama;
I have repeatedly endured old age, diseases, and manifold latent impressions, as well as the intense pairs of opposites in this world.

Then, at one time, out of disillusionment with the world and because I had been deeply humiliated and oppressed, I, being intensely afflicted by suffering, abandoned the ways of worldly life and practiced this path.
Having experienced [the truth] in this world, I have followed this way.
14,016.037 Then, through the grace of my own self, this perfection was attained by me.
14,016.038 I shall not come here again; I behold the worlds [from afar]. From the attainment of perfection until the creation of beings, my own destiny is auspicious.
"O best of the twice-born, this supreme perfection has been attained by me;
henceforth I shall go from here to the even higher state,
the undisturbed station of Brahman— let there be no doubt in you regarding this."
"O scorcher of foes, I shall not return again to this mortal world.
