I am pleased with you, O one of great wisdom; tell me, what may I do for you?
Whatever you have come here desiring, the time for that has now arrived."
"I recognize that purpose for which you have come to me.
Before long, however, I shall depart by the very path for which I urged you on.
O wise one, I am deeply pleased with your conduct."

"Ask whatever you desire, and I shall speak until it is satisfied for you. I hold your intelligence in high regard and I greatly honor it, since I have been awakened by you; for you are indeed wise, O Kāśyapa."
Vāsudeva said:
Then, having grasped his feet, he asked questions that are very difficult to utter;
and he, the best among the upholders of dharma, answered them all.
Kāśyapa said:
How does the body fall away, and how is it reborn?
And how, while wandering through the miserable cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), is one completely liberated?
14,017.003 How does the self, having joined with that body, abandon it? And once released from the body, how does it attain another?
14,017.004 And how does this man experience his own performed actions, both auspicious and inauspicious?
"Where does one enjoy [the fruits of action], or where do the deeds of one who is bodiless (videha) abide?
The Brahmin said:
"Thus urged, the Siddha replied to those questions."
O Vārṣṇeya, listen to my words regarding this sequence:
it is established that in this very [system], the life-prolonging rites are traditionally held to yield auspicious fruits.
The Siddha said:
Whatever actions one performs in this world that bring about longevity and fame, when those [fruits] have entirely exhausted themselves upon the assumption of another body, [one departs].
One whose self is overwhelmed by the exhaustion of life pursues perverted courses;
and when destruction is imminent, his intellect turns away from the truth. This occurs because he likewise fails to understand his own nature, strength, and the [proper] time.
One who lacks self-control partakes excessively of things that are contrary to those [wholesome ones]. When he indulges in all such extremely painful things,
or eats to excess, or does not eat at all;
He eats food that is spoiled, food containing poison, or food that is mutually incompatible; he eats heavy food or even ordinary food when his previous meal is not yet digested,
or he indulges in excessive physical exercise or sexual intercourse.
Whether due to constant greed for activity or from the suppression of natural urges,

or by consuming food excessively rich in tastes, or by indulging in daytime sleep— at a time when it is undigested and before the [proper] time has arrived— one thus personally provokes the bodily humors (doṣas).
Through the provocation of his own faults, he incurs a disease ending in death; or else, he resolves upon such things as hanging. By these causes, the living being falls away from the body.
Listen now correctly as that which is called life is being described:
when the vital heat (ūṣman) becomes agitated within the body, impelled by a fierce wind,
it circulates throughout the body and indeed obstructs all the vital breaths (prāṇas).

When the vital heat (*ūṣman*) becomes excessively powerful and is provoked within the body, it shatters the seats of the life-force; know these to be the *marman* (vital points). Then, accompanied by pain, the life-force immediately departs as it flows out.
"O best of the twice-born, know this: when the vital organs are being severed, a living being casts off the body, its self overwhelmed by agonizing pains;
all creatures are perpetually agitated by birth and death."
O bull among the twice-born, they are seen abandoning their bodies; furthermore,
a human being experiences exactly the same kind of agony during the transition into the womb and when the vital organs are being displaced.
Then that man, with his joints broken, undergoes dissolution by water,
just as he had attained dependence upon the five elements;
provoked by coldness within the body and impelled by a violent wind.
That wind which is established within the five elements and in the prāṇa and apāna, having released the embodied being with difficulty, moves upward;
it indeed abandons the body, and the person is seen to be breathless.
Devoid of heat, breathless, stripped of splendor, and unconscious—
that man who has been utterly abandoned by Brahmā is said to be dead.
Through those channels by which the embodied being perceives the objects of the senses, [he once lived].
By those very [elements], one does not perceive the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that arises from food;
he who acts within that very body is the eternal soul (*jīva*).
Whatever may be joined among them in various combinations here and there, [that is the soul].
Know that to be the vital point (marmman) as it is seen in the scriptures;
for when those vital points are pierced, he [the wind],
surging forth from there, enters the heart of the living being and swiftly obstructs the *sattva*.
Then that conscious being perceives nothing at all;
his knowledge being shrouded by darkness while the vital organs are closed up,
that life-force, deprived of its support, is blown away by the wind.
Then, having heaved that great and terrible sigh,
as he departs, he quickly causes that insentient body to tremble. That life-force, fallen from the body, is enveloped by its own past actions.
Marked by their own auspicious merits or even by their sins, they are reborn; for Brahmins endowed with knowledge and who have correctly reached certainty through sacred revelation,
perceive that other person— whether they have performed meritorious deeds or not— by means of these signs.
Just as those with sight perceive a firefly flickering here and there in the darkness,
so do the perfected ones (siddhas) possessing the eye of knowledge behold the living soul (jīva) with their divine vision.
Falling away, being born, and entering a womb—
these three states of his are seen here according to the scriptures. This earth is the field of action, where living beings abide.
Then, having performed good and evil deeds, all embodied beings receive their retribution;
even here in this world, they obtain various high and low enjoyments according to their own actions.
But one who has performed evil deeds here, having gone to hell by virtue of those actions—
Downward that sinful man is cooked intensely in hell;
this downward course is miserable, where men are roasted.
Therefore, liberation is very difficult to attain; for that reason, the self must be protected with great care.
Now, listen to me as I describe in truth those places where living beings, having ascended,
reside; having heard that, you shall attain a definitive understanding through the certainty of action.
Know that all the forms of the stars, this lunar orb, and the solar orb which shines resplendent in the world by its own light— these are the abodes of men who have performed meritorious deeds.
And when their karma is exhausted, they all fall away again and again;
even there in heaven, there is a distinction of low, high, and middling status.
Even there, there is no contentment upon seeing a more radiant splendor.
Thus, all these destinies have been described individually.
Hereafter, I shall speak of the conception of the embryo;
listen attentively, O twice-born one, as I explain it correctly.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"There is no destruction here of actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
rather, having reached field after field, they ripen accordingly."
Just as a fruit-bearing tree, when it comes into flower, yields abundant fruit,
so too does merit performed with a pure mind become vast;
and likewise, evil committed with an evil mind becomes great.
For here, the self proceeds toward action only after placing the mind at the forefront. Listen further to how a man, enveloped by desire and anger, enters the womb as directed by his past actions.
The semen, mixed with the blood and having entered the womb of the woman,
obtains a field born of karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Due to its subtlety and its unmanifest nature, it does not cling anywhere.

Having entered the body of Brahmā, that eternal Brahman is the seed of all beings; by it all living creatures live. That *jīva* (individual soul), having entered the limbs of the embryo part by part, [animates them].
Established immediately within the seats of the vital breaths, he takes hold [of them] with his consciousness;
then that embryo, endowed with sentience, causes the limbs to throb.
For it is just like molten metal poured into a mold, taking on the form of a statue.
Know that the entry of the living soul into the womb is just like that;
just as fire enters a lump of iron, heating it thoroughly,
so too, you should understand, is the manifestation of the living soul in the womb.
Just as a burning lamp provides shelter by illuminating,
even so does consciousness illuminate the bodies;
whatever action it performs, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Everything performed in a previous body must necessarily be experienced;
thus, that [karma] is exhausted, yet again another is accumulated,
as long as one does not realize the Dharma established in the yoga of liberation.
In this regard, O best of beings, I shall proclaim that Dharma by which one indeed becomes happy while revolving through various successive births;
a wise person should perform those acts which are said to bestow auspicious results.
Generosity, religious observance, celibacy, and the maintenance of vows as prescribed;
self-restraint, tranquility, and compassion for all living beings;
self-control, kindness, and the avoidance of taking what belongs to others.
Where on earth there is the avoidance of harming living beings,
service to mother and father, worship of deities and guests, reverence for teachers, compassion, purity, and constant restraint of the senses— [that is heaven].
The promotion of virtuous deeds is called the conduct of the good;
the Dharma practiced by the good is established in right conduct (*sadācāra*). It serves both purposes: it leads to the goal of heaven and likewise bestows liberation.

From that, Dharma arises, which protects the eternal subjects. Thus one should always look toward the virtuous, for therein this established order is fixed; conduct reveals Dharma, in which the virtuous are firmly grounded.
That eternal Dharma has been deposited within them; he who fully attains that Dharma shall not fall into an evil state.
Therefore, the world, having become deluded regarding the paths of Dharma, is restrained by it.
But that yogin who is liberated excels over these;
for just as it is for a man living according to dharma,
so too shall his crossing over saṃsāra come to pass after a long time.

Thus every living being experiences the karma performed in the past; all that is the cause by which this person, having been humiliated, has come here. And by whom was his taking of a body previously ordained?

"Thus there is this doubt in the world, and I shall explain that hereafter. Having fashioned a body for himself, Brahmā, the grandfather of all beings, created the three worlds in their entirety, including all things mobile and immobile."
Then he created Pradhāna, which is the consciousness of embodied beings;
by this all this is pervaded, and which they know as the supreme in the world. Here that is called the perishable (kṣara), but the other is the immortal, the imperishable (akṣara).
The first-born Prajāpati created all beings, both stationary and moving, by means of the three pairs, each separately;
such is the ancient revelation.
The Grandfather established for him the measure of time,
as well as the transition among beings and their return once more—
just as some wise man here, having perceived the self in a previous birth, [remembers it].
Whatever I shall declare will all be established exactly as it is:
he who always correctly perceives pleasure and pain as impermanent, and views the body as a collection of impurities, subject to destruction, and bound by karma.
Remembering that whatever happiness there may be is all suffering, one who understands the primary principle will cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to traverse,
which is beset by birth, death, and disease.
He perceives consciousness equally in all sentient beings;
then, seeking the supreme state, he becomes disenchanted with everything.
O best of men, I shall explain his instruction to you exactly as it is.
"O Brahmin, understand from me in its entirety this supreme knowledge of the eternal and immutable state as it is being proclaimed. The Brahmin said:
He who is absorbed in the single path, remaining silent and not thinking of anything at all,
having abandoned each preceding stage, shall become one who is free from worldly undertakings;
he is a friend to all, patient with all, equally disposed toward all, and has conquered his senses.
Free from fear and anger, and having abandoned desire, such a man is liberated.
He who behaves toward all beings as toward himself— self-restrained and pure—
should always act according to the rule, with his senses under control.
Free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of pride, he is indeed liberated in every respect.
He who is equal toward both life and death, as well as toward pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and the liked and the disliked— he too is released.
He does not envy anyone, nor does he despise anything;
free from the pairs of opposites, with a self devoid of passion, he is indeed liberated in every respect.
He who has no enemies, no kinsmen, and no offspring anywhere—[he is truly free].

Having abandoned dharma, artha, and kāma, and being free from longing, he is liberated. He who is neither a follower of dharma nor a follower of adharma, who has destroyed previously accumulated [karma],
whose self is tranquil through the exhaustion of the elements (dhātu), and who is free from dualities— he is released.

Free from action and free from desire, seeing the world as impermanent, unstable, and powerless, and constantly deluded by the cycle of birth and rebirth; possessing a mind of detachment and always observing the faults inherent in suffering.
He brings about liberation from the bondage of the self almost immediately. Having seen the self—which is without odor, taste, touch, sound, or possession; formless and unknowable—he is liberated.

He who perceives that which is devoid of the qualities of the five elements, formless, untainted, without attributes, yet the enjoyer of attributes— he is liberated. Having abandoned all mental and physical volitions through the intellect, [he attains liberation].
Gradually he attains nirvāṇa, like a fire without fuel;
liberated from all forms of existence, free from the sense of "mine," and without possessions,
he who wanders with his collection of senses stilled is indeed liberated.

Liberated from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he then attains the eternal Brahman— the supreme, utterly tranquil, immovable, divine, and imperishable. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed science of yoga (*yogaśāstra*).

"Listen to me as I explain correctly that instruction by which yogins, having realized the perfected Self, perceive it within the world. By means of those gateways through which one constantly directs [the mind], one perceives the Self within the self."
Having withdrawn the senses, one should fix the mind upon the Self;
having first performed intense austerity, one should then begin to apply oneself [to yoga].
An ascetic who has abandoned all formative intentions and is free from hypocrisy and egoism—
The wise sage, inspired by his intellect, beholds the Self within himself.
If this virtuous man is able to yoke the self to the Self,
then, established in solitude, he beholds the Self within himself.
Constantly restrained, ever-disciplined, self-possessed, and having conquered the senses—
one who is thus well-disciplined perceives the Self by means of the self,
just as a person, having seen someone in a dream, recognizes him upon waking, saying, "This is he."
One who is well-disciplined perceives the self as being of such a nature,
just as someone might extract a blade of grass from a *muñja* reed and display it; in that same way,
the yogi beholds the self extracted from the body.
They say the body is the *muñja* grass and that which rests within the self is the *iṣīkā* reed. This is declared by those who know yoga to be the unsurpassed illustration.
For when the embodied being perceives the self as properly disciplined, [he sees it thus].
At that time, no one has power over him, not even he who is the lord of the three worlds.
He assumes various bodies at will,
and having properly disciplined himself, he abides in the Self alone.
Having turned away from old age and death, he neither exults nor grieves;
disciplined and self-controlled, he exercises lordship even over the divinity of the gods,
and having cast off this impermanent body, he attains the immutable Brahman.
Even when the worlds are perishing, no fear arises in him;
even while beings are being afflicted, he is not afflicted by anything—
by the terrible miseries and sorrows born of attachment and affection.
One whose self is disciplined, who is free from longing, and whose mind is peaceful, cannot be shaken. Weapons do not pierce him, nor does death exist for him.
There is nothing anywhere in this world more blissful than this.
Through yoga, he is forever liberated from saṃsāra within his own self; when,
having properly disciplined himself, he beholds the Self within the self alone,
he sleeps in happiness, with the suffering of old age completely turned away.
Having abandoned this human body, he attains whatever bodies he desires;
at that very time, he no longer longs even for Śatakratu himself. However, one who is practicing yoga must never, under any circumstances, fall into despondency.
But hear how one who is devoted to the practice of solitary virtue should apply himself to yoga:
having mentally visualized the direction previously seen in the city where he dwells,
his mind should be directed toward the interior of that city and not toward the outside.

Standing within the city, in whatever dwelling one may reside, one should fix the mind— both internally and externally— upon that very dwelling; having mentally surveyed the entire dwelling, one should likewise focus it upon the body in which it resides.
Having restrained the collection of the senses in a soundless, deserted forest, one should direct the mind toward that body alone and not outwardly in any way;
with one-pointed concentration, one should contemplate the entire interior of the body.
"One should contemplate the teeth, the palate, the tongue, the throat, and likewise the neck; one should also contemplate the heart and the ligaments of the heart.
Thus was that intelligent disciple addressed by me, O Madhusūdana.
14,019.036c He asked once again about this dharma of liberation, which is so difficult to explain:
14,019.037a "How is this food, once it has been eaten and eaten, digested within the stomach? How does it turn into chyle, and how is blood produced?"
14,019.037 Thus it nourishes the flesh, the fat, the sinews, and the bones.
14,019.038 How do all these bodies of embodied beings grow? And how does the strength increase as the body grows?
14,019.038e The departure of the lifeless and the various impurities [is explained]; 14,019.039a From where does this [being] exhale or inhale again?
14,019.039c And abiding in what location does this Self reside within the self?

"O sinless Blessed One, if the individual soul (jīva) sustains the body by means of its movement, what color does it have, and of what nature is the mind that it establishes within the frame? You ought to tell me this according to the truth."
"O Mādhava, O mighty-armed subduer of enemies, having been thus questioned by that brahmin, I replied exactly as I had heard it:
'Just as one who has placed [grain] in his own storehouse becomes intent on the storehouse and its contents.'"
Likewise, having cast the mind into one's own body with the gates [of the senses] motionless,
one should seek the Self therein and avoid negligence. Thus constantly striving, with a joyful soul, in no long time—
One attains that Brahman by seeing which one becomes a knower of Pradhāna;
yet it is not to be grasped by the eye, nor even by all the senses.
Only by means of the mind as a lamp is the Great One seen within the self.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
and with ears everywhere in the world, He exists pervading everything.
The living being perceives the Self as having departed from the body.
Having cast off that body of his and maintaining the absolute Brahman alone,
he beholds the Self with his mind as if smiling;
having thus made that his refuge, he then attains liberation in me.
"O best of the twice-born, I have told you this entire secret. I take my leave; I shall now depart to accomplish my purpose. Go, disciple, as you please.
Thus addressed by me at that time, O Kṛṣṇa, was that disciple of great asceticism.
"Go as you wish, O Brahmin, your doubts having been severed.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Pārtha, having spoken these words to me at that time, that bull among the twice-born—"
"Relying perfectly upon the *mokṣadharma*, he vanished right there.
O Pārtha, was this heard by you with a one-pointed mind? For even then, while standing on your chariot, you indeed heard this very thing."
"O Pārtha, it is my opinion that this is not easily understood by one who is confused, nor by a man who lacks discernment, who is undisciplined, and whose self is unrefined.
O bull of the Bharatas, this which has been declared is a profound secret of the gods."
"O Pārtha, has this not been heard by any other mortal?
For no other man besides you, O sinless one, is worthy to hear this;
it is not easily understood today by one whose inner self is confused."
For the world of the gods, O son of Kuntī, is filled with those who perform ritual actions;
nor is this cessation of mortal form desired by the gods. For that which is the eternal Brahman, O Pārtha, is the supreme goal.

14,019.055c Where one attains immortality, casting off suffering and being forever happy; 14,019.056a For by thus adhering to dharma, even those who are of low birth— women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras— they too attain the supreme goal.
How much more so, O Pārtha, those Brāhmaṇas or Kṣatriyas who are deeply learned,
always devoted to their own duty, and intent upon the world of Brahmā?
This has been taught with its underlying reason, as well as the means for its accomplishment.
The fruit of spiritual accomplishment is liberation and the definitive resolution of suffering;
O bull among the Bharatas, what other happiness could there possibly be beyond this? O Pāṇḍava, you are learned, full of faith, and possessed of great prowess.
The mortal who abandons the worldly system as being devoid of essence shall, by these means, swiftly attain the supreme goal.
This much alone is to be said; there is nothing more than this.
"For one who is constantly disciplined for six months, O Pārtha, yoga proceeds.
Vāsudeva said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
14,020.001c O Pārtha, this is the dialogue between a husband and wife known by the name "Fearlessness.
14,020.002a A certain Brāhmaṇī, having seen a Brāhmaṇa who had reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, sitting in a secluded place, spoke to her husband:
"To what world shall I go, having taken refuge in you as my husband— you who have abandoned your duties, who sit idle, who are a miserly farmer, and who lack discernment?
We have heard it said that wives attain the worlds won by their husbands."
"Having obtained you as my husband, what destiny indeed shall I go to?
Thus addressed, he, whose soul was tranquil, spoke to her as if smiling:
"O blessed one, O sinless one, I do not find fault with these words of yours."
Whatever exists here as an object of perception, the visible, and the audible—
this very thing is what those engaged in action determine to be "action, action. Deprived of knowledge, they are governed by delusion through their actions.
In this world, no state of actionlessness is perceived as being material;
whether by deed, mind, or speech, whether auspicious or inauspicious, action—
consisting of the various distinctions of embodied forms such as birth and so forth— subsists among living beings.
While the visible objects and ritual acts were being destroyed by the Rākṣasas,
I beheld with my own self that abode situated within the self,
where that Brahman free from dualities resides, together with Soma and Agni.
The wise man, constantly supporting all beings, engages in sexual union;
there, Brahmā and the others, being disciplined, worship that Imperishable One,
where the learned, firm in their vows, peaceful in soul, and masters of their senses abide.
It is not to be smelled by the nose, nor is it to be tasted by the tongue;
it is not to be touched by the sense of touch, but is perceived by the mind alone.
It cannot be grasped by the eye, and it is something beyond all that is heard.
It is without smell, without taste or touch, without form or sound, and immutable;
from it the system (tantra) proceeds, and in it it is established— namely,
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna.
From that very source they proceed, and into that same source they enter.
Between the *samāna* and the *vyāna*, the *prāṇa* and *apāna* circulate. When one is asleep, both the *samāna* and the *vyāna* dissolve into it.
Between the *apāna* and the *prāṇa*, the *udāna* remains pervading them;
therefore, the *prāṇa* and *apāna* do not leave a man who is lying down.
That by which the vital breaths are extended upward is called *udāna*.
Therefore, those who discourse on Brahman resolve upon austerity as the means to attain that state. Among all those embodied beings who prey upon one another,
Vaiśvānara Agni is indeed established within them in a sevenfold manner.
The nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear as the fifth,
along with the mind and the intellect— these seven are indeed the flames of Vaiśvānara.
Likewise, that which is smelled, that which is tasted, that which is seen, that which is touched, and that which is heard [are their objects].
That which is to be thought and that which is to be understood—these are my seven sacrificial fuels (samidhas).
The smeller, the eater, the seer, the toucher, and the hearer as the fifth;
the thinker and the understander—these seven are the supreme officiating priests.
O fortunate one, behold always that which is to be smelled, drunk, seen, touched, and likewise heard; that which is to be reflected upon and understood—
just as the seven classes of priests offer oblations in the seven fires, sevenfold, within the seven.
Having properly cast [the elements] into their own sources, the wise produce [beings];
they are proponents of the doctrine that the instrument, action, and agent constitute liberation.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—
Mind and intellect—these seven are designated as the source (yoni). All the qualities (guṇas), having become oblations, enter the mouth born of fire;
and after dwelling within for a time, they are born again from their own sources.
And right there they cease at the dissolution that brings about the state of the elements;
from that, smell is produced, from that, taste is produced,
from that, form is produced, and from that, touch is born.
From that, sound is produced; therein doubt arises.
From that, certainty is born; the wise know this birth to be sevenfold.
It was grasped in this very manner by the ancients.
"Filled by the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti), they become completely filled with splendor.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history (itihāsa)."
O beautiful lady, understand here the dialogue between the senses and the mind, as well as the nature of the ordinance of the ten hotṛ-priests.
[These are] the ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, the nose, the two feet, and the two hands.
The generative organ and the anus— these, O beautiful lady, are the ten sacrificial priests (*hotṛ*). Sound, touch, form, taste, smell, speech, action, movement,
and the discharge of semen, urine, and feces are the ten oblations (*havis*).
O beautiful lady, the quarters, the winds, the sun, the moon, the earth, fire, and Viṣṇu; Indra, Prajāpati, Mitra, and the ten fires—these are the ten.
O beautiful lady, the ten sense organs are the officiating priests and the ten oblations.
The sense objects are indeed the sacrificial fuel offered into the ten fires;
the mind is the dipping-spoon, wealth is the purifier, and supreme knowledge is the clarified butter.
It is heard in the sacred tradition that this entire world was thus well-differentiated.
Then, free from discursive thoughts, she examined the mind.
Having heard that the mind is indeed a ladle, the mind is called "manas. Between those two, there was no separation; it was immovable and characterized by sound.
Like a naked woman feeling ashamed, she looked about for a garment. From that were born the social classes (*varṇa*), as well as the vowels (*svara*) and the sacred formulas (*mantra*).
And Prajāpati told this to us regarding Sarasvatī.
14,021.002 All that is to be known here, the mind, perceives through knowledge;
the seed is within the body that sustains the self, but the knower is the sustainer of the body.
14,021.003 The sustainer of the body is the *gārhapatya* fire; therefore, another [fire] is brought forward.
Then the Ahavaniya fire is concentrated within that oblation;
from that, Vācaspati was born, who observes all things equally. Indeed, form becomes manifest, and the mind runs after it.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
Why did speech come into being first, and why did the mind come into being afterwards?
For when a sentence is conceived by the mind, it is then brought forth by speech.
"By what application of consciousness is the intellect and the mind thus established? By whom was it raised up, and who indeed can restrain it?
The Brahmin said:
The vital breath (apāna), becoming its lord, impels it toward exhalation;
they call that mental faculty "mind" (manas), and therefore the mind perceives it.
Since you ask me this question concerning speech and mind, [I shall explain].
Therefore, I shall relate to you that very dialogue between those two. Having approached both speech and mind, the self of beings (bhūtātman) asked them:
"Tell me which of us is superior; O Lord, resolve our doubt."
"O Blessed One, [the Lord] then said to Sarasvatī, 'The mind alone. Then Speech said to him, 'I am indeed the fulfiller of your desires. [The Lord replied:
'Know that both the stationary and the moving are my two minds.'"
The immobile [Mantra] resides indeed in my presence, while the mobile [Mantra] resides within your domain.
Should anyone enter your domain—even by means of a mantra, a letter, or even a single vowel—that is called the "mobile mind"; therefore, you are more venerable.

"O beautiful Sarasvatī, because you came to me of your own accord and spoke, therefore, having reached your breath, you shall not speak again. For the goddess Speech always dwells within the interval between the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (apāna)."
Being thus impelled, O highly fortunate one, she breathed out even without her vital breath (prāṇa) and ran toward Prajāpati, saying, "Be gracious, O Blessed One!
Thereupon, Prāṇa appeared once more, nourishing Speech.
Therefore, having attained the breath, speech never speaks at all;
though it is resonant by nature, it proceeds as eternally silent.
And of these two—the resonant and the silent—it is the silent one that is indeed superior.
Like a cow, this [speech] flows with the most excellent essence;
for she, the proclaimer of Brahman, flows perpetually and eternally. By virtue of her divine and non-divine power, O lady of radiant smiles, she is the cow of speech.
"Behold the interval between these two subtle, flowing streams. While words had not yet arisen, being impelled by the desire to create,
what did the goddess Sarasvatī speak first?"
That which arises in the body through the *prāṇa*,
and from *prāṇa* one attains *apāna*; having become *udāna*, it departs, casting off the body.
"By means of the vyāna, one pervades the entire sky;
from there, one becomes established here in the samāna"—
thus indeed did he speak previously.
Therefore, the mind is superior because of its immobility;
likewise, the goddess is superior because of her mobility.
The Brahmin said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history concerning the procedure for the seven hotṛ-priests as it was, O blessed lady:
the nose, the eye, the tongue, the skin, and the ear as the fifth.
Mind and intellect—these seven are the Hotṛ-priests, each residing separately. Though they exist within that subtle space, they do not perceive one another.
Know these indeed to be the seven Hotṛ-priests by their very nature, O beautiful lady.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"In such a subtle space, how is it that those holy ones do not see one another?
What is their nature, O Blessed One? Tell me this, O All-pervading Lord."
The brahmin said:
"Lack of knowledge regarding the qualities is ignorance; knowledge of the possessor of the qualities is true discernment. These [beings] never understand the qualities of one another."
The tongue, the eye, as well as the ear, the skin, the mind, and the intellect—these do not perceive odors; it is the nose that perceives them.
The nose, the eye, as well as the ear, the skin, the mind, and the intellect likewise [do not perceive them].
The tastes do not perceive [them]; it is the tongue that perceives them.
The nose, the tongue, as well as the ear, the skin, the mind, and the intellect—these do not perceive forms; it is the eye that perceives them.
The nose, the tongue, the eye, the ear, as well as the intellect and the mind—these do not perceive tactile objects; rather, it is the skin that perceives them.
The nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, the mind, and the intellect likewise [do not perceive them].
They do not perceive sounds; it is the ear that perceives them.
The nose, the eye, the ear, the skin, the tongue, and the intellect as well—[these are the sense organs].
The nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, the ear, and the intellect as well [are likewise engaged].
They do not perceive through doubt; the mind perceives them.
The nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, the ear, and the mind itself do not reach the final certainty; the intellect reaches that certainty.
In this regard, O beautiful lady, they cite this ancient history concerning the dialogue between the senses and the mind. The mind said:
Without me, the sense of smell does not perceive odors; the tongue does not perceive taste;
the eye does not grasp form; the skin does not perceive touch;
and the ear, deprived of me, does not perceive sound in any way whatsoever.
I am the eternal, preeminent being among all creatures. Deprived of me, the senses always shine no more than empty houses or fires whose flames have been extinguished.
"Even with their senses striving, all living beings do not attain the objects of the qualities, just as one cannot obtain wet or dry wood [for fire] without me.
The senses said:
"This would indeed be true, just as you think it to be,
if you were to enjoy these pleasures— which are for our sake— without us;
or if, once we have perished, [you were to receive] the libations and the sustenance of life."
"You enjoy pleasures and you enjoy flavors; it is according to what you think.
Or, "If, while we are dissolved and the objects of sense remain present, he enjoys pleasures as if they were real by mere volition alone," [then so be it].
14,022.021a Now, if you think that success will always be achieved for our purposes, 14,022.021c then perceive form with the sense of smell, and perceive taste with the eye.
14,022.022a Perceive fragrance with the ear, and perceive solidity with the tongue.
Take up sound with your skin and touch with your intellect as well;
for the powerful have no restraints, whereas restraints belong to the very weak. Accept unprecedented enjoyments; you ought not to eat what has been left over.
Just as a disciple runs toward his teacher for the sake of what has been heard, and having received that which was heard, he attends to the meaning of what was heard;
so do you conceive of the objects shown by us.
Whether in dreams or while awake, [he perceives] those yet to come and those already past;
and for those small-minded beings who have fallen into despondency,
the preservation of their lives is seen once the task has been accomplished for our sake.
For even after considering many intentions and attending to dreams,
you, tormented by hunger, run only toward sense-objects,
as if having entered a house without a door.
Experiencing objects through mere volition,
he constantly attains peace at the exhaustion of the vital breaths,
just as a blazing fire does upon the consumption of its fuel.
Granted that we have attachment to our own qualities,
and granted that there is no perception of each other's qualities;
yet, apart from us, there is no perception of you.
"Even apart from you, joy would not attend us.
The Brahmin said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
O fortunate one, such is the ordinance of the five *hotṛ*s here as it is:
*prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, *samāna*, and *vyāna*. Indeed, the wise know these five *hotṛ*s to be the supreme state of being.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"Your former view was that there are seven Hotṛ-priests by nature;
now let the state beyond the five Hotṛs be explained."
The Brahmin said:
"Sustained by the prāṇa, the apāna wind is born from it;
sustained by the apāna, the vyāna wind proceeds from that."
The wind gathered by the *vyāna* then gives rise to the *udāna*;
the wind gathered by the *udāna* then fully proceeds as the *samāna*.
In former times, they went and questioned Prajāpati, who was born first.
"Tell us who among us is the eldest; he shall be our superior.
Brahmā said:
"He in whom, when he has dissolved, all others go to their dissolution..."
He in whom all the vital breaths of living beings abide,
and who, when he has departed, they follow once more—
he is indeed the best; go wherever you desire.
The Prāṇa said:
"When I am dissolved, all the vital breaths within the bodies of living beings go to dissolution."
"And when I have moved on, they move again;
behold me, for I am the foremost, as I dissolve.
The Brahmin said:
Then Prāṇa dissolved away, and once more he began to move.
Then Samāna and Udāna spoke these words, O auspicious lady:
"You do not remain here pervading all this as we do."
"O Prāṇa, you are not the best among us, for Apāna is under your control.
Prāṇa then moved away again, and Apāna addressed him:
"When I am dissolved, all things go to dissolution."
All the vital breaths within the bodies of living beings circulate again once I have moved;
behold me, for I am the supreme, now withdrawn.
"I am the best among all; hear the reason why.
To him as he was speaking, Vyāna and Udāna then said:
"O Apāna, you are not the best, for Prāṇa is under your control."
Then the apāna moved forward, and the vyāna spoke to him again:
"I am the best of all; hear the reason why.
When I have dissolved, all things go to dissolution."
All the vital breaths within the bodies of living beings circulate again once I have moved;
behold me, for I am the supreme one, now withdrawn.
Then Vyāna dissolved away, and once again he began to move.
Prāṇa, Apāna, Udāna, and Samāna said to him:
"O Vyāna, you are not the best among us; for Samāna is indeed under your control."
Vyāna moved about once more, and Samāna spoke again:
"I am the best of all; hear the reason why.
When I have dissolved, all things go to dissolution."
All the vital breaths within the bodies of living beings move again once they have entered into me;
behold me, for I am the supreme, as I dissolve away.
Then the *samāna* dissolved away and began to move once more. Then the *vyāna* spoke to the *samāna*, and likewise the *prāṇa* and *apāna* spoke.
The *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna* all addressed him.
"O Samāna, you are not the best; Vyāna alone is under your control.
"I am the best among all; hear for what reason!
Thereupon, Udāna quickly dissolved away, and Samāna spoke again.
Then Samāna moved about, and Udāna spoke to him:
"I am the foremost of all; hear the reason why.
When I have dissolved, [all beings] go to dissolution."
All the vital breaths within the bodies of living beings move again once I have moved;
behold me, for I am the supreme, as I dissolve away.
Then Udāna dissolved away, and once more he moved about. Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, and Vyāna spoke to him:
"O Udāna, you are not the best; Vyāna alone is under your control."
Then Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, spoke to those who had assembled:
"Are you all superior, or are none of you superior? You all possess one another's characteristics;
each is preeminent in his own domain, and all are protectors of one another."
The five vital airs (vāyu) are distinguished as being both one and stable, and one and unstable; my very self alone is manifested in many ways. As friends to one another, they sustain one another.
"Go in safety; may it be well with you; support one another.
The Brahmin said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
The dialogue between Nārada and the seer Devamata.
Devamata said:
"For a living being who is being born, what indeed functions first?"
"Whether it be prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, or udāna—
Nārada said:
That by which this living being is created, that [principle] precedes all others."
The pair of vital breaths should be understood as that which moves transversely and that which moves upwards.
Devamata said:
By what is this living being created, and who else precedes it?
"Tell me definitively, moreover, about the pairs of vital breaths—those moving horizontally and those moving upward.
Nārada said:
"Joy arises from mental resolve, and it also arises from sound."
It is born from taste and also born from form;
it is born from touch and also born from smell. This is the nature of udāna: joy arising from union.

From desire semen is produced; from desire the vital essence (rasa) is produced. When the semen and blood have been brought together by the *samāna* and *vyāna* breaths, the *prāṇa* first proceeds from the semen mixed with the blood.
When the semen is transformed by the *prāṇa*, the *apāna* then proceeds;
these two, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, form a pair that moves downward and upward respectively.
Both *vyāna* and *samāna* are likewise called a pair that moves transversely.
"Agni indeed is all the deities"—such is the teaching of the Veda. Knowledge endowed with intelligence is born among the Brāhmaṇas;
its smoke is the form of *tamas*, and its ash is *rajas* from which excellent seed arises.
The *sattva* arises in that place where the oblation is cast;
those who know the sacrifice understand the two libations (*āghāra*) to be the *samāna* and the *vyāna*.
The *prāṇa* and *apāna* are the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), and between them is the consumer of the oblation (*hutāśana*).
The Brahmins know this form of the *udāna* to be supreme.
Listen as I explain that which is called "beyond the pairs" (*nirdvaṃdva*):
day and night constitute a pair, and between them lies the consumer of oblations (fire).
The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of *udāna*:
both paths [of inhalation and exhalation] as a pair, and the fire between them. The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of *udāna*.
Truth and falsehood are a pair; between them is the fire.
The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of *udāna*.
Both the auspicious and the inauspicious are a pair; between them is the fire.
The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of *udāna*. Existence and non-existence constitute that duality; between them is the fire.
The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of *udāna*.
First, the *samāna* breath expands that action through the *vyāna*;
then, for the third time, it is again resolved by the *samāna*. For the sake of peace, there is the *vāmadeva*, and peace is the eternal Brahman.
The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of the *udāna*.
As long as there are the substances and qualities, so long will the lamp continue to shine;
when the substances and qualities are exhausted, the light goes to its disappearance.
For this person is manifest through the quality of *sattva*; he masters manifestation.
O Brahmin, understand this; indeed, I shall speak further to you:
even by means of a thousand [efforts], the dull-witted man suffers, while the wise man prospers in happiness.
Thus should the accomplishment of the Dharma be understood through its means;
for the wise person who knows the means attains ultimate happiness. It is like a man who sets out on a journey somewhere without provisions.
"By great affliction one proceeds, or perishes even midway;
in the same way, O man, the fruit of actions is to be understood. For a person, the vision of the auspicious and inauspicious is the means for attaining the supreme good within the self."
Just as one might set out on foot upon a long journey,
suddenly turned toward the vision of reality after never having seen it before,
so too does one reach the path here by means of a swiftly moving chariot.
Just as one might travel by means of a horse-drawn vehicle, such is the course of the wise. Having ascended a high mountain, one indeed beholds what lies upon the earth;
by means of a chariot one sees the charioteer, and by means of consciousness one perceives the conscious self.
As long as there is a path for a chariot, one proceeds by means of a chariot;
when the path for a chariot has ended, the wise man abandons the chariot and goes on foot.
In this same way, the intelligent person proceeds, knowing the method for the application of reality.
Having understood the ever-increasing [teachings] of the one of great intelligence,
he who, out of delusion, attempts to plunge into the terrible great ocean with his own two arms will undoubtedly meet his destruction.

Just as a wise man, without a boat and without a skilled helmsman, might wade through water that is too deep to cross, yet successfully crosses over by himself; once he has crossed and reached the further shore, he would leave the boat behind, free from attachment.

14,024.020d@002_0027 It has been explained by the previous method, just as in the case of charioteers and infantrymen. 14,024.020d@002_0028 Lest one, having fallen into delusion through delusion, should meet with destruction;
14,024.020d@002_0029 so it is for one overcome by the sense of "mine" who laments right there.
Just as it is not possible to ascend a boat and travel upon dry land, nor is it prescribed that one who has ascended dry land can go upon the waters; so too,
an action performed by the mind remains distinct and situated in its own particular sphere.
Just as an action is performed in the world, so does its result arise. Where there is neither smell, nor taste, nor form, touch, or sound—
when the mind then conceives [an object] through the intellect, that they declare to be the Pradhāna.

That which is the Pradhāna is unmanifest; the quality (*guṇa*) of the unmanifest is the Mahat. The qualities of the Mahat, which constitutes the Pradhāna, are traditionally taught as follows: just as the manifest possesses the nature of a seed, so too does it possess the nature of procreation.
We have heard that the Great Self (Mahān Ātmā) and the Vasus possess the nature of seeds;
from the seed-nature, however, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is produced again and again,
and the five great elements (mahābhūta) indeed possess the nature of both seed and sprout.
They say that which possesses the nature of a seed does not produce anything at all; the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of all beings have the mind as their distinguishing characteristic.
The Brahmins know this to be the supreme form of the *udāna*.
The Brahmin said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history concerning the manner in which the ritual procedure for the four officiating priests (cāturhotra) is prescribed."
The ritual procedure for all of that shall be taught according to the rules;
listen to me as I speak, O blessed lady, of this supreme secret:
the instrument, the action, the agent, and liberation—such, O beautiful woman, is the summary.
These four are the Hotṛ priests by whom this world is pervaded. Listen now to the complete and exhaustive account of the instruments of these Hotṛs:
the nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear as the fifth.
Mind and intellect— these seven are to be known as the causes of the qualities (guṇas).
Odor, taste, form, sound, and touch as the fifth,
that which is to be thought, and that which is to be understood— these seven are the causes of action (karma).
The smeller, the eater, the seer, the toucher, and the hearer as the fifth;
the thinker and the knower—these seven are to be known as the causal agents.
Possessing qualities, they consume their own qualities, both auspicious and inauspicious.
"And I am devoid of qualities here"— these seven are the causes of liberation for the wise who understand each their own station according to the rule;
those qualities, having become deities, constantly consume the sacrificial oblation.
For the ignorant man who eats food with a sense of "mine-ness" is constantly destroyed by that sense of "mine-ness" as he cooks for his own sake;
indeed, the eating of forbidden food and the drinking of intoxicants destroy him.

He destroys that food, and having destroyed it, the wise man is himself destroyed. For the wise master, knowing this food, produces it again; he is born from that food, and therein lies the transgression called "subtle."
That which is understood by the mind, and that which is uttered by speech;
that which is heard by the ear, and that which is seen by the eye;
that which is touched by the sense of touch, and that which is smelled by the nose.
Having restrained these offerings, with the mind as the sixth, in their entirety,
the fire that carries the oblation blazes for me, purifying through its qualities;
my sacrifice of yoga has commenced, arising from the mind through the Brahman of knowledge.

The *prāṇa* is the hymn of praise (*stotra*), the *apāna* is the ritual recitation (*śastra*), and the renunciation of everything is the excellent sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Brahmā is my witness to the rite, the performer is the *adhvaryu*,
the one who has offered praise is the *praśāstṛ*, that scripture is the manual, and liberation (*apavarga*) is its fee.
Regarding this, people who know Nārāyaṇa recite these Ṛgvedic verses:
"In ancient times, when they bound the sacrificial animals for the god Nārāyaṇa, there they sang the Sāman hymns; these they cite as an illustration."
"O timid one, understand from me that the god Nārāyaṇa is the self of all.
The Brahmin said:
"There is one teacher; there is no second teacher."
"I act exactly as I am commanded. "I declare that which dwells within the heart; this Person, abiding in the heart, governs as the Ruler."
Driven by that very [desire], one flows like water down a slope.
There is no second teacher other than this one;
I declare that it dwells within the heart.
Always instructed by that preceptor,
all the Dānavas were utterly defeated;
there was but one kinsman, and no second besides him.
I speak of him who dwells in the heart;
instructed by him, kinsmen become possessed of true kinship,
and the Seven Seers shine in the sky.
There is no second listener other than that one who dwells in the heart; it is him whom I address.
Having lived as a student with that teacher, dwelling in the teacher’s house—
Śakra has attained the immortality of all the worlds.
There is no second hater; I declare that he who dwells within the heart is that [enemy].
Always instructed by that preceptor,
all the serpents were indeed hated by the world.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
Before Prajāpati, there was a consultation between the serpents and the celestial sages.
Seated around Prajāpati, the celestial sages, the Nāgas, and the Asuras asked him, "Tell us that which is for our highest good."
To them who were inquiring after the highest good, the Blessed One spoke:
"Om"—the single-syllabled Brahman. Having heard this, they fled in all directions.
As they were fleeing, for the sake of his own instruction—
The disposition toward biting was already present in the serpents from the very beginning;
the disposition toward deceit arose naturally among the Asuras. The gods were intent upon giving, while the great seers were devoted solely to self-restraint.
Having approached a single Teacher and refined by a single word,
all— the serpents, celestial rishis, and dānavas— have reached various conclusions;
yet this one hears what is being spoken and grasps it exactly as it is.
While he was thus questioning, another teacher agreed with him; with that teacher's approval, the ritual action was subsequently undertaken.
The teacher, the knower, the enemy, and the hater were all established within his heart.

Wandering in the world with evil, he becomes an evildoer; wandering in the world with virtue, he indeed becomes a doer of good. But he who delights in the pleasures of the senses acts according to his desire, driven by passion.
He who is always observant of vows and devoted to the conquest of the senses is a *brahmacārī*. But he who has abandoned the performance of ritual duties and rests solely in Brahman,
having become one with Brahman while moving through the world— he too is a *brahmacārī*.

The sacred word (*brahman*) itself is his fuel, the sacred word is his fire, and the sacred word is his sacrificial grass; the waters are the sacred word, the teacher is the sacred word—he is fully absorbed in the sacred word.
The wise know this to be such a subtle form of celibate discipline (*brahmacarya*).
Having understood this, those who perceive through the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) followed it accordingly.
The Brahmin said:
[The body] has the volitions of its biting flies and mosquitoes, and grief, joy, cold, and heat as its weather.

Having crossed that great and difficult fortress— filled with the darkness of delusion, infested by the serpents and reptiles of greed, a path where sense-objects are the sole calamity, and obstructed by desire and anger— I have entered this vast forest.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"O one of great wisdom, where is that forest? What trees and what rivers are there?
What mountains and hills are there, and how far away is that forest?"
The Brahmin said:
"In the state of being separate, there is nothing whatsoever equal to that;
in the state of being non-separate, there is nothing whatsoever more distant than that."
14,027.005 There is nothing shorter than that, nor is there anything greater than that;
there is nothing more painful than that, and no other happiness is equal to it. 14,027.006 Having entered that, the twice-born neither grieve nor do they rejoice.
They do not fear anyone, nor does anyone fear them. In that forest, there are seven great trees,
seven fruits, and seven guests.
There are seven hermitages and seven meditative absorptions;
there are also seven initiations—this is the nature of the forest.
There are five-colored divine flowers and fruits.

Producing flowers and fruits that are golden or of two colors, the trees stand there pervading that forest. Producing flowers and fruits that are golden or of two colors, the trees stand there pervading that forest.
14,027.010a Trees there that produce divine flowers and fruits of four colors stand pervading that forest.
14,027.011a [They produce] auspicious flowers and fruits of three colors.

Producing flowers and fruits that are fragrant and of a single color, the trees stand there pervading that forest. Producing flowers and fruits that are fragrant and of a single color, the trees stand there pervading that forest.
Releasing many flowers and fruits of indistinct colors, two great trees stand pervading that forest;
releasing [these], the great trees remain, pervading that forest.
For here there is one benevolent fire, the Brāhmaṇa;
here the five sense-faculties serve as the fuel-sticks.
From these, the seven liberations arise as the initiatory rites.
The virtues are the fruits, and the guests are those who hope for fruit;
there, the seven great seers receive hospitality.
When they have been honored and have vanished, another forest shines forth.
Those virtuous ones who attain that tree of the Pratijñā— fruitless yet endowed with the shade of peace,
the refuge of knowledge, the water of contentment, and the sun within the field-knower (kṣetrajña)—
for them there is no fear again.
Neither above, nor below, nor across can its end be found.
Seven radiant mothers dwell there, facing downward, ever-present.
They bestow all the essences upon living beings,
as well as everything and impermanence itself;
they are established right there, and from there they arise again.
The seven perfected *saptarṣis*, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
together with Yaśas, Varcas, Bhaga, Vijaya, Siddhi, and Tejas—
these seven luminaries likewise follow the sun.
In brief, there are hills and mountains there,
as well as rivers and streams carrying water that originates from Brahmā. There,
at the confluence of those rivers in a secluded spot, is the Vaitāna fire-altar.

14,027.022c Since those who are self-contented and self-controlled go directly to the Grandfather (Brahmā), 14,027.023a Those whose desires have been thinned, who are firm in their vows, and whose sins have been burnt away by austerity, 14,027.023c having absorbed the self into the Self, they worship Brahmā.
Regarding this, those people who know the forest of knowledge recite even a verse:
"Having intended that as a forest, it became [the forest] just as [one might intend] a wise man.
The Brahmins know this divine forest to be exactly like this.
Having understood this, they acted according to what was pointed out by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
The Brahmin said:
"I do not smell odors; I do not perceive tastes."
I do not see form, nor do I touch it;
nor do I hear various sounds;
nor do I entertain any conceptual thought whatsoever.
One's own nature desires desirable objects;
one's own nature hates all hateful things.
Desire and hatred arise from one's own nature.
Having established the prāṇa and apāna breaths within the bodies of living beings,
and having observed other impermanent states within them,
I shall perceive the elemental self (bhūtātman) in the body.
While abiding in that [state], one cannot be affected in any way by desire and anger, nor by old age and death;
for one who does not desire all objects of desire, [there is no affliction].
And for me, who does not harbor hatred toward any faults, there is no staining by inherent natures,
just as a drop of water leaves no mark upon a lotus leaf.
But when the non-eternal bodies have thus come together with this eternal [self], they become eternal for it as it perceives their many inherent natures.
The web of enjoyments does not cling to his actions, just as the web of rays does not cling to the sun in the sky.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
O illustrious lady, learn now of that dialogue between the Adhvaryu and the Yati. Seeing the animal being sprinkled with water during the sacrificial rite,
the seated Yati spoke to the Adhvaryu, censuring him, saying, "This is an act of violence."
The Adhvaryu replied to him: "This goat shall not perish;
this creature will be united with what is more auspicious, provided that this sacred scripture is indeed so.
For that portion of it which is of the earth shall go to the earth.
Whatever lotus-like [parts] he has, they enter into the waters;
his eye enters the sun, his ears the quarters, and his breath the very sky. For one who abides in this process of dissolution, there is no fault whatsoever.
The ascetic said:
"If you perceive that there is spiritual welfare for the goat in its separation from life,
then since this sacrifice is being performed for the sake of the goat, what is your purpose in it?"
"May your mother, father, brother, and even your friend give their consent to you.
Having brought him forward, consult with him especially since he is dependent on others. You ought to ask those who would thus grant their approval."
Having heard their consent, it is possible for an investigation to be conducted:
"The life-breaths of this goat have been returned to their own sources;
only the body remains, motionless—this is my opinion."
But with a body that is equal to fuel and devoid of consciousness,
those desiring to fulfill their sacrificial obligations regard the fuel known as "livestock" as the object of injury; yet,
"non-injury is the highest of all dharmas"— this is the instruction of the elders.

We know that whatever action is non-violent, that is what ought to be done. "Non-violence" is the proposition; if I were to speak further than this, it would be possible to state many kinds of refutations of your position.
"Non-violence toward all living beings is always pleasing to us;
we establish this through direct perception, for we do not rely on what is beyond the senses.
The Adhvaryu said:
You enjoy the quality of fragrance from the earth; you drink the juices consisting of water; you behold the form of lights; you touch the qualities born of the wind;
you hear the sound born of space; and with the mind, you contemplate thought.

"You consider all these beings to be [identical with] the vital breath (*prāṇa*); you are constantly engaged in taking away that breath, for you abide in violence. There is no movement without violence—what do you think of this, O twice-born one?"
The ascetic said:
This duality of the self consists of the imperishable (akṣara) and the perishable (kṣara). Therein, the imperishable is true being; the perishable is said to be its inherent nature (svabhāva).

For one who is liberated from these states— vital breath, tongue, mind, the quality of goodness (sattva), and inherent nature along with passion (rajas)— who is free from dualities, free from longing,
equal toward all beings, devoid of the sense of "mine," and self-conquered;
"For one who is completely liberated on all sides, no fear exists anywhere.
The Adhvaryu said:
"O best among the wise, one should dwell here only with the virtuous."

"Having heard your opinion, my own mind has become enlightened; O Blessed One, awakened by the thought that you are the Blessed One, I speak thus. To deliberate upon your view and to perform this sacrifice, there is no fault on my part, O twice-born one."
The Brahmin said:
Thereafter, the ascetic remained silent by virtue of his realization, and the Adhvaryu priest, freed from delusion, proceeded with the great sacrifice.
"Thus do the Brahmins know such liberation, which is exceedingly subtle;
having known it, they practice it while observing with the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
The Brahmin said:
In this regard, O beautiful lady, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Kārtavīrya and the Ocean. There was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms.

By him, with his bow, the earth as far as the ocean's edge was conquered. Once, while wandering on the shore of the sea, he—proud of his strength—showered the ocean with hundreds of arrows; so we have heard.
Having paid homage to him with palms joined in reverence, the ocean said:
"O hero, do not release your iron shafts; tell me, what may I do for you? Let not the living beings who take refuge in me be struck by the great arrows discharged by you."
"O tiger among kings, they are being slain; O Lord, grant them freedom from fear.
Arjuna said:
"If there were anyone anywhere who, as a wielder of the bow, was equal to me in battle—"
"Tell me of him who would sit against me in battle.
The Ocean replied:
"O King, if the great seer Jamadagni has been heard of by you..."
"His son ought to extend hospitality to you in the proper manner.
Thereupon, that king, overcome by great anger, set out;
having reached that hermitage, he sought out Rāma himself.
Together with his kinsmen, he acted in opposition to Rāma and caused distress to the high-souled Rāma;
thereupon, the splendor of Rāma, who possesses immeasurable power, blazed forth.
O lotus-eyed one, as he was then consuming the enemy armies,
Rāma then took up his axe and suddenly severed that thousand-armed one, like a tree with a thousand branches.

Seeing him slain and fallen, all his kinsmen gathered together; taking up swords and spears, they surrounded the descendant of Bhṛgu. Rāma also, quickly taking up his bow and mounting his chariot, [proceeded].
Discharging showers of arrows, he scattered the royal army.
Then some kṣatriyas, having slain Jamadagni,
entered mountain fastnesses like deer tormented by a lion.
Because they did not perform their own prescribed duties out of fear of them,
and because they no longer saw the Brāhmaṇas, the subjects fell into the state of *vṛṣalatva*.
These are the Dramiḍas, Kāśas, Puṇḍras, along with the Śabaras.
Having fallen into the state of *vṛṣalas* through their deviation from the duty of the Kṣatriyas,
the Kṣatriya race was then repeatedly procreated by the twice-born among the women whose heroes had been slain; however, Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, cut them down once more.
At the conclusion of twenty-one sacrifices, O Rāma, a divine and sweet voice, heard by all the worlds, spoke from the bodiless ether:
"Rāma, Rāma, turn back! My son, what merit do you perceive?"
"Having repeatedly deprived these kinsmen of the warrior caste of their lives,
[you have acted thus]; likewise, O highly fortunate one, the grandfathers headed by Ṛcīka then said to that great-souled man, 'Desist!'"
Unable to endure the slaughter of his father, Rāma spoke to those sages:
"You ought not to restrain me here.
The fathers said:
"O best among victors, you ought not to slay these wretched kshatriyas;
for it is not fitting for you, being a Brahmin, to kill kings.
The fathers said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history;
having heard it, O best of the twice-born, you should act accordingly.
There was a royal sage named Alarka, who was a man of great asceticism.
A knower of dharma, true to his word, high-souled, and observer of great vows, he—
having conquered this earth as far as the ocean's edge with his bow and having performed a most difficult feat— fixed his mind upon the subtle.
Then, as he stood at the foot of the tree, a reflection arose in him,
O high-minded one, regarding that subtle [reality] for which he had renounced his vast kingdom.
Alarka said:

"Strength has been born from my mind; having conquered the mind, victory is certain. Surrounded by enemies, I discharge my arrows elsewhere [from this mind], for it is this embodied mind that desires to do all these things out of fickleness."
"O Alarka, I shall discharge extremely sharp-pointed arrows at your mind.
The mind said:
"These arrows will not pierce me in any way whatsoever, O Alarka."
"They will pierce your very vitals; with your vitals pierced, you shall die. Look for other arrows with which you might destroy me.
Having heard that, he reflected and then spoke these words.
"Your intellect hankers here after all the objects of the senses;
therefore, I shall discharge sharpened arrows against that intellect.
Alarka said:
"Having smelled many fragrances, he becomes greedy for those very same ones;
therefore, I shall discharge sharpened arrows at the sense of smell.
The sense of smell said:
"O Alarka, these arrows will by no means pierce me;
they will only pierce your own vital organs, and with your vitals pierced, you shall die.
Look for other arrows with which you might destroy me."
Having heard that, he reflected and then spoke these words.
Alarka said:
"Having enjoyed these sweet flavors, she now hankers after them once again."
"Therefore, I shall discharge sharpened arrows against your tongue.
The tongue said:
"O Alarka, these arrows will not pierce me by any means whatsoever."
"Those very arrows shall pierce your vital organs; with your vitals pierced, you will die. Look for other arrows with which you might destroy me.
Having heard this and reflected upon it, he then spoke these words.
14,030.015 Alarka said:
"Having touched various sensations with the skin, it craves those very same sensations;
therefore, I shall tear the skin apart with various heron-feathered arrows."
The skin said:
"O Alarka, these arrows shall not pierce me in any way;
they will pierce only your own vital organs, and with your vitals pierced, you shall die."
"Look for other arrows with which you may destroy me.
Having heard that, he reflected and then spoke these words.
Alarka said:
"Having heard various sounds, one becomes greedy for those very things;
therefore, I shall discharge sharpened arrows at the sense of hearing.
The ear said:
"O Alarka, these arrows will not pierce me in any way;
rather, they will strike your own vital organs, and then you shall lose your life.
Look for other arrows with which you might destroy me."
14,030.020c Having heard that, he reflected and then spoke these words.
14,030.021 Alarka said:
14,030.021a "Having indeed seen various states of being, one becomes greedy for those very things."
"Therefore, I shall discharge sharpened arrows against your eye.
The Eye replied:
"O Alarka, these arrows will not pierce me by any means whatsoever."
"14,030.022c They will pierce your very vital organs; with your vitals pierced, you shall die.
14,030.023a Look for other arrows with which you might destroy me.
Having heard that, he reflected and then spoke these words.
Alarka said:
"This goal is manifold, yet it is determined by wisdom;
therefore, I shall discharge sharpened arrows against the intellect."
Buddhi said:
"O Alarka, these arrows shall not pierce me by any means;
rather, they will pierce your own vital organs, and with your vitals pierced, you shall die."
"Look for other arrows with which you may destroy me.
The fathers said:
"Thereupon Alarka, having undertaken severe and most difficult austerities..."
Despite his supreme power, he could not find a single arrow among these seven;
then the lord, with a perfectly concentrated mind, reflected upon this.
Having pondered for a long time, O best of the twice-born, Alarka [thought as follows].
14,030.027c That best among the wise did not find any higher excellence than yoga.
14,030.028a Having made his mind one-pointed and remaining motionless, he established himself in yoga.
14,030.028c The valiant one swiftly struck down the senses with a single arrow.
Having entered his own self through yoga, he attained supreme perfection.
And the royal seer, filled with wonder, sang this verse:
"Alas, what a tragedy that we formerly governed the kingdom!"
"In the past, kingdoms were served by those possessed by thirst for enjoyments;
later, through yoga, I realized that there is no happiness higher than this.
Know this also, O Rāma, and do not slay the Kṣatriyas."
"Perform severe austerity; then you shall attain the highest good.
The Brahmana said:
"Thus addressed by his ancestors, that son of Jamadagni performed severe austerity."

Established in this, the highly fortunate one attained a success that is difficult to reach. Having been thus addressed by his ancestors, the illustrious son of Jamadagni then undertook severe austerity and attained supreme perfection.
The Brahmin said:
"There are indeed three enemies in the world, which are traditionally held to be ninefold by way of their qualities. Joy, rigidity, and arrogance—these three are the qualities of the *sattva* mode."
Grief, anger, and excessive agitation—these are known as the qualities of *rajas*. Sleep, lassitude, and delusion—these three are the qualities of *tamas*.
Having cut these down with showers of arrows, remain steadfast and unwearied.
One whose self is tranquil and who has conquered the senses is capable of conquering enemies. Regarding this,
people who know the ancient cycles recite these verses sung by King Ambarīṣa while he was ruling his kingdom:
"When the vices had arisen and the virtuous were being oppressed,
it is heard that Ambarīṣa seized the kingdom by force.
Having restrained the great evils and having honored the virtuous,"
He attained great perfection and uttered this verse:
"The faults have for the most part been conquered by me; all enemies have been slain. Yet one fault remains, and it must be destroyed, though it has not yet been slain by me."
Endowed with this, a living being does not attain freedom from craving;
like one tormented by thirst, he runs toward low ground and does not perceive it. Impelled by this, a man here commits even what ought not to be done.
Cut down that greed with sharp swords; cut it down!
For from greed arises craving, and from that, anxiety ensues. One who is full of longing acquires an abundance of qualities belonging to the realm of passion (rājasa).
Upon attaining that [state], however, one acquires predominantly tamasic qualities.
Bound again and again by these defects, the embodied soul,
having indeed experienced rajasic enjoyments, is born and exerts itself toward further action.
Bound by the body through those qualities,
he is born again and again and performs actions here;
when birth is exhausted, his body is shattered and scattered.
One goes to death again in one's own birth;
therefore, having thoroughly examined this greed and restrained it through fortitude within oneself, one should desire sovereignty.
"One should know that this kingdom is nothing else;
for the king who was conquered here is my one [treasure]," thus sang the illustrious King Ambarīṣa in these verses.
14,031.013c Having set aside sovereign power and cut away greed alone,
14,032.001 the Brāhmaṇa said:
14,032.001a "In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
O beautiful lady, there was a conversation between a brahmin and Janaka.
King Janaka, for the sake of discipline, spoke to a brahmin who had sat down during some sacred discourse, saying: "You must not dwell within my domain."
Thus addressed, the brahmin then replied to that best of kings:
"O King, declare the extent of the territory that remains under your control;
O Lord, I wish to dwell in the domain of another king."

"O lord of the earth, I wish to carry out your word according to the scriptures. When he had been addressed thus by the illustrious brahmin, the king sighed repeatedly and hotly, and did not reply to him.
As that king of immeasurable prowess sat there lost in meditation,
a sudden dejection overcame him, like a planet eclipsing the radiant sun.
Then, having regained his composure once that dejection had passed away, the king—
Then, after what seemed like a mere moment, he spoke these words to that brahmin:
"While this ancestral kingdom and its subject territory remain under my control,
I have not found a wife, though I have searched this entire earth."
When I did not find him on the earth, I searched Mithilā; when I did not find him there, I searched among my own subjects;
and when I did not find him among them, then dejection came over me.
Then, at the end of my despondency, my intelligence returned to me once more.
By means of it, I no longer consider anything to be an object of attachment, nor do I consider everything to be my domain;
even this self is not mine, nor is the entire earth mine.

"O best of the twice-born, I consider that as it is for me, so it is for others. Dwell here as long as you have the energy; enjoy as much as you desire, while this ancestral kingdom and its subject people remain under our control."
Tell me, relying upon what understanding have you abandoned the sense of "mine," or having determined what understanding is it that every object is indeed yours,
such that you do not perceive any object as being exclusively yours?
Janaka said:
"In this world, all undertakings in every action are known to be finite;
yet I have not found that from which it could be said, 'This is mine.'"
"Whose is this? "Whose is the property?"—thus I pondered upon the words of the Vedas;
I could not find through my intellect anything that might be "mine.
Having resolved upon this understanding, I have abandoned the sense of "mineness."
Listen, however, to that wisdom by knowing which my domain extends everywhere:
I do not desire for my own sake even the fragrances that reach the nose;
therefore, the earth has been conquered by me and remains perpetually under my control.

I do not desire flavors for my own sake, even as they remain within my mouth; therefore, the waters have been conquered by me and remain perpetually under my control. I do not desire form or light for my own sake through the eye.
Therefore, light has been conquered by me and remains perpetually under my control. I do not desire for my own sake those sensations of touch that reside in the skin;
therefore, wind has been conquered by me and remains perpetually under my control.

I do not desire sounds, even those that have reached my ears, for my own sake; therefore, sounds are conquered by me and remain perpetually under my control. I do not desire the mind, which is always within the mind, for my own sake.
My mind has been conquered; therefore, it remains perpetually under my control.
Indeed, all these undertakings are for the sake of [offering] to the gods, the ancestors, the spirits, and guests.
Then, smiling, the Brahmin spoke again to Janaka:
"Know that I am Dharma, who has come here today for the purpose of testing you.
You are the nave of this wheel of Brahman, whose hub is the intellect and which never turns back."
Of the wheel whose rim is composed of living beings, he alone is the setter-in-motion.
The Brahmin said:
"O timid one, I do not move about in the world in that manner."
Thus you conjecture about me with your own intellect:
"I am a Brahmin, I am liberated, I am a forest-dweller;
likewise, I am a householder and a celibate student."
"O auspicious lady, I am not as you perceive me with your eye.
This entire world, whatever exists within the realm of the moving, is pervaded by me.
Whatever creatures there are in the world, whether mobile or immobile,"
Know me to be their ender, like fire to pieces of wood.
Whether it be sovereignty over the entire earth or even over the triple heaven—such is the understanding this intellect possesses; indeed, this intellect alone is my wealth.
There is but one path for the Brahmins, by which those who know that [reality] proceed: whether in households, in forest dwellings, in the service of teachers, or among mendicants,
they worship that single Intellect with many undistracted signs.

Those whose intellect is characterized by tranquility, regardless of their various marks or stages of life, attain that single state just as rivers reach the ocean. This path is traversed by means of the intellect; it is not traversed by the body.
Actions have a beginning and an end; the body is a bondage of actions.
Therefore, O blessed one, you have no fear regarding the next world;
devoted to the contemplation of my nature, you shall attain my very self.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"This cannot be understood by one of small intellect, nor by one whose self is undisciplined. My own understanding is manifold, limited, condensed, and confused."
"Tell me, however, the means by which this wisdom may be obtained;
I consider that to be the supreme cause from which it proceeds.
The brahmin said:
