"Know that the Brāhmaṇī woman is the lower fire-drill (araṇī) and the Guru is its upper fire-drill;
by churning with austerity and sacred learning, the fire of knowledge is born from them.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"That which is this mark of Brahman, designated as the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña)—
where indeed is that characteristic by which it can be grasped?
The Brāhmaṇa said:
It is without marks and devoid of qualities; no cause for it exists.
I shall explain the very means by which it might be grasped, or perhaps not. Even when correctly taught, it is perceived [only] as if by bees.
The notion of action arises from a lack of true understanding, like relying on the marks of knowledge [when they are absent].
Regarding liberation, it is not taught that "this is to be done" or "this is not";
rather, for one who sees and hears, the intellect arises toward those things which pertain to the Self.
One should conceive as many portions as possible here—
both manifest and unmanifest in form, by the hundreds and thousands—
all of them endowed with diversity and all of them having perceptible causes.
"Since nothing further exists beyond that, it will be realized through practice.
Vāsudeva said:
"Then, however, the mind of that Brahmin woman [was fixed] upon the dissolution of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*)."
From the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) alone, another Knower of the Field proceeds beyond.
Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, where indeed is that Brāhmaṇī, and where is that bull among Brāhmaṇas?"
"O Acyuta, tell me who those two were by whom this perfection was attained.
Vāsudeva said:
"Know, O Brāhmaṇa, that my mind is the Brāhmaṇa; know that my intellect is the Brāhmaṇī."
"That which is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), that indeed am I, O Dhanañjaya.
Arjuna said:
"You ought to explain to me that which is the supreme Brahman, the object to be known."
"Indeed, by your grace, my mind delights in the subtle.
Vāsudeva said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
14,035.002c A dialogue concerning liberation between a disciple and his teacher:
14,035.003a A certain intelligent disciple questioned a seated Brāhmaṇa, a teacher of rigid vows, 14,035.003c saying, "O scorcher of foes, what indeed is the highest good?"
"O Brahmin, I have taken refuge in the Blessed One, who is the ultimate goal of supreme beatitude. I entreat you with my head bowed; please consider what I shall say to you.
To his disciple who spoke thus, O Pārtha, the teacher replied:
"Tell me what you wish to hear, O twice-born one, regarding that in which you have doubt.
Being thus addressed by his preceptor, O best of the Kurus, he who was devoted to his teacher joined his palms in reverence and questioned him; listen to that, O high-minded one.
The disciple said:
"From where have I come, and from where have you come? Tell me that which is the supreme truth.
From what are all beings born—the stationary and the moving?"
By what do living beings subsist, and what is the nature of their life-span? O Brahmin, what is truth, what is austerity, and what qualities are proclaimed by the virtuous?
What paths are auspicious, what is happiness, and what is evil action?
"O Blessed One, O best of beings, O brahmin-sage, you ought to answer these questions of mine according to reality, exactly as they are and in accordance with truth;
for who else besides you is capable of answering these questions here?"

"Speak, O best among those who know the Dharma; my curiosity is supreme. You are celebrated throughout the worlds as one skilled in the meaning of the Dharma of Liberation; there is no one else to be found who can sever all doubts."
"We are indeed afraid of saṃsāra and likewise desirous of liberation.
Vāsudeva said:
"To him who had approached and was questioning me correctly,"
To a disciple endowed with virtues, who is tranquil, obedient to his guru,
who has become like a shadow [to him], self-controlled, an ascetic, and a celibate student;
to one of noble birth, of excellent character, devoted, and a proclaimer of Brahman.

O best of the Kuru lineage, O subduer of enemies, that wise preceptor of firm vows answered all those questions correctly, O Pārtha. He spoke this dharma proclaimed by Brahmā and practiced by the foremost of sages.

We know that knowledge alone— which is to be fully attained through the science of the Vedas and which consists of the contemplation of the true nature of reality— is the supreme renunciation and the highest austerity;
for he who knows, through firm conviction, the unassailable essence of knowledge.
He who perceives the Self abiding in all beings is considered to have attained the state of omnipresence; the wise man who perceives both union and separation,
as well as unity and diversity, is thereby liberated from suffering.
He who desires nothing and conceives no egoistic notions,
even while remaining in this world, is fit for becoming Brahman;
he is a knower of the reality of the qualities of primordial matter (pradhāna) and a knower of the ordination of all beings.

Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. Born from the seed of the Unmanifest, the Great Tree consists of the intellect as its trunk, has great egoism as its branches, and the sense organs as the hollows of its sprouts.
It is a particular manifestation of the great elements, possessing distinct branches;
it is ever-leaved, ever-flowering, and always yielding auspicious fruit.
It is the livelihood of all beings, the eternal seed of Brahman.
Having known this in its true essence through supreme knowledge that cuts away [ignorance], and having severed [the bonds] and attained immortality, one abandons birth and death,
as well as the determination regarding the past, future, and present, and regarding dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
O one of great wisdom, today I shall proclaim to you that eternal, ancient path, known by the hosts of Siddhas, which,
once understood here, enables wise men to attain perfection in this world.
In former times, the ṛṣis— Bṛhaspati, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Bhārgava, Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Viśvāmitra, and Atri— approached one another, desiring to know [the truth] among themselves.
Having traversed all the paths and become exhausted by their own labors,
those twice-born ones, placing the aged Ṛṣi Āṅgirasa at their head,
beheld Brahmā, free from all taint, in the abode of Brahmā.
Having prostrated before that high-souled one as he sat at ease, the great seers, endowed with humility, asked him about this supreme spiritual welfare:
"How should one perform action rightly? How may one be liberated from evil?"
What paths would be auspicious for us? What is truth, and what is evil action?
By what do both paths of karma arise, and by what does one attain greatness? [Tell us of] the dissolution and liberation of beings, their origin and their passing away.
14,035.021 Thus addressed by the best of sages, I shall fully declare to you that which the Great-grandfather spoke; listen, O disciple, according to the tradition.
14,035.022 Brahmā said:
"From Truth (satya) all beings—both the stationary and the moving—are born;
they live by means of austerity (tapas). Know this, O you of excellent vows.
Having returned again to their own source, they proceed according to their own karma."
Truth indeed is endowed with all virtues and is fixed in five characteristics:
Brahman is truth, austerity is truth, and Prajāpati himself is truth. From truth all beings are born; the great existent world is composed of truth.
Therefore, O brahmins, those who rely on truth, who are constantly devoted to yoga, who have transcended anger and distress, and who are self-restrained, serve as the bridges of dharma.
These learned ones, mutually disciplined, are the promoters of the bridge of dharma.
I shall fully declare those eternal principles that sustain the worlds:
the fourfold knowledge, as well as the four social classes and the four stages of life separately;
for the wise have declared that Dharma is a single reality with four feet, which is eternal.
"O twice-born ones, I shall declare to you the auspicious path that brings security,
which was formerly traversed by the wise for the sake of attaining the state of Brahman. Listen now as I speak of that supreme path, so difficult to comprehend."
O highly fortunate ones, understand in its entirety the supreme state:
they say that the stage of the student (brahmacarya) is the first station;
the householder’s life (gārhasthya) shall be the second, and after that, the forest-dweller’s life (vānaprastha).
Beyond that, however, one should know the supreme state of the inner self (*adhyātma*):
light, space, the sun, wind, Indra, and Prajāpati.
As long as one does not attain the inner self, so long does one not perceive these.
14,035.031e I shall declare the means for that; listen to it hereafter.
14,035.032a For the twice-born who dwell in the forest, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air, the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is prescribed.
The householder stage is prescribed for all social classes;
the wise declare that this dharma is characterized by faith.
Furthermore, the lifelong student and the ascetic are distinct categories of the religious student.
Thus have these paths leading to the gods been proclaimed to you— paths frequented by the wise and steadfast, which serve as bridges of dharma through their deeds.
He who, firm in his vows, practices the dharma according to each of these individually, [attains the goal].
From time, one always perceives the origin and dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, I shall explain the principles (tattvas) according to their true nature and cause,
as they abide within their objects and exist in their respective parts.
The Great Self, as well as the Unmanifest and likewise the Ego; the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five great elements;
and the specific qualities of the five elements—this is the Vedic revelation.
These twenty-four principles have been fully proclaimed to you.
Now, he who knows the origin and dissolution of all these principles—
that wise man does not fall into delusion regarding any living beings.
He who knows the principles as they truly are,
as well as all the qualities and all the deities,
having shaken off evil and being released from bondage;
He enjoys all the stainless worlds.
Brahmā said:
That is unmanifest, unsurpassed, all-pervading, eternal, and firm.

One should know the city with nine gates, consisting of the three qualities and the five elements; it has eleven enclosures, with the mind as its defining characteristic, and intellect as its master— this is the supreme eleventh.

There are three streams which flow into this [body] again and again; these very channels proceed as being composed of the qualities (guṇas). Darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva)—these they call the qualities.

All these five elements, characterized by the three qualities (guṇas), are mutually paired, mutually dependent for their subsistence, mutually supportive, mutually following one another, and mutually interwoven.
Tamas has sattva as its mate, and rajas is the mate of sattva;
likewise, sattva belongs to rajas, and tamas is the mate of sattva. Where tamas is restrained, there rajas proceeds.
Where *rajas* is restrained, there *sattva* prevails.
One should know that *tamas* is of the nature of night, consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), designated as delusion (*moha*),
characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*), and invariably present in evil deeds.
This form is indeed seen as associated with *tamas*, yet it is also observed as being essentially characterized by activity (*pravṛtti*). Rajas is said to be the cause of transformation;
it is active within all beings and is observed to have the characteristic of origination.
Luminosity among all beings, lightness, and faithfulness— such is the nature of *sattva*, and lightness is thus esteemed by the virtuous.
Indeed, the true essence of these qualities will be explained through reasons and non-reasons.
Know from me those things in their true nature, both in brief and in detail:
delusion, ignorance, lack of renunciation, indecision regarding actions,
sleep, arrogance, fear, greed, grief, and the disparagement of good deeds.
Lack of mindfulness, lack of ripening [of karma], nihilism, and a broken way of life; lack of distinction, blindness, and a disposition toward inferior qualities;
the pride of having accomplished what was not done, and the pride of knowledge regarding what is ignorance—these are the marks of one who has fallen from yoga.
Lack of friendliness, a perverted state of being, lack of faith, and a deluded disposition;
crookedness, lack of mindfulness, sinful action, and thoughtlessness;
heaviness, a depressed state of mind, blackness, and a downward course.
O Brahmins, all these qualities are proclaimed to be of the nature of *tamas*;
likewise, whatever other fixed states exist in this world that are designated as delusion (*moha*),
they are all regulated by *tamas* and are therefore qualities of *tamas*.
Constant talk of slander against gods, brahmins, and the Vedas; lack of generosity, arrogance, delusion, anger, as well as intolerance,
and envy toward living beings— this is held to be the tamasic mode of conduct.
Whatever undertakings are in vain, whatever gifts are in vain,
and this which is called eating in vain— this is held to be the mode of conduct belonging to *tamas*. Excessive speech, lack of endurance, envy, and excessive pride [are likewise].
Lack of faith is indeed considered a tamasic disposition.
Those who in this world are such as these— evil-doers, men who have transgressed the bounds of conduct— they are all people characterized by tamas.
I shall declare the fixed destiny of those who perform evil deeds:
they go to the downward state of hell, or to the animal realm;
they become stationary beings, cattle, or beasts of burden.
Flesh-eaters and venomous serpents, worms, insects, and birds; those creatures born from eggs and all quadrupeds as well;
the insane, the deaf, the mute, and others afflicted with loathsome diseases.

Immersed in darkness, those of evil conduct, characterized by their own past actions, are known as the "downward-streaming" (avāk-srotas); these, being dominated by tamas, are submerged in darkness. Hereafter, I shall describe their advancement and increase.
Just as those performers of meritorious deeds obtain the worlds of the righteous,
so too [it is for] those who have practiced otherwise, those who have increased in their ritual acts,
and for the Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to their own duties and desire what is auspicious.
"By means of ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), those who strive ascend upwards to attain the same world (*salokatā*) as the gods;
they go to heaven—such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). But those who have understood otherwise, though increased in their own ritual acts..."
Those humans here who possess the nature of returning again—
having fallen into evil wombs as Caṇḍālas, mutes, or those with speech impediments—
attain the castes in successive order, one after another.

Having transcended the womb of a Śūdra, those other qualities of darkness (tāmasa) come together within the stream and exist in the quality of darkness. Attachment to sensual desires is known as "great delusion" (mahāmoha).
Even the sages, the munis, and the gods, desiring happiness, are deluded in this matter.

Darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), and that which is called the darkness of anger (tāmisra)— death is known as blinding darkness (andhatāmisra), while anger is said to be darkness (tāmisra).
O Brahmins, all this regarding *tamas*—in terms of its nature, its qualities, its origin, and its true essence—has been proclaimed to you according to the rule.
Who indeed understands this correctly? Who indeed perceives this rightly?
He who perceives reality in that which is unreal— that is the defining characteristic of darkness (*tamas*). The qualities of *tamas* have been proclaimed to you in many ways,
and *tamas*, both its higher and lower aspects, has been described exactly as it is.
"For the man who always knows these qualities,
he is liberated from all qualities characterized by darkness.
Brahmā said:
"O best of beings, I shall declare to you the nature of *rajas* according to its true essence; listen, O highly fortunate ones, to its qualities and conduct in every respect.
It is a composite, a form, exertion, pleasure and pain, cold and heat."
Sovereignty, war, peace, logical argumentation, discontent, and forbearance;
strength, heroism, pride, anger, as well as exertion and strife;
envy, desire, calumny, combat, possessiveness, and protection.
The afflictions of execution and imprisonment, as well as buying and selling;
the hacking away at the vital secrets of others by saying "cut," "sever," and "pierce";
harsh and cruel abuse; and the misappropriation of another's wealth.
Worldly concern, anxious thought, envy, and reproach; false speech, false giving, conceptualization, and reproach;
censure, praise, commendation, majesty, and gratification.
Attendance, service, devotion, thirst, reliance, array, misconduct, negligence, burning anguish, and grasping—
these and whatever other formative forces (saṃskāras) operate individually in this world.

"May I never experience distress or lack of confidence regarding men, women, living beings, material objects, or places of refuge; and may my vows, observances, and acts of giving always be free from worldly desires."
Various meritorious acts (*pūrta*) joined with benedictions,
as well as the utterances of *svadhā*, *namas*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*; both officiating at sacrifices and teaching— these they likewise call "acceptance" (*parigraha*).
Giving and receiving, penances, and auspicious rites;
"May this be mine, may that be mine"— affection arising from qualities, as well as malice, deceit, dishonesty, and pride.
Theft, violence, slander, remorse, and sleeplessness;
arrogance, hypocrisy, and passion; devotion, affection, and exhilaration;
gambling, idle gossip, and those relationships formed with women.
Dancing, instrumental music, singing, and whatever other attachments there may be—
all these qualities, O Brahmins, are proclaimed to be of the nature of *rajas*.
They are the mental conceptions regarding the states of beings— past, present, and future— upon this earth.

Constantly devoted to the threefold set of goals— namely dharma, artha, and kāma— they rejoice in the fulfillment of all desires, acting according to their will. These are known as the arvāk-srotas (downward-streaming), who are composed of *tejas* and enveloped by *rajas*.
In this world, they rejoice, being born again and again;
they strive for what pertains to the afterlife as well as for what pertains to this world. People of passionate nature (rājasa) strive for success that brings about rebirth.
They give, they receive, they mutter prayers, and they likewise offer oblations.
Thus have the qualities of passion (rajas) been described to you in their many forms,
as well as the proper conduct associated with those qualities.
"For the man who always knows these qualities is liberated from all qualities pertaining to *rajas*.
Brahmā said:
14,038.001a Hereafter I shall proclaim the third, supreme quality,
14,038.001c which is beneficial to all beings in the world, the irreproachable dharma of the virtuous: 14,038.002a joy, delight, exaltation, clarity, and indeed happiness.
Absence of wretchedness, absence of agitation, contentment, faithfulness, forgiveness, fortitude, non-violence, equanimity, truthfulness, straightforwardness,
freedom from anger, lack of envy, purity, dexterity, and prowess.

Knowledge is in vain, conduct is in vain, service is in vain, and effort is in vain for one who is thus engaged in dharma; such a person attains infinity in the hereafter. Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from expectations, and equal toward all things—such is he.
"Unassailed by desire"— this is the eternal dharma of the virtuous:
confidence, modesty, forbearance, renunciation, purity, vigilance,
benevolence, lack of delusion, compassion toward all beings, and freedom from backbiting.
Joy, contentment, wonder, humility, virtuous conduct,
rites of pacification, purity, auspicious intelligence, and liberation;
equanimity, the holy life, and renunciation in every respect.
Freedom from possessiveness, absence of desire for rewards, and the state of not selling the Dharma; giving in vain, sacrificing in vain, studying in vain, and observing vows in vain;
likewise, receiving gifts in vain, practicing Dharma in vain, and performing austerities in vain.
Whosoever in this world abide in such conduct, taking refuge in the True Being (sattva), those Brahmins established in the womb of Brahman are wise and possessors of right vision;
having abandoned all evils, they are indeed free from sorrow, ageless, and immortal.
Having reached heaven, those wise ones indeed exercise their power here and there; possessing mastery, self-control, and lightness of mind,
those great-souled ones manifest transformations like the gods who dwell in the third heaven.

14,038.013a These are known as the *ūrdhvasrotas* gods, the products of transformation (*vaikārika*). 14,038.013c Having reached heaven, they indeed transform by their own nature (*prakṛti*) here and there.
14,038.013e Whatever they desire, all that they enjoy and distribute.
"O best of the twice-born, this conduct characterized by *sattva* has thus been described to you.
By understanding this according to the prescribed rule, one obtains whatever one desires.
The qualities of *sattva* have been proclaimed in detail."
And as it has been said regarding the very nature of the qualities:
"The man who always understands these qualities enjoys the qualities; he is not consumed by them."
Brahmā said:
It is not possible here to describe the qualities individually in their entirety;
for rajas, sattva, and likewise tamas are seen to be inseparable.
They are attached to one another and depend upon one another for their livelihood;
they all rely on one another and likewise follow one another. As long as *sattva* exists, so long does *tamas* persist; of this there is no doubt.
As long as there is darkness (*tamas*), goodness (*sattva*), and passion (*rajas*), so long is it said to exist here.
Joining together, they carry out their course in association, moving in groups;
for these, whose nature is to function in combination, proceed by means of causes and non-causes.
Of those [qualities], which exist in mutual relation through their excesses and absences,
that [state] exists as both non-deficient and entirely distinct. Where darkness is predominant, it exists in the state of the animal realm.
In that [state], rajas should be known as slight, and sattva as even less than that. Where rajas is predominant, one should know that it belongs to the middle stream;
there, tamas is slight, and sattva is even less than that.
When sattva is predominant and follows the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas),
it should be known that rajas is there in small measure, and tamas is even smaller than that. Sattva, which is transformative (vaikārika), is the source and the illuminator of the sense organs.
For no other entity whatsoever is prescribed as superior to *sattva*.
Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle;
and people of *tamas*, joined with the lowest quality, go downward.
Darkness (tamas) is in the Śūdra, passion (rajas) in the Kṣatriya, and goodness (sattva) is supreme in the Brāhmaṇa;
thus do these three qualities revolve among the three castes.
Indeed, even from afar they are seen moving together in a company.
We have never heard of darkness, goodness, and passion existing in isolation from one another.
Upon seeing the rising sun, base thieves would be struck with fear;
travelers, afflicted by thirst and sharing in suffering, would be tormented.
The Sun is designated as *sattva*, while wicked thieves are like *tamas*. The distress of travelers is said to be the quality of *rajas*.
Manifestation is *sattva* in the Sun, and heat is the quality of *rajas*.
An eclipse occurring during its [the moon's] nodes should be known as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Thus, among all luminaries, the three qualities (guṇas) revolve;
they proceed by turns, in various ways, in their respective places.

In stationary beings, darkness (tamas) prevails in the state of animal existence; those characterized by passion (rājasas) undergo transformation, while the state of affection (sneha-bhāva) is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). Day is to be known as threefold, and night is likewise ordained as threefold.
Months, half-months, and years, as well as the seasons and the junctions;
gifts are given in three ways, sacrifice proceeds in three ways;
the worlds are threefold, the Vedas are threefold, the sciences are threefold, and the goals of existence are threefold.
The past, the present, and the future; dharma, artha, and kāma; as well as prāṇa, apāna, and udāna—these indeed are the three qualities.
Whatever exists here in this world, all that is contained within these very three.

The three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—proceed from the unmanifest and are indeed eternal; this is the ancient creation of the qualities. Tamas is the unmanifest, auspicious, eternal, unborn, and the primordial source.

Nature (prakṛti), modification (vikāra), dissolution (pralaya), the primary matter (pradhāna), and origin and destruction (prabhavāpyayau); that which is neither increased nor diminished, which is unshakable, immovable, and eternal;
both the existent and the non-existent—all that is known as the Unmanifest (avyakta) and possessed of the three qualities (triguṇa).
These 14,039.023 names should be known by men who contemplate the inner self (adhyātma).
He who knows all these unmanifest names and qualities according to their true nature, as well as all the exclusive destinies, [attains liberation].
Having cast off the body and knowing the truth of the distinctions,
he is liberated from all qualities and free from affliction.
Brahmā said:
From the Unmanifest, the Great Self (Mahān Ātmā), the great-minded one, was first produced.
He is said to be the origin of all qualities and the first creation.
The Great Self is called Mati, Viṣṇu, Viśva, and the powerful Śambhu.
Intellect (*buddhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), as well as manifestation (*khyāti*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and memory (*smṛti*)—
by these synonymous terms the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*) is conceptualized.
Knowing it, the learned Brahmin does not fall into delusion.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, he exists pervading all. This Person of great radiant splendor is seated within the heart of everyone.
14,040.005c Aṇimā, laghimā, prāpti, īśitva, and the imperishable light (jyotis).

14,040.006a Therein are the worlds of the wise, those who are devoted to renunciation, 14,040.006c the meditators, those constantly engaged in yoga, those true to their word, and those who have conquered their senses.
Whosoever are possessed of knowledge, free from greed, and have conquered their anger; those wise ones who are serene-minded, devoid of "mine-ness," and free from egoism—
all these, being liberated, indeed attain greatness.
He who knows the supreme, meritorious goal of the Great Self—
that wise man does not fall into delusion in any of the worlds. Viṣṇu himself becomes the self-existent Lord in the primordial creations.
For thus does a man know the Lord who dwells in the cave of the heart,
the ancient Person of universal form,
the golden one, the supreme goal of the wise.
That wise one stands having transcended the intellect.
Brahmā said:
That which was first produced as the Great One is called the ego (ahaṃkāra).
The second creation is said to be that which arose as "I" (ahaṃ).

It is known as the ego (ahaṃkāra), the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and the transformative (vaikārika). From the luminous (taijasa) aspect comes the element of consciousness; it is the progenitor of creatures and Prajāpati himself.
The god who is the source of the gods and the creator of the three worlds from the mind— because he conceives of all that as "I," he is called the Abhimānin (the Ego-maker).
For the sages of purified soul who are constantly devoted to the knowledge of the supreme self...
This is the eternal world for those who have perfected the sacrifices of Vedic study;
by means of egoism, he who takes up these qualities— the creator of beings, Bhūtādi— thus brings forth creation.
The Vaikārika [ego] sets all this in motion;
likewise, by its own radiance, it colors the world.
Brahmā said:
From ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), the five great elements (mahābhūta) are indeed produced:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
Beings become deluded regarding these five great elements.
When sound, touch, form, taste, and smell have ceased, and at the end of the destruction of the great elements, when the dissolution has arrived,
O wise ones, a great fear arises in all living beings.
Whatever being is born from this [source] dissolves back into it;
they dissolve in reverse order and are born in successive order.
Then, when all beings, both stationary and moving, have dissolved, [the world remains].
Then those wise ones, possessing mindfulness, are never dissolved.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are joined with action and cause; they are impermanent and designated as delusion.
Bound by the procreation of greed, they are indeed indistinguishable and possess nothing;
being mere aggregates of flesh and blood, they subsist upon one another. These are the "external selves"—miserable and wretched in their conduct.
Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna—
these five winds are fixed as the inner self;
together with speech, mind, and intellect, the world consists of these eight principles.
He whose skin, nose, ears, eyes, tongue, and speech are restrained,
whose mind is pure, and whose intellect is unerring—
he for whom these eight fires never burn his mind; ||| 14,042.010–011 ||| [he is truly liberated].
He goes to that auspicious Brahman from which nothing further exists. And those eleven sense organs that they speak of specifically,
O twice-born ones, I shall describe them as having been produced from the ego (ahaṃkāra).
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the two feet, the anus, the generative organ, the two hands, and speech shall be the tenth.
This is the collection of sense organs, and the mind is the eleventh.
One should first conquer this village; thereafter, Brahman shines forth.
They say there are five organs of perception and five organs of action;
they also say that, in reality, the five beginning with hearing are endowed with the intellect.
And those other [faculties] associated with action are likewise without distinction;
however, the mind should be known to exist in both cases, and the intellect (buddhi) shall be the twelfth.
Thus have these eleven sense-faculties been described by me in their proper order.
Having understood these things, the wise consider that [their purpose] has been accomplished.
Hereafter, I shall explain all the various faculties (*indriya*). There are three abodes for living beings; a fourth does not exist.
Land, water, and likewise space, as well as birth, which is fourfold—
namely, egg-born, sprout-born, sweat-born, and womb-born—
this is observed to be the fourfold birth of the multitude of living beings.
One should know that even immobile beings, as well as those that move through the air, those born from eggs, and all reptiles,
as well as sweat-born worms and similar creatures, are likewise [to be understood].

This second type of birth is said to be the most inferior. However, those beings which are born by piercing through the earth due to the passage of time, the best of the twice-born call them *udbhijja* (those born from sprouts).

O best of beings, know that those beings born from a womb— whether they have two feet or many feet, and even those moving horizontally— are likewise [of this nature]. Furthermore, the eternal source of Brahman should be understood here as being twofold.
"Austerity and meritorious action—this is the doctrine of the wise.
Action is to be understood as twofold: sacrifice and giving at the ritual;
for one who is born, sacred study is meritorious—such is the instruction of the elders."
O best of the twice-born, he who knows this according to the rule shall be liberated;
understand that he is indeed released from all sins. Space is the first element; it is called the ear with respect to the internal self.
Likewise, sound is the *adhibhūta*, and the quarters (*diś*) are the *adhidaivata* therein;
the second element is wind (*māruta*), which is renowned as the *adhyātma* of the skin,
while the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) is its *adhibhūta*, and lightning (*vidyut*) is the *adhidaivata* therein.

The third light, they say, is called the eye with respect to the internal self; its corresponding objective element (adhibhūta) is form, and the sun is the deity there (adhidaivata). The fourth is to be known as water, and the tongue is held to be the internal self.
Taste is to be known as the *adhibhūta*, and water is the *adhidaivata* therein;
taste is the *adhibhūta* here, and Soma is the *adhidaivata* therein. Earth is the fifth element, and the sense of smell is held to be the *adhyātma*.
Likewise, smell is the *adhibhūta* (the elemental correlate), and the wind is the *adhidaivata* (the presiding deity) therein.
This is recorded as the fourfold rule regarding the five elements.
Hereafter, I shall explain all the threefold nature of the sense organs.

"Regarding the feet, those Brahmins who perceive the truth say they are the *adhyātma* (the internal self). As for the *adhibhūta* (the objective realm), it is that which is to be traversed; Viṣṇu is the *adhidaivata* (the presiding deity) therein.
The downward movement and the *apāna* breath, as well as the anus, are considered the *adhyātma*."
The emission is the *adhibhūta*, Mitra is the *adhidaivata* therein. Procreation is the organ of generation (*upastha*) called the *adhyātma*;
likewise, semen is the *adhibhūta*, and Prajāpati is the deity (*daivata*).
"Those people who know the inner self say that the two hands are the *adhyātma*;
but actions are the *adhibhūta*, and Śakra is the *adhidaivata* therein.
Speech, preceded by the mind, is said here to be the *adhyātma* belonging to the Viśvedevas."
The object of speech (adhibhūta) is fire, and its presiding deity (adhidaivata) therein is Agni.
They say that the internal self (adhyātma) is the mind, which follows the five elements; the object of thought (adhibhūta) is that which is to be thought, and its presiding deity is the Moon.
Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is thus the internal [principle] that brings about all saṃsāra;

conceit (*abhimāna*) is the external element (*adhibhūta*), and Rudra is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*) therein. They say that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the internal [principle] which ranges over the six sense organs.
The elemental (adhibhūta) is to be known as Viṣṇu, and Brahmā is the presiding deity (adhidaivata) therein.

Thus has this rule concerning the self (adhyātma) been declared to you by me exactly as it is. For those who know dharma, O wise ones, knowledge of this has indeed been attained here by the intelligent.
The senses and the objects of the senses, as well as the five great elements—
one should contemplate all these together by means of the mind. When the mind has entirely ceased, the happiness of birth is no longer desired.
That is considered happiness by the wise, for those beings endowed with knowledge.
Hereafter, I shall explain the auspicious cessation toward all beings, whether by gentle or harsh means, which brings about a subtle state of being.
"Free from merit and demerit, unattached, solitary, and uninterrupted—
this, they say, is the conduct of a Brahmin, a singular state of happiness.
Like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, the wise man should withdraw his desires from every side."
The man who is free from passion and liberated in every respect is always happy. Having restrained desires within himself, with craving extinguished and composed,
being a friend to all beings and full of loving-kindness, he attains the state of Brahman.
Through the restraint of all the senses that seek their objects,
and by the sage’s renunciation of inhabited lands, the internal fire is kindled;
just as a fire fanned by fuel shines forth as a great light.

Likewise, through the cessation of the senses, the Great Self shines forth when one perceives all beings within the heart of the self with a tranquil mind; for this very mind is indeed established within the heart in this world.
Then, from its own source, it attains that which is subtler than the subtle, the unsurpassed.
Fire is form; water is the flow; wind is indeed touch;
earth is the bearer of mire, the terrible; and space is likewise hearing.
Those who know the inner self say that what is visible is indeed the sun;
it is possessed by passion and grief, enveloped by the five streams,
joined with the five elements, having nine gates, and two deities.

The body is defined as that which is subject to impurity, invisible, composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), consisting of the three elements (*tridhātuka*), delighting in attachment, and deluded. It is difficult to master in this world of living beings, for it is dependent upon the principle of *sattva*.
Indeed, this very wheel of time (kālacakra) revolves in this world;
it is a terrible, bottomless great ocean known as delusion (moha).
It emits and withdraws [all things], awakening the entire world together with the gods.

Through the restraint of the senses, he abandons desire, anger, fear, delusion, malice, and falsehood— those things which are so difficult to cast off. He for whom these three qualities and five elements have been conquered in this world [is liberated].
Then, in the sky, his supreme and infinite station is perceived—
[a river] with Kāma as its bank, boundless in its limits, bringing fear to the current of the mind,
possessing the five senses as its great banks, and having the speed of the mind as its vast waters.
Having crossed the river with its difficult-to-navigate depths, one should conquer both desire and anger.
Freed from all defects, one then beholds that which is supreme;
fixing the mind within the mind, one perceives the Self within the self.
The all-knowing one beholds the Self within himself among all beings;
transforming himself here and there into both one form and many forms,
he perceives fixed forms just as a hundred lamps [issue] from a single lamp.
He is indeed Viṣṇu and Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and Prajāpati;
for he is the Ordainer and the Disposer, the Lord whose face is turned in every direction. He shines as the heart of all beings, the Great Self.
The assemblies of brahmins, the gods and asuras,
the yakṣas, piśācas, ancestors, birds,
the hosts of rākṣasas, and all the hosts of bhūtas [gazed upon him].
And the great seers always offer praise.
Brahmā said:
"Among human beings, the Kṣatriya is the royal caste, characterized by the middle quality."
Among vehicles, the elephant is the foremost; among forest-dwellers, the lion;
among all animals, the sheep; and among those dwelling in holes, the rat.
Among cattle, the bull is the chief, and among women, the man.
The *nyagrodha*, the *jambū* tree, the *pippala*, the *śālmali*,
as well as the *śiṃśapā*, the *meṣaśṛṅga*, and the *kīcaka* bamboos—
these are the kings of trees in this world; of this there is no doubt.
Himavat, Pāriyātra, Sahya, Vindhya, and Trikūṭavat;
Śveta, Nīla, Bhāsa, and the mountain Kāṣṭhavat;
Śubhaskandha, Mahendra, and likewise the Mālyavat mountain.
These are the kings of the mountains, as well as the hosts of the Maruts;
Sūrya is the lord of the planets, and Candramas is the lord of the constellations;
Yama is the lord of the ancestors, and the ocean is the lord of the rivers.
Varuṇa is the king of the waters; Mitra is said to be the lord of living beings.
Arka is the sovereign of hot things; Indu is said to be the lord of the luminaries. Agni is eternally the lord of spirits; Bṛhaspati is the lord of the Brāhmaṇas.
Soma is the lord of herbs; Viṣṇu is the best among the powerful. Tvaṣṭṛ is the sovereign of forms; Śiva is the lord of animals.
Likewise, Yajña is the master of sacrificial fees, and the Ṛṣis are the masters of the Vedas.
The northern direction belongs to the wise; the majestic Soma is the king of the Brahmins;
Kubera is the lord of all Yakṣas, and Purandara is the lord of the gods. This is the creation beginning with the elements, and Prajāpati is the progenitor of all creatures.
Among all beings indeed, I am the great one consisting of Brahman;
there exists no being superior to me or even to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu is the king of kings over all, the great one consisting of Brahman.

We recognize him as the Lord; he is the all-pervading one, he is Prajāpati. For he is indeed the sovereign of humans, kiṃnaras, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as of all the gods, dānavas, and nāgas.
Among all those who follow Bhaga and the gods, she who is the great goddess Māheśvarī, known as Pārvatī, is the fair-eyed one;
know her to be the goddess Umā, the most excellent and auspicious among women.
The Apsarases are the wives of the Vasus, who are full of delight;
likewise, kings are devoted to dharma, and Brāhmaṇas are characterized by dharma.
Therefore, a king should strive here for the protection of the twice-born.
For those kings in whose realm the virtuous suffer,
they are deprived of all their own merits and, after death, go along the downward path. But those kings in whose realm the virtuous are protected—
"O best of the twice-born, know that these great-souled ones rejoice in this world and, after death, attain infinity itself. Hereafter,
I shall declare the definitive characteristics of dharma."
Dharma is characterized by non-violence, while adharma is characterized by violence;
the gods are characterized by light, and human beings are characterized by action;
space is characterized by sound, and wind is characterized by touch.
The characteristic form of the luminaries is light; water has the characteristic of taste; the earth is the support of all beings and has the characteristic of smell;
and speech, composed of vowels and consonants, has the characteristic of truth.

The characteristic of the mind (*manas*) is said to be thought (*cintā*), while intellect (*buddhi*) is so called because of its subsequent determination. One who contemplates objects with the mind determines them through the intellect; for intellect is characterized by determination—of this there is no doubt.

Great meditation has the unmanifest as its characteristic, while the mark of the virtuous is the unmanifest itself; yoga has activity as its characteristic, and knowledge has renunciation as its characteristic.
Therefore, having placed knowledge at the forefront, a wise person should renounce in this world.
The renunciant endowed with knowledge attains the supreme goal;
having transcended the pairs of opposites, he reaches that state which is beyond darkness, death, and old age.
Thus have I duly described to you that which is conjoined with the characteristics of dharma.
Henceforth, I shall correctly explain the apprehension of qualities.
That odor which belongs to the earth is indeed perceived here by the sense of smell;
and likewise, the air residing within the nose is ordained for the cognition of odor.
The essence of water is taste, which is constantly perceived by the tongue;
likewise, Soma resides in the tongue and is ordained for the cognition of taste. And the quality of light is form, which is perceived by the eye.
Likewise, the sun, residing in the eye, is ordained for the cognition of form; and the wind, belonging to the realm of air, is perceived by the skin,
and that wind, residing in the skin, is ordained for the cognition of touch.

Sound is the quality of space, and it is perceived by the ear; all the quarters of space are said to reside in the ear for the cognition of sound. Thought is the quality of the mind, and it is perceived by means of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The element of consciousness (cetana) residing in the heart is established as the knowledge of the mind (manas).
Likewise, the intellect (buddhi) functions through determination (adhyavasāya), and the Great One (mahat) through meditation (dhyāna).
Having reached certainty, there is constant apprehension of the unmanifest (avyakta); of this there is no doubt.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is eternal, devoid of attributes, and does not grasp signs;

therefore, the Knower of the Field is signless and characterized solely by knowledge. The Unmanifest (avyakta) is designated as the Field (kṣetra), the source and place of dissolution of the qualities (guṇas).
I always see, I discern, and I hear that which is dissolved [in the field];
the Puruṣa knows that, and therefore he is called the Kṣetrajña (Knower of the Field).
Likewise, the Kṣetrajña perceives the entire operation of the Guṇas.

From beginning to middle to end, the insentient being that is being created does not know itself as it is created again and again; no one indeed knows the Truth, but the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) alone finds it.

That which is beyond the qualities (guṇas) and that which has become the qualities— the Great (mahat) which is further beyond— that knower of reality (tattvavid), having here abandoned both the qualities and the [evolvent] principle (tattva),
and with his defects (doṣas) exhausted, enters the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) after leaving behind the qualities.
Free from dualities, free from salutation, and likewise free from the utterance of *svadhā*,
he is immovable, homeless, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Supreme, and the All-pervading Lord.
Brahmā said:

I shall explain in accordance with reality everything regarding the beginning, middle, and end, as well as the very means of apprehension, together with their names and characteristics. First comes the day, then the night; the months are traditionally said to begin with the bright fortnight (śukla).
The constellations beginning with Śraviṣṭhā, the seasons beginning with Śiśira,
the earth as the source of odors, and the waters as the source of tastes;
light as the source of forms, and wind is said to be the source of touch.
Sound has space as its origin; this is the quality produced by the elements. Hereafter, I shall declare the supreme origin of the elements:
the sun is held to be the origin of lights, and fire is the origin of the elements.
The Sāvitrī is the foremost of all branches of knowledge; Prajāpati is the foremost of the gods;
the syllable Om is the foremost of all Vedas; and the vital breath is the foremost of all speech. Whatever is established in this world is said to be derived from the Sāvitrī.
The Gāyatrī is said to be the first among meters; the goat, the first among animals;
cows, the first among quadrupeds; the twice-born, the first among humans;
the hawk, the first among birds; and the oblation, the highest among sacrifices.
O best of the twice-born, among all those that crawl, the serpent is the eldest;
and among all the ages (*yugas*), the Kṛta is the first—of this there is no doubt. Likewise, gold is the foremost of all gems, and barley is the foremost of herbs.
Among all things that are to be chewed and eaten, food is said to be supreme;
among all liquids and drinks, water is the best. And among all beings, whether stationary or otherwise, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The field of Brahmā is eternally meritorious; the Plakṣa tree is remembered as its first-born.
Among all the Prajāpatis, I am the foremost—of this there is no doubt. Viṣṇu, whose nature is inconceivable, is remembered as my very self, the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū).
Among all mountains, Mahāmeru is remembered as the first-born;
likewise, among the cardinal and intermediate directions, the upward direction was born first.
Similarly, the triple-pathed Gaṅgā is remembered as the first-born of rivers.
Likewise, among all lakes and wells, the ocean is the foremost;
he is the sovereign lord and master of all gods, dānavas, bhūtas, piśācas, uragas, rakṣasas, humans, kiṃnaras, and yakṣas.

Viṣṇu, the great one composed of Brahman, is the origin of the entire universe; there exists nothing higher than him in the three worlds. And among all the stages of life (āśramas), the householder’s stage is the foremost; of this there is no doubt.
The Unmanifest is the beginning of the worlds, and it is also the end of everything. Days end in sunset, and the night ends in sunrise.
Suffering always ends in happiness, and happiness always ends in suffering.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall. Unions end in separation, for life ends in death.
Everything created ends in destruction; for one who is born, death is certain.

For in this world, everything—whether stationary or moving—is indeed impermanent. Sacrifices, gifts, austerity, study, vows, and observances—all these end in destruction; yet there is no end to knowledge.
"Therefore, one whose self is serene and composed through pure knowledge,
being free from 'mine-ness' and free from egoism, is released from all evils.
Brahmā said:
It has the essence of intellect as its trunk, the mind as its pillar, and the collection of sense organs as its binding;
it has the great elements as its supporting beams and blinking as its encircling frame;
it is pervaded by old age and sorrow, and is the locus for the movement of diseases and calamities.
This world, which investigates space and time, resounds with the sounds of toil and exertion;
it revolves through day and night, is encircled by cold and heat,
is afflicted by the extremes of pleasure and pain, and is pinned down by hunger and thirst.
Marked by the shifting of shadow and sunlight, agitated by the closing and opening of eyes,
crowded with people in a terrible delusion, this present world-process is insentient, reckoned by months and half-months, and full of hardship.
It has the accumulation of darkness as its mud and the impulse of passion as its current;
it is radiant with the ornaments of living beings and a mandala consisting of a multitude of virtues;
it has the vocal body as its navel and revolves through the mass of sorrows.
Joined with action and its causes, it is an extensive expansion of passion;
it is reckoned as greed and longing, arising from knowledge that is [otherwise] secluded;
it is surrounded by fear and delusion, and it produces the confusion of living beings.

The wheel of time (kālacakra) revolves—endowed with joy and delight, yet grasping desire and anger; beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa); unattached, originating from the Unmanifest (avyaya), swift as thought, and unwearied.
This Kālacakra, joined with the pairs of opposites and devoid of consciousness, emits and withdraws the world together with the gods,
and it truly brings about the progression and cessation of the Kālacakra.
The man who knows this eternally is not deluded among living beings;
liberated from all afflictions and transcending all dualities, that sage,
freed from all sins, attains the supreme goal.
The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
these four stages of life (āśramas) are proclaimed to all have their root in the householder stage.
Whatever tradition (āgama) has been celebrated here in this world [is based upon it].

To reach the end of that [life] is better; this is the eternal fame. Having been previously consecrated by the sacraments and having duly observed his vows, he, a knower of the Vedas, should perform the return ceremony upon being born into a family distinguished by its virtues.
Devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, following the conduct of the virtuous, and having conquered his senses,
he should indeed perform the five great sacrifices with faith. Eating only what remains after serving the deities and guests, he should be intent upon the duties prescribed by the Vedas.
Engaged in sacrifice and the giving of gifts according to his ability and according to rule,
the sage is not restless with his hands or feet, nor restless with his eyes, nor restless with his speech or limbs; such is the sphere of conduct for the disciplined man.

He should always wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), be dressed in white garments, and be pure in his vows. Self-restrained through self-control and charity, he should always associate with the disciplined. Having conquered his genitals and his belly, he should be friendly toward all and intent upon the conduct of the disciplined.
One should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water. One should constantly and untiringly maintain three [vessels]:
one for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), and one for washing the feet.

One [Veda] is for the purpose of performing purificatory rites; thus, having studied this triad, one should likewise engage in teaching, as well as sacrificing for oneself and officiating at sacrifices for others,
giving gifts, and receiving them— one should practice this sixfold mode of livelihood.
There are three occupations here which constitute the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from those who are pure. As for the other three occupations that remain, they are as follows:
Giving, study, and sacrifice—these are indeed the practices joined with dharma.
One who knows dharma should apply vigilance to these three activities.
A sage is self-controlled, friendly, endowed with patience, and equal toward all beings.
A Brahmin, being pure and performing all this according to his ability,
thus disciplined and firm in his vows, shall conquer heaven as a householder.
Brahmā said:
Thus, by this aforementioned path and according to the prescribed rule, he has studied to the best of his ability; likewise, remaining a celibate student (*brahmacārin*),
the wise sage is devoted to his own duty and restrains all his senses.
Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of his guru, pure and dedicated to truth and righteousness,
he should eat food only when permitted by his guru, never disparaging it; he may subsist on sacrificial offerings or alms, and should be disciplined in his standing, sitting, and movements.
Offering oblations into the fire twice a day, having become pure and composed,
he should always carry a staff made of *bilva* or *palāśa* wood; likewise,
he may wear a garment of linen, cotton, or even the skin of a deer.

All the clothing of a twice-born man should be dyed saffron-red; his girdle should be made of muñja grass, he should wear matted hair, and likewise remain constantly purified by water. He should wear the sacred thread, be devoted to Vedic study, and never neglect his fixed vows.

Likewise, always performing the libation to the deities with pure water, the celibate student who acts with self-restraint and devotion is highly praised. Thus disciplined, with vital energy drawn upward and mind composed, he shall conquer heaven.

Relying upon the supreme state, he does not transmigrate through births; though conditioned by all formative forces (*saṃskāra*), he likewise practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Having gone forth from the village into the forest, the sage should dwell as one who has renounced the world.
Clad in skins or bark garments, he should personally perform his ablutions every morning;
dwelling constantly in the forest, he should never enter a village again. Honoring guests at the proper time, he should also provide them with shelter.
Subsisting on fruits, leaves, roots, and śyāmāka grain, he should,
remaining vigilant, consume everything grown in the wild— from water and air down to grass— in the prescribed sequence according to his initiation.
One should honor a guest who has arrived with offerings of roots and fruits;
whatever food one may have, one should always give alms from it without weariness.
And, having first honored the deities and guests, one should always eat while restraining one's speech.
With a mind free from agitation, eating sparingly, and taking refuge in the deities; self-controlled, friendly, endowed with forbearance, and maintaining his hair and beard;
offering oblations, devoted to the study of sacred texts, and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Always renouncing the body, skillful, ever-dwelling in the forest, and composed— thus disciplined and having conquered his senses, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) shall conquer heaven.
Whether he be a householder, a student (brahmacārī), or again a forest-dweller, [he attains the same].
14,046.017c He who desires to abide in liberation should resort to the highest mode of life.

14,046.018a Having granted fearlessness to all beings, he should practice actionlessness (naiṣkarmya). 14,046.018c Being intent on the welfare of all beings, friendly, and with all senses restrained, he is a sage (muni).
One should always enjoy with contentment and without longing whatever food comes to one unasked for, not prepared in anticipation,
and obtained by chance; one should eat only as much as is necessary for sustenance, solely for the maintenance of life.
One should eat what is obtained through dharma and should not follow the dictates of desire;
one should by no means accept anything other than food and clothing. One should accept only as much as is required for sustenance, and not otherwise.
One should never accept gifts from others, nor should one ever give them;
rather, the wise man, out of compassion for living beings, should always share his own wealth.
He should not take the property of others, nor should he accept anything that has not been offered.

Having enjoyed any object whatsoever, one should certainly not desire it again. One who has duties to perform here should take earth, water, stones, leaves, flowers, and fruits as they are found, without making them his own.
He should not live by the craft of an artisan, nor should he desire a second meal;
he should be neither a hater nor a teacher, remaining free from worldly attachments.
He should eat food purified by faith and avoid omens.
Living in a state of simplicity and unattached to all beings, having established a lack of conscious connection with them,
he should wander for alms when the fire has gone out and the people have already eaten;
once the clatter of the eating bowls has ceased, the knower of liberation should seek alms.
He should not rejoice upon gaining [alms], nor become dejected when failing to gain them.
He should not beg for excessive alms, but seek only what is necessary for the maintenance of life.
Eating in moderation and awaiting the proper time, he should wander for alms with a concentrated mind.
One should not desire common gain, nor should one enjoy it when highly honored;
for a mendicant should feel revulsion toward gain obtained through being highly honored.
[He should avoid] things that are fermented, sour, bitter, astringent, and pungent.

While eating, one should not relish savory or sweet flavors; one should eat only as much as is necessary for sustenance, solely for the maintenance of life. One who knows liberation should seek a livelihood without causing obstruction to other beings.
While begging for alms, he should never beg from anyone else; he should not proclaim the Dharma to others, but should wander free from passion in solitude—
in an empty house, a forest, at the foot of a tree, or likewise by a river.
For the sake of shelter, he may resort to a mountain or a cave;
during the summer he should stay one night in a village, or during the rainy season he may dwell in one place.
His path is indicated by the sun, and he should traverse the earth like an insect.
Out of compassion for all living beings, he should wander the earth while keeping this in view;
he should not make accumulations of goods and should avoid dwelling in affectionate attachment.
One who knows liberation should always perform his necessary duties with pure water.
A person should always touch water that has been drawn out;
non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness, and straightforwardness,
as well as freedom from anger, lack of envy, self-restraint, and constant avoidance of backbiting.
One should be disciplined in these eight observances with the senses restrained;
one should always practice a conduct that is sinless, free from deceit, and straightforward. One should avoid actions associated with worldly desires and those involving violence.

One should neither perform nor cause to be performed the dharma of gathering the world; having transcended all states of being, one should wander as one who is light. Being equal toward all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
One should not cause anyone else to tremble with fear, nor should one tremble before anyone;
being trustworthy toward all beings, such a person is said to be foremost among those who know liberation. One should not dwell on the future, nor should one brood over the past.
One who is concentrated and awaits the proper time should remain indifferent toward what is occurring;
one should never defile anything by means of the eye, the mind, or speech,
nor should one perform any wicked act, whether openly or in secret.
Having withdrawn the senses from all sides, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, one whose senses,
mind, and intellect are stilled should gaze with the senses extinguished—
free from dualities, free from salutations, and even free from the utterance of *svāhā*.
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, and likewise free from the pursuit of acquisition and preservation; free from desire toward all beings, free from attachment, and without support;
all-knowing and liberated from everything—he is released, of this there is no doubt.
Without hands, feet, or back; without head or belly; devoid of qualities and actions; absolute, stainless, and stable;
and indeed without smell, taste, touch, form, or sound.

Those who perceive the Self—which is without skin, bone, or marrow, and even without flesh; which is free from anxiety, imperishable, eternal, and ever-present within the heart; and which dwells in all beings—they are not dead.
There, neither the intellect, nor the senses, nor the deities prevail;
neither the Vedas, nor sacrifices, nor the worlds, nor austerity, nor prowess have any effect there,
where the attainment of the wise is said to be beyond the grasp of signs.
Therefore, one who knows the Dharma, who observes the vows of Dharma,
and who relies on the secret Dharma, being wise, should conduct himself in an unrecognizable manner.
Without being deluded, he should act with the appearance of a fool, practicing the Dharma without causing it to be defiled.
One should practice dharma in such a manner that others always hold one in contempt, thereby not defiling the path of the virtuous;
for he who is thus perfected in conduct is called the best of sages.
The senses and the objects of the senses, the five great elements,
the mind, the intellect, as well as the self, the unmanifest, and likewise the Puruṣa—
having enumerated all this and having completely renounced it, one becomes stainless.

Then, liberated from all bonds, he attains heaven. Having thus reckoned this at the time of his end, the knower of reality, resorting to solitude, should meditate; then, being without support, he is released.
Freed from all attachments like the wind moving through space, with his store of karma exhausted and free from fear, he attains the supreme state. Brahmā said:
The elders who perceive with certainty say that renunciation is austerity;
the Brahmins established in the source of Brahman know that supreme Brahman is knowledge. The supreme Brahman, which is based upon Vedic wisdom, is not far away.
Free from duality, devoid of qualities, eternal, inconceivable, secret, and supreme—
that state the wise perceive through knowledge and austerity;
they are cleansed of darkness, purified, having transcended passion, and stainless.

Those seekers of the supreme who are people knowing Brahman and constantly devoted to renunciation travel the path of security through austerity. They say that austerity is a lamp and right conduct is the accomplisher of dharma.

We know that knowledge alone is supreme, and renunciation is the highest austerity. But he who knows, through the ascertainment of reality, the unobstructed knowledge of the Self abiding in all beings— he is considered to have attained the state of omnipresence.
The wise person who perceives both co-dwelling and separation, as well as unity and diversity, is liberated from suffering. He who desires nothing at all and holds nothing in contempt—
Remaining even in this very world, he is fit for becoming Brahman—
knowing the truth of the qualities of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), knowing the ordainment of all beings,
free from possessiveness, and free from egoism; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Free from duality, free from salutation, and likewise free from the utterance of *svadhā*,
one attains through tranquility alone that which is devoid of qualities, eternal, and non-dual.
Having abandoned all action consisting of the qualities, whether auspicious or inauspicious, the living being [reaches this state].
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Born from the seed of the Unmanifest, the Great Tree consists of the intellect as its trunk, has the great ego as its branches, and the various senses as its hollows.
The great element Viśākha, possessing special branches and sub-branches,
ever-leaved and ever-flowering, yielding fruits both auspicious and inauspicious,
the livelihood of all beings, is the eternal Brahma-tree.
Having cut through and split apart this [bondage] with the supreme sword of knowledge, and having abandoned immortality to attain [liberation], one should indeed cast off both death and birth—
the wise man, by means of the sword of the knowledge of reality.

Having abandoned the snares of attachment that give rise to death, birth, and old age, one who is free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism is liberated; of this there is no doubt. These two birds are eternal companions, yet they are devoid of consciousness.
But beyond these two is that which is traditionally known as the conscious one (cetana).
It is insentient (acetana) and joined with an aggregate of material elements (sattva-saṃghāta);
yet, through its connection with the principle of being (sattva), the inner self (antarātman) perceives.
14,047.016c That Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), whose intellect perceives the aggregate of the constituents (sattva-saṃghāta),
transcends the qualities (guṇas) and is liberated from the noose of death.
14,048.001 Brahmā said:
Some consider it a tree composed of Brahman; some, a great [entity] composed of Brahman;
some, the unmanifest Puruṣa; and some, the supreme, stainless [state].
All of these, they believe, originate from and dissolve into the unmanifest.
If one should become equanimous at the time of death for even the duration of a single breath,
having attained the Self, he is fit for immortality. Even if it be for only the duration of a blink of an eye, having restrained the self within the Self—
Through self-serenity, he attains the imperishable state reached by the wise. Then, having repeatedly restrained his vital breaths through breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
he proceeds beyond that for ten, twelve, or even twenty-four [breaths].
Thus, one whose self is serene obtains whatever he desires from the past;
from the unmanifest, when *sattva* is predominant, one is fit for immortality. Those who know that truth praise nothing here as superior to *sattva*.
"O twice-born ones, we know the Puruṣa who abides in the *sattva* through inference; it is not possible to understand that Puruṣa otherwise.
[His qualities are] forbearance, fortitude, non-violence, equanimity, truthfulness, and straightforwardness."

Knowledge, renunciation, and then relinquishment—this is held to be the mode of conduct characterized by *sattva*. By this very inference, the wise consider that *sattva* and the *puruṣa* are one; there is no doubt in this matter.
Some wise men who are well-established in knowledge say:
"The identity of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the principle of being (*sattva*) is not tenable;
therefore, that they are eternally distinct has not been properly considered."
Separateness and co-nascence should be understood according to reality;
likewise, unity and diversity are accepted as the method of the wise. Indeed, both unity and separateness are observed in the case of the gnat and the udumbara fruit.
"Just as a fish might be in water, such is the union of these two;
their connection is like that of drops of water upon a leaf of the *kokanada* lotus.
Thus spoke the Guru.
When the Grandfather of the World had spoken thus,
those best of the twice-born sages, having fallen once more into doubt, questioned him again.
The ṛṣis said:
"What among the duties is considered here to be most worthy of performance? We perceive the various courses of dharma as if they were contradictory:
some say it exists after the body [has perished], while others say this is not so."
Some regard everything as doubtful, while others regard it as free from doubt;
some say that what is impermanent is permanent, and others say that what exists does not exist.
Some say that what is of a single form is twofold, and others say it is a mixture.

"14,048.016e Some maintain that there is one, others that they are distinct, and still others that they are many; 14,048.017a thus do the wise Brāhmaṇas, who perceive the true nature of reality, believe. 14,048.017c Others wear matted hair and deerskins, while some are shaven-headed and unrestrained."
Some desire non-bathing, while others likewise desire bathing; some desire food, and some are devoted to fasting.
Some praise action, while others praise tranquility.
Some [discuss] both place and time, while others say, "This does not exist.
Some praise liberation, some various kinds of enjoyments;
some desire wealth, and others likewise poverty.
Some say that the means for worship exists, while others say it does not; some are devoted to non-violence, while some are intent on violence;
some say [the goal is attained] through merit and fame, while others say this is not so.
Some others are devoted to true contemplation, while some remain in a state of doubt;
some are established in suffering, others in pleasure, and still others in meditation. Some wise ones are established in sacrifice, and others in giving.
Some praise everything, while others say that not everything [should be praised].

Some praise austerity (*tapas*), while other people praise the study of sacred texts (*svādhyāya*). Some praise knowledge and renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), while those who contemplate the elements praise inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
When the Dharma has been thus set forth, O best of gods, people run in many directions; being utterly bewildered, we do not arrive at a certainty.
People set out thinking, "This is the highest good," or "That is the highest good."
"For whoever is devoted to whatever dharma always honors that very thing.
In this matter, our wisdom has been frustrated and our minds have become distracted. O best of beings, we wish to know this: what is the highest good?"
"Beyond this, you ought to speak of that which is secret:
by what cause does the connection between the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña* exist?
Thus addressed by those brahmins, the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, [replied].
To them, the wise and righteous-souled one explained everything exactly as it is.
Brahmā said:
"Ah, O best of beings, I shall indeed declare to you that which you ask of me."

Listen to what has been said by the Guru upon approaching his disciple; having heard all of this here, let it be properly understood. Non-violence toward all living beings is considered the highest duty.
This state is undisturbed, supreme, and characterized by dharma.
The elders who perceive certainty declare that knowledge is the highest good;
therefore, through pure knowledge, one is liberated from all sins.
Those in the world who are intent on violence, those who follow the conduct of nihilists,
and those possessed by greed and delusion— these indeed go to hell.
But those who, unwearied, perform actions joined with desire for rewards...
They rejoice in this world, being born again and again— those wise ones who, full of faith, perform their duties,
who are united with yoga that is not for worldly gain, and who are steadfast seers of the truth.

Henceforth I shall declare how the union and the separation of the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña* occur; listen to that, O best of beings. This relationship is said here to be that between the object and the subject.
The Puruṣa is eternally the subject, and Sattva is traditionally held to be the object.
This has been explained by the previous analogy, just like the gnat and the udumbara fruit;
the insentient Sattva does not know that it is being enjoyed.
But he who truly understands him who eats and that which is eaten—

[they say] the *sattva* (being) is impermanent, joined with dualities, and consists of the qualities (*guṇas*). The Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), however, is free from dualities, partless, eternal, and consists of that which is beyond the qualities.

When he is thus perceived as equal everywhere, having attained right consciousness, the wise man always experiences the quality of *sattva* like a lotus leaf in water; though intertwined with all the qualities (*guṇas*), he is not defiled by them.
Just as a flickering drop of water resting upon a lotus leaf is unattached,
even so the person (puruṣa) is undoubtedly unattached. It is certain that the essence (sattva) of the person consists of nothing more than material substance.
Just as there is substance and an agent, so too is there a conjunction between these two.
Just as someone, taking a lamp, travels through the darkness,
so do those seeking the supreme proceed by means of the lamp of *sattva*.

As long as there are the qualities of its constituent substance, so long does the lamp shine; when the qualities of its substance are exhausted, the light goes to its disappearance. In this same way, while the quality of *sattva* is manifest, the *puruṣa* is held to be unmanifest.
O Brahmins, understand this; indeed, I shall speak further to you:
even with a thousand [teachings], one of dull intellect does not attain growth.
That state has been reached, having gone to which one no longer grieves.

O fortunate one, you too, through this Brahman-splendor as it has been described, are clearly possessed of the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*); thus, being wise, you shall prosper in happiness. Furthermore, even by means of a fourth part [of that splendor], the wise man prospers in happiness.
In this way, the accomplishment of Dharma should be understood through skillful means;
for the wise person who knows these means attains ultimate happiness. It is like a man setting out on a journey somewhere without provisions for the road.
With great effort one proceeds, yet one may perish along the way;
likewise, it should be understood that regarding actions, the fruit may or may not come to pass.
For a person, this is the manifestation of the auspicious and inauspicious results within oneself that lead to one's own ultimate welfare.
Just as one might suddenly set out on foot upon a long journey never seen before, being devoid of the vision of reality; yet,
by means of a swift-moving chariot, traverse that very same path here.
Just as one might travel by means of a horse-drawn vehicle, such is the path of the wise.
Having ascended a high mountain, one should not look down upon those on the ground;
from his chariot, he should observe the charioteer struggling and unconscious.
As long as there is a path for a chariot, he travels by chariot;
when the path for a chariot is exhausted, the wise man abandons the chariot and proceeds.
In this way does the intelligent one proceed, knowing the method for the application of reality.
Having understood this, the one of great intelligence [should proceed] from one stage to the next;
for just as one who plunges into the terrible great ocean without a boat would undoubtedly meet his death by his own arms alone through delusion.
Just as a wise man who knows how to navigate might board a boat and,
remaining untiring, plunge into the water and surely cross over quickly;
having crossed, he would leave the boat behind and go to the further shore free from possessiveness.

14,049.028 Just as it was explained by the previous analogy regarding the chariot-rider and the foot-soldier, so too [the fool], having fallen into delusion through affection like a boatman on a ship, being overcome by the sense of "mine," revolves right there. 14,049.029 Just as a boatman on a ship [is deluded], so he, overcome by the notion of "mine," revolves in that very place.
Just as it is not possible to mount a boat and move about on dry land,
so too, having mounted a chariot, one's movement is not ordained upon the waters. In this way, various actions performed are distinct according to their respective domains.
Just as an action is performed in the world, so does its result arise. That which possesses neither smell nor taste, nor form, touch, or sound—
what the sages perceive through their intellect, they declare to be Pradhāna.
The mind considers the sense of taste, the touch of form, and sound to be like itself; and that which is beyond even that is perceived by the intellect (*buddhi*).
In this regard, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the primary source, and the Great One (*mahat*) is the quality (*guṇa*) of the unmanifest.

The quality of Mahat, which is the primary principle (pradhāna), is indeed ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra). And the quality of that which has ego-consciousness as its primary principle is the production of the gross elements (mahābhūta).
For it is traditionally held that the objects of the elements are their qualities, existing in their distinctness.
Just as the nature of the seed is unmanifest, so too is its nature to produce;
we have heard that the Great Self (Mahat) possesses the nature of the seed and is also production. Furthermore, the ego (ahaṃkāra) possesses the nature of the seed and is repeatedly production.

The five great elements (mahābhūta) indeed possess the nature of producing seeds; they are said to have the quality of being seeds, yet they do not themselves perform the act of production. Know that the specific qualities (viśeṣa) of those five elements are their distinguishing characteristics.
In that regard, space is said to have one quality, wind two qualities, light three qualities, and water four qualities;
earth, teeming with moving and stationary beings, is to be known as having five qualities.
The goddess who creates all beings is the revealer of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these five qualities of the earth should be known, O best of the twice-born.
Earth always possesses fragrance, and fragrance is said to be of many kinds.
