I shall describe in detail the many qualities of that fragrance:
it is pleasant and unpleasant, sweet, sour, and likewise pungent.
Pervasive, compact, oily, dry, and clear—
thus the odor of earth is known to be of ten kinds.
Sound, touch, form, and taste are recorded as the qualities of water.
I shall now describe the knowledge of taste; taste is traditionally held to be manifold:
sweet, sour, pungent, bitter, astringent, and likewise salty.
Thus, taste, which consists of water, is known to have a sixfold extension.
Sound, touch, and likewise form—light is said to possess these three qualities. Form is the specific quality of light, and form is remembered as being manifold:
white, black, red, blue, yellow, and likewise orange.
Short, long, thick, square, minute, and round—
thus the form of fire is said to have twelve varieties;
it should be constantly understood by Brahmins who know the Dharma and speak the truth.
Sound and touch are to be known; wind is said to possess two qualities. Furthermore, touch is the specific quality of wind, and touch is remembered as being of many kinds:
hot, cold, pleasant, painful, oily, and even clear.
Hard, sticky, smooth, slippery, harsh, and soft—
thus is the quality of wind said to be twelvefold in its extent by the Brahmins who are perfected, knowers of dharma, and seers of reality, according to the prescribed rule.
Therein, space possesses a single quality, which is traditionally known as sound alone.
I shall describe in detail the many qualities of that sound:
Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and likewise Pañcama.
Beyond this, however, the *niṣāda* and the *dhaivata* are to be known;
sound, moreover, may be desired or undesired, compact or differentiated.
Thus, sound originating from space (*ākāśa*) should be understood as being of many kinds.

Space is the highest element; beyond that is the ego (ahaṃkāra). Beyond the ego is the intellect (buddhi); beyond the intellect is the Self (ātman). Beyond that is the Unmanifest (avyakta); beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa.
He who knows the higher and the lower among beings, having attained whom one enjoys infinity—
he whose self has become the self of all beings goes to the imperishable Self.
Brahmā said:
Just as the mind is the lord of these five elements in both their restraint and their release,
so too is the mind alone the eternal presiding principle over the great elements and the self of the beings.
Intellect proclaims sovereignty; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is said to be all things. The mind yokes the senses, just as a charioteer yokes good horses;
the Knower of the Field always yokes the senses, the mind, and the intellect.

Mounted upon that chariot, which is joined with the great elements and equipped with the restraint of the intellect, that self of beings (bhūtātman) courses everywhere; it is joined with the collection of the senses and has the mind as its charioteer.

The great chariot, composed of Brahman, has the intellect as its constant restrainer. The wise man who thus always knows this chariot composed of Brahman— that steadfast one does not fall into delusion in any of the worlds.
From the unmanifest (avyakta) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa), teeming with mobile and immobile beings,
illuminated by the radiance of the moon and sun, adorned with the circles of planets and constellations,
and decorated on all sides by networks of rivers and mountains.
Constantly adorned with various kinds of waters,
it is the livelihood of all beings and the refuge of all who possess breath. This is the eternal forest of Brahman, in which the knower of the field (kṣetravid) moves.

Whatever beings there are in this world, whether stationary or moving, they dissolve first; afterwards, the qualities produced by the elements [dissolve]. From the qualities come the five elements; such is the aggregate of beings.
Gods, humans, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas—
all these are created by their own inherent nature, not from actions nor from a cause.
These Brahmins, the creators of the universe, are indeed born again and again.

Produced from them, they dissolve back into those very five great elements at the proper time, just as waves dissolve into the ocean. From the elements that create the universe, he goes to the great elements.
Released even from the five elements, one shall go to Prajāpati.
The Lord Prajāpati created all this through austerity alone;
likewise, the ṛṣis attained the Vedas through austerity.
Furthermore, by the gradual practice of austerity, those who subsist on fruits and roots,
being composed in mind, behold the three worlds here through their ascetic power;
they [attain] medicinal herbs, antidotes, and all various branches of knowledge in every respect.
14,050.016c By austerity alone they attain success, for austerity is the root of all accomplishment.

14,050.017a Whatever is difficult to obtain, difficult to learn, difficult to overcome, or difficult to follow— 14,050.017c all that is to be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable.
The drinker of spirits, the slayer of a Brahmin, the thief, the destroyer of an embryo, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
by means of well-performed austerity alone, they are liberated from that sin.
Humans, ancestors, gods, cattle, beasts, and birds [are likewise purified].
Whatever other beings there are, whether mobile or immobile,
they always attain perfection through asceticism by being constantly devoted to it.
Likewise, through asceticism, the highly fortunate gods have gone to heaven.
Those who, unwearied, perform actions joined with desire for rewards,
yet are possessed by egoism, [remain] in the presence of Prajāpati;
whereas those who are free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism through pure meditative yoga [attain liberation].
14,050.022c Those high-souled ones attain the great and supreme world, 14,050.023a having reached it through the yoga of meditation, with minds ever serene;
14,050.023c by virtue of self-mastery, they enter the unmanifest state of accumulated bliss.
Having attained the yoga of meditation, free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism,
they enter here the unmanifest, the great, and supreme world. Having arisen from the unmanifest itself, he who knows the proper time has departed once again.
Freed from both *tamas* and *rajas*, and abiding solely in *sattva*, he is liberated from all sins; being partless (*niṣkala*), he abandons everything.
One should know him as the *kṣetrajña*; he who knows him is a knower of the Veda.
Having approached the mind through the mind, the sage should sit restrained; becoming one whose mind is the mind itself, this is the eternal secret.
That which begins with the unmanifest and ends with the specific elements is known as characterized by ignorance.
14,050.028c Understand, therefore, how this characteristic is defined by the qualities (guṇas). 14,050.029a Death consists of two syllables, while the eternal Brahman consists of three syllables.
14,050.029c "It is mine" is death; "it is not mine" is the eternal.
Some men of very dull intellect praise action;
but those who are Buddhas, the Great-Souled Ones, do not praise action.
By action a living being is born, embodied and composed of sixteen constituents.
Ignorance creates the person who is ungraspable and consumes the immortal.
Therefore, those who see the further shore are without attachment to ritual acts;
this person is known to consist of knowledge, not of action.
He who knows this immortal, eternal, ungraspable, perpetually imperishable,
self-controlled, and unattached [Self] shall not die. He who knows this unprecedented, immortal, eternal, and undiscriminating [Self]— [he too shall not die].
14,050.033c He who finds this Self, which is ungraspable and the consumer of immortality,
14,050.033e becomes ungraspable and immortal— he who is steadfast through these means.
14,050.034a Having cast aside all volitions and having restrained the self within the Self, [he attains it].
He knows that auspicious Brahman from which nothing further exists; through the very clarity of his being,
he attains serenity,
for the characteristic of serenity is like the experience of a dream.

This is the destination of those who are liberated and firmly established in knowledge; they perceive all activities as arising from transformation. This is the destination of the unattached; this is the eternal Dharma.

This is the attainment of those possessed of knowledge; this is their irreproachable conduct. All of that is achieved through non-attachment alone, by means of the destruction of desire and hope. [One acts] with equanimity toward all beings, free from longing and devoid of expectations.
This state can be attained everywhere by one who perceives with equanimity.
O best of brahmin-sages, I have thus related all this to you;
practice accordingly, and you shall swiftly attain perfection.
The Teacher said:
"Having been thus addressed by Brahmā, their preceptor, those high-souled sages acted accordingly and thereby attained the worlds."
"O highly fortunate one, you too, O pure-souled one, should properly carry out these words of Brahmā as they have been spoken; from that, you shall attain perfection. Vāsudeva said:

Thus addressed by his preceptor regarding the supreme dharma, O Kaunteya, that disciple then performed everything and subsequently attained liberation. And having accomplished his purpose, O perpetuator of the Kuru lineage, that disciple [departed].
14,050.043c He has attained that state, reaching which one does not grieve.
14,050.044 Arjuna said:
14,050.044a Who indeed was that brahmin, O Kṛṣṇa, and who was the disciple, O Janārdana?
"If this is indeed to be heard by me, then tell it to me, O All-pervading Lord.
Vāsudeva said:
"O mighty-armed one, know that I am the teacher and the mind is my pupil."
"O Dhanañjaya, out of affection for you, this secret has been told to me. O perpetuator of the Kuru lineage, if you have constant love for me,
then having heard this concerning the supreme self (*adhyātma*), practice it correctly, O observer of noble vows."
Then, O joy of the Kurus, when this dharma has been properly practiced, you,
with your soul purified of all sins, will attain absolute liberation.
This very thing was also said previously when the time for battle had arrived.

"O mighty-armed one, [I have been away] for 14,050.048c years; therefore, O Phalguna, set your mind upon this at my request. O best of the Bharatas, O lord, it has been a long time since I last saw my father; I wish to see him with your consent."
14,050.050 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,050.050a Having spoken these words, Dhanañjaya replied to Kṛṣṇa:
14,050.050b "Do whatever you desire; as the Lord of all, protect us."
Homage to you, O Soul of all the worlds, Nārāyaṇa, higher than the highest!

In this Kali age, penance is impossible due to the impurity of the mind; ritual action is destroyed by ignorance; even charity is marred by defects regarding wealth. Therefore, one should simply remember [you].
"O Vāsudeva, salutations to you! If our minds are resolved to go,
O Kṛṣṇa, let us indeed depart this very day for the city named after the elephant, Hastināpura,
so that we may meet there with the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Having obtained the permission of the invincible one, you ought to go to your own city.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Kṛṣṇa urged Dāruka, saying, "Let it be yoked!"
In just a moment, Dāruka announced, "It is ready.
And so the Pāṇḍava urged his attendants forward, saying, "Prepare yourselves;
we shall set out for the city named after the elephant."

Thus addressed, O lord of the people, those soldiers prepared themselves and reported to Pārtha of immeasurable splendor that they were ready. Then Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava mounted their chariot and set forth.
O lord of the people, as the two of them took delight in various wonderful conversations,
Dhananjaya, possessed of great splendor, addressed these words once more to Vāsudeva who was seated upon the chariot, O best of the Bharatas.
"O scion of the Vṛṣṇi clan, through your grace the king has attained victory;
his enemies have been slain, and the kingdom has been secured free from thorns.
O Madhusūdana, by your protection, the Pāṇḍavas now have a true protector."
"Having obtained you as our raft, we have crossed the ocean of the Kurus.
Protect us, your devoted dependents, both in this world and in the next.
O Viśvakarman, homage be to you, the soul of the universe, the source of the universe!"
"O Kṛṣṇa, O high-minded one, act in such a way that I may always know you as you truly are and remain constantly devoted to your mind,
O Madhusūdana; for the sacrificial fire is eternally born from your splendor."
Your delight consists of play, O Lord; heaven and earth are Your illusion.
All this universe—whatever is here, whether stationary or moving—is centered in You;
for You indeed manifest the entire eternal multitude of beings.
The earth and the intermediate space, as well as all things mobile and immobile;
your smile is the stainless moonlight, and the seasons are the manifestations of the senses. The wind is your ever-moving breath, and eternal death is your anger.
O high-minded one, the goddess Padmā Śrī is eternally present in you as well;
delight, contentment, fortitude, and patience reside in you, as do all this world of moving and unmoving beings. O sinless one, you alone are declared to be the dissolution at the ends of the ages.

Even in an exceedingly long time, O lotus-eyed one, your qualities and your supreme self cannot be fully described by me; salutations to you! You are known to me, O invincible one, through Nārada and likewise through Devala.

From Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself, as well as from the grandfather of the Kurus, everything has been entrusted to you; you alone, O lord of men, are the sovereign ruler. And that which was spoken by you, O sinless one, was imbued with grace.
"O Janārdana, I shall duly perform all of this;
and this most wonderful deed has been accomplished by you out of a desire for our welfare—
that the sinful Kaurava, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, has been slain in battle."

"That army was indeed consumed by you; it was by me that it was conquered in battle. That deed was performed by you, through whose wisdom and prowess victory was obtained by me over Duryodhana in the conflict."
The means for the slaughter of Karṇa has been duly demonstrated,
as well as that of the wicked Saindhava and Bhūriśravas;
therefore, you yourself must deliberate and act for our benefit in whatever way is appropriate.
"O delighter of Devakī, whatever has been said to me by you with affection, that I shall do; for I have no hesitation in this matter. And having approached King Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is righteous—"
"O knower of dharma, O sinless one, I shall urge you toward your departure. For this return to Dvārakā is pleasing to me, O Lord;
and before long, O Madhusūdana, you shall see your maternal uncle."
Thus conversing with the invincible Baladeva and other bulls among the Vṛṣṇis, the two of them arrived at the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) and both entered it,
which was filled with joyful people.
Having gone to the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which resembled the abode of Śakra,
they beheld, O great king, the lord of men Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as well as the highly intelligent Vidura and King Yudhiṣṭhira.
And [he saw] the invincible Bhīmasena, the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra seated there, and the unconquered Yuyutsu;
as well as the highly wise Gāndhārī, Pṛthā, and the beautiful Kṛṣṇā.
Subhadrā and all those women of the Bharata lineage likewise stood surrounding Gāndhārī;
then those two tamers of foes approached King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having announced their own names, they grasped his feet;
likewise, those two high-souled ones grasped the feet of Gāndhārī, Pṛthā, and Dharmarāja, as well as those of Bhīma.
And those two high-souled subduers of enemies likewise paid homage at the feet of the great-souled Bhīma;
those two high-souled ones of great prowess likewise paid homage at his feet.
Having honored the steward and inquired after his unchanging welfare,
and having embraced that high-souled great chariot-warrior, the son of the Vaiśya woman,
they both then sat beside the aged king together with them.
Then at night, O great king, the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra dismissed the leaders of the Kurus and Janārdana to their homes. Having received the king's permission, they went each to his own residence.
The heroic Kṛṣṇa went directly to the house of Dhanañjaya. There, honored according to custom and provided with all his desires,
the wise Kṛṣṇa slept, accompanied by Dhanañjaya as his companion.
When the night had turned to dawn, having performed their morning rites,
those two highly honored men went to the palace of Dharmarāja,
where the high-minded Dharmarāja sat together with his ministers.

Then, having entered that place, those two of great strength beheld Dharmarāja seated there like the King of the Gods, just as the two Aśvins might behold him. Having approached the king, those two— the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and the bull of the Kurus— [stood before him].

Having been permitted by that king who was indeed filled with joy, the two of them sat down. Then that wise king, the best of monarchs and foremost among speakers, seeing that both were desirous of speaking, addressed these words to them.
"I consider you two heroes, the scions of the Yadu and Kuru lineages, to be desirous of speaking. Speak, and I shall do everything for you both without delay; do not hesitate.
When this was said, Phalguna then spoke to Dharmarāja.
When the King of Dharma had spoken thus, Phalguna, skilled in speech, approached him with humility and replied: "O King,
this powerful Vāsudeva has been living here for a long time."
"O Hero, having obtained your permission, he wishes to see his father; if you so deem it right, let him go with your leave to the city of Ānarta. You ought to grant him permission."
14,051.042 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lotus-eyed one, may you be blessed! O Madhusūdana, go this very day to the city of Dvāravatī to see the lord, the son of Śūra."
"O mighty-armed Keśava, your departure pleases me;
my maternal uncle has not been seen by you for a long time, nor has Queen Devakī.
O Mādhava, [go to see] your maternal uncle Vasudeva and Baladeva."
O one of great wisdom, you should worship them according to their merit in my name;
and you should always remember me, as well as Bhīma, the best among the strong,
Phalguna, Nakula, and Sahadeva, O Mādhava.
"O mighty-armed one, having looked upon the Ānartas and your father, as well as the Vṛṣṇis, you should return again to my horse sacrifice, O sinless one. Therefore,
go now, taking with you various jewels and riches."
"And whatever else is pleasing to you, O Sātvata, take that as well;
for by your grace, O Mādhava, this entire earth has come into our possession,
O hero, and our enemies have been slain."
"For those devoted to you, neither heaven nor liberation is difficult to attain.
O cloud that extinguishes the fire of sin, [you have done this] today within the thicket of saṃsāra.
While the Kuru prince Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, was speaking thus—
Vāsudeva, the best among men, spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, today indeed the jewels, the wealth, and the entire earth belong to you alone."
"And whatever other wealth there is in my house,
you alone are its eternal master, O Lord. Having been addressed thus, he was then honored in return with the words, "So be it."
The valiant elder brother of Gada, having been honored by the son of Dharma according to the prescribed rites, greeted his father’s sister and circumambulated her.
Then, having been duly welcomed by her,
and likewise by all those headed by Vidura,
the elder brother of Gada departed from the city of Nāgapura.
With his divine chariot drawn by four horses, Hari,
having placed the beautiful lady Subhadrā upon the chariot with the consent of Yudhiṣṭhira, [departed], O Janārdana.
And likewise, the mighty-armed one set forth surrounded by the citizens, along with his father’s sister;
he was followed by him whose banner bears the foremost of monkeys.
Sātyaki, the two sons of Mādravatī,
the fathomless-minded Vidura,
and Bhīma himself, who possesses the prowess of a king of elephants, [all approached] Mādhava.
Having turned back those who increase the glory of the Kuru kingdom,
the heroic Janārdana then spoke in haste to Dāruka, as well as to Vidura and all the others.
"Urge on the horses! said Sātyaki then;
thereupon Janārdana, the crusher of enemy hosts, proceeded, followed by the heroes of the Śini clan.
Just as Śatakratu, having slain the hosts of his enemies, ascended to heaven, so did the powerful [Arjuna] proceed toward the city of Anarta.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As the descendant of Vṛṣṇi was thus departing for Dvārakā, those bulls among the Bharatas,
the harassers of foes, embraced him and turned back along with their retinues;
and Phalguna embraced the descendant of Vṛṣṇi again and again.
He beheld him again and again until they were out of range of sight; and then Pārtha, with great difficulty, withdrew his gaze that had been fixed upon Govinda, as did the unconquered Kṛṣṇa.
Hear from me as I recount those many portents of wondrous form that appeared at the departure of that great-souled one. A wind blew with great force ahead of his chariot.
Making the path free of pebbles, dustless, and thornless, Vāsava also rained down pure and fragrant water,
as well as divine flowers, before the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
As that mighty-armed one was traveling through the level desert lands,
he then beheld the best of sages, Uttaṅka, of immeasurable splendor; indeed,
he saw him approaching, known by the name of Udaṅka.
Having honored that great seer of perfected asceticism, renowned throughout the ends of all worlds,
the radiant one with broad eyes— being himself honored by the sage in return—
then inquired after his well-being.
Having been asked about his welfare by him, and having honored Madhusūdana,
Uttaṅka, the best of Brahmins, then questioned Mādhava:
"O Śauri, having gone there to the abode of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, [did you see them?]"
"You have established an unshakable bond of brotherhood; you ought to explain that to me.
O Keśava, bull among the Vṛṣṇis, having made a pact with those heroes, you have returned to us who are your most beloved kinsmen."
"O scorcher of enemies, will the five sons of Pāṇḍu and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra roam through the worlds together with you?
And will the kings indeed find happiness in their own kingdoms?"
"O Mādhava, now that the Kauravas have been pacified by you as their protector, O dear one,
has that expectation which I always placed in you been made fruitful regarding the Bharatas, O Kṛṣṇa?"
Vāsudeva said:
"O Brahmin, I made every effort toward brotherly concord with the Kauravas;
yet those who delight in unrighteousness could not be reconciled by me."
When they could not be easily established in equanimity,
then they all, along with their sons and kinsmen, met their destruction;
for it is not possible to overstep destiny, whether by intelligence or by force.
"O great seer, O sinless one, surely all of this is known to you.
They overstepped my counsel, as well as that of Bhīṣma and Vidura;
indeed, they have brought about for me the very conflict with Bhīṣma."
Then, having encountered one another, they went to the abode of Yama.
Only the five Pāṇḍavas remained, their friends slain and their sons killed;
and all the Dhārtarāṣṭras were destroyed, along with their sons and kinsmen.
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken these words, Uttaṅka, filled with intense anger,
replied to him with his eyes wide open in rage:
"Since the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas were not protected by you, O Kṛṣṇa, despite your power— "
"Since my beloved kinsmen have been restrained and turned back by you through force,
O Madhusūdana, I shall undoubtedly curse you, for you are possessed by wrath."
"O Mādhava, while you were capable,
you treated the best of the Kurus with deceitful conduct, since you overlooked them.
Vāsudeva said:
"Listen to this in detail as I speak it, O descendant of Bhṛgu;
accept my conciliation, for you are indeed an ascetic, O Bhārgava.
Having heard this concerning the supreme self (*adhyātma*), you should truly release your curse this very day."
"No man is able to overcome me with little ascetic merit. Nor do I wish for the destruction of your penance, O best of those who recite prayers;
your ascetic power is exceedingly great and radiant, and your gurus have been well-pleased."
"O best of the twice-born, I know of your lifelong celibacy since childhood;
therefore, I do not wish for the expenditure of this ascetic merit acquired with such great difficulty.
Uttaṅka said:
"Tell me truly, O Keśava, about the irreproachable nature of the supreme self (adhyātma).
Having heard it, I shall declare what is for my welfare, or else a curse upon you, O Janārdana.
Vāsudeva said:

Know that darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva) are states dependent upon me. As the presiding lord over maintenance, creation, and dissolution, I am designated by the names Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Īśa.
At times, through the quality of darkness, I am Rudra; when established in the quality of goodness, I am Viṣṇu.
Likewise, O twice-born one, know that even in the quality of passion (rajas), Brahmā follows other qualities through his attributes;
he is the self of the syllable Om, consisting of the three qualities, and the source of sound and the rest, as well as all things moving and unmoving,
and likewise the Rudras and Vasus— all these, know them to have me as their origin.
"Know for certain that all beings abide in me and I also abide in all beings; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.
Likewise [I dwell] within all the hosts of Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas."
"O twice-born one, know that the Gandharvas and Apsarases likewise originate from me;
as do the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas,
Nāgas, and Apsarases."
That which they call both existent and non-existent, the unmanifest and the manifest,
the imperishable and the perishable— all this has me as its essence.
O Sage, whatever duties have been ordained for the four stages of life (āśramas), [all these have me as their essence].
Know that even divine actions are entirely composed of me;
the non-existent, the existent, and the existent-nonexistent— the entire universe which is beyond both existence and non-existence— from that eternal God of gods there is nothing higher.

"O descendant of Bhṛgu, know me to be the Vedas originating from the syllable Om; likewise, know me here as the sacrificial post, the Soma, and that which nourishes the thirty gods in the sacrifice. O joy of the Bhṛgus, know me also as the Hotṛ priest and the oblation."
The Adhvaryu and the Kalpaka also [offer] the sacrificial oblation most perfectly consecrated;
and at the great sacrifice, the Udgātṛ praises me with the sounds of song. O Brahman, during the rites of expiation, those who recite the propitiatory and auspicious mantras praise me.

The best of the twice-born constantly praise Viśvakarman. Know, O best of the twice-born, that Dharma is my eldest son, born of my mind, dear to me, O Brahmin, and whose very nature is compassion for all beings.
There,
O best of the twice-born, wandering indeed through many wombs among both existing and deceased men,
I [acted] for the sake of protecting dharma and for the sake of establishing dharma.
O Bhārgava, through various costumes and forms throughout the three worlds,
I am Viṣṇu, I am Brahmā, and I am Śakra; I am the origin and the dissolution of the entire multitude of beings, as well as their creator and their destroyer.
Even as all beings persist in unrighteousness, I too, in every shifting age, establish the bridge of dharma; desiring the welfare of all creatures, I enter into various wombs.
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, when I abide in the womb of a deity, then I perform everything like a god; of this there is no doubt.
But when I abide in the womb of a Gandharva, O descendant of Bhṛgu..."

O Bhārgava, when I am in the state of a Gandharva, I then perform all the activities of a Gandharva; and when I am in the womb of a Nāga, I then conduct myself like a Nāga; and likewise, I move about appropriately within the wombs of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
While I was still among human beings, I piteously entreated you,
yet you, overcome by delusion, did not accept my beneficial words;
and I terrified the Kurus by pointing out a great danger.
Having become as if enraged, they were then shown their true state as it is:
joined with unrighteousness here and overtaken by the law of time, yet slain in battle according to dharma, they have gone to heaven; of this there is no doubt.
"O best of the twice-born, the Pāṇḍavas have indeed attained renown throughout the worlds.
I have related all this to you that you asked of me.
Uttaṅka said:
"O Janārdana, I recognize you as the creator of the world;
surely this is your grace toward me—of this I have no doubt.
And my mind, O Acyuta, is perfectly serene, being absorbed in your true nature."
"Know, O scorcher of foes, that my anger has ceased.
If I am worthy of some favor from you, Janārdana, I wish to see your divine form; show it to me."
14,054.004 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, with a pleased soul, he revealed that form to him—
the eternal Vaiṣṇava form which the wise Dhanañjaya had beheld.
He beheld the great-souled one, possessing universal form and mighty arms—
the supreme Vaiṣṇava form,
endowed with immense splendor.
Resembling a thousand suns, radiant and like fire,
it stood pervading the entire sky, facing every direction.
Having seen that supreme, wondrous Vaiṣṇava form of Viṣṇu, [he was struck with awe].
Seeing that divine form, the brahmin was filled with wonder.
Uttaṅka said:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Soul of All, Nārāyaṇa, higher than the highest!"
O Supreme Self, O Lotus-navelled One, O Lotus-eyed One, O Mādhava!
Salutations to You, who are Hiraṇyagarbha in form, the deliverer from the cycle of existence, the Ancient Puruṣa, and the Inner Controller.
I bow to you, the sun that dispels the cataract of ignorance, the great medicine for the disease of existence, and the one who reaches the far shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra*; be my refuge.
I bow to you, who are to be known through all the Vedas as the sole object of knowledge, and who consist of all the gods.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, the eternal one, who is dear to those devoted to you. Out of compassion, you ought to deliver me here from suffering and delusion;
O Janārdana, protect me, for I am bound by many sinful deeds.
O Viśvakarman, let there be homage to you, whose form is such as this:
by your two feet the earth is pervaded, and by your head the sky is covered;
that which is between heaven and earth is encompassed by your belly.
O Acyuta, you have covered all these quarters with your two arms;
O God, withdraw again this supreme and imperishable form.
I wish to see you once more in your own eternal form.
14,054.009 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,054.009*0112_01 Seeing the sage with a terrified mind, the high-minded Janārdana Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with a very serene heart, [spoke].
14,054.009*0112_02 Janārdana, being delighted with a most gracious mind.
O Janamejaya, Govinda, his soul serene, then said to him, "Choose a boon. To him Uttaṅka then spoke this:
"O you of great splendor, this alone is sufficient as a boon from you today."
"O Kṛṣṇa, this form of yours which I behold is both the source and the dissolution [of all things].
To him Kṛṣṇa spoke again: "Do not hesitate in this matter;
this must certainly be done, for my vision is never in vain."
Uttanka said:
"O Lord, if you consider this to be something that must certainly be done, then I desire water wherever I wish; for such is indeed difficult to find in these desert lands."
14,054.013 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having withdrawn that splendor, the Lord spoke to Uttaṅka:
"When there is something to be desired, I am to be thought of. Having said this, he went to Dvārakā.
Then, on one occasion, the venerable Uttaṅka, thirsty and desiring water,
wandered about in the desert and remembered Acyuta. Thereupon, the wise man [beheld] a naked outcaste covered in filth and mud.
In that desert, the best of the twice-born beheld a terrifying being surrounded by a pack of dogs,
girt with a sword and bearing a bow and arrows;
beneath that stream, he saw abundant water.
Remembering him, the Mātaṅga spoke as if laughing:
"Come, O Uttaṅka, descendant of Bhṛgu; receive water from me. For great compassion has arisen in me upon seeing you afflicted by thirst."
Thus addressed by him, that sage did not welcome the water; and that wise man hurled harsh words at Acyuta. Again and again, Mātaṅga said to him, "Drink!"
Filled with anger and with an agitated inner self, he did not drink.
Having been thus refused by that high-souled one because of his firm resolve,
O Great King, he vanished right there along with his dogs.
Seeing him thus, Uttaṅka’s mind was filled with shame;
he felt that he had been deceived by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies.
Then, by that very same path, [Kṛṣṇa appeared], bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The mighty-armed one arrived, and Uttaṅka said to him:
"O best of men, O Lord, it was not proper for you to give such water to the foremost of brahmins by means of a stream from a *mātaṅga*."
Having spoken these words, the wise and highly intelligent Janārdana,
consoling Uttaṅka with gentle speech, said this:
"In whatever form you have chosen, which is indeed appropriate for me to give,"
"Indeed, such a thing was granted to me, yet you do not perceive it.
For I spoke to the lord Purandara, the wielder of the thunderbolt, on your behalf, saying:
'O Lord, grant amṛta to Uttaṅka in the form of water.'"

"O descendant of Bhṛgu, that Lord of the Gods said to me repeatedly, 'A mortal cannot attain immortality; grant him another boon. Thus was the husband of Śacī addressed by me when I declared, 'The nectar must be given.'"
Having propitiated me, the Lord of the Gods spoke this once again:
"O one of great splendor, if it must certainly be given, I shall become a Mātaṅga and bestow the nectar upon the high-souled Bhārgava."
"If the descendant of Bhṛgu accepts the nectar in this way today,
O Lord, I shall go to give the nectar to the descendant of Bhṛgu;
for he has rejected me, saying, 'I will not give it,' O Bhārgava."
Having thus made that agreement, Vāsava, in that very form,
approached you;
and though he stood before you offering the nectar of immortality, he was rejected by you.

O Blessed One, appearing in the form of a Caṇḍāla, your transgression was indeed very great; however, O invincible one, I shall once again make your desire fulfilled— specifically, your longing for water.
"O Brahmin, on those days when you have a desire for water,
then clouds filled with water shall appear in the desert;
and they will provide you with flavorful water, O descendant of Bhṛgu."
"They shall be known as the Uttaṅka-clouds and will attain great renown.
Having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, that brahmin became filled with joy.
Even today, O Bhārata, the Uttaṅka-clouds rain down in the desert.
Janamejaya said:
By what austerity was Uttanka endowed, that great ascetic who became desirous of pronouncing a curse upon the all-powerful Viṣṇu?
14,055.002 Vaiśampāyana said:
O Janamejaya, Uttaṅka was endowed with great ascetic power;
devoted to his guru and full of splendor, he did not worship anyone else.
O Bhārata, this was the desire of all the sons of the sages: "May we indeed attain the status of a teacher’s son toward Auttaṅki.
O Janamejaya, among the many disciples of Gautama—
Then, Uttaṅka’s affection and love increased even further. Gautama became filled with joy because of his self-restraint and purity, his valorous deeds, and his perfect service.
Then Gautama, having given leave to thousands of disciples,
did not wish to grant permission to Uttaṅka out of his supreme affection for him.
O dear one, in due course, old age overcame that great sage.
And at that time, the sage, who was devoted to his guru, did not perceive [the danger].
Then once, O king of kings, Uttaṅka went out to fetch firewood and brought back a great load of wood.

But he, O King, his soul overwhelmed by the burden, exhausted and hungry, crushed that load of wood upon the earth, O subduer of enemies. A matted lock of hair, radiant like silver, became entangled in the wood.
Then, together with the logs, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Thereupon, crushed by the weight and overcome by hunger, that descendant of Bhṛgu,
seeing that state of his own age, then wept with a piteous voice.
Then his daughter, whose eyes resembled lotus petals,
who possessed beautiful hips and large eyes, and who was knowledgeable in dharma, bowed her head at her father’s command and caught the tears with her hand.
Her two hands fell down, scorched by those teardrops;
indeed, the earth was not able to bear those falling tears. Then Gautama, with a joyful heart, spoke to the brahmin Uttaṅka.
"14,055.014c Why, dear one, is your mind today so overcome with grief here?
14,055.014e Speak freely, O brahmin-sage; I wish to hear your words.
14,055.015 Uttaṅka said:
With my mind directed toward you, desiring to do what is pleasing to you, and being absorbed here in devotion to you and following after your very nature,
this old age was not perceived by me, nor was my own happiness recognized.

"O best of the twice-born, though you have dwelt with me for fourteen thousand five hundred and sixteen years, you have not granted me leave to depart. For disciples even inferior to me, having been permitted by you, have attained [liberation] by the hundreds and thousands."
Gautama said:
"O bull among the twice-born, because I was intent on pleasing you and serving my guru, a great length of time passed by me without my even realizing it."
"However, O Bhārgava, if you have the desire to go today,
take leave from me and go home without delay.
Uttaṅka said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me what I may give for the sake of my guru;
having offered that, O Lord, I shall depart with your permission.
Gautama said:
"Indeed, the virtuous say that the satisfaction of one's gurus is the true sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
For you, O Brahmin, as you have practiced [this], I am truly satisfied; of this there is no doubt.
Know me to be thus fully satisfied, O scion of Bhṛgu."
"O twice-born one, since you shall indeed become a youth of sixteen years today,
I give to you my own daughter as your wife. For no other woman than her is worthy to serve your splendor."
Then, having become a youth, he accepted that illustrious woman;
and, permitted by his preceptor, he spoke to the preceptor’s wife:
"What shall I give to you? Command me for the sake of my preceptor."
"For I desire for you that which is dear, even at the cost of my life or my wealth.
Whatever jewel there may be in this world that is difficult to obtain and truly marvelous, I would bring it back through ascetic power; of this I have no doubt."
Ahalyā said:
"I am well-pleased with you, my son, as is the Blessed One forever. That is sufficient; may it be well with you. Go, dear child, wherever you wish."
14,055.028 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,055.028a But Uttaṅka, O great king, spoke these words once again: 14,055.028c "Command me, O mother, for I must do what is pleasing to you."
Ahalyā said:
"The two divine jeweled earrings are known to be with the wife of Saudāsa;
bring them back to me—blessings upon you—and a great service will have been rendered to your preceptor."
Having promised "So be it," O Janamejaya,
he then departed in order to bring those [medicines] for the sake of pleasing his preceptor’s wife.
Thereupon, Uttaṅka, that bull among brahmins, proceeded with great speed.
In order to beg the jeweled earrings from the man-eater Saudāsa,
Gautama Uttaṅka said to his wife, "Uttaṅka is not to be seen today.
Thus questioned, she told him that he had indeed gone for the sake of the earrings.
Then he said to his wife, "This was not done rightly by you;
that king has surely been cursed and will certainly kill that brahmin.
Ahalyā said:
"O Blessed One, that Brahmin was commissioned by me today while I was unaware [of his identity].
By your grace, no fear whatsoever shall befall him.
When she had spoken thus, Gautama said to his wife, "So be it."
14,055.035c Uttaṅka, too, beheld that king in the empty forest.
14,056.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,056.001a Having seen the king in such a state, looking so terrible, he [approached].
The brahmin felt no distress at seeing one with a long beard, drenched in the blood of men; then the king,
of great splendor and like Yama himself in causing fear, rose up and spoke to him.
"By good fortune, O auspicious one, you have come into my presence at the sixth mealtime,
O best of the twice-born, while I was searching for food.
Uttaṅka said:
"O King, know that I have come here wandering as one seeking wealth for my preceptor.
For the wise say that one who is striving for the sake of a preceptor must not be harmed.
The king said:
"O best of the twice-born, my meal is ordained for the sixth period;
yet, being hungry, I am truly unable to let it pass today.
Uttaṅka said:
"So be it, O Great King; however, let an agreement be made with me:
having accomplished the purpose of my preceptor, I shall return again under your command. And that object which was promised by me to the preceptor, O best of kings—"
"O Indra among kings, he is dependent upon you; therefore, O lord of men, I beg of you. For you bestow jewels of every kind upon the foremost of Brahmins;
you are a giver, O tiger among men, and you are a worthy recipient here on this earth."
"Know me also, O best of kings, as the alms-bowl for receiving gifts. Having presented wealth to my preceptor, which is now at your disposal, O subduer of enemies,
I shall return to your power again by our agreement, O Indra among kings."
"I promise you this truth; there is nothing false in it here.
Never before have I spoken an untruth even in jest, so how could it be otherwise now?
Saudāsa said:
"If the purpose of my preceptor depends on me, it is already accomplished;
and if I am worthy of receiving a gift now, then tell me what it is.
Uttaṅka said:
"O bull among men, you have always been considered by me as one worthy of receiving gifts.
Therefore, I have come to you to beg for the jeweled earrings.
Saudāsa said:
"O Brahmin-sage, these two beautiful jeweled earrings belong to my wife;
choose some other object as your boon, and I shall give that to you, O observer of noble vows.
Uttaṅka said:
"Enough of your excuses, if we are an authority for you! Give me the earrings, O King, and be true to your word.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the king spoke these words again to Uttaṅka:
"Go, O best of men, and at my word say to the queen, 'Give [it] to me.
Surely, when she is thus spoken to by you with my message, that lady of pure smiles will comply."
"O best of the twice-born, he will give those earrings to you; of this there is no doubt.
Uttaṅka said:
"O lord of men, where might I be able to see your wife?"
"Why do you yourself not approach your wife?
Saudāsa said:
"You shall see her today at some forest waterfall."
"Indeed, at this sixth period [of the day], she cannot be seen by me today. Thus addressed, O bull of the Bharatas, Uttaṅka departed;
and having seen Madayantī, he informed her of his purpose.
Having heard the words of the slave, O Janamejaya, that large-eyed woman then replied to the highly intelligent Uttaṅka:
"It is even so, O great Brahmin; you do not speak untruth, O sinless one."
"You ought to bring some token of recognition here;
for these two divine jeweled earrings of mine are known to the gods,
the yakṣas, and the great serpents."
Desirous of avoiding [us] by various means,
they constantly watch for vulnerabilities;
yet these serpents have cast this down upon the earth.
Just as Yakṣas and gods might seize a jewel after it has been touched by leftovers,
so too might they assault you while you are under the power of sleep.
O bull among the twice-born, these [openings] are indeed always unassailable;
yet, by one who is vigilant, they are guarded against the gods, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas.
For they flow with gold by day and by night, O best of the twice-born.
14,056.025c At night, it exists eclipsing the radiance of the lunar mansions and the stars.
14,056.026a For those who have donned these, O Blessed One, whence could there be fear of hunger or thirst?
14,056.026c And no fear ever arises from poison, fire, or wild beasts.
"When these two are fastened with a small [clasp], they become small; when fastened with a fitting one, they indeed arise in that same proportion.
Such are these two earrings of mine, most highly honored."
"Bring that token of recognition, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having approached Mitrasaha, he requested that token of recognition.
Then that best of the Ikṣvākus gave him a token of recognition.
Saudāsa said:
"This path is not secure, nor is any other path known to exist."
"Having understood this, my wish, give me the jeweled earrings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, Uttaṅka then spoke these words to his wife.
Having heard this, she then gave those two jeweled earrings to him.
Having obtained the earrings, she spoke again to the king:
"O King, I wish to hear what this secret matter is."
Saudāsa said:
"By the very nature of things, Kṣatriyas indeed honor Brahmins;
yet, many faults also arise for us from the Brahmins."
"O Brahmin, though I am bowed before the twice-born, I have incurred a fault from you.
Accompanied by Madayantī, I see no other course of action;
O best among those who possess a way, I perceive no other refuge whatsoever."
O best of the twice-born, for one who has gone to the gate of heaven or remains here on earth,
it is not possible— especially for a king who has acted in opposition to the twice-born—
to remain established in the world of men or to prosper in happiness after death.
"These two jeweled earrings of mine have been given by me to you because they were desired;
fulfill for me now that agreement which was made by you today.
Uttaṅka said:
"O King, I shall do exactly so here; I will return again under your control.
However, O scorcher of foes, I intend to ask you a certain question.
Saudāsa said:
"Speak, O Brahmin, according to your desire; I shall answer your words.
I shall sever your doubt today; I have no hesitation in this matter.
Uttaṅka said:
Those who perceive the subtleties of dharma declare that a friend is one with whom speech is shared;
they know him to be a thief who behaves dishonestly toward his friends.
O King, you have now attained the state of being my friend.
"O best among the wise, grant me that even-mindedness which you possess.
Today I have achieved my purpose here, as has your cannibalistic self;
tell me whether it is appropriate for me to come into your presence or not."
Saudāsa said:
"O best among the foremost of the twice-born, if it is appropriate for me to say here,
O best of the twice-born, you must not come near me under any circumstances."
"O scion of the Bhrigu lineage, I perceive this to be for your own welfare;
for if you come here, O Brahmin, death will surely befall you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by the wise king with words that were appropriate and beneficial,
he took leave of the king and departed for Ahalyā,
taking the divine earrings to do what was pleasing to his preceptor’s wife.
With great speed, he set out toward the hermitage of Gautama;
having bound those two earrings exactly as Madayantī had instructed regarding their protection, he carried them in his black antelope skin.
Driven by hunger, he saw a *bilva* tree laden with a heavy burden of fruit; overcome by hunger, he climbed it,
O subduer of enemies, having fastened his black antelope skin to its branches.
Then that bull among the twice-born caused the *bilva* fruits to fall;
as he was thus dropping them, his vision being stolen away by the *bilva* fruits,
O Lord, those *bilva* fruits fell right upon that very antelope skin.
At that time, when those two earrings had been fastened by the best of brahmins,
the binding was then shattered by blows from *bilva* fruits;
together with the earrings, that deerskin fell suddenly from the tree.
When that black antelope skin, its binding loosened, had fallen to the earth,
a certain serpent born of the lineage of Airāvata, becoming swift, beheld those two jeweled earrings there.
Having bitten the anthill with his mouth, he then entered it for the sake of the earrings. Seeing that the earrings were being carried away by the serpent,
he fell from the tree in agitation, overcome by grief and extreme anger.
Taking up a wooden staff, he then dug into the anthill for thirty-five days without distraction, O Bhārata; at that time,
the limbs of that bull among the twice-born were consumed by anger and resentment.
Unable to endure that unbearable force, the Earth,
her limbs pierced by wooden stakes, trembled violently in great distress.
Then, as the brahmin seer continued to dig into the surface of the earth, [the earth shook].
Having resolved to create a path to the world of the Nāgas,
the immensely powerful wielder of the thunderbolt approached that region in a chariot yoked with bay horses and beheld the best of the twice-born.
But he, having become a brahmin, being pained by his [Uttaṅka’s] suffering, said to Uttaṅka: "O dear one, this is truly not possible for you;
for the world of the Nāgas is thousands of yojanas from here."
"O best of the twice-born, since those two earrings were carried away by the serpent,
I do not consider this task of yours to be achievable with a wooden staff.
Uttaṅka said:

"O Brahmin, if I am unable to obtain the earrings in the world of the Nāgas, I shall give up my life before your very eyes, O best of the twice-born. Since he was unable to make his resolve otherwise, [he departed].
Then Vajrapāṇi joined his staff with the vajra-weapon. Thereupon, O Janamejaya, the earth, being rent asunder by those blows of the vajra, opened a path to the world of the Nāgas.
By that path, he then entered the world of the Nāgas;
he beheld the world of the Nāgas extending for thousands of yojanas,
adorned with divine rampart walls embellished with jewels and pearls.
O highly fortunate one, he beheld ponds made of gold,
as well as rivers with crystal stairways and clear waters;
and he saw many trees frequented by flocks of various birds.
That descendant of Bhrigu beheld the gate of that world,
five yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length;
but upon seeing the world of the Nagas, Uttaṅka then became despondent.
O dear one, he became hopeless again regarding the recovery of the earrings.
Then, O Kauravya, a horse with a black and white tail and copper-colored face and eyes, as if blazing with energy, spoke to him there.
"Blow into this drinking vessel for me;
then, O Brahmin, you shall obtain [the earrings], for the two earrings have been brought here by the son of Airāvata.
Do not feel any disgust, my son, regarding this matter in any way."
"For this was indeed practiced by you at that time in the hermitage of Gautama.
Uttaṅka said:
"How may I recognize you with respect to the teacher's hermitage?"
"I wish to hear that which was previously practiced by me; for that is what I desire to hear.
The horse said:
"Know me to be the preceptor of your preceptor, the blazing Jātavedas (the Fire-god)."
"O child, for you have always honored me on behalf of my preceptor;
O Brahmin, descendant of Bhṛgu, you have constantly worshipped me with purity. Therefore, I shall grant you a blessing; act accordingly and do not delay."
Thus addressed by Citrabhānu, Uttaṅka acted accordingly;
and Ghṛtārcis, being well-pleased, blazed forth with a desire to consume him.
Then, O Bhārata, as he was being blown [into flame] from the pores of his skin—
A dense smoke, terrifying to the world of the Nāgas, suddenly appeared.
O Bhārata, by that smoke which increased so rapidly,
O great king, nothing at all could be discerned in the world of the Nāgas.
O Janamejaya, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the entire residence of Airāvata and among the Nāgas headed by Vāsuki.
O Bhārata, their dwellings did not shine, being obstructed by smoke.
Like forests and mountains shrouded in mist,
their eyes reddened by smoke and scorched by the heat of the fire,
they approached to ascertain the resolve of the exceedingly radiant descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having heard the resolve of that great seer of fierce splendor,
they all, with agitated minds, performed worship according to the prescribed rites;
all the nāgas, led by the old and the young, stood with palms joined in reverence.
Prostrating with their heads, they said, "Be gracious, O Blessed One.
Having thus propitiated the Brahmin and offered him water for his feet and the guest-offering (arghya),
those serpents presented him with two divine earrings of supreme value.

Then, having been honored by the Nāgas there, the powerful Uttaṅka circumambulated the fire and departed for the abode of his preceptor. Having gone quickly, O King, he reached the residence of Gautama.
O sinless Janamejaya, he then presented the two divine earrings to the wife of his preceptor;
and that best of the twice-born related everything exactly as it had happened to the preceptor and to the Nāgas headed by Vāsuki.
Thus, O Janamejaya, having traveled through the three worlds, that great-souled one brought back those two divine jeweled earrings.
Such was the power of that sage Uttaṅka, O bull of the Bharata race.
"Endowed with supreme ascetic power, you ask me that which you inquire.
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, after Govinda had granted the boon to Uttaṅka,"
14,058.001c After this, what did the mighty-armed and highly illustrious one do?
14,058.002 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,058.002a Having granted the boon to Uttaṅka, he set forth together with Sātyaki.
Govinda, with his great horses of swift speed, reached Dvārakā itself;
having traversed lakes, rivers, and various forests,
he then arrived at the beautiful city of Dvāravatī.
O great king, while the festival of Raivataka was underway,
the lotus-eyed one arrived, followed by Yuyudhāna;
that mountain was then adorned with various forms and diverse decorations.
O bull among men, that great mountain shone on all sides with golden *kāśa* grass,
with excellent golden garlands and likewise with flowers,
as well as with garments and *kalpa* trees everywhere.
Constantly adorned with golden lamp-trees,
the place became as bright as day within its caves and waterfalls;
it was surrounded on all sides by variegated banners equipped with bells.
Resounding with the voices of men and women, it was as if filled with song;
O Bhārata, it became exceedingly beautiful to behold, like Mount Meru surrounded by hosts of sages, with men and women who were intoxicated and joyful in appearance.
The sound of those singing on the lord of mountains was as if it would touch the heavens; filled with the shouts and exultations of those who were heedless, intoxicated, and utterly maddened,
the earth became truly enchanting with the sounds of "kilakila."
It was delightful, possessing marketplaces and shops, and provided with various foods, edibles, and places for recreation;
it was filled with heaps of garments and garlands, and resounded with the music of lutes, flutes,
and drums.
With food and drink mixed with *surā* and *maireya* liquor being given incessantly to the wretched, the blind, the miserable, and others,
the supreme splendor of that great mountain shone forth most auspiciously.
O hero, that mountain, filled with meritorious dwellings frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds,
was the pleasure-grove of the Vṛṣṇi heroes at the great festival of Raivataka;
crowded with mansions, it shone like the world of the gods.
And then, O bull of the Bharatas, having attained the presence of Kṛṣṇa,
the gods, Gandharvas, and Ṛṣis praised him from their hidden state—
he who is the accomplisher of all dharmas and the destroyer of the Asuras.
You are the creator, the object of creation, the support, and the cause; you are the knower of dharma and the Vedas.
O Lord, we do not understand what is being done by you through your illusory power (māyā);
we know only this much: that you are the Supreme Lord, our refuge.
"O Govinda, [we offer] proximity to Brahmā and the others, refuge, and homage.
When the son of Devakī was thus praised and worshipped by humans,
that king of mountains indeed became like the abode of Śakra.
Then, being honored, he entered his auspicious palace; Govinda and Sātyaki likewise went to their own abodes. Having been away for a long time, he entered with a joyful heart.
Having performed a deed difficult to accomplish, like Vāsava among the Dānavas,
the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas then approached the high-souled Vārṣṇeya as he arrived, just as the gods approach Śatakratu.

Having honored them and inquired after their welfare, the wise and intelligent one rejoiced; filled with joy, he engaged in conversation with those wise men. Seeing that Kṛṣṇa had arrived, the wielder of the mace embraced him with affection.
Wearing a garland of forest flowers, Balarāma embraced Keśava;
and Kṛṣṇa, having respectfully saluted his brother Rāma,
joyfully greeted his father and likewise his mother.
Embraced and consoled by those two, the mighty-armed one sat down, surrounded by all those Vṛṣṇis. Having rested and having had his feet washed, that one of great splendor was at ease.
Being questioned by his father regarding that great battle, Kṛṣṇa related it to him.
Vasudeva said:
"O Vārṣṇeya, I have heard of that most wonderful conflict."
"O son, among men who constantly engage in the opening of discourses,
you alone, O mighty-armed one, are both an eyewitness and a knower of the facts.
Therefore, O sinless one, describe the battle to me exactly as it happened."
Just as that unsurpassed battle took place between the high-souled Pāṇḍavas and Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa, Śalya,
and others, as well as with many other kṣatriyas who were skilled in weapons.
"Of those who possessed various dress and forms and dwelt in various lands"—
having been addressed thus by his father in the presence of his mother, the lotus-eyed one related how the heroes of the Kurus had met their death in battle.
Vāsudeva said:
"The deeds of the high-souled Kṣatriyas are most wonderful;
because of their great number, they cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years."

"Listen to me as I describe, in brief and according to their importance, the deeds of the lords of the earth, O you of immortal luster. Bhīṣma became the commander-in-chief, the leader of eleven armies."
Kauravya was like Vāsava among the Kauravas and the gods;
Śikhaṇḍin, the leader of the sons of Pāṇḍu and commander of the seven armies,
became protected by the wise Savyasācin.

That battle between those high-souled Kurus and Pāṇḍavas lasted for ten days; it was truly immense and hair-raising. Then, in that great conflict, Śikhaṇḍin [attacked] the son of Gaṅgā, who was not fighting.
Śikhaṇḍin, together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, struck that highly effulgent son of Gaṅgā, who was no longer fighting, with many arrows; thereupon,
that sage-like warrior met his end while lying upon a bed of arrows.
When the southern solstice had passed and the northern solstice had arrived,
Drona— the best among those skilled in weapons—
became the commander-in-chief of the Kaurava lord, like Kavya for the lord of the Daityas.
Surrounded by the remaining nine *akṣauhiṇīs*, O best of the twice-born, that hero who delights in battle was protected by Kṛpa, Vṛṣasena,
and others; having formed a military array for the great war, he struck down the great chariot-warriors.
Fierce as Death himself, he scorched the people in the night battle; meanwhile,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, a master of great weapons, became the leader of the Pāṇḍavas,
protected by Bhīma like Varuṇa by Mitra.

Surrounded by his fivefold army, the high-minded one, seeking to reach Droṇa and remembering the insults to his father, performed great deeds in battle. In that encounter between Droṇa and the son of Pṛṣata, those lords of the earth [fought].
Heroes arrived from various directions and for the most part met their death;
that battle continued for five days and was exceedingly terrible. Then Drona, overcome by exhaustion, fell under the power of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then Karna became the commander-in-chief of Duryodhana’s army,
surrounded in battle by the five remaining akṣauhiṇīs;
whereas the sons of Pāṇḍu had three divisions protected by Bībhatsu.
With the majority of their foremost heroes slain, they stood firm.
Then, having encountered Pārtha like a moth encountering fire,
Sauti met his death on that second, terrible day.
On the second day, he was then struck down by Phalguna; having scorched all the Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas with the fiery energy of his weapons,
Karṇa, along with his son, was extinguished in battle by the splendor of Pārtha.
When Karṇa was slain, the Kauravas, devoid of enthusiasm and robbed of their vigor,
surrounded the Lord of Madra with three akṣauhiṇīs.
The Pāṇḍavas, however, whose mounts were mostly killed, [surrounded] Yudhiṣṭhira.

Devoid of energy, they surrounded him with the remaining fourteen thousand and fifty-nine akṣauhiṇīs. King Yudhiṣṭhira of the Kurus slew the King of Madra after performing a most difficult feat on that half-day.
When Śalya had been slain, the high-minded Sahadeva, possessed of immeasurable prowess, killed Śakuni, the bringer of that calamity.
When Śakuni was struck down, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son became deeply dejected.
With mace in hand and the majority of his soldiers slain,
he fled; the powerful Bhīmasena, filled with rage,
pursued him and beheld him standing within the waters of Lake Dvaipāyana.
Then, having surrounded him on all sides with their remaining troops,
the five Pāṇḍavas sat down joyfully near him as he lay in the lake.
But he, having quickly plunged into the water, was severely wounded by the word-arrows [of their speech].
Rising up with mace in hand, he stood ready for battle. Then,
while the lords of the earth looked on, that King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was slain by Bhīmasena through his prowess in the great conflict.
Then that Pāṇḍava army, sleeping in its camp at night,
was slaughtered by the son of Droṇa, who could not endure the killing of his father. Together with me, they were deprived of their sons, their strength, and their friends.
With Yuyudhana as his second, the five remaining Pāṇḍavas survived.
Together with Kṛpa and the Bhoja prince, the son of Droṇa escaped from the battle; and Yuyutsu, the descendant of Kuru, was also released by taking refuge with the Pāṇḍavas.
When Suyodhana, the lord of the Kauravas, had been slain along with his followers,
Vidura and Saṃjaya presented themselves before Dharmarāja.
Thus, O Lord, did that battle unfold for eighteen days.
14,059.035c Where those protectors of the earth, having been slain, dwell in heaven.
14,059.036 Vaiśampāyana said:
O great king, as they were listening to that hair-raising tale, [the hairs on their bodies stood on end].
Then, for the Vṛṣṇis, there arose sufferings, joys, and afflictions.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the powerful Vāsudeva was thus speaking, then—
At the conclusion of the story of that Mahābhārata war in the presence of his father,
O Bhārata, that high-minded hero passed over the slaughter of Abhimanyu,
lest it be unpleasant for Vasudeva.
"The high-minded Vasudeva, upon hearing of the great calamity— the slaughter of his daughter's son— might become consumed by pain and grief.
Subhadrā, however, [learned] that her son had been killed in battle.
"Tell me, O Kṛṣṇa, of the slaughter of Saubhadra!"— saying this, she fell to the ground,
proclaiming there the great slaughter of Abhimanyu in battle.
Then Vasudeva beheld her fallen upon the earth.
Upon seeing him, he too fell to the earth,
fainting from grief; then, O great king, Vasudeva, overwhelmed by pain and sorrow due to the slaughter of his grandson, spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa.
"O lotus-eyed one, you are indeed renowned on earth as one whose word is truth.
O slayer of enemies, since you do not announce to me today the slaughter of my grandson, tell me the truth regarding the death of my sister's son, O Lord."
"How was he, whose eyes were like yours, slain by enemies in battle?
Alas, O Vārṣṇeya, death is indeed difficult for men to attain at any time other than when it is ordained,
since my heart does not shatter into a hundred pieces from this grief."
"What did he say to you in battle regarding his mother Subhadrā,
and also to me, O lotus-eyed one— my beloved with the restless eyes?
Having turned his back on the fray, was he perhaps not slain by the enemies?"
"O Govinda, I hope that your face was not distorted by him in battle?
For that powerful lord of great splendor, O Kṛṣṇa, as if boasting in my presence,
spoke of his own victory out of childishness."
"O Keśava, tell me this: does that boy lie slain upon the earth, his body disfigured by Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the others?
For he [defeated] Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Karṇa, the best of chariot-warriors."
"My daughter's son used to constantly vie with me in battle. To his father, who was thus lamenting in great distress, Govinda, himself even more sorrowful, spoke these words.
He did not distort his face at the forefront of the battle,
nor did he turn his back on that difficult-to-cross fray;
having struck down kings by the hundreds and thousands in their multitudes.

O Lord, if he were constantly fighting alone against a single opponent, even the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) would not be able to slay him in battle; yet he has been exhausted by Droṇa and Karṇa and has fallen under the power of the son of Duḥśāsana.
When the son of Pṛthā had been challenged by the Saṃśaptakas in battle,
he was then surrounded in the fray by Drona and others who were filled with rage.
Thereupon, having wrought a very great slaughter of the enemy in battle for his father’s sake—
"O Vārṣṇeya, your grandson has fallen under the power of Duḥśāsana’s son.
Surely he has gone to heaven; cast off your grief, O high-minded one, for truly, noble men never despond when they encounter calamity."

He by whom Droṇa, Karṇa, and others—who were equal to Mahendra in battle—were held at bay; how could he not attain heaven? O invincible one, cast off your grief and do not fall under the sway of anger.
For that conqueror of enemy cities had attained a destination purified by weapons.
When that hero was slain, this sister of mine, Subhadrā,
afflicted with grief, approached Pṛthā and wailed like a female osprey.
Having approached Draupadī, she, being distressed, asked:
"Noble lady, where are all my children? I wish to see them.
Hearing her words, all those Kuru women [responded].
Embracing her with both arms, they cried out like those in extreme distress.
Then Bhadrā said to Uttarā, "O auspicious lady, where has your husband gone?
Inform him quickly that I am coming."

"O daughter of Virāṭa, surely having heard my voice before, he would have quickly rushed out from his palace; why does your husband not come? O Abhimanyu, are your maternal uncles, those great chariot-warriors, well?"
"All of them spoke auspiciously to you as you arrived here eager for battle.
O subduer of enemies, tell me today about the combat as it was before;
why do you not answer me now as I lament here?"
Having heard these and other such lamentations of the daughter of Vṛṣṇi,
Pṛthā, afflicted with great sorrow, then spoke these words slowly:
"O Subhadrā, by Vāsudeva and likewise by Sātyaki in battle..."
To her who was thus lamenting, Sātyaki then said:
"This child, protected by his father, has been slain by the law of time. Such is the nature of mortals; do not grieve, O delight of the Yadus."
"O you of restless eyes, your son, who was difficult to overcome, has indeed attained the supreme goal. You were born into a great lineage of high-souled Kṣatriyas; do not grieve, O lotus-eyed one."
"Look toward the northern direction, O auspicious one; do not grieve. For this passionate woman, being pregnant, will soon give birth to a son.
Having thus consoled her, O descendant of the Yadu clan, Kuntī—
Having cast aside his invincible grief, he indeed performed the *śrāddha* for him; then,
having obtained the permission of the king and of Bhīma— who both knew what was right—
the twins, who were like Yama himself, gave gifts in great abundance.
Then, O best of the Yadus, having given many cows to the Brahmins,
the daughter of the Vṛṣṇis rejoiced and said this to the daughter of Virāṭa:
"O illustrious daughter of Virāṭa, you should not feel any distress here."
"O lady of beautiful hips, protect my infant still within the womb for the sake of its father.
Having spoken thus, O one of great luster, Kuntī then became silent;
and having obtained her permission, I brought this Subhadrā here.
"Thus has your grandson met his end, O Mādhava. Cast off your grief, O invincible one, and do not set your mind on sorrow.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of his son, the righteous son of Śūra then cast off his grief and performed an unsurpassed *śrāddha* ceremony;
likewise did Vāsudeva for his high-souled nephew.
The mighty-armed one constantly performed the funeral rites for his beloved father;
he fed six million Brahmins according to the prescribed rules, providing them with food endowed with every excellent quality.
Having covered [the Brahmins] with these gifts, the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa then dispelled their thirst for wealth; that event was hair-raising. He gave them gold, cows, as well as beds and clothing.
Then the Brahmins said, "It is abundant.
Then Vāsudeva of the Daśārhas, Baladeva, Satyaki,
and Satyaka performed the *śrāddha* for Abhimanyu.
14,061.006e Extremely tormented by grief, they found no peace;
14,061.007a likewise, the heroic Pāṇḍavas in the city of Nāgasāhvaya, deprived of Abhimanyu, indeed attained no tranquility.

O Indra among kings, for many days thereafter, the daughter of Virāṭa, afflicted by grief for her husband, did not eat; that was a great and piteous sight. Indeed, the fetus remaining within her womb began to perish.
Then, while that embryo was still being held within her womb,
Vyāsa, having perceived it with his divine eye, arrived there;
and the wise one, having approached, spoke to Pṛthā of the large eyes.
"And you, O lady of great splendor, must cast off this grief.
A son of great luster shall be born to you,
O illustrious one, through the power of Vāsudeva and by my own pronouncement."
"And at the end, he shall protect the earth for the Pāṇḍavas.
O Bhārata, looking toward Dhanañjaya while Dharmarāja looked on, Vyāsa spoke these words as if gladdening him.
"O mighty-armed one, a high-minded grandson shall be born to you;
he will indeed protect the earth as far as the oceans.
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, O crusher of enemies, cast away your grief."

"There is no need for you to deliberate on this; it shall indeed come to pass as truth. O joy of the Kurus, that which was previously spoken by Kṛṣṇa, the hero of the Vṛṣṇis, will happen exactly so; let there be no doubt in you regarding this."

"Having gone to the imperishable worlds of the gods, won by his own self-effort, he is not to be mourned by you, O dear one, nor likewise by the other Kurus. Thus addressed by the grandfather, that righteous-souled Dhanañjaya [was consoled].

O great king, having cast off his grief, he then became joyful in appearance. O knower of dharma, even your father, O high-minded one, grew in that womb in due time, like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Then Vyāsa urged the king, the son of Dharma,
toward the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and thereupon he vanished. Having heard those words of Vyāsa, the wise Dharmarāja likewise [prepared].
14,061.019c "O dear one, having lost his wealth, he set his mind on departing.
Janamejaya said:
14,062.001a "O Brahmin, having heard these words spoken by the high-souled Vyāsa,"
What did the king do then regarding the horse sacrifice?
And how did he obtain that jewel which had been placed upon the surface of the earth by Marutta? Tell me this, O best of the twice-born.
14,062.003 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Dvaipāyana, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
summoned all his brothers and spoke these words at that time.
[He addressed] Arjuna, Bhīmasena, and the two sons of Mādrī, the twins;
[he spoke of] Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, and Vṛkodara.
"O heroes, you have heard the words spoken out of friendship by that high-souled one."
This was spoken by the wise Kṛṣṇa out of a desire for the welfare of the Kurus—
by the great Vyāsa, who is advanced in asceticism, a well-wisher seeking the prosperity of his friends, a teacher of virtuous character, and a performer of wondrous deeds.
"O wise Pāṇḍavas, having fully recalled those words spoken by Bhīṣma and the intelligent Govinda, I desire to carry them out correctly;
for that is indeed for the benefit of us all, both in the future and at present."
"And the auspicious words of those who discourse on Brahman regarding the consequences [of such deeds]—
O best of the Kurus, this entire earth has indeed been depleted of its jewels;
and Vyāsa described that vast wealth of Marutta, O kings."

"O best of the Kuru lineage, when the king had thus spoken— 'If this is highly esteemed by you, or if you consider it appropriate, then let us all bring it; or what do you think, Bhīma?'"— 14,062.009–14,062.010a.
14,062.010c Bhīmasena, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the best of kings:
14,062.011a "O mighty-armed one, what you have spoken regarding the bringing back of the wealth described by Vyāsa is pleasing to me."

"O Lord, O Great King, if we could obtain here that wealth of the son of Avikṣita, it would be as good as accomplished; such is my thought. Therefore, let us [approach] with prostrations the high-souled Girīśa."
Therefore, may prosperity be yours; let us propitiate Kapardin,
that all-pervading Lord of the gods, along with his attendants—
him who holds the trident in his hand and possesses three eyes.
We pay homage to Śambhu, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is without beginning or end;
by propitiating the Protector of the World and the Chief of the Gaṇas through our speech, intellect, and actions, we shall surely attain our goal.
And those *kiṃkaras* of fierce appearance who guard that wealth will become submissive when the Bull-bannered Lord is pleased;
for that Supreme Lord, the God whose soul is gracious, is the master of his devotees.

The Lord grants even immortality; how much more so gold? In the past, when Jiṣṇu was dwelling in the forest, he, being pleased, gave him the great Pāśupata weapon, as well as the Raudra and Brahmaśiras weapons—how much more so wealth?
"For we are all devoted to him, and he is well-disposed toward us. It is through his grace, O delighter of the Kurus, that we have obtained this kingdom,
now that Abhimanyu has been slain and Dhananjaya has made his vow."
For the sake of slaying Jayadratha, Arjuna, together with Keśava, propitiated the Teacher of the World in a dream during the night and obtained a divine weapon. Then,
when the night had turned to dawn, the Lord [spoke] in the presence of Phalguna.
With his spear, he struck down the army right before the eyes of Savyasācin.
O King, who could even have dared to attack that army at that time in their minds, when it was protected by Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa— those great archers and strikers?
Except for the god Maheśvara, who possesses many forms and is the great archer,
and by his grace alone, your enemies have been slain; he, moreover,
will bring the horse sacrifice to completion.
O Bhārata, having heard these words spoken by Bhīma, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, became exceedingly pleased;
and those headed by Arjuna also joyfully said, "So be it."

Having resolved to fetch the jewels, all the Pāṇḍavas ordered their army to march under an auspicious constellation and on a fixed day. Then the sons of Pāṇḍu departed after having had the Brāhmaṇas pronounce blessings.
Having first worshipped Maheśvara, the best of gods,
with sweetmeats, milk-rice, meat, and likewise with cakes,
they offered prayers to the Great-souled One and departed, exceedingly joyful.

Then, as they were about to depart for that place, the foremost of the twice-born and the citizens, with hearts full of joy, uttered auspicious benedictions. Thereupon, having circumambulated them and prostrated themselves with their heads bowed, they departed.
The sons of Pāṇḍu set out with the Brāhmaṇas and the sacred fires,
having taken leave of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was stricken with grief for his sons,
along with his wife and the large-eyed Pṛthā.
Having left the Kuru prince Yuyutsu, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, behind at Mūla,
the heroic Pāṇḍavas— established in their observances and pure in their vows— set forth, being honored by the citizens and by wise Brahmins.
14,063.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then they set forth joyfully, with their men and mounts greatly delighted,
filling the earth with the great roar of their chariots.
Being praised with hymns by *sūtas*, *māgadhas*,
and *bandins*, and surrounded by their own army like the Ādityas by their own rays,
they had a white parasol held over their heads.
There, Yudhiṣṭhira shone like the lord of stars on a full-moon night;
that bull among men, the Pāṇḍava, duly and properly accepted the blessings of victory from the joyful people along the road.
Likewise, O King, the soldiers who followed the king—
their tumultuous clamor stood still, pervading the very heavens—
as they passed by lakes, rivers, forests, and groves.
The great king passed beyond [the mountain] and reached the very peak;
in that region, O Indra among kings, where that supreme wealth was located,
the Pāṇḍava king established his camp together with his soldiers.
O best of the Bharatas, at that time, in an auspicious and level place,
he placed the Brahmins— endowed with austerity, knowledge, and self-restraint— at the forefront,
as well as his family priest, O Kauravya, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.

Before the encampment was established, the Brahmins, together with the family priest, performed the rites of pacification according to the rules and surrounded the king on all sides. Having placed the king and his ministers in the center according to the prescribed ordinance, they took their positions.
The twice-born constructed a settlement with six roads and nine divisions,
and they also established a dwelling for the rutting lordly elephants according to the prescribed rites.
Having had this done, that lord of kings spoke thus to the brahmins:
"O best of the twice-born, regarding this task on this auspicious lunar mansion and day,
you should do exactly as you deem fit. Let there be no delay here, lest we suffer the loss of time."
"O best of Brahmins, having thus resolved, let that which must follow be performed.
Hearing these words of the king, the Brahmins, together with the family priests, spoke these words joyfully, desiring to do what was pleasing to Dharmarāja.
"Today indeed the constellation and the day are auspicious;
let us strive for that which is most excellent in our rites.
O King, let us dwell here today with water."
"Let the fast also be observed by you today.
Having heard those words of the best of the twice-born,
the lords of men observed the fast for that night.
They remained there, well-pleased, upon beds of kusha grass,
