like blazing sacrificial fires at rituals;
then that night passed for those great-souled ones.
While they were listening to the words uttered by the Brahmins,
then at the clear dawn, those bulls among the twice-born spoke these words to the king, the son of Dharma.
The brahmins said:
"O King, let an offering be made today to the great-souled Tryambaka;
having performed the offering, we shall then strive for our own purpose."
14,064.002 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,064.002a Having heard the words of those brahmins, Yudhiṣṭhira 14,064.002c offered an oblation to the Lord of the Mountains according to the prescribed rule.
Having gratified the fire with clarified butter duly consecrated,
and having prepared the sacrificial oblation (caru) perfected by mantras, the domestic priest then set forth,
O lord of men, taking with him flowers purified by mantras.
Then, having offered an oblation of sweetmeats, milk-rice, and meats,
as well as various beautiful flowers and diverse parched grains,
he who had mastered the Vedas performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* rite entirely according to the prescribed rules.
After that, he performed an excellent offering for the *kiṃkaras*,
as well as for Kubera, the lord of the *yakṣas*, for Maṇibhadra,
and for other *yakṣas* who are lords of spirits.
With *kṛsara* mixed with meat, and with *nivāpa* offerings combined with sesame seeds,
the domestic priest presented jars upon jars of boiled rice;
meanwhile, the lord of the earth gave thousands of cows to the Brahmins.
O King, he then assigned an offering for the night-roaming spirits;
that place of the God of Gods shone exceedingly, filled with the fragrance of incense and covered with *sumana* flowers.

Having performed worship to Rudra and all his attendants in every way, the king, placing Vyāsa at the head, proceeded toward the treasure-house of jewels. Having honored the Lord of Wealth, he prostrated himself and offered salutations.
Having worshipped all the treasures, beginning with Śaṅkha, as well as all the guardians of the treasures, with various *sumanas* flowers, cakes, and *kṛsara*,
that valiant one, having caused the foremost of the twice-born to pronounce auspicious blessings, [proceeded].
Established in splendor by the sound of their auspicious proclamations (*puṇyāha*),
that best of the Kurus, filled with joy, had that treasure excavated.
Then there were vessels, water-jars, and beautiful bowls made of *aśmantaka* stone.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, had thousands of golden jars, basins, pitchers, and vardhamānaka vessels, as well as many other diverse containers, brought out.

Their characteristic mark, O King, was also a great hollowed palm; their vessel was three hundred thousand [in weight], O monarch, and it weighed half a *tulā*. And there, O lord of people, was the vehicle of the son of Pāṇḍu.
Sixty thousand camels, twice as many hundreds of horses,
and elephants numbering one hundred thousand, O great king;
likewise, there were carts, chariots, and female elephants in equal numbers.
There was no counting the number of donkeys and men;
this was the wealth that Yudhiṣṭhira brought forth.
It consisted of twenty-four thousand loads, measured by the *bhāra*.
Having placed those articles upon them and worshipped them once more, the son of Pāṇḍu set out toward the city called after the elephant (Hastināpura) for the sake of Mahādeva,
having been granted leave by Dvaipāyana and placing his family priest at the head.
At every *goyuta*, that bull among men would halt his march.
O King, that great army proceeded toward the city,
its burden of wealth causing great hardship, yet bringing joy to the leaders of the Kurus.
14,065.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, the heroic Vāsudeva also arrived at the city named after the elephant (Hastinapura) together with the Vṛṣṇis.
Having understood the agreement regarding the horse sacrifice as it was stated by the son of Dharma, that bull among men, while proceeding toward his own city,
was accompanied by the son of Rukmiṇī and by Yuyudhāna.
Then, placing Baladeva at their head and accompanied by Subhadrā, [the Yadavas set out] with Cārudeṣṇa, Sāmba, Gada, Kṛtavarman, the heroic Sāraṇa, Niśaṭha, and Ulmuka.
Desiring to see Draupadī, Uttarā, and Pṛthā,
and also to console those Kṣatriya women whose lords had been slain,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, upon seeing them arrived, [received them].
The high-minded Vidura accepted it according to the prescribed rites,
and Kṛṣṇa, that bull among men, of great splendor, dwelt right there, duly honored by Vidura as well as by Yuyutsu.
While those Vṛṣṇi heroes were dwelling there, O Janamejaya,
your father Parīkṣit, the slayer of enemy heroes, was born, O King. But that king, O great monarch, was afflicted by the Brahmā weapon.
The corpse became motionless, increasing both joy and sorrow;
the sound of the people there, who were shouting lion-roars in their excitement,
entered all the quarters of space and then subsided once more.
Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Yuyudhāna, entered the inner apartments with great haste, his senses and mind deeply distressed. There he beheld his paternal aunt approaching in great urgency.
"O King, the women of the kinsmen cried out repeatedly, 'Run after Vāsudeva! while Draupadī and the illustrious Subhadrā followed behind,
wailing piteously with loud lamentations."
Then, O tiger among kings, having approached Kṛṣṇa, Kuntī, the daughter of a king, spoke with a voice choked with tears:
"O Vāsudeva, O mighty-armed one, Devakī has truly given birth to noble offspring through you."
"You are our refuge and our foundation; this lineage depends entirely upon you.
O Lord, O hero of the Yadu clan, this son of your sister’s son was killed by Aśvatthāman while still in the womb; restore him to life, O Keśava!"
"O delighter of the Yadus, O Lord, this was indeed promised by you during the Aiṣīka battle:
'I shall restore to life a child who has died. That very child, O dear one, is born dead; behold him, O bull among men."
O Mādhava, you ought to protect all of us— Uttarā, Subhadrā, Draupadī, and myself,
as well as the son of Dharma, Bhīma, Phalguna, Nakula,
and the invincible Sahadeva.
"O descendant of Daśārha, the lives of the Pāṇḍavas and my own depend upon this man; likewise, the funeral offerings for Pāṇḍu, my father-in-law,
and for the beloved and worthy Abhimanyu rest with him— may you be blessed."
"O Janārdana, you should today produce joy even for the deceased;
for Uttarā, O slayer of enemies, will surely relate the pleasant words of Abhimanyu, O Kṛṣṇa, because of her love for you— of this there is no doubt."
Long ago, O descendant of Daśārha, the son of Arjuna said to the daughter of Virāṭa:
"O blessed lady, your son shall go to the family of his maternal uncle;
having gone to the clan of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, he will master the science of archery."
"O dear one, the invincible son of Subhadrā, the slayer of enemy heroes, out of affection recounted these various weapons and the entire science of polity;
of this there is no doubt."
"Therefore, O Madhusūdana, we bow down here before you and entreat you:
for the sake of the welfare of this lineage, perform the highest good.
Having spoken thus to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the large-eyed Pṛthā—
Raising their arms in the agony of grief, they and the others fell to the ground;
and all of them, O Great King, with eyes clouded by tears, said:
"O Lord, the nephew of Vāsudeva has been born dead."
When this had been said, Janārdana then received Kuntī;
and as she lay fallen upon the ground, O Bhārata, he comforted her.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Pṛthā had risen, Subhadrā, seeing her brother,
then cried out, afflicted with grief, and spoke these words:
"O lotus-eyed one, behold the grandson of the wise son of Pṛthā!"
When the Kurus were utterly exhausted and their life-span was spent,
a blade of grass was raised by the son of Droṇa for the sake of Bhīmasena;
it fell instead upon Uttara, as well as upon Vijaya and myself.
"O Keśava, this [grief] burns within my heart;
O invincible Lord, it is because I do not see the son of my son.
What indeed will the righteous-souled Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira say?"
And Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and those two sons of Mādravatī,
having heard that Abhimanyu’s son was born and yet dead,
felt as if they had been robbed by the son of Droṇa, O Vārṣṇeya; so did the Pāṇḍavas.
"O Kṛṣṇa, Abhimanyu was dear to his fathers; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard that he has been defeated by the weapon of Droṇa’s son, what indeed will they say?
O Janārdana, what do I think but that beyond this there will be further sorrow?"
"O Kṛṣṇa, subduer of enemies, from the son of Abhimanyu— who was born dead—
I, along with this Pṛthā and Draupadī, now seek your favor, bowing my head before you. Behold us, O Puruṣottama!"
O Mādhava, when the son of Droṇa was destroying the embryos of the Pāṇḍavas,
O crusher of enemies, you, being enraged, spoke to the son of Droṇa:
"O base man, O wretch of a Brahmin, I shall frustrate your desire!"
"I shall restore to life the son of the son of Kiritin"—
having heard these words and knowing your power,
O invincible one, I entreat you that the offspring of Abhimanyu may live.
"O tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, if you do not fulfill these auspicious words after having promised them, consider me as dead.
O hero, if this son of Abhimanyu does not come back to life,"
"O invincible one, while you are alive, what can I possibly do with you?
O invincible hero, restore to life this dead son of Abhimanyu—
your own son with eyes like yours— just as a rain-cloud revives the crops."
For you, O Keśava, are righteous-souled, truthful, and of true prowess;
therefore, O subduer of enemies, you ought to make those words of yours come true.
For even if you so desired, you could bring these dead people back to life, even all the three worlds.
O giver of honor, while you live,
what need is there to speak of all the Pāṇḍavas? How much more so for this beloved son born of your sister’s daughter, who has died?
"O Kṛṣṇa, I know your power; therefore, I say this to you:
grant this supreme favor to the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Whether you consider them as your own kin, O mighty-armed one, or rather as those whose sons have been slain."
"Knowing that she has sought refuge in me, you ought to show compassion here.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Indra among kings, having been addressed thus, the slayer of Keśin was overwhelmed with grief."
"So be it," he declared aloud, as if gladdening those people;
for by that speech, the Lord, that bull among men, then refreshed those people, just as one afflicted by heat is refreshed by waters.
Then, O tiger among men, he quickly entered your father’s birth-chamber,
which had been duly honored with white garlands and with jars filled to the brim with water placed in every direction.
O mighty-armed one, with ghee, *tinduka* embers, and mustard seeds,
and with stainless weapons laid out and fires on all sides, Acyuta was attended by beautiful elderly women for the sake of service.
Surrounded by skillful and expert physicians, O hero, that radiant one beheld on all sides various articles for warding off demons,
which had been duly prepared by skilled men.
Seeing that birth-chamber of your father thus prepared, Hṛṣīkeśa became joyful and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
While the descendant of Vṛṣṇi was speaking thus with a cheerful countenance, [the chamber appeared] at that time.
Draupadī, having gone quickly, spoke these words to the daughter of Virāṭa:
"O blessed lady, here comes your father-in-law, the slayer of Madhu— the ancient seer of inconceivable soul, the unconquered one— approaching your side."

She too, restraining her voice which was choked with tears and holding back her tears, the queen became well-veiled, gazing at Kṛṣṇa as if he were a god. Thus, that ascetic woman, with a heart tormented by grief, [remained].
Seeing Govinda approaching, she lamented piteously:
"O lotus-eyed Janārdana, behold these two children here, deprived of their protector;
both Abhimanyu and I have been struck down alike."
"O Vārṣṇeya, O slayer of Madhu, O hero, I propitiate you with my head bowed low. Restore to life this son of mine, who has been consumed by the weapon of Droṇa’s son.
Whether it be by Dharmarāja or by Bhīmasena," [he said].
"O lotus-eyed one, this must have been the word spoken by you:
'O Lord, let this blade of grass kill my mother while she is unaware.
Otherwise, I alone would have perished, and this [catastrophe] would not have come to pass."

Having committed this cruelty— striking down this child while still in the womb with the Brahmā weapon, and cutting him to pieces with the Brahmā weapon while he remained in the womb— what fruit does the evil-minded son of Droṇa reap?
O destroyer of enemies, bowing my head to you, I entreat you:
O Govinda, I shall give up my life if he does not return to life. For, O virtuous one, many were the desires I had for him.
"O Keśava, since those fourteen thousand and six hundred and eighteen have been slain by the son of Droṇa, why indeed do I continue to live?
O Kṛṣṇa, O Janārdana, my mind was once full to its very lap with the thought, 'By good fortune,
I shall offer my salutations [to my sons],' but that has now been rendered futile."
"O bull among men, O Kṛṣṇa, now that this heir of Capalākṣa is dead, all the desires in my heart have been rendered fruitless. For it is said,
O Madhusūdana, that Capalākṣa was exceedingly dear to you."
"Behold this son of his, struck down by the Brahmā weapon!
He is ungrateful and cruel, just like his father,
who has now gone to the abode of Yama, abandoning the prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas."
"O Keśava, O hero, I made this vow at the front of the battle:
'When Abhimanyu has been slain, I shall come to you without delay. But I did not do that, O Kṛṣṇa; cruel that I am, I was too fond of life."
"What indeed will the son of Phalguna say now that she has arrived there?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus lamented piteously like one possessed, that ascetic woman—
Utterly wretched and longing for her son, she fell to the ground on her back.
Seeing her fallen there, deprived of her kinsmen and attendants,
Kuntī cried out in the agony of her grief, as did all the women of the Bharata lineage.
O King, for a mere moment that encampment of the Pāṇḍavas became unbearable to behold, resounding with the cries of those in distress.
And for a moment, O Indra among kings, she was tormented by grief for her son.
O hero, at that moment Vairāṭī was overwhelmed by fainting.
But having regained consciousness, O bull of the Bharatas,
Uttarā placed her son on her lap and spoke these words:
"O son of one who knows the Dharma, you perceive this as unrighteousness,
you who do not offer a salutation to the foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis.
My son, go and speak my words to your father."
"O hero, it is difficult for living beings to die when their time has come, by any means whatsoever.
For I, who am now bereft of you—my husband—and my son, continue to live even though I ought to be dead; I am one whose well-being is destroyed and who possesses nothing."
"Or rather, O mighty-armed one, permitted by the King of Dharma,
I shall consume fierce poison or enter the fire. Or else, dear father, this death of mine is difficult to achieve, even in a thousand ways."
The heart of one bereft of husband and sons does not break. Arise, my son; behold this sorrowful great-grandmother—afflicted, overwhelmed, wretched, and submerged in an ocean of grief.
"Behold the noble Pāñcālī and the ascetic Sātvatī;
behold me as well, afflicted by great sorrow like a doe pierced by a hunter.
Arise and look upon the face of the wise Lord of the World."
With eyes like the petals of a lotus, his glance as tremulous as a fawn’s— seeing Uttarā thus lamenting and fallen once more,
all those women raised her up again.
Then, rising again with fortitude, the daughter of the lord of the Matsyas,
with palms joined in reverence, prostrated herself on the ground before the lotus-eyed one.
Having heard her extensive lamentation, that bull among men—
Then, having touched water, Kṛṣṇa withdrew that Brahmā weapon.
Acyuta, the descendant of Daśārha, promised him his life;
and the pure-souled one spoke, making it heard throughout the entire world.
"I do not speak falsely regarding this answer; this shall come true. While all embodied beings look on, I shall restore him to life.
Never before have I spoken a falsehood, even in jest."
"Since I have never turned my back in battle, by that truth may this man live; and as righteousness is dear to me, and especially the Brahmins,
so may this son of Abhimanyu, though born dead, come back to life."

"By this truth— that I am not aware of ever having had a conflict with Vijaya— may this child who has died come back to life. By this truth that truth and righteousness are eternally established within me."
"Even as this infant has died, let Abhimanyu’s son live! Just as Kaṃsa and Keśin were slain by me in accordance with righteousness,
by that truth let this child be restored to life here!"
"If my celibacy remains intact and truth is firmly established in me,
and if my sovereignty is unimpeded, by that power let this child live!
O bull of the Bharatas, when Vāsudeva had spoken thus, that child—
With his lotus-like foot, worshipped by Brahmā and Rudra,
that lotus-eyed one touched him from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head; as soon as he was touched by Kṛṣṇa, that boy, the son of Abhimanyu, [was restored].
"O great king, he gradually regained consciousness and began to move slowly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, when the Brahmā weapon was withdrawn by Kṛṣṇa,"
Then that house was illuminated by your father’s splendor;
consequently, all the *rakṣasas* perished, abandoning that dwelling.
And a voice arose in the sky, saying, "Excellent, Keśava! Excellent!"
That blazing weapon then returned to the Grandfather; thereupon,
O lord of men, your father regained his life-breaths and that boy began to move according to his energy and strength.
O King, those women of the Bharata lineage then became joyful;
at the command of Govinda, they caused the Brahmins to recite auspicious prayers.
Then, all of them, being delighted, praised Janārdana.
Like those who have reached the further shore after gaining a boat, the women of the lions of the Bharatas—
Kuntī, the daughter of Drupada, Subhadrā, and likewise Uttarā,
as well as the other wives of those lions among men— became joyful in their hearts.
There, the Mallas, Naṭas, Jhallas, Granthikas, Saukhaśāyikas,
and the hosts of Sūtas and Māgadhas indeed praised Janārdana with blessings containing the names of your Kuru lineage, O bull among the Bharatas.
O great king, the vast multitude of people, filled with joy, offered their salutations. Then,
O Bhārata, at the appropriate time, Uttarā, together with her son, rose up and affectionately greeted the delighter of the Yadus.

Then, being pleased, he gave her many jewels in abundance; likewise, the other tigers among the Vṛṣṇis did so. And the Lord Janārdana, who is true to his promise, O great king, bestowed a name upon her after that of your father.
"Since this son of Abhimanyu was born when his lineage had been nearly extinguished,
let his name be Parikṣit," he said then. O lord of men, that son of yours grew up in due course of time.
O Bhārata, he was a delight to the minds of all the world;
this King Parīkṣit shall be equal to his grandfather.
O hero, O Bhārata, your father will be born after ten months.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, those best of men, arrived bringing a vast quantity of jewels—
vessels resembling the peaks of Mount Meru, jars, and various containers,
as well as great amounts of gold, both wrought and unwrought.
At every *gauruta* along that path, they traveled while resting with their beasts of burden, who were afflicted by the weight;
remembering the Supreme Lord,
O King, there was not a single person there who was not oppressed by the load, except for the king himself.
"Even Bhīma and the others carry [the burden] for the sake of the sacrifice, how much more so ordinary people?
Hearing that they had arrived nearby, the bulls among the Vṛṣṇis went forth;
and the men adorned the city called after the elephant with floods of garlands.
O lord of men, the citizens also decorated their houses with various colorful banners and diverse flags; likewise,
they performed many kinds of worship in the temples of the gods.
Then Vidura, desiring to do what was pleasing to the sons of Pāṇḍu, gave instructions.
The royal roads there were adorned with flowers,
and that city shone forth, its roar resembling the surging tide of the ocean.
With dancers performing and the sounds of singers,
that city then became like the abode of Vaiśravaṇa; and,
O King, there were thousands of bards and men accompanied by women.
In various secluded places all around, it was beautifully adorned; and banners fluttering in the blowing wind seemed, at that time,
to point out the Kurus of the south and the north.
Then a man stationed at the king’s court made this proclamation:
"Today there shall be a festival lasting the entire night, characterized by precious ornaments.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Hearing that the Pāṇḍavas had arrived nearby, Vāsudeva, the crusher of enemies, set out with his ministers and a circle of friends, desiring to see them. He proceeded forth accompanied by his host of well-wishers.
Having met together according to custom, O King,
those Pāṇḍavas,
along with the Vṛṣṇis, entered the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) in a body.
By the sound of the hooves and wheel-rims of that vast army,
heaven, earth, and the sky were completely filled with noise. Then,
placing their treasury at the front, they entered their own city.
The Pāṇḍavas, with joyful hearts, together with their ministers and circles of friends,
approached King Dhṛtarāṣṭra according to custom;
announcing their own names, they bowed at his feet.

O tiger among kings, those best of the Bharatas then paid their respects to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and after him to Gāndhārī, the daughter of Subala, as well as to Kuntī; and having met with Vidura, the son of a Vaiśya woman, they honored him.

Being thus honored, O lord of the people, those heroes shone with splendor. Then, O Bhārata, those heroes heard that supreme, wonderful, diverse, great, and marvelous account of the birth of your father.
Having heard of that deed of the wise Vāsudeva, they honored Kṛṣṇa, the joy of Devakī, who is worthy of worship. Then,
after a few days had passed, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, arrived.
The one of great splendor arrived at the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura). All the leaders of the Kurus paid him honor according to tradition;
together with the tigers among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, they then waited upon him.
Having recounted various kinds of stories there,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, spoke these words to Vyāsa:
"O Blessed One, by your grace this jewel has been recovered."
"I desire to employ that [horse] in the great Horse Sacrifice (vājimedha).
Therefore, O best of sages, I wish for your permission;
we are all dependent upon you and the high-souled Kṛṣṇa."
Vyāsa said:
"O King, I grant you leave; let that which follows be performed. Perform the horse sacrifice according to the rules, accompanied by the prescribed sacrificial fees."
"O Indra among kings, the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is indeed the purifier of all sins. By performing it, you shall truly become free from sin; there is no doubt about this.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Thus addressed, that righteous-souled Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira, O descendant of Kuru, set his mind upon the performance of the horse sacrifice. Having obtained the permission of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the king—
Having addressed Vāsudeva, the eloquent one spoke these words:
"O best of men, the goddess Devakī is blessed with a noble son because of you.
O mighty-armed Acyuta, do what I shall say to you here."
"O delight of the Yadus, we enjoy these pleasures acquired through your power;
for by your prowess and your wisdom, this earth has been conquered by you. Consecrate yourself [for sacrifice], for you are our supreme teacher."
"O knower of dharma, O Lord, if you perform this sacrifice, I shall be freed from sin;
for you are the imperishable sacrifice, you are everything, you are dharma, and you are Prajāpati.
Vāsudeva said:
"O mighty-armed subduer of foes, it is you alone who ought to speak this;
it is my firm conviction that you are the refuge of all beings.
And today, you shine preeminently through righteousness among the heroes of the Kurus."
"O King, we have become subordinate to you; O King, you are considered by us as our elder.
Perform the sacrifice with my permission; the rite has already been secured by me. O Bhārata, employ us in whatever task you desire."
"O sinless one, I promise you truly: I shall do everything for you.
O Bhārata, when you have performed the sacrifice, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the two sons of Mādravatī will likewise have fulfilled their desires."
14,071.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having been thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, took leave of Vyāsa and then spoke these words.
"Since you know the truth regarding the horse sacrifice according to the proper time, then initiate me; for this sacrifice depends upon you. Vyāsa said:
"O son of Kuntī, I, Paila, and likewise Yājñavalkya shall undoubtedly perform whatever rites are required at the proper time. For on the full moon day of Caitra, your initiation shall take place."
"O bull among men, let the materials for your sacrifice be gathered.
Let the charioteers who are experts in the science of horses, as well as the Brahmins who know that science,
examine a horse fit for sacrifice for the successful accomplishment of your rite."
Having abandoned that earth girt by the oceans according to the scriptures,
let him wander about, O King, increasing your fame under his own name,
[traversing] the earth whose girdle is the sea.
"O Yaśovardhana, while wandering about, he was protected by you for a long time.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, that Pāṇḍava, the lord of the earth, replied, "So be it."
O Indra among kings, he performed everything exactly as it had been told by the teacher of the Veda;
and all the necessary materials, O Indra among kings, were duly prepared.
Then the righteous son of Dharma, having gathered those materials, [proceeded].
The one of immeasurable soul reported this indeed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
Then the highly effulgent Vyāsa said to the king, the son of Dharma:
"We are ready for your initiation at the proper time and in the proper manner."

"O Kaurava, let the wooden sword (*sphya*), the seat of grass (*kūrca*), and whatever else may be suitable there be made of gold; let it all be fashioned of gold. Furthermore, let the horse be released today upon the earth according to the prescribed order."
"And let him wander well-guarded according to the scriptures, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Brahmin, this horse has been released by me upon this earth."
"He will roam there according to his desire; let the necessary arrangements be made for that.
O Sage, you ought to tell us who shall protect the horse as it wanders over the earth, moving at its own will."
14,071.014 Vaiśampāyana said: Thus addressed, O king of kings, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana replied:
"The younger brother of Bhīmasena is the foremost of all archers."
Victorious, enduring, and bold, he shall protect him;
for he is capable of conquering the earth, being the slayer of the Nivātakavacas. For in him reside divine weapons as well as a celestial physical frame.
A divine bow and two quivers shall follow him;
for he is skilled in both dharma and artha and proficient in all branches of knowledge. O best of kings, he will guide your horse according to the scriptures.
The mighty-armed prince, dark-complexioned and lotus-eyed,
that hero who is the father of Abhimanyu, will follow him;
so too will the radiant Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, of immeasurable prowess.
"O lord of the people, Nakula is capable of protecting the kingdom;
and Sahadeva, O descendant of Kuru, being wise and highly illustrious, shall duly attend to the entire management of the household."
The scion of the Kuru lineage performed all that according to the prescribed rule,
and he also gave instructions to Phalguna regarding the horse.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Come, O Arjuna, O hero; let this horse be protected by you.
For you alone are worthy to guard it; no other mortal whatsoever is capable.
And as for those lords of men, O mighty-armed one, who may advance against you—"

"O sinless one, you must act in such a way that no conflict arises with them. O mighty-armed one, you must announce this sacrifice of mine in its entirety to the kings; let it be known that we shall depart at the appointed time."
Having spoken thus to his brother Savyasācin,
that righteous-souled one appointed Bhīma and Nakula to the protection of the city,
and likewise assigned Sahadeva, the lord of warriors, to the administration of the household.
Having obtained the permission of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Yudhiṣṭhira [prepared for the sacrifice].
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the time for initiation had arrived, those great officiating priests (ṛtvij) then...
They initiated the king for the horse sacrifice according to the prescribed rites. Having performed the animal sacrifices, that son of Pāṇḍu,
the highly effulgent Dharmarāja, shone resplendently together with his officiating priests while consecrated for the rite.

And that horse, O King, was released for the sake of the horse-sacrifice by Vyāsa himself— that expounder of the Veda endowed with immeasurable splendor— in accordance with the scriptural injunctions.
Then, O King, that king born of Dharma, having been initiated, shone forth brilliantly.
Wearing a golden garland and a golden necklace, blazing like a fire,
clad in a black antelope skin, holding a staff, and dressed in linen garments, that son of Dharma shone with even greater splendor, like Prajāpati at a sacrifice.
Likewise, O lord of the people, all his officiating priests were dressed in identical attire;
and Arjuna himself appeared like a blazing fire. Dhananjaya, whose horses are white, urged on that black antelope-colored steed.
O protector of the earth, by the command of Dharmarāja according to the prescribed rites, he—
wielding the Gāṇḍīva bow and wearing his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors,
O King— pursued that horse with great joy, O protector of the world.
O King, O Lord, from that time on, the city was filled with people including even the children,
who were eager to see Dhananjaya, the best of the Kurus, as he was about to depart.
From the mutual crowding of those crowds, a heat as if of fire arose.
Desirous of seeing that horse and its attendant,
O great king, a roar arose from the men who were watching Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, filling all ten directions.
"Here goes the son of Kuntī, and here is the radiant horse,
whom that mighty-armed one follows while grasping his supreme bow.
Thus did the noble-minded Jiṣṇu hear the words of those who were speaking.
"May it be well with you; go safely and return again," O Bhārata—so said others, O lord of men, as they spoke these words:
"We do not see him in the crush of the crowd; only this bow is visible."
"This is indeed the bow Gāṇḍīva, renowned for its terrifying roar. May it go safely on a path free from harm and fear.
We shall see him returned again"—thus they spoke.
O bull of the Bharata race, he repeatedly heard such sweet words being uttered by men and women;
and there was a disciple of Yājñavalkya who was skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
Accompanied by Pārtha, that master of the Vedas set out for the sake of peace;
and many Brāhmaṇas, O protector of the earth, who were masters of the Vedas,
as well as Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, followed that high-souled one.
O great king, O best of men, that horse wandered according to its destination over the earth already conquered by the Pāṇḍavas through the power of their weapons; and there,
those battles which had occurred involving the Pāṇḍava took place.
"O hero, I shall describe to you those various and great [tirthas]. O King, subduer of enemies, that horse first circumambulated the earth from the north; listen to that, O lord of the earth."
Crushing the kingdoms of the earthly rulers, that best of steeds,
along with the great car-warrior Śvetāśva, then slowly traversed the earth.
At that time, there was no counting the kings by the tens of thousands who were there.
O great king, those Kṣatriyas whose kinsmen had been slain fought on;
O King, there were many Kirātas of deformed appearance who bore swords and bows,
as well as various other Mlecchas who had previously been humiliated in battle.
And many noble kings of the earth, whose men and mounts were filled with joy and who were fierce in battle, encountered the son of Pāṇḍu;
thus did battles take place here and there, O lord of the earth.

O King, O sinless one, I shall describe to you those great battles fought on both sides by Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, against the rulers of the earth dwelling in various lands— battles that were fierce and extensive.
14,073.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
There occurred a battle between Kirīṭin and the Trigartas,
who were born of enmity and were great car-warriors renowned for having slain the sons and grandsons [of their enemies].
Having learned that the sacrificial horse had arrived,
those heroes, clad in armor, surrounded it at the border of the kingdom;
they were chariot-warriors with quivers fastened, mounted on well-adorned, excellent horses.

O King, having surrounded the horse, they proceeded to seize it. Then Kirīṭin, the subduer of enemies, reflecting upon what those kings intended to do, restrained those heroes with conciliatory words.
Disregarding him, they all then struck him with arrows;
Kirīṭin warded off those who were shrouded by darkness and dust.
Then, O Bhārata, Jiṣṇu spoke as if laughing:
"Turn back, you who are ignorant of dharma; life itself is better for you!
For that hero, as he was about to depart, was indeed restrained by Dharmarāja [Yudhiṣṭhira], who said:
'O Pārtha, these kings whose kinsmen have been slain must not be killed by you.'"
Then, having heard those words of the wise Dharmarāja, he said to them, "Turn back! yet they did not turn back.
Then, [he encountered] Sūryavarman, the king of the Trigartas, in battle.
Spreading a net of arrows, Dhanañjaya laughed aloud.
Then, filling all the directions with the roar of their chariots and the sound of hooves and wheel-rims, they rushed toward Dhanañjaya.
Then, O king of kings, Sūryavarman released hundreds of straight-knotted arrows at the son of Pṛthā, displaying his lightness of hand;
likewise did the other great archers who were his followers.

Desirous of slaying Dhanañjaya, they released showers of arrows. O King, the Pāṇḍava cut down those many arrows with numerous shafts released from his bowstring and feathered nocks; they then fell to the ground.
The energetic Ketuvarmā, his younger brother, being young,
fought on behalf of his brother against the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Seeing Ketuvarmā rushing toward him in the battle, [the Pāṇḍava]—
Bībhatsu, the slayer of enemy heroes, struck them with sharpened arrows.
When Ketuvarman was struck down, the great car-warrior Dhṛtavarman quickly turned his chariot around and covered Jiṣṇu with a shower of shafts.
Seeing that swiftness of the boy Dhṛtavarman, the heroic and highly energetic Guḍākeśa was exceedingly pleased;
he could not then perceive him taking up his arrows nor aiming them.
The son of Pākaśāsana beheld him scattering arrows indeed; he, however,
honored Dhṛtavarman in that battle,
mentally gladdening him for a moment in the fray.
Enraged in battle, the son of Kuntī did not strike back, as if smiling;
he was amazed at seeing that feat of the young son of Subhadrā,
like a snake in a fury, while the Kuru hero looked on with a smile.
"O Great King, out of affection, he did not deprive him of his life. While being thus protected by Pārtha of immeasurable splendor,
Dhṛtavarman then released a sharp arrow at Vijaya."
14,073.022a Pierced deeply in the hand by him while shooting swiftly,
Vijaya (Arjuna) released the Gāṇḍīva out of pain; it then fell to the ground,
O Lord, from the hand of Savyasācin as he let go of the bow.
O best of the Bharatas, its form was like that of Indra’s weapon; O Bhārata, it appeared like the rainbow of Śakra. When that divine great bow had fallen, O King—
In that great battle, Dhṛtavarman let out a loud, resonant laugh. Then Jishnu, filled with rage, wiped the blood from his hand,
took up his divine bow, and rained down a shower of arrows.
Then a tumultuous roar, reaching to the heavens, arose from various beings who were loudly praising that deed. Then,
beholding him enraged like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time—
The Trigarta warriors, rushing forward with speed, surrounded Jishnu. Then, having approached with the intent to rescue Dhṛtavarman, they hemmed in Guḍākeśa; at that, Dhananjaya grew enraged.
Then, with sharp iron arrows resembling the thunderbolt of great Indra, he swiftly slew eighteen of their warriors. Seeing them broken, Dhananjaya acted with haste.
Laughing loudly, he struck them with arrows resembling venomous serpents;
all those great car-warriors of the Trigartas,
their spirits broken and afflicted by Dhananjaya’s shafts, fled in every direction.
For those who remained after the slaughter, having witnessed Pārtha’s prowess in the past, spoke to that tiger among men, the slayer of the Saṃśaptakas:
"We are all your servants; we are all under your command."
"Command us, O Pārtha, for we stand here as humble servants.
We shall do everything that is pleasing to you, O delighter of the Kurus.
Having heard these words, he then spoke to them all.
"O kings, protect your lives; accept this command! "Come, O monarchs, for the supreme full moon of Caitra has arrived.
Let the horse sacrifice of Yudhiṣṭhira be witnessed by you."
14,074.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having reached Prāgjyotiṣa, that best of horses roamed about;
there, the son of Bhagadatta, fierce in battle, went forth.

O best of the Bharatas, King Vajradatta fought with the horse of the son of Pāṇḍu once it had reached the borders of his territory. That king, the son of Bhagadatta, having marched out from his city, [encountered him].
Having violently seized the approaching horse, he fled toward the city.
Beholding him, the mighty-armed bull of the Kurus then swiftly took up his *gāṇḍīva* bow and rushed forward in haste.

Then, bewildered by the arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, that hero, King [Jayadratha], abandoned his horse and rushed toward Pārtha. Having entered the city once more, that best of kings donned his armor.
Having mounted that preeminent elephant, the great car-warrior went forth, longing for battle,
with a white umbrella held over his head and a white yak-tail whisk being waved before him.
With a fly-whisk being vigorously fanned [over him], that great car-warrior then approached Pārtha,
the great car-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas,
and out of childishness and delusion, he challenged the Kaurava in battle.
Then, filled with rage, he dispatched toward the one with white horses an elephant resembling a mountain, its temples and mouth flowing with rut,
like a cloud pouring down rain, capable of warding off the elephants of enemies.
That elephant, arrayed for battle like a treatise on warfare, was three *sāhasra* in size and intoxicated with the frenzy of combat. Urged on by that king,
the mighty beast then shone with its goad as if it were about to leap into the sky.

O King, O Bhārata, seeing him charging toward him, the enraged Dhanañjaya, standing on the ground, fought the one mounted upon an elephant. Then Vajradatta, filled with fury, swiftly released [his weapon] at Dhanañjaya.
Then Arjuna, with arrows dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva that travel through the sky, cut those lances— which resembled fire and were as swift as locusts—
into two and three pieces while they were still in mid-air before they could reach him.
Seeing those lances thus severed, the son of Bhagadatta swiftly discharged unobstructed arrows toward the Pāṇḍava.
Then Arjuna, even more rapidly, [discharged] straight-flying arrows with golden shafts.

Enraged, he dispatched [the weapon] against the son of Bhagadatta. Pierced by those [arrows] in that great battle, the highly energetic Vajradatta fell to the earth, severely struck; yet his consciousness did not desert him.
Then, having once again mounted his excellent elephant in battle, he,
seeking victory, calmly urged it toward Vijaya.
Thereupon, Jishnu [discharged] arrows at him that were like sloughed-off venomous serpents.
Enraged, he dispatched [arrows] that were like blazing fires. Pierced by them, the great elephant, streaming with blood,
then shone like Himavat, the lord of mountains, with its many waterfalls.
14,075.001 Vaiśampāyana said: O bull of the Bharatas, thus did that battle between Arjuna and the lord of men continue for three nights, like the battle between Śatakratu and Vṛtra.
Then, on the fourth day, the mighty Vajradatta laughed a loud laugh and spoke these words:
"Arjuna, Arjuna! Stay! You shall not escape from me alive."
"Having slain you, I shall offer water to my father according to the prescribed rites.
By you, my aged father Bhagadatta—your friend and my father's ally—was killed while he was old and honored; therefore, fight me today as a child."
Having spoken thus, O Kauravya, the enraged Vajradatta, lord of men,
dispatched his elephant toward the Pāṇḍava.
That king of elephants was sent forth by the wise Vajradatta.
As if about to spring into the sky, he rushed toward the Pāṇḍava; O great king, with a spray discharged from his trunk, he drenched Phalguna like a dark cloud drenching a mountain.
Sent by that king, he rushed toward Phalguna, repeatedly roaring like a cloud with the thunderous sound from his gaping mouth;
urged on by Vajradatta, he was like a lordly elephant in rut as if dancing.
O King, he swiftly approached the great car-warrior of the Kauravas. Seeing Vajradatta’s elephant charging toward him,
the powerful slayer of enemies took refuge in his Gāṇḍīva bow and did not tremble.
O Bhārata, remembering the obstruction to his mission and his former enmity toward that king, the Pāṇḍava became violently incensed;
then, filled with rage, the Pāṇḍava [struck] that elephant with a net of arrows.
Then, like the shore restraining the ocean, he checked that foremost of serpents; though restrained by Arjuna through his prowess,
that best of nāgas stood with his limbs pierced by arrows, like a porcupine bristling with quills.
Seeing his elephant repulsed, O King, the son of Bhagadatta,
overwhelmed with rage, loosed sharp arrows at Arjuna.
But Arjuna, O great king, [fended them off] with arrows capable of destroying shafts.
He warded off those who were shooting, and it was like a marvel.
Then, becoming even more enraged, the king, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa,
dispatched a great lord of elephants, powerful and like the wind.

Seeing him charging toward him, the powerful son of Pākaśāsana discharged an iron arrow, blazing like fire, at the elephant. O King, that elephant was struck violently in its vital organs by that shaft.

14,075.018c He suddenly fell to the ground like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt. 14,075.019a Struck by Dhanañjaya’s arrow, that falling serpent shone like a great mountain entering the earth, crushed by a thunderbolt.

When that elephant had fallen, the Pāṇḍava said to King Vajradatta, who had descended to the ground, "Do not be afraid. Then the one of great splendor spoke: "Yudhiṣṭhira told me as I was setting out [for battle]."
"O Dhanañjaya, those kings must not be slain by you under any circumstances.
O tiger among men, let all this be accomplished by this much alone.
Furthermore, O Dhanañjaya, the warriors also must not be killed by you in battle."
"Furthermore, all kings, together with their circle of friends, must be told:
'May you witness Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse sacrifice.
Having heard these words of my brother, O lord of men, I do not kill you."
"Arise! You have no fear; go in safety, O King. You shall come again, O Great King, when the next full moon of Caitra has arrived;
then the horse sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja shall take place."
Thus addressed, that king, the son of Bhagadatta,
having been defeated by the Pāṇḍava, then replied with the words, "So be it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having then conquered and pacified the king who was the son of Bhagadatta,
O Bhārata, and having released the horse as it proceeded toward the Saindhavas,
a battle then ensued between the Saindhavas and that Diademed One (Kiritin).
O great king, those who remained after the slaughter, as well as the sons of the slain,
having heard that Śvetavāhana had entered their territory,
went out to meet that bull among the Pāṇḍavas, unable to endure him.
Having seized that horse at the border of the territory, those men, who were like poison,
felt no fear of Bhīmasena, the son of Pṛthā, who stood close behind them. They remained not far away, bows in hand, near the sacrificial steed.
They encountered Bibhatsu standing on foot;
then those kings of great prowess,
those tigers among men who had previously been humiliated in battle, surrounded him, desiring victory.
Proclaiming their names, lineages, and various deeds,
they then showered Pārtha with a rain of arrows.
Discharging those sharp shafts capable of repelling even lordly elephants, they assailed him.
Desiring victory in battle, they surrounded the son of Kuntī.
Without even considering that hero of fierce deeds in combat,
all those brave warriors, stationed upon their chariots, fought against him who was on foot.
They struck down that hero, the slayer of the Nivātakavacas,
the destroyer of the Saṃśaptakas, and the killer of the ruler of the Sindhus.
Then, with a thousand chariots and ten thousand horses...
Having hemmed in the son of Kuntī, they fought with great joy,
O Kauravya, those heroes remembering the slaughter in battle of the wise Jayadratha, the king of Sindhu, by Savyasācin.
Then, like clouds, they all released a rain of arrows;
covered by them, Pārtha shone like the sun amidst the clouds.
That bull among the Pāṇḍavas was seen completely enveloped by those shafts.
O Bhārata, like a bird moving within a cage, [he was hemmed in];
then, O King, when the son of Kuntī was afflicted by arrows, a cry of "Alas! arose from everyone, and the three worlds became filled with dust, while the sun turned crimson with that dust.
Then, O great king, a hair-raising wind blew;
Rāhu swallowed both the sun and the moon simultaneously;
and meteors, scattering in every direction, struck down the sun.
O King, there was a trembling of the great mountain Kailāsa;
and the Seven Sages, as well as the celestial sages, overcome by fear and filled with pain and grief, shed very hot tears.
O King, at that time, during those portents of calamity, a hare quickly pierced the orb of the moon and fell; it was then reversed,
appearing like a reddish-brown donkey, bearing a bow and accompanied by lightning.
Covering the sky, the clouds released flesh and blood. O best of the Bharatas, when the world was thus enveloped by that shower of arrows upon the hero, it was as if a miracle had occurred.
As he was completely overwhelmed by that shower of arrows,
through his confusion, the Gāṇḍīva bow and even the hand-guard fell from his hand. When he had fallen into that state of stupor, an even greater shower of arrows [fell].
When the great car-warrior had lost his life-force, the Saindhavas quickly released their arrows. Then,
perceiving that Pārtha was overcome by a swoon, all the denizens of heaven became terrified in mind and turned toward performing rites for his pacification.
Then all the celestial rishis, as well as the seven rishis and the brahmin rishis, chanted prayers for the victory of the wise son of Pṛthā.
Thereupon, O King, the splendor of Pārtha was kindled by the gods.
Standing firm like a mountain in battle, that wise man, skilled in supreme weapons,
drew his divine bow; and from it, O joy of the Kurus,
there arose again and again a great sound like that of a mechanical engine.
Then that lord, Pārtha, rained showers of arrows upon his enemies with his bow, just as the Lord of the Gods rains down rain;
thereupon all those Saindhava warriors, together with their king, [were overwhelmed].
Covered by arrows like moths by fire, they could no longer be seen.
At the sound of that [weapon], they were terrified and fled, afflicted by fear;
stricken with grief, the Saindhavas shed tears and even fell into a deep sleep.
O King, that best of men, the powerful slayer of enemies, moving everywhere like a whirling circle of fire, struck them all with nets of arrows;
that mass of shafts was like a magical illusion.
Like Mahendra wielding the thunderbolt, he discharged [his weapons] in all directions;
having torn asunder that army which resembled a mass of clouds,
that best of the Kauravas, radiant as the sun, shone like the sun in autumn.
14,077.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then the hero who wields the Gāṇḍīva, standing firm for battle,
shone in the conflict, invincible like the immovable Himavat mountain.
Then those Saindhava warriors, O Bhārata, once again took their positions, highly agitated and discharging showers of arrows.
The one of great heroism, having forcibly overcome them as they stood firm once more, [proceeded].
Then the son of Kuntī spoke with gentle words to those who were about to die:
"Fight with your utmost strength and strive for my slaughter;
perform all your duties, for a great danger has come upon you."
"I shall fight you all, warding off your snare of arrows. Stand firm with minds set on battle; I shall humble your pride.
Having spoken thus in anger, the Kuru prince, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, then—

Then, O Bhārata, remembering the words of his eldest brother, the high-souled Dharmarāja had said: "O dear one, Kṣatriyas who desire victory must not be slain in battle; rather, they are to be conquered."
Then Phalguna, that bull among men, reflected:
"I was told by the lord of men, 'The kings are not to be slain.
How may those auspicious words of the King of Dharma not prove false here?"
"Let not the kings be slain, and let the command of the king be fulfilled. Having reflected thus, he who was devoted to the welfare and pleasure of his brother,
that knower of dharma, then spoke these words to the Saindhavas, who were maddened by battle.
I shall not slay children or women among you who stand their ground;
nor will I kill anyone who, defeated in battle, says, "I am yours.
Having heard these words of mine, do what is for your own benefit.
"Otherwise, you shall fall into distress, tormented by me.
Having spoken thus to those heroes, that bull among the Kurus fought with them—
calm and unagitated, against those who were agitated and eager for victory.

Then, O King, the Saindhavas released hundreds of thousands of straight-knotted arrows at the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow. He [then] [encountered] those cruel, oncoming shafts, which were like the venom of poisonous serpents.
Dhananjaya cut them down with sharpened arrows while they were still in mid-air;
having severed those swift, stone-sharpened shafts feathered with heron plumes,
he pierced each one in that battle with ten arrows of his own.
Then, remembering that Jayadratha had been slain, the Saindhava kings once again hurled spears and javelins at Dhanañjaya;
but the high-minded Kirīṭin rendered their resolve futile.
Having cut all those [weapons] down in mid-air, the Pāṇḍava shouted with joy.
Likewise, as those warriors, greedy for victory, were charging forward,
he struck off their heads with straight-knotted *bhalla* arrows.
As they were fleeing, running back again,
and turning around, their noise was like that of the full great ocean.
While being slaughtered then by Pārtha of immeasurable splendor, they...
14,077.020c Fighting Arjuna according to their strength and according to their energy,
14,077.021a then, in that battle, by Phalguna with his straight-knotted arrows, 14,077.021c most of them were rendered unconscious, their mounts and soldiers exhausted.
Then, perceiving that they were all utterly exhausted, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s daughter Duḥśalā took her young grandson—
the heroic son of Suratha who was innocent of any fault— and set out on a chariot.
For the sake of pacifying all the warriors, she approached the son of Pāṇḍu.
Having reached Dhanañjaya, she then let out a cry of distress.
And the lord Dhanañjaya, seeing her, cast aside his bow.
Having laid down his bow according to the prescribed rites, Pārtha then said to his sister, "What shall I do? And she spoke these words to him:
"O best of the Bharatas, this infant is the son of your sister's son."
"O hero, he greets you; behold him, O bull among men.
Thus addressed, Arjuna then asked his father, "Where is he? Thereupon, O King, Duḥśalā spoke these words.

"O hero, his father, tormented by grief for his son and afflicted by despair, met his death; learn from me how that happened. O sinless one, having previously heard that his father had been killed in battle by you..."

O Dhanañjaya, having heard that you had arrived as a horse-tamer for the sake of battle, he who was already afflicted by the grief of his father’s death gave up his life, O sinless one, at the mere mention of your name, "Bībhatsu."
"Afflicted by grief, my son fell to the earth and died. O Lord, seeing him fallen,
I have now come to you seeking refuge, having taken hold of his son."
Having spoken thus with a piteous voice, the daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra released her tears;
then, distressed, she spoke to Pārtha, who stood there dejected with his face cast down:
"Look upon me, your sister, and look upon your sister’s son."
O knower of dharma, O upholder of the Kuru lineage, you ought to show compassion toward me;
disregard that dull-witted King of the Kurus and Jayadratha,
so that Parikṣit, the slayer of enemy heroes, may be born from Abhimanyu.
"O mighty-armed one, thus was this grandson of mine born from Suratha;
O tiger among men, taking him with me,
I have come into your presence for the sake of peace among all warriors— listen now to these words of mine."
"O mighty-armed one, here has come the grandson of that dull-witted man. Therefore, you ought to show favor to this boy.
O subduer of enemies, he is propitiating you with his head bowed along with me."
"O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, he entreats you: 'Be at peace.
O Pārtha, show favor toward this child who has lost his kinsmen and knows nothing; O knower of dharma, do not fall under the sway of wrath."
"Forgiving this ignoble and cruel man, who has utterly transgressed against his own grandfather, you ought to show him favor. While Duḥśalā was speaking thus piteously, Dhanañjaya—
Remembering Queen Gāndhārī and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
he, afflicted by pain and grief, spoke while censuring the duty of the Kṣatriyas:
"Fie on that base Duryodhana, who was greedy for the kingdom and full of pride!"
"Because of whom all my kinsmen have been led by me to the abode of Yama"—
having spoken thus, Jaya offered many words of consolation and showed her favor;
then, embracing her with affection, he sent her back toward her home.
And Duḥśalā, having restrained those warriors from the great battle and having paid homage to Pārtha, departed toward her home with her auspicious countenance.
Then, that bull among men, having utterly defeated the Saindhava warriors, [proceeded].
Having thus defeated those heroic Saindhavas, Dhananjaya once again pursued that horse which moved according to its own will;
O lord of the people, the hero followed that sacrificial steed in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Like the constellation Mṛga in the sky, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
and that horse roamed at will through various regions as they pleased, according to their desire, thereby increasing the fame of Pārtha’s deeds.
O bull of the Bharata race, as that horse was thus wandering in due order,
it reached the territory of the lord of Maṇipura along with the son of Pāṇḍu.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having heard that his heroic father had arrived, the noble King Babhruvāhana went forth with humility, preceded by Brahmins bearing offerings of honor (*arghya*). Dhananjaya, however, [beheld] the Lord of Maṇipūra thus approaching.

The wise one did not approve, remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya. Then the righteous-souled Phalguna, filled with indignation, said to him: "This conduct of yours is not fitting; you stand outside the dharma of a Kṣatriya."

"Why, my son, did you not fight me as I approached the border of your realm, when I was a sacrificial horse being protected by Yudhiṣṭhira? Fie on you, O evil-minded one, who are unskilled in the duty of a Kṣatriya!"
"O you who, when I arrived for battle, instead received me with peaceful words—
there is no purpose whatsoever in your living here,
you who have welcomed me with conciliation as if I were a woman when I came for war."
"O evil-minded one, if I were to come to you having laid down my weapons,
then this conduct of yours would be appropriate, O lowest of men.
Having understood these words spoken by her husband, the daughter of the serpent...
Unable to endure it, Ulūpī burst through the earth and approached him.
There she saw her son, O Lord, reflecting with his face cast down,
being repeatedly rebuked by his father who was eager for battle.
Then Ulūpī, the daughter of a serpent, whose every limb was beautiful and who was well-versed in the dharma of the Kṣatriyas, approached him and spoke these words:
"Know me to be Ulūpī, your mother, born of a serpent."
"O son, follow my word; it will result in the highest dharma for you.
Fight this Dhananjaya, the best of the Kurus and a tamer of foes, O subduer of enemies.
For in this way he will surely be pleased with you; of this there is no doubt."

Thus encouraged by his mother, O bull of the Bharatas, that king Babhruvāhana, possessed of great splendor, set his mind upon battle. Having donned his golden armor and his radiant helmet, he prepared for the fray.
The wise one ascended that great chariot, which was crowded with hundreds of quivers,
equipped with all necessary implements, yoked to horses swift as thought, fitted with excellent wheels and appurtenances, and adorned with golden ornaments.
Having raised his most highly honored golden lion-standard,
King Babhruvāhana set out toward Pārtha.
Then, the hero approached the sacrificial horse protected by Pārtha.
He had it seized by men skilled in the training of horses.
Seeing the steed captured, Dhananjaya, with a joyful heart,
stood on the ground and restrained his son, who was mounted upon his chariot, in that battle.
Then that king afflicted the hero with thousands of volleys of sharp arrows resembling the venom of poisonous serpents. An incomparable battle ensued between those two, the father and the son.
Resembling the battle between the gods and the asuras, as both sides were filled with joy,
Babhruvāhana— that tiger among men— laughing, pierced Kirīṭin in the region of the collarbone with a straight-knotted arrow.
Like a serpent entering an anthill, it entered along with its feathers;
having pierced through the son of Kuntī, it then entered the surface of the earth. Suffering intense pain, the wise hero clung to his excellent bow.

Having entered into divine splendor, he shone as if restored from death. Then, O lord of the earth, that bull among men, having regained consciousness and praised his son, the son of Śakra spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one, my child, son of Citrāṅgadā! Seeing this deed worthy of you, my son, I am filled with joy.
Here, I release these arrows for you; remain firm in battle, my son."

Having spoken thus, the slayer of enemies, laughing, rained down extremely sharp iron arrows upon his heroic son, O bull among the Pāṇḍavas. He [the son] [received] those [arrows] released from the Gāṇḍīva, which possessed a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt of Indra.
The king cut every one of those iron arrows into three pieces each.
Then Pārtha, with divine shafts, struck down from the chariot his [the king's] gold-adorned standard,
which resembled a golden palm tree, using a razor-headed arrow.

Laughing, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas rendered the king’s horses— huge-bodied and possessed of great speed and prowess— lifeless. Then the king, exceedingly enraged, quickly descended from his chariot.
On foot, he fought his father, the Pāṇḍava, out of anger;
yet the bull among the Pāṇḍavas,
the son of the wielder of the thunderbolt, being well-pleased by his son’s prowess, did not excessively afflict him.
As his father turned away while being struck, Babhruvāhana,
the lord of the earth, pierced him in the heart with a firm arrow;
then the powerful one tormented him once more with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, out of childishness, Babhruvāhana powerfully pierced his father in the heart with a sharp, well-feathered arrow;
that shaft was radiant with energy, like a blazing fire.
O King, that arrow, having pierced the vital organ of the Pāṇḍava and causing extreme pain, entered the earth.
O King, being thus deeply pierced by his son, Dhanañjaya, the joy of the Kurus,
fell to the ground afflicted by a swoon.
When that hero, the bearer of the burden of the Kauravas, had fallen,
the son of Citrāṅgadā also quickly fell into a swoon,
having exerted himself in battle and seeing his father slain.
Already deeply pierced by Arjuna with volleys of arrows,
he too fell, embracing the earth at the forefront of the battle. Seeing his lord slain and his son fallen upon the ground, [he was overcome].
Terrified, Citrāṅgadā entered the field of battle;
with a heart tormented by grief, that beautiful woman wept as she then beheld her husband, the lord of Maṇipūra, slain.
14,079.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having lamented in many ways, that lotus-eyed woman,
though difficult to overcome, fainted from grief and fell to the ground.
Having regained consciousness, the goddess, assuming her divine form,
beheld Ulūpī, the daughter of the serpent, and spoke these words:
"Ulūpī, look at your husband lying slain in battle."
"Because of you, my son, though but a child, has fallen in battle against one who conquers assemblies.
Surely you are noble, O lady, surely you know the dharma, and surely you are devoted to your husband;
yet because of you, this husband of yours has fallen, slain in the field of battle."
"But this is a grievous offense against you all, O Dhanañjaya;
forgive me as I entreat you, and restore Dhanañjaya to life.
Surely you, noble lady, are a knower of dharma, renowned throughout the three worlds, O auspicious one."
"Since you do not grieve here for having caused your husband to be slain by your son,
I do not grieve for my slain son, O daughter of a serpent; rather,
I grieve only for my husband, to whom this hospitality was offered."
Having spoken thus to the goddess Ulūpī, the daughter of the serpent,
that illustrious woman approached her husband and said this:
"Arise, O my beloved, you who desire to do what is pleasing to me, the foremost of the Kurus."
"O mighty-armed one, this horse has been released by me for you.
Surely, O hero, this sacrificial horse of Dharmarāja must be pursued by you; why then do you lie upon the surface of the earth?"
"O joy of the Kurus, the lives of the Kurus are dependent upon you.
Why then, you who grant life to others, have you abandoned your own life?
O Ulūpī, look well upon your husband slain in battle."
Having incited your son and caused him to be slain, you do not grieve. Let this boy sleep at his pleasure upon the ground, having entered the state of the departed;
let the red-eyed Guḍākeśa, the victorious one, live well.
"O fortunate one, there is no fault in men having many wives;
however, such a thought should not occur to you regarding women.
For this friendship was established by the Creator as eternal and immutable."
Recognize our friendship; let there be true union between us.
If you do not show me my husband alive today after having him killed by his son, I shall surely give up my life this very day.
"O timid one, I, afflicted by grief and deprived of both husband and sons, shall surely sit here in a fast unto death while you look on; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus to her co-wife, the daughter of the serpent, Caitravāhinī—
Then, O lord of men, she sat in silence, observing a fast unto death.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having lamented thus and ceased, she grasped her husband’s feet.
The queen sat down, gazing at her son with a sigh of relief. Then,
having regained consciousness once more, King Babhruvāhana looked at his mother on the field of battle and spoke.
What indeed could be more painful than this: that my mother, who was raised in comfort,
lies upon the ground mourning her deceased husband,
a hero who was the slayer of enemies in battle and the foremost among all wielders of weapons?
"Alas, she beholds me slain in battle— a death so difficult to endure!
Oh, how firm must be the heart of this queen that it does not shatter as she gazes upon her slain husband, broad-chested and mighty-armed!"
I consider death here difficult for a man to attain while the journey has not yet reached its end—that point where neither I nor my mother shall be separated from life.
Alas, what a pity! That the golden breastplate of the Kuru hero lies upon the earth.
"Behold here this discarded man, slain by me, his son!
O Brahmins, behold my heroic father lying upon the earth on the hero’s bed, struck down by me, his son!"
"Let the Brāhmaṇas appointed by the chief of the Kurus to follow the horse perform propitiatory rites today for this one who has been slain by me in battle.
And what expiation, O Brahmins, do you prescribe for me here today?"
For twelve years, this cruel and wicked man has practiced a life of hardship after slaying his father on the field of battle; today,
indeed, he remains here cruelly clad in my father’s skin.
"Even as my father eats from his own skull today,
there is indeed no other atonement for me than killing my father now.
Behold, O daughter of the best of Nāgas, your husband slain by me."
"O auspicious lady, by slaying Arjuna in battle today, I have done what is pleasing to you.
I too shall now go the way frequented by my ancestors;
I am unable to sustain myself by my own power."

"O Mother, when I am dead, and likewise when the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow is dead, may you remain full of joy; O Queen, I swear this by my own soul. Having spoken thus, the king was then overwhelmed by pain and grief.
Having touched water, O Great King, he spoke these words out of sorrow:
"Let all beings, both stationary and moving, listen,
as well as you, my mother, O best of serpent-women, so that I may speak the truth."
"If my father Jaya, the bull of the Bharatas, does not rise [to fight],
I shall wither away my body right here on this battlefield. For there is no atonement to be found anywhere for one who has slain his own father."
Afflicted by the murder of my elder, I shall certainly fall into hell. For by killing a heroic Kṣatriya, one is liberated by the gift of a hundred cows;
but having slain my father in this way, the expiation for me is insurmountable.
"For this Dhananjaya, son of Pāṇḍu, is indeed one of great splendor;
and my father was a righteous soul—where, then, can there be atonement for me?
Having spoken thus, O King, the prince who was the son of Dhanañjaya [fell silent].
Having touched water, the high-minded one became silent and sat down to fast unto death.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that time, when the king, the lord of Maṇipūra, had thus sat down to fast unto death...
O scorcher of foes, when he was overcome with grief for his father along with his mother,
Ulūpī then thought of the life-restoring jewel (saṃjīvana-maṇi); and that jewel, the ultimate refuge of the serpents, then appeared before her.
Having taken him up, O Kauravya, the daughter of the lord of the Naga kings then spoke these heart-gladdening words to the soldiers:
"Arise! Do not grieve, my son; this Jiṣṇu has not been slain by you."
"He is invincible by men or even by the gods led by Indra; however,
this illusion named Mohinī has been employed by me today for the sake of pleasing your illustrious father, that lord among men."
"O son, this Kaurava, the slayer of enemy heroes, has indeed come here, O King, while you were fighting in battle, desiring to see your strength. Therefore,
my son, I have urged you toward this combat."
"O son, O lord, do not suspect even the slightest evil in yourself.
This seer is of great splendor, the eternal and immutable Puruṣa.
For even Śakra himself, my son, is not able to defeat him in battle."
"O Lord of the People, this divine jewel has been brought by me for you,
which constantly restores to life those lords of serpents who have died. O powerful one, place it upon your father's chest."

"O son, you shall see the Pāṇḍava restored to life once again. Having been addressed thus, that doer of no evil, possessed of immeasurable splendor, then placed the jewel upon the chest of his father’s son out of paternal affection.

When that jewel was placed upon him, O hero, the lord Jiṣṇu returned to life; with his eyes cleansed of blood, he rose up like one awakened from sleep. Seeing that high-souled and wise one risen and restored to consciousness, [he beheld him].
Seeing his father restored to health, Babhruvāhana paid him homage.
O Lord, when that tiger among men had risen once more, endowed with splendor, Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, rained down divine and holy flowers.
Unstruck drums resounded with the roar of thunderclouds, and a great sound arose in the sky, crying "Excellent! Excellent!
Then the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, having risen, was fully restored.
Embracing Babhruvāhana, he smelled his head;
then, seeing his mother standing nearby, emaciated by grief and accompanied by Ulūpī,
Dhanañjaya questioned her.
"O slayer of enemies, why does this entire battlefield appear filled with grief, wonder, and joy? If you know, tell me;
and for what reason has your mother come to the field of battle?"
"Who is this daughter of the lord of serpents, Ulūpī, who has come here?
I know that this battle was fought by you at my word;
I wish to know the reason for the arrival of these women."
Then, having been thus questioned, the wise lord of Maṇipūra bowed his head in supplication and said, "Let Ulūpī be asked.
Arjuna said:

"O delight of the Kuru lineage, what is the purpose of your arrival? O daughter of a serpent, do you likewise wish for the welfare of the mother of the Lord of Maṇipura and of this king on the field of battle?"
"O lady with tremulous eyes, do you perhaps desire my welfare? O lady of broad hips and auspicious appearance,
have I, out of ignorance, or this Babhruvāhana, done anything unpleasant to you?"

"And does the princess Citrāṅgadā, your co-wife, she of the beautiful hips who moves like the spring breeze, commit no offense whatsoever? Then the daughter of the Lord of Serpents spoke to him, smiling.
"You have not offended me, nor has King Babhruvāhana,
nor his mother who stands before me like a servant.
Listen to how all this was undertaken by me."

"O Dhananjaya, you should not feel anger toward me; I propitiate you with my head bowed low. O sinless Kauravya, this was done by me solely for the sake of pleasing you. Listen, O mighty-armed one, to the whole matter in its entirety."
O Pārtha, this expiation has been made for that which was done by you in the Mahābhārata war when the king, the son of Śantanu, was slain unrighteously;
for Bhīṣma was not struck down by you while he was actually engaged in combat, O hero.
But Śikhaṇḍin, having been engaged in combat with him, was slain by you while relying upon him. If you should give up your life without performing the funeral rites for him,
you will certainly fall into hell because of that sinful deed.
This peace, O protector of the earth, which you have obtained from your son, was ordained by the Vasus and Gaṅgā, O high-minded one; for indeed,
this was heard by me in the past as it was told by the Vasus.
When King Śāntanu had been slain and they had come to the bank of the Gaṅgā,
the Vasu gods bathed in the great river and, having gathered together,
spoke these terrible words at that time with the consent of Bhāgīrathī.
"O beautiful lady, this Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, has been slain by Savyasācin while he was not fighting in the battle, being engaged with another. Therefore,
O auspicious one, because of this indignity, we too [shall fight] Arjuna."
"Let us join him with a curse," they said, and she replied, "So be it.
Having informed my father of that, my senses were deeply distressed;
and he, upon hearing it, fell into the utmost despondency.
My father, having gone to the Vasus, entreated them on your behalf;
after propitiating them again and again, they spoke thus to him:
"O illustrious one, the young lord of Maṇipura shall [be born] once more."
"He shall strike him down to the earth with arrows while he stands in the midst of battle;
when this is done, O Lord of Nagas, he will be released from his curse.
Having been told "Go" by the Vasus, he related this to me.
Having heard that, you have been liberated by me from that curse;
for even the King of the Gods could not defeat you in battles. A son is considered one's own self; therefore, you were defeated here by him.
"In my opinion, there is no fault in this; or how do you consider it, O Lord?
When he had been addressed thus, Vijaya, with a serene soul, spoke these words:
"O Queen, everything that you have done is very dear to me."
Having spoken thus, Jaya then addressed his son, the lord of Maṇipūra,
while Citrāṅgadā, the daughter of the Kuru lineage, was listening:
"The horse sacrifice of Yudhiṣṭhira shall take place during the coming full moon of Caitra."
"O King, you should go there together with your ministers and accompanied by your two mothers.
Having been addressed thus by Pārtha, the wise King Babhruvāhana, his eyes clouded with tears, spoke these words to his father.
"O knower of dharma, at your command I shall come to the great horse-sacrifice as the server of the twice-born;
however, for the sake of showing me favor, please enter your own city."
"O Śatrughna, together with your two wives, let there be no hesitation on your part in this matter.
Having dwelt here happily in your own home, free from all affliction, O Lord,
you shall once again set out in pursuit of the horse, O best among victors."
Thus addressed by his son,
the ape-bannered son of Kuntī then smiled and spoke to the son of Citrāṅgadā:
"O mighty-armed one, it is known to you how I am observing this initiation."
"O large-eyed one, I shall not enter your city as long as this sacrificial horse proceeds according to its will. May you be well; I shall depart, for no place remains for me here."
Having been duly honored there by him, that subduer of Pāka,
permitted by his two wives, departed, O best of the Bharatas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having traversed this earth as far as the edge of the ocean,
that steed turned back, O King, facing toward the city named after the elephant. And as he returned, the radiant wearer of the diadem followed him.
At that time, he arrived by chance at the city of Rājagṛha.
When he had come near, the heroic King, the grandson of Jarāsaṃdha’s son,
established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, challenged him to battle.
Then, having emerged from the city, Meghasandhi— charioteer, archer, and shield-bearer— rushed toward the foot-soldier Dhanañjaya.
And having approached Dhanañjaya, the highly energetic Meghasandhi [attacked him].
"O Great King, out of childishness and not from skill, he spoke thus:
'Why is this horse being led like one among women, O Bhārata? I shall seize this horse; strive to set him free!'"
If you were not previously conciliated by my fathers when they were distressed in battle, then surely you have reached the further shore of the arts of war.
"I shall provide you hospitality; strike me, or I shall strike you.
Thus addressed, the Pāṇḍava replied to him as if laughing:
"It is my established vow that I must ward off anyone who creates an obstacle for me."
"O King, this must surely be known to you as well, through your eldest brother:
strike according to your strength; I harbor no anger.
Having been addressed thus, the Lord of Magadha struck the Pāṇḍava first.
Scattering thousands of arrows like the thousand-eyed Indra pouring down rain,
the heroic wielder of the Gāṇḍīva then, O bull of the Bharatas, effortlessly rendered those shafts futile with arrows dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva.
Having rendered his flood of arrows futile,
he whose banner bears the monkey discharged blazing shafts that resembled serpents with flaming mouths;
[he struck] upon the standard, the flagstaffs, the chariot mechanism, and the horses.

While [the wheel] was being protected by Pārtha on other parts of the chariot— neither on the body nor on the charioteer— the Magadha king, regarding his own prowess as supreme, discharged arrows at Phalguna’s body.
Then the hero who wields the Gāṇḍīva bow, having been struck by the king of Magadha,
shone like a great palāśa tree in full bloom during the spring.
Though he was not being slain, that king of Magadha continued to strike the bull among the Pāṇḍavas.
O descendant of Kuru, he stood there for the sake of beholding that hero of the world;
but Savyasācin, filled with rage, drew his bow with great force,
rendered the horses lifeless, and struck off the head of the charioteer.
With a razor-sharp arrow, he cut down his great and variegated bow;
he then struck down his hand-guard, his banner, and his standard. Deprived of his horses, his bow, and his charioteer, that king was deeply distressed.

Seizing his mace, the impetuous one rushed with speed toward the son of Kuntī. As he was charging, [Arjuna] swiftly cut that gold-adorned mace into many pieces with numerous arrows feathered with vulture plumes.

That mace, shattered and its jeweled bindings broken, fell upon him in a thousand fragments like a female serpent casting off its slough. Deprived of his chariot, his bow, and his mace, he stood there.
The wise Arjuna, the leader at the forefront of battle, did not wish to strike him.
Then, to him who was dejected yet remained established in the duty of a Kṣatriya,
the one whose banner bears the ape spoke these words with conciliation:

"O son, this duty of a Kṣatriya has been sufficiently demonstrated; you may now depart. O King, this feat performed by you in battle while still a youth is truly great. Yet, Yudhiṣṭhira’s command remains: 'The kings must not be slain.'"
"O King, because of that you live, even though you have wronged me in battle.
Thinking thus, the King of Magadha realized he had been rebuked;
understanding this to be the truth, he honored him with palms joined in reverence.
"I am defeated; may you be blessed! I do not venture to fight here anymore.
Tell me whatever task must be done by me for you today, and it shall be considered as already accomplished.
Having thus consoled him, Arjuna spoke these words once more.
"You must come for our king’s horse sacrifice on the full moon of Caitra.
Having been addressed thus, he replied, "So be it," and Sahadeva’s son honored that horse and Phalguna, the best of warriors, according to the prescribed rites.
Then that lion-like king went once more wherever he desired;
along the shore of the ocean, he passed through the lands of the Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras,
and Keralas, and here and there encountered numerous and vast armies of Mlecchas.
