"O King, Dhananjaya conquered [all] with his bow, Gāṇḍīva.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, the Pāṇḍava whose steeds are white was honored by the ruler of Magadha."
Taking his stand in the southern direction, he caused that horse to roam;
then, turning back again, that powerful horse, moving at will,
reached the beautiful city of the Cedis known as Śukti.
O King, having been honored there by Śiśupāla’s son, the son of Śarabha,
with the honor and worship due to a warrior,
that mighty and excellent horse then departed.
Having received due honors there from the Kāśīs, Andhras, Kosalas, Kirātas, and Taṅgaṇas, that son of Pāṇḍu,
the son of Kuntī, returned and then proceeded toward the Daśārṇas.
There, a powerful lord of the earth named Citrāṅgada [dwelt];
with him, Vijaya had a most terrifying battle.
And having brought even him under his control, the diadem-wearing Kṛṣṇa, that bull among men—
He went to the territory of Ekalavya, the king of the Niṣādas;
then the son of Ekalavya challenged him to battle,
and he engaged in a hair-raising conflict with the Niṣādas.

Then the heroic son of Kuntī, undefeated in battles, conquered him as well in combat— he who had risen up to obstruct the sacrifice. Having defeated that Nishāda prince, O great king, the son of Indra [Arjuna]—
Having been honored, he set out once more toward the southern ocean.
There too, the diadem-wearing hero engaged in battle with the Dravidas, the Andhras, the fierce Māhiṣakas, as well as those from Kollagiri.
Having conquered them as well with no excessive violence, Vijaya then,
following the course of his horse, proceeded toward Surāṣṭra;
and having reached Gokarṇa, he also went to Prabhāsa.
Then that glorious horse, fit for the sacrifice of the Kuru king, reached the beautiful city of Dvāravatī, which was protected by the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
Having thrown down that best of horses, the young princes of the Yādavas [seized it].
O King, as they were then departing, Ugrasena restrained them.
Then, having emerged from the city, the lord of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas,
accompanied by Vasudeva, the maternal uncle of Kirīṭin, [departed].
Having approached the best of the Kurus, they both stood before that foremost of the Bharatas, honoring him with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rites; then,
permitted by them, he proceeded toward where the horse had gone.
Then that horse gradually traversed the vast western region of the ocean, and from there he went to Pañcanada;
from there as well, O descendant of Kuru, the horse proceeded to the territory of Gāndhāra.
Then, followed by the son of Kuntī, he roamed at will;
there, a terrible battle took place between that high-souled one and the King of Gāndhāra,
the son of Śakuni, who pursued their former enmity.
14,085.001 Vaiśampāyana said: The heroic son of Śakuni, a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) among the Gāndhāras, advanced against Guḍākeśa, surrounded by a vast army.
Unable to endure the slaughter of King Śakuni, those warriors, accompanied by a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots adorned with garlands of flags and banners,
advanced together against Pārtha with their bows drawn.

The righteous-souled and unconquered Bībhatsu spoke to them these words of Yudhiṣṭhira, yet they did not accept his beneficial advice. Though restrained by Pārtha with conciliatory words, they remained filled with indignation.

Surrounding the horse, they advanced; then the Pāṇḍava grew enraged. Thereupon, with razor-sharp arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva whose tips were blazing, Arjuna severed their heads as if without even the slightest effort.
Being slaughtered by Pārtha, O great king, those [Gāndhāras], afflicted intensely by the rain of arrows, abandoned their horses in confusion and retreated;
and even while being pierced by those Gāndhāras, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas [remained].
Repeatedly commanding them, the radiant hero struck off their heads.
While those Gāndhāras were being slaughtered on all sides in the battle,
that king, the son of Śakuni, opposed the Pāṇḍava.
To that king who was fighting, firmly established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, Pārtha said: "By the command of the King, kings are not to be slain by me.
Enough with this battle, O hero; there shall be no defeat for you today."
Thus addressed, deluded by ignorance and disregarding those words,
he covered Śakrasamakarman with arrows.
Pārtha [then struck] his helmet with a feathered crescent-headed shaft.
Without any agitation, he struck off Jayadratha’s head, just as [Arjuna had done].
Seeing that, all those Gāndhāras were filled with wonder;
they also understood that the king had not been killed because he so desired it.
But the son of the king of Gandhāra, intent on flight, shone together with those very terrified men like a small deer surrounded by its frightened herd;
while they were thus running about right there, Pārtha pursued them with great speed.
With broad-headed arrows of straight joints,
he severed their heads; yet some did not realize that their uplifted arms had been struck down by arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, broad and impelled by Pārtha.
Then that army— its men, elephants, and horses bewildered,
and the majority of it slain or shattered— turned back again and again;
for not a single one could be seen before that hero of preeminent deeds.
Even those enemies who might withstand his great arrows while being struck down by them—
then the mother of the king of Gāndhāra, preceded by his aged ministers, came forth in fear, bringing forward an excellent offering of honor (*arghya*).
She, remaining unperturbed, restrained her son who was intoxicated by the frenzy of battle;
she then sought to appease Jiṣṇu, the doer of effortless deeds.
Having honored her, the son of Kuntī then showed his favor.
And consoling the son of Śakuni, he spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, it is not pleasing to me that you have formed this intention;
O slayer of foes, O sinless one, you are indeed my brother, though you wish to fight against me."

"O King, it is because you remember your mother Gāndhārī and because of what Dhṛtarāṣṭra has done that you still live, while your followers have been slain. Do not be thus; let this enmity cease, and let such a thought never again enter your mind."
"You must come to our king’s horse sacrifice on the next full moon of Caitra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Pārtha followed that horse which roamed at will.
The Gandhāras who had survived the slaughter returned to their own city;
then the horse turned back toward the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Yudhiṣṭhira heard of its return through a spy.
Having heard that Arjuna was well, his heart became joyful;
and having heard of Vijaya’s deeds in the land of Gandhāra as well as in other regions at that time, the king became exceedingly pleased.
At that very time, on the twelfth day of the fortnight of Māgha,
having observed the auspicious constellation, the high-minded and highly energetic Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira summoned all his brothers.
Then, at that time, the Kaurava, the best among the upholders of dharma, the foremost of speakers, addressed these words to Bhīma, Nakula,
and Sahadeva after calling out to Bhīma of terrible prowess.
"Here comes that Bhīmasena, your younger brother, together with his horse,
just as the men who follow Dhananjaya have told me.
The time has arrived, and the horse is now close at hand."
"O Vṛkodara, this is the full moon of Māgha; the month is now at its conclusion.
Therefore, let the learned Brāhmaṇas, who have mastered the Vedas, set out to find a sacrificial site for the successful accomplishment of the horse sacrifice."
Thus addressed, Bhīma carried out that command of the king; hearing from the monarch that Savyasācin was approaching, he was filled with joy. Then Bhīmasena set forth together with wise architects.
Placing at the forefront Brahmins skilled in the rituals of sacrifice,
he then [prepared] that site, praiseworthy for its sacrifices and endowed with every auspicious mark—
a place featuring the village of Śālacaya, complete with its main streets and watchtowers.
The Kuru prince measured out the sacrificial ground according to the prescribed rules;
it was crowded with hundreds of palaces and featured floors inlaid with the finest jewels. There were the assembly hall, the quarters for the wives, and also the northern fire-sanctuary.
He caused it to be constructed according to the prescribed rites, adorned with jewels and gold; he erected pillars variegated with gold and massive archways,
having provided pure gold for the sacrificial grounds.
The righteous-souled king caused inner apartments to be constructed according to the prescribed rules here and there for the rulers dwelling in various lands,
as well as dwellings for the Brāhmaṇas who had assembled from diverse regions.
Bhīma had various kinds of things made in great numbers;
likewise, O Great King, Bhīmasena dispatched messengers by the king’s command to those monarchs of unwearied deeds.
Those best of kings came for the sake of the Kuru lord,
bringing with them many jewels, women, horses, and weapons. As they were settling into their camps by the thousands, [the earth trembled].
The roar, like that of the surging ocean, seemed to touch the very heavens.
Rising to meet them and paying homage, he announced the arrival of the brahmins to the lotus-eyed king.
As those guests arrived, the king—whose eyes were like lotuses—[honored them].
The King of Dharma, that tiger among men, ordered food and drink, as well as superhuman beds; he also assigned various stables for the mounts, provided with rice, sugarcane, and milk.
Indeed, the various castes were gathered there separately, each honored more than the one preceding it;
likewise, at that great sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja,
many hosts of sages who were exponents of the Veda assembled.
O lord of the earth, those who were the most eminent among the twice-born and had assembled there with their disciples— the Kaurava received them all and escorted them as far as their lodgings.
Then, having personally abandoned all deceit, the highly resplendent Yudhiṣṭhira—
after which the architects, craftsmen, and others who were there,
O King, completed the entire sacrificial ritual and reported it to the King of Dharma.
Having heard that everything had been performed without reproach, the King of Dharma,
the steadfast monarch, together with his brothers, became filled with joy;
and may that glorious Lord be a bestower of merit upon all people.
14,087.001 Vaiśampāyana said: When that sacrifice had commenced, eloquent men who were skilled in dialectic, desiring to defeat one another, uttered many logical arguments.
The kings beheld that supreme arrangement of the sacrifice,
O descendant of Kuru, which had been prepared by Bhīma like that of the Lord of the Gods.
There they saw archways made of gold.
There were many beds, seats, and pavilions adorned with jewels; the kings saw no vessel there— not a jar, a bowl, a cauldron, a pitcher, or a water-pot— that was not made of gold.
And he [prepared] sacrificial posts made of wood as prescribed in the scriptures, adorned with gold,
of great splendor, and duly fashioned at the proper time;
and whatever animals there were, O Lord, whether born on land or in water.
Those kings beheld all of them brought together:
cows and buffaloes, as well as aged women,
aquatic creatures, beasts of prey, and birds.
They beheld beings born from a womb, born from eggs, born from sweat, and born from sprouts; they saw creatures of the mountains, the marshlands, and the forests,
O King, all brought there according to rule by the command of the monarch.
Seeing the entire sacrificial enclosure thus overflowing with cattle, wealth, and grain, the kings were filled with supreme wonder; and there,
various kinds of food were being distributed incessantly.
There was an abundance of highly refined and opulent food for both the Brahmins and the Vaiśyas. While a full hundred thousand Brahmins were eating there,
drums with the resonance of thunderclouds were struck again and again.
Then, day after day, he let out shouts of joy again and again;
thus did that sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja proceed. O King, there were many heaps of food, like mountains, distributed therein.
The people beheld streams of curd and lakes of clarified butter.
Indeed, O King, the entire Jambūdvīpa, filled with various provinces,
appeared gathered in one place during that great sacrifice of the king.
There, O bull of the Bharata race, thousands of men from here and there arrived, bringing with them vast quantities of wealth. These kings were adorned with garlands and polished jeweled earrings.
Then, by the hundreds and thousands,
they served those foremost of the twice-born with various kinds of food and drink; those men who were followers gave to the brāhmaṇas the very same foods that the king himself consumed.
14,088.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen the kings and lords of the earth who had assembled there, all of whom were knowers of the Vedas,
King Yudhiṣṭhira then spoke to Bhīmasena.
"These tigers among men who have arrived here are the lords of the world;
let worship be offered to them, for these lords of men are worthy of honor.
Thus addressed, he acted accordingly at the command of the illustrious king.
O Bhārata, the highly energetic Bhīmasena was there together with the twins;
then Govinda, accompanied by the Vṛṣṇis, approached the son of Dharma—
he who is the Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice, and known through all the Vedāntas.
The gods, sages, and brahmins, having mentally worshipped Keśava,
rose up from their seats; then Mādhava,
the best among all living beings, entered there, placing Baladeva at his head.
Accompanied by Yuyudhāna, Pradyumna, Gada, Niśaṭha, Sāmba, and likewise Kṛtavarman—
the mighty-armed Bhīma paid them the highest honor.
Those bulls among men entered their jewel-adorned dwellings. Then,
at the conclusion of the conversation in the presence of Yudhiṣṭhira, Madhusūdana spoke of Arjuna, who had been worn down by many battles.
The son of Kuntī questioned that subduer of enemies again and again;
the King of Dharma, the lord of the world, spoke to his brother Jiṣṇu:
"O King, a trusted messenger from my residence in Dvārakā has arrived."
"He who saw the best of the Pāṇḍavas, emaciated by many battles,
and reported that the mighty-armed one was nearby, said to me, 'O Lord,
perform the necessary rites for the successful accomplishment of the horse sacrifice, O son of Kuntī.'"
Thus addressed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, replied to him:
"By good fortune, O Mādhava, that Jiṣṇu is well and approaches us;
tell me what he, the leader of the Pāṇḍava forces, has commanded."
"O delighter of the Yadus, I wish for you to explain that here.
When this was said, O tiger among kings, the eloquent lord of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas then spoke these words to the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O Great King, that man said this to me:
'O Kṛṣṇa, at the proper time, these words of mine must be spoken to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Kings will come from all directions toward the Kauravas. "
"An individual worship of each of them must be performed; this is indeed appropriate for us.
O giver of honor, the king should be informed of these words of mine:
"That which might occur during the bringing of the *arghya* offering shall not be considered an emergency."
"The king ought to do this, and may you also grant your consent;
otherwise, O King, these subjects might perish again through hatred toward their ruler.
And that man spoke these other words as well, O son of Kuntī:
"O King, listen as I recount to you the wealth of Dhanañjaya:
the lord of Maṇipura,
my son Babhruvāhana, who is possessed of great splendor and dear to me, shall come to our sacrifice."
"O Lord, you should honor him according to the prescribed rites for my sake;
for he is devoted and constantly attached to me," said [Kṛṣṇa].
Having heard these words, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [acted accordingly].
Having rejoiced at those words of his, he spoke these words:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, this pleasant thing which you deign to speak has been heard."
O Lord, this [account] of yours, which resembles the essence of nectar, gladdens my mind. Indeed,
it has been heard by me, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that there were many battles fought by Vijaya against various kings at various places.
"For on account of Manu, that son of Pṛthā has always been deprived of happiness;
though the wise Vijaya is so exceedingly brilliant, my mind is grieved.
O Vārṣṇeya, I constantly reflect upon the son of Kuntī in solitude."

O son of Pāṇḍu, that man constantly experiences extreme suffering. What inauspicious mark, O Kṛṣṇa, exists upon his body— though it is otherwise honored with every auspicious sign— by which he undergoes these miseries?
"That son of Kuntī has always been a partaker of extreme suffering;
yet, I do not see anything blameworthy in the limbs of Bībhatsu.
If this is indeed something I ought to hear, you should explain it to me."
Thus addressed, Hṛṣīkeśa, Viṣṇu— the enhancer of the Bhoja kings— having meditated for a very long time, spoke to the king:
"O King, I do not perceive anything unfavorable regarding him."
Except for the two calves of this exceedingly tall man, who is a lion among men,
that tiger among men is constantly yoked to his journeys;
for I see no other reason why this conqueror should be a partaker of such hardship.

Having been addressed thus with these truths by the wise Kṛṣṇa, that best of the Kurus said to the tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, "So be it," O Lord. But Draupadī Kṛṣṇā looked askance at Kṛṣṇa with resentment.

Hṛṣīkeśa, the slayer of Keśin, accepted her affection just as Dhananjaya himself would; for he was the friend of his friend. There, Bhīma and the others, as well as the Kurus and the Yādavas, [were present].
O Lord, having heard those stories of Dhanañjaya containing such diverse meanings, they were filled with wonder. While they were thus engaged in conversation concerning Arjuna,
a messenger arrived from the high-souled Vijaya with a message.

Having approached the best of the Kurus and paid his respects, that wise man announced to him that Arjuna, that tiger among men, had arrived. Upon hearing this, the king’s eyes became clouded with tears of joy.

On that occasion, he indeed gave away much wealth for the sake of announcing pleasant news. Then, on the second day, a great sound increased as that tiger among men, the leader of the Pāṇḍavas, was approaching.
Then a cloud of dust arose from that horse as it moved about,
appearing just like that of Uccaiḥśravas;
there Arjuna heard the joyful voices of the men.
"By good fortune you are well, O Pārtha; blessed is King Yudhiṣṭhira!
For who else but Arjuna could have returned after conquering the entire earth along with its kings and having caused that best of horses to wander?"
"Among those high-souled kings of the past, such as Sagara and others,
we have never heard of any such deed performed even by them.
Nor will future rulers of the earth ever do this."
"O best of the Kuru lineage, that which you have performed here is indeed difficult to accomplish"—
hearing such words from those men, pleasant to the ear,
the righteous Phalguna entered the sacrificial arena.
Then the king, together with his ministers and Kṛṣṇa, the joy of the Yadus,
placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, went out to meet him.
He, having saluted the feet of his wise father, Dharmarāja, [proceeded further].
Having honored Bhīma and the others as well, he embraced Keśava;
embraced by him, whose nature is gentle and who is a vessel of nectar, [Bhīma] attained great happiness.
Having met with them and been honored by them, he in turn honored them according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having reached the shore like one who has crossed to the further bank, that righteous-souled one found rest.
At that very time, however, the wise King Babhruvāhana,
accompanied by his two mothers, arrived in the land of the Kurus.
There, O child, he approached the elders— the Kurus and other kings—
and having met all the Kurus, he was greeted by them all. Having saluted those mighty-armed ones, he was in turn welcomed by them.
14,089.026 He entered the excellent residence of his paternal grandmother Kuntī.
14,090.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,090.001a Having entered the dwelling of the Pāṇḍavas according to custom, he...
Accompanied by his two mothers, the self-controlled one,
bowing low with humility according to tradition, there paid homage at the feet of Kuntī and Gāndhārī.
With a most beautiful chant, she addressed her grandmother;
likewise, Queen Citrāṅgadā and the daughter of the Kauravya also approached Pṛthā and Kṛṣṇā together with humility.
And according to custom, Kuntī gave Subhadrā and the other women of the Kuru lineage [to Arjuna]; then she bestowed various jewels upon them both.
And Draupadī, Subhadrā, and the other women also gave gifts.
There those two queens dwelt upon costly beds and seats,
highly honored by Kuntī herself out of her desire to do what was pleasing to Pārtha;
and that king of great heroism, Babhruvāhana, was also honored.
He approached King Dhṛtarāṣṭra according to the prescribed rites,
as well as King Yudhiṣṭhira and the other Pāṇḍavas, including Bhīma;
having approached them, the one of great splendor greeted them with humility.
Embraced by them with affection and honored according to tradition,
those great car-warriors, being delighted, gave him abundant wealth.
In the same way, that protector of the earth [honored] Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the discus and the mace.
Like Pradyumna attending upon Govinda with humility,
he waited upon him; to that king, Kṛṣṇa gave a highly precious and honored chariot, adorned with gold, yoked to divine horses, and most excellent.

Dharmarāja, Bhīma, the twin sons of Mādrī, and Phalguna likewise each honored him, who was so worthy of respect, individually and exceedingly. Then, on the third day, the sage who was the son of Satyavatī—
Approaching Yudhiṣṭhira, the eloquent one spoke these words:
"O son of Kuntī, begin the sacrifice from this day forth, for it is now your time;
the auspicious hour for the sacrifice has arrived, and the officiating priests urge you."
"O Indra among kings, this sacrifice of yours is named Ahīna and is characterized by various options;
because of the abundance of gold, it is known as Bahusuvarṇaka.
In this very manner, O Great King, make the sacrificial fee threefold."
"O King, let your state become threefold, for the Brahmins are the authority in this matter. By performing three horse-sacrifices here accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
O lord of men, you shall cast off the sin incurred by the slaughter of your kinsmen."
"For this is indeed the supreme purifier, the purifier of all purifiers,
which you shall attain, O joy of the Kurus, at the final ablution of the horse sacrifice.
Thus addressed by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, that radiant hero—
Then the righteous king entered upon the initiation for the sake of attaining the horse sacrifice;
the lord of men performed the great Vājimedha sacrifice,
which was provided with abundant food and sacrificial fees and endowed with all desirable qualities.
There, O King, the officiating priests who were knowers of the Vedas performed the rituals;
wandering about, they were learned in the scriptures and well-trained according to the rules. Among them, there was no lapse, nor was there any omission of the offerings.

There, those bulls among the twice-born performed the rites both in their proper sequence and with due application. Having duly performed the *pravargya* ceremony, O King, those best of the twice-born, who were knowers of dharma, likewise performed the *abhiṣava* according to the prescribed rules.

Then, O King, having pressed the Soma, those best of Soma-drinkers performed the libations in their proper sequence according to the scriptures. There, no one was miserable, nor did anyone become poor.
Whether hungry, distressed, or even an ordinary man,
Bhimasena of great splendor constantly caused food to be given to those seeking food, always by the command of the king.
And the officiating priests,
skilled in the ritual arrangements and possessing the eye of knowledge regarding the meaning of the scriptures, performed all the rites day after day.
Among the members of that wise king’s assembly, there was no one who was not learned in the six Vedāṅgas.
A twice-born man who is not observant of vows, who lacks a preceptor, or who is incapable of debate is not [fit for this].

Then, O bull of the Bharatas, when the time arrived for the erection of the sacrificial posts, six were made of Bilva wood, six of Khadira wood, and an equal number of all other varieties, along with fuel-sticks of Bilva.
In the sacrifice of the Kuru king, the officiating priests caused two sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) made of *devadāru* wood to be fashioned, and one made of *śleṣmātaka* wood;
all of these they duly prepared in accordance with the scriptures.
O bull among men, at the command of Dharmarāja, that Bhīma caused other sacrificial posts made of gold to be fashioned for the sake of beauty;
O royal sage, they shone forth, adorned with garments.
The king approached the gods like the Seven Sages approach the deities in heaven. There, golden bricks were prepared for the purpose of the sacrificial altar;
the construction there shone like that of Prajāpati Dakṣa himself.
That altar of his consisted of four layers and measured eighteen cubits; it was shaped like Garuḍa, constructed with threefold layers, and adorned with golden wings.
Then the wise ones offered the sacrificial animals according to the scriptures.
14,090.032 Directed toward each respective deity, they employed birds and beasts,
14,090.033 as well as bulls mentioned in the scriptures and those that dwell in the water;
all of these they utilized there in the rite of piling the sacrificial fire.
Three hundred animals were likewise bound to the sacrificial posts;
and for that high-souled son of Kuntī, the king, there was the jewel among horses as the preeminent offering.
That sacrifice of his shone brightly, crowded with celestial ṛṣis in person.
It was crowded with hosts of Gandharvas, graced by throngs of Apsarases,
adorned with the songs of Kimpuruṣas and embellished by Kinnaras;
it was surrounded on all sides by the dwellings of Siddhas and Brahmins.
In that assembly were the constant disciples of Vyāsa, the best of the twice-born,
who were the authors of all the Śāstras and skilled in the rituals of sacrifice; Nārada was also there, as was the highly effulgent Tumburu.
Viśvāvasu, Citrasena, and other Gandharvas skilled in song— experts in singing and proficient in dances—
then delighted those Brahmins during the intervals between the sacrificial rites.
14,091.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having duly pacified the other sacrificial animals, those best of the twice-born brahmins sacrificed that horse according to the scriptures.

Then, O King, having consecrated the horse according to the prescribed rites, those bulls among sacrificers— experts in sacrificial acts and authors of all the scriptures— caused Drupada’s daughter to lie down beside it.
O King, with three thousand one hundred and nine kalās,

according to the prescribed rite, those bulls among the twice-born, having extracted the omentum of that [victim], cooked it without distraction according to the scriptures and the rules, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then Dharmarāja, together with his younger brothers, smelled the scent of the smoke from the omentum according to the prescribed rite, which at that time removes all sins.
O lord of men, as for those other limbs of the horse that remained—
All sixteen wise officiating priests together offered those [oblations] into the fire. Having thus completed that sacrifice of the king, who possessed the splendor of Indra,
the venerable Vyāsa, along with his disciples, offered blessings upon that monarch.

Then Yudhiṣṭhira, according to the prescribed rites, bestowed a thousand crores of gold coins upon the members of the assembly, and the earth upon Vyāsa. Having accepted the earth, O King, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, [bestowed it].
He spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of the Bharatas and the soul of righteousness:
"O best of kings, this earth is now offered to you;
let a ransom be given to me, for Brāhmaṇas are seekers of wealth."
The high-minded and wise Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, replied to those brahmins in the midst of the great-souled kings:
"In the great horse sacrifice, the earth is traditionally prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."

"O best of Brahmins, this earth has been conquered by Arjuna and brought by me to you priests; I shall enter the forest. Divide this earth into four parts, according to the measure of the fourfold sacrificial office (cāturhotra)."

"O best of sages, I do not wish to take the property of a Brahmin; for this has always been my view, O sinless ones, as well as that of my brothers. When he had spoken thus, those brothers and Draupadī—
"So be it," they said, and that was hair-raising.
Then, O Bhārata, a voice arose in the sky saying, "Excellent! Excellent!
And likewise, the sound of the throngs of twice-born ones praising resounded.
Thus addressed, the sage Dvaipāyana, honoring him in the midst of the brahmins, spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"This [cow] was given to me by you; I now give it back to you."
"Let gold be given to these twice-born ones, but let the earth remain yours.
Then Vāsudeva said to the King of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira:
"You ought to do exactly as the venerable Vyāsa has said."
Thus addressed, that best of the Kurus, his soul filled with joy along with his brothers,
bestowed as a sacrificial fee for the rite three times ten million times ten million [gold pieces].
No other lord of men in this world shall ever do such a thing.
14,091.020c That which was performed by the lion of the Kurus, imitating Marutta; 14,091.021a having accepted that wealth, the lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
the wise one, gave it to the officiating priests, and they divided it into four parts.
Having given that gold as the ransom for the earth, Yudhiṣṭhira—
purified of sin and having conquered heaven— rejoiced together with his brothers.
At that time, the officiating priests [received] that boundless heap of gold.
They distributed [the wealth] among the twice-born according to their enthusiasm and according to their strength.
Whatever was in the sacrificial enclosure— be it gold, even ornaments,
as well as archways, sacrificial posts, jars, vessels, and bricks— [all were given away].
Authorized by Yudhiṣṭhira, all those twice-born ones divided that entire [wealth].
Immediately thereafter, the Kṣatriyas took wealth from the Brāhmaṇas,
as did the multitudes of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and likewise other Mleccha tribes.
After a long time, they brought that gold from here and there;
then all those brahmins, satisfied by that wealth from the high-souled Dharmarāja, departed for their homes in great joy.
The illustrious and highly effulgent Vyāsa gave his own share of that vast quantity of gold to Kuntī as a respectful greeting at her feet.
Having received that gift of affection from her father-in-law, she was delighted in heart.
Then Pṛthā performed a very great act of merit in the world;
having gone to the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*), the king, together with his brothers, was freed from sin and shone while being honored, like Mahendra among the gods.
And the Pāṇḍavas, surrounded then by the assembled kings,
shone, O great king, like the planets amidst the hosts of stars.
Then he bestowed various jewels even upon the kings.
Elephants, horses, ornaments, women, garments, and gold—
that boundless flood of wealth— King Pārtha, as he distributed it throughout the circle of the earth, shone like Vaiśravaṇa himself.
And having summoned the heroic King Babhruvāhana,
he then bestowed upon him vast wealth and sent him back to his home;
likewise, O bull among kings, [he sent] that young grandson of Duḥśalā.
In his own kingdom, protected by his ancestors,
the self-controlled Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira joyfully consecrated them all; having honored those kings with due distinction, he sent them all on their way.

Having honored the high-souled Govinda, the mighty Baladeva, and likewise thousands of other Vṛṣṇi heroes such as Pradyumna and others according to the prescribed rites, O great king, that one of great splendor—
Accompanied by his brothers, the king, the subduer of enemies, dispatched [the messengers].
Thus did that sacrifice of the wise Dharmarāja take place,
with a vast flood of food, wealth, and jewels, and oceans of *surā* and *maireya* liquors.

O bull of the Bharatas, there were many lakes with ghee for mud, mountains of food, and canals with cream of curd for their mire; and the cry arose, "Let the various kinds of snacks and sweetmeats be prepared! Let them be eaten!"
Even as animals were being slaughtered there, no end to them could be seen; at that time, the place became delightful with intoxicated, mad, and joyful people, with young women singing,
and with the sounds of mṛdaṅga drums and conchs.
"Let it be given! Let it be enjoyed!"—thus there was a great clamor day and night without restraint, "Let it be drunk! Let it be given!"
Men dwelling in various countries spoke of that place, which resembled a great festival and was crowded with exceedingly joyful people, saying:
"Having rained down streams of wealth, as well as objects of desire, jewels, and riches..."
Free from sin, that best of the Bharatas, having accomplished his purpose, entered the city.
Janamejaya said:
"At the sacrifice of my grandfather, the wise son of Dharma—"
"Whatever wonder occurred, you ought to tell it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen, O tiger among kings, to this great and supreme marvel."

O Lord, O best of the Bharatas, when the great horse sacrifice was concluded, when the foremost of the twice-born, as well as kinsmen, relations, and friends, had been gratified, and even the poor, the blind, and the wretched were satisfied— then [what occurred]?
O Bhārata, while the great gift was being proclaimed in all directions and showers of flowers were falling upon the head of Dharmarāja,
O sinless one, Nakula, with his golden flanks, then emerged from his burrow.
O lord of the people, he let out a roar like a thunderbolt;
having uttered that roar once, terrifying the beasts and birds,
the great cave-dweller, bold and fearless, spoke these human words.
"O lords of men, this sacrifice of yours is not equal to that of a generous man who lives by gleaning grains and resides in Kurukṣetra, even if he offers only a prastha of barley meal.
O lord of the people, having heard those words of Nakula, [the king...]
All those bulls among brahmins were filled with supreme wonder.
Then, gathering together, those twice-born ones questioned Nakula:
"From where have you come to this sacrifice, this assembly of the virtuous?"
"What is your supreme strength? What is your learning? What is your ultimate refuge?
How may we know you, who censures our sacrifice—a sacrifice performed by officiating priests who are experts in the ritual rules and have not violated the entirety of the sacred tradition?"
Whatever was to be done has been performed according to the scriptures, according to what is right, and as it was prescribed.
Those worthy of worship have been honored here according to rule by one whose eye is the scripture;
the fire has been offered oblations purified by mantras, and gifts have been given without stinginess.

The best of the twice-born were gratified there by various kinds of gifts; the Kṣatriyas by fair combat; the ancestors by the Śrāddha offerings; the Vaiśyas by protection; and excellent women by the fulfillment of their desires.
The Śūdras were satisfied by his compassion, the common folk by the remnants of his gifts,
and our kinsmen and relatives by the King’s purity; the gods were gratified by his holy oblations, and those who sought refuge by his protection.
"O you who are true to your word, tell us what is the truth here among the twice-born;

speak as you have heard it and as you have seen it, for you are questioned out of a desire for the welfare of the brahmins. You are one whose words are trustworthy, you are wise, and you bear a divine form."
"Having met with these brahmins, you ought to speak the truth. Thus questioned by those twice-born ones, Nakula laughed and said:
"O brahmins, these words spoken by me are neither false nor uttered out of pride."

"O lords of men, whatever little I have said and whatever you have heard from me— that this sacrifice of yours is not equal to a single measure of barley-meal given by a generous man living in Kurukṣetra who subsists on the gleanings of grain."
"O best of the twice-born, this must certainly be told by me to you;
listen with undistracted minds as I recount it, O bulls among the twice-born—
whatever supreme wonder has been experienced and seen by me."
[The story] of how a twice-born man dwelling in Kurukṣetra, who lived by the gleaning of grains, attained heaven together with his wife, sons, and daughters-in-law according to his conduct;
and how half of my own body was turned to gold.
Nakula said:
"O twice-born ones, I shall indeed describe to you the supreme fruit of giving— that which is obtained through righteous means, even if it be small, when bestowed upon a Brahmin."
In the field of dharma, Kurukṣetra, which was crowded with many who knew the dharma,
there lived of old a certain twice-born man who subsisted by gleaning, following the practice of the pigeon. He dwelt in austerity together with his wife, his son, and his daughter-in-law.
Accompanied by his daughter-in-law as the fourth, that virtuous and self-controlled brahmin, firm in his vows, would eat at the sixth mealtime together with them;
yet sometimes, at that sixth mealtime, no food was found for him.
O best of the twice-born, that man sometimes ate at the sixth mealtime;
O brahmins, understand that during a terrible famine, no store of food remained for him who lived like a pigeon.
At that time, having exhausted his collection of medicinal herbs and being destitute of wealth,
no food was to be found for him whenever mealtime arrived.
Then, overcome by hunger, they all set out.
Then, while the sun was scorching at midday during the bright fortnight,
that brahmin, established in austerity and afflicted by heat as well as hunger,
failed to obtain any gleaned grain together with his attendants.

Afflicted by hunger in that very same way, that best of the twice-born, his life-breaths barely sustained, passed that time after touching water according to the prescribed rite. Then, when the sixth period had elapsed, he procured a prastha of barley.
Those ascetics made a *prastha* of barley into flour; having performed their prayers and daily rites and offered oblations into the fire according to the rules,
all those ascetics divided it portion by portion, each taking a *kuḍava*.
Then, while they were eating, a certain brahmin guest arrived.
Seeing that guest there, they became joyful in heart.
Having greeted him and then asked after his welfare, they welcomed the guest.
Those of pure mind, self-controlled, endowed with faith and self-restraint;
free from malice, devoid of anger, virtuous, and free from envy; having abandoned pride, conquered wrath, and knowing the Dharma—these are the best of the twice-born.
Having announced their own lineage and their status as fellow celibate practitioners to one another,
they then led the guest, who was afflicted by hunger, into the hut.
"O sinless one, here is the water for honor (*arghya*), here is the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and here is this seat (*bṛsī*) for you."
"O Lord, these pure groats have been acquired through self-restraint;
please accept them, O best of the twice-born, for they are given by me—may prosperity be yours! Having been addressed thus, the brahmin then accepted a *kuḍava* measure of the groats.
O Indra among kings, he ate [the food], yet he did not attain satisfaction.
Seeing that twice-born man overcome by hunger,
he who lived by gleaning reflected upon how he might provide food so that the man would be satisfied.
"O King, his wife said, 'Let my share be given;
let this best of the twice-born depart as he pleases, well-satisfied.
To that virtuous woman who was speaking thus, that righteous bull among the twice-born [replied]:"
Knowing her to be overcome by hunger, that bull among brahmins did not welcome those barley-meals; for the wise man, at that time, inferred [her state] from his own experience,
knowing her to be aged, afflicted by hunger, exhausted, emaciated, and a woman of ascetic toil.
Then he spoke to his wife, who was trembling and reduced to skin and bone:
"O beautiful one, even among insects, moths, and wild beasts, women are to be protected and supported; you ought not to speak thus."
A man who is shown compassion by his wife, nourished and protected by her,
may fall from radiant glory and fail to attain the higher worlds.
Service, the continuity of the lineage, and the pursuit of virtue, pleasure, and wealth [depend upon her].
Dharma depends upon one's wife for the sake of both the ancestors and oneself.
That man who, being incapable of protecting his wife, does not do so through his own effort,
incurs great infamy and goes to the hells.
Having been addressed thus, she then said: "O twice-born one, for us both, dharma and artha are equal.
Be gracious to me and accept this fourth part of a prastha of barley-meal.
Truth, pleasure, dharma, and heaven are all won through virtuous qualities."
O best of the twice-born, women are dependent upon their husbands for everything they desire. The mother provides the season, the father provides the seed, but the husband is the supreme deity.
Indeed, it is through the grace of the husband that women obtain both pleasure and the fruit of sons.
"For you are my lord because of your protection, and my husband because of your support;
you are the granter of boons because of the gift of a son—therefore, accept these barley-meals from me. You are overcome by old age, aged, afflicted by hunger, and exceedingly weak."
"When you too are exhausted from fasting and emaciated," thus addressed by her, he took the barley meal and spoke these words:
"O best of beings, O twice-born one, please accept this barley meal once more."
Having accepted those [gifts] and eaten them, the twice-born man did not attain satisfaction.
Observing him, the one who lived by gleaning became filled with anxiety. Then his son spoke to his father, whose mind was dejected:
Bowing down with humility,
the son spoke these words,
which were full of reason: "O best of men, take these parched grains and give them to the brahmin."
"14,093.030c Thus, I consider this to be a virtuous deed; therefore, I shall do this.
14,093.031a For you, O best of the twice-born, must be protected by me with every effort.
14,093.031c For this nourishing of an aged father is indeed desired by the righteous."
"For this purpose of obtaining a son was ordained for youth, while protection [of the world] belongs to old age;
such is the sacred tradition (śruti), O brahmin-sage, renowned throughout the three worlds.
By the mere sustenance of life, penance can indeed be performed by you."
"For life is indeed the supreme dharma, established within the bodies of embodied beings.
The father said:
"Even though you are a thousand years old, in my eyes you are still but a child."
"For once a father has begotten a son, he indeed becomes one who has fulfilled his duty. O Lord, I know that hunger is powerful in children;
I am old, I shall sustain myself, so be strong, my little son."
"O son, though my age is advanced, hunger does not afflict me;
for I have practiced austerities for a long time, and I have no fear of death.
The son said:
"I am your offspring, your son; for a son is so called because he provides protection. A son is remembered as one's own self (*ātman*); therefore, protect yourself here by means of yourself.
O brahmin-sage, I am your son; I must be protected by you at all times."
"Now, however, let these parched grains be given to this hungry one.
The father said:
"In beauty, you are my equal, as are you in character and self-restraint."
"Parīkṣit has been tested by me in many ways, and therefore I accept these barley-meals from you. Having said this— by means of his humility, his intellect, his conduct, and likewise his patience—
the best of the twice-born, with a joyful soul, took those barley-meals.
As if laughing, he then gave them to that Brahmin;
yet even after eating those barley-meals, he was not at all satisfied,
and that best of the twice-born, who lived by gleaning, became filled with shame.
Standing there, that virtuous daughter-in-law, desiring to do what was pleasing to the Brahmin,
took the barley meal and, filled with joy, spoke these words to her father-in-law:
"O Brahmin, through your lineage, my own lineage shall continue."
"Take these barley groats for my guest and give them to me;
through the fulfillment of your labor, imperishable worlds are indeed promised to you. Through a grandson, one attains those realms where, having gone, one does not grieve."
For just as the triad of Dharma and the others constitutes a triad, so too does the triad of fires;
likewise, for one's sons and grandsons, this triad indeed becomes an inexhaustible means to heaven.
We have heard it said that a son is called "putra" because he rescues (trāṇāt) his ancestors.
"Accompanied by sons and grandsons, she will certainly attain the worlds of the righteous.
Śvaśura said:
"Indeed, seeing you with limbs wasted by wind and sun, and your complexion turned pale..."

"How can I, becoming a destroyer of dharma, take the parched grain from you who are emaciated by your observance of vows, whose mind is overwhelmed by hunger, and who are of auspicious conduct? O auspicious lady, you ought not to speak thus."

"How shall I ever see you at the sixth mealtime, observing your vows, endowed with virtue and purity, living in hardship and fasting? You are a young woman afflicted by hunger; as such, you must always be protected by me."
"You are indeed exhausted from fasting, O delighter of your kinsmen. The daughter-in-law said:
"You are truly my guru's guru, since you are the deity of my deities."
"O God beyond gods, O All-pervading Lord, therefore please accept these barley-meals from me.
My body, my life-breath, and my merit exist solely for the sake of serving my guru;
by your grace, O Brahmin, I shall attain the worlds I desire."
"O twice-born one, you ought to take these parched grains, considering that they are to be looked after by me, or because of your firm devotion, or thinking, 'This is my concern.
The father-in-law said:
"By this constant excellence of character and conduct you shine, O virtuous lady;
for you, endowed with the vows of dharma, observe the proper behavior toward your elders.
Therefore, I shall take the barley meal; O daughter-in-law, you do not deserve to be deceived."
"O highly fortunate one, you are indeed the best among the upholders of dharma; having counted [the grains], you have reached 14,093.054c.
Having said this, she took those barley-meals and gave them to the twice-born man.
Thereupon, the brahmin became satisfied with that virtuous and high-souled man.
With a joyful soul, he spoke these words to that bull among the twice-born;
at that time, the eloquent one was Dharma himself, the best of the twice-born, embodied in human form.
"By your pure gift, which has been acquired with effort through righteous means..."
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased that you have given according to your ability.
Oh, your gift is being proclaimed in heaven by the inhabitants of heaven!
Behold, a rain of flowers has fallen from the sky upon the earth."
O Mahāmati, having gone swiftly for infinite celestial years,
the divine sages, gods, gandharvas, and those who lead the gods,
as well as the messengers of the gods, stood there praising him, struck with wonder by his generosity.
The Brahman-sages dwelling in celestial chariots and those who have gone to the world of Brahmā long for a sight of you; go to heaven, O bull among the twice-born!
All your ancestors who have gone to the world of the Pitṛs have been delivered by you.
And many others yet to come, throughout very many ages,
[have attained their goal] through celibacy, sacrifice, charity, and likewise through austerity and straightforward dharma; therefore, O twice-born one, go to heaven.
"O you of excellent vows, because you practice asceticism with supreme faith,
the gods are pleased with this of yours, O best among the foremost of the twice-born;
for all the deities are not so pleased by the asceticism of a self-controlled man as they are by this."

"Since you have renounced all this property with a pure heart at a time of great hardship, heaven has been won by you through this deed. For hunger drives away wisdom and dispels the understanding of dharma."
When one's knowledge is overwhelmed by hunger, one indeed abandons fortitude.
But he who conquers hunger certainly conquers heaven;
when one takes delight in giving, then righteousness does not perish.

Disregarding affection for your sons and affection for your wife, and recognizing Dharma alone as supreme, you did not take account of craving. For men, the acquisition of wealth is a minor matter; giving to a worthy recipient is superior to that.
Time is superior to giving, and faith is even more supreme than that. Indeed, the gateway to heaven is extremely subtle; it is not seen by men due to delusion.
It is the bolt of heaven, with greed as its seed, guarded by passion, and difficult to overcome.

But men who have conquered anger and subdued their senses— Brahmins endowed with austerity who give according to their ability— behold that [state]: one with a thousandfold power sees a hundred, and one with a hundredfold power sees ten.
"Whoever gives water according to their ability is recorded as having a fruit equal to all [other gifts]. For King Rantideva, though possessing nothing,
gave water with a pure mind, O Brahmin, and thereby ascended to the heights of heaven."

"O dear one, Dharma is not so pleased by gifts of great fruit given away as he is satisfied by even small gifts that are obtained righteously and purified by faith. King Nṛga gave thousands of cows to the twice-born."
By giving away a single cow belonging to another, he fell into hell;
whereas King Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, by the gift of his own flesh,
attained the worlds of the merit-makers and rejoices in heaven, O observer of noble vows.

O Brahmin, for men who possess wealth, merit is acquired through their own power; for the virtuous, it is what they have earned by their own efforts. But that merit of men which is devoid of effort is like a roar at that time—it is not equal to the merit gained through various sacrifices duly accumulated.
Anger destroys the fruit of giving; through greed, one does not go to heaven.
For one who lives by righteous conduct and knows how to give through austerity enjoys heaven, even more so than by performing many Rājasūya sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.

"O sinless one, even with many horse-sacrifices, this fruit is not equal to yours; for by means of a single measure of barley-meal, you have conquered the world of Brahmā. O Brahmin, go as you wish to the stainless abode of Brahmā."
"O best of the twice-born, a divine vehicle has appeared for all of you. Ascend it as you please; I am Dharma, behold me!
For your body has been purified by you, and your fame shall endure forever in the world."
"Go to heaven together with your wife, your son, and your daughter-in-law.
Having been addressed with these words by Dharma, that twice-born man ascended the vehicle and,
accompanied by his wife, son, and daughter-in-law, departed for heaven.
When that wise brahmin had departed for heaven, accompanied by his son,
his daughter-in-law, and his wife— the four of them, all knowers of dharma— I then emerged from the cave,
drawn out by the scent of the barley meal and the moisture of the water.
By the crushing of divine flowers by that virtuous man, by those fragments of his gifts,
and by the ascetic power of that Brahmin, my head has been turned to gold— indeed,
by the subtle gift of that one who was true to his promise.
"O brahmins, one half of my body has been made of gold;
behold this vast expanse produced by the ascetic power of that wise man.
O twice-born ones, he thought, 'How might my other side become just like this?'"
"Delighted, I have visited ascetic groves and sacrifices again and again;
yet, having heard of this sacrifice of the wise Kuru king,
I came with the highest hope, and I have not been turned into gold."
Then, O best of the twice-born, I laughed and said those words:
"In no way is this sacrifice equal to a measure of barley-meal.
For by those measures of barley-meal, I was then turned into gold.
"Indeed, this great sacrifice is not equal to those [other gifts] in my opinion;
in my view, this sacrifice is not equal to a single measure (*prastha*) of barley-meal.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having spoken thus to all the best of the twice-born at the sacrifice, O King, Nakula then vanished from sight, and those brahmins returned to their homes. All this has been related to you by me, O conqueror of enemy cities.
Whatever wonder occurred during that great horse sacrifice,
O King, you should not feel any astonishment regarding that sacrifice in any way;
for thousands of millions of sages have gone to heaven through their ascetic penances.
"Non-malice toward all beings, contentment, good conduct, and straightforwardness; austerity, self-restraint, truthfulness, and charity—these are considered equal.
Janamejaya said:
"O Lord, kings are devoted to sacrifice, great seers are devoted to austerity,
and Brahmins are intent upon tranquility— peace and self-restraint.
Therefore, there is nothing in this world equal to the fruits of sacrifice."
"Such is my understanding, and this is undoubtedly so:
for many kings, O best of the twice-born, having sacrificed with various rites,
attained supreme fame in this world and, after death, departed from here to heaven."
The thousand-eyed king of the gods,
the all-pervading one of great splendor, attained the entire sovereignty of the gods through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
O best of the twice-born, kings likewise [attain their status] through sacrifices and extensive austerities.
Having attained supreme fame in this world, they now abide in heaven—
just as King Yudhiṣṭhira, preceded by Bhīma and Arjuna,
is equal to the king of the gods in both prosperity and prowess.
14,094.006a Then why did that Nakula censure that sacrifice— 14,094.006c the Aśvamedha, the great sacrifice of that high-souled king?
14,094.006d For this reason, O Great King, Nakula censured it.
"O King of great intelligence, O Lord of the Earth, the Dharma is subtle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O bull among men, [the king asked about] the foremost ritual procedure of the sacrifice and its fruit."
"Listen to me as I speak, O King, O Bhārata, exactly as it happened here.
Long ago, while Śakra was performing a sacrifice and the sacrificial rites were spread out, all the great seers spoke to the officiating priests who were busily engaged in their duties."
While the fire was being offered oblations by the Hotṛ priest endowed with many virtues,
and while the gods were being summoned and the supreme ṛṣis remained present, O King,
the Brahmins then [proceeded] with their own scriptures, accompanied by excellent voices.
Then, O great king, at that time of the ritual immolation, when the animals had been seized by tireless and agile bulls among the *adhvaryu* priests,
the great seers were filled with compassion.
Then, seeing the wretched animals, those sages whose wealth was their asceticism approached Śakra and said: "This sacrificial rite is not auspicious;
it is a lack of discernment on your part, even though you desire great merit."
"O Purandara, herds of animals are not prescribed for sacrifice according to the sacred injunctions. O Lord, this undertaking of yours is a destroyer of dharma;
this is not the dharma practiced by those who follow dharma, for violence is never called dharma."
"If you so desire, let them perform your sacrifice according to the sacred tradition alone;
through a sacrifice performed according to the prescribed rules, your merit shall be exceedingly great. O Thousand-eyed One, perform the sacrifice with seeds that have been stored for three years."
"O Śakra, when this great Dharma is contemplated, it is realized. But Śatakratu, following the sway of pride and delusion, did not accept those words spoken by the seers who perceive reality.

A very great dispute arose among those Śakra and the great seers, O Bhārata, as to whether sacrifices should be performed with moving beings or even with stationary ones. Then those seers, who perceive the truth, became weary of the dispute.
Then, having entered into an alliance with Śakra, they questioned King Vasu, who had fallen into doubt regarding the Dharma: "O high-minded one, speak the truth!
O illustrious king, how is the traditional authority (*āgama*) regarding sacrifices remembered?"
"Sacrifices should be performed with animals fit for the altar, as well as with seeds and even goats.
Having heard those words of theirs, the king, without considering their relative strength or weakness, declared: "Sacrifices must be performed with whatever has been brought forth."
Having spoken thus, that king entered the subterranean realm (rasātala),
O King, after having uttered a falsehood here as the lord and master of the Cedis.
Therefore, in a matter of doubt, one should not speak at all, even if one is highly learned.
Having abandoned Prajāpati, the self-existent Lord,
that unwise man who, desiring merit, performs a sacrifice with wealth acquired through unjust means or long since passed away, does not enjoy the fruit of his dharma.
But that wicked-souled man who is a hypocrite regarding the Dharma gives gifts to the Brahmins merely to inspire confidence in the world;
having obtained wealth through sinful deeds, the unrestrained Brahmin—

Filled with passion and delusion, he attains a defiled state in the end. The gifts given by that evil man, whose intellect has been destroyed, perish even though they were extensive, for they do not reach the realm of sentient beings.
For that evil-minded man who is engaged in unrighteousness, who is harmful,
and who is wicked, no fame arises from giving, either in this world or after death;
for his mind is intent on hoarding, having fallen under the sway of greed and delusion.
One of evil intent causes living beings to tremble through violence;
even if such a person, having acquired wealth through greed, performs sacrifices and gives gifts,
he does not attain success by that action because of its wicked origin.

For he who might give or perform sacrifices does not enjoy the fruit of that after death, because of his acquisition of wealth through evil means. O those whose wealth is austerity, [even] gleaning, roots, fruits, vegetables, or a vessel of water— 14,094.029d*0191_01 **** **** He who indeed might give or sacrifice, 14,094.029d*0191_02 does not enjoy its fruit after death because of the acquisition of wealth through sin. 14,094.030a Gleaning, roots, fruits, vegetables, or a vessel of water, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Having given gifts according to their means, righteous men go to heaven.
This great dharma consists of renunciation, charity, compassion for all beings,
as well as celibacy, truthfulness, kindness, fortitude, and forgiveness.
This is the eternal root of the eternal dharma. Indeed,
it is heard that in ancient times there were Brahmins and kings such as Viśvāmitra and others—
Viśvāmitra, Asita, and Janaka the lord of the earth.
Kakṣasena, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and King Sindhudvīpa—
these and many other kings, rich in asceticism, attained supreme perfection through truthfulness and gifts acquired by righteous means.
"O Bhārata, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those who have taken refuge in austerity— purified by the fire of the duty of giving (dāna-dharma)— they go to heaven.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, if everything exists through a renunciation that accords with the Dharma,
then explain all of this to me, for you are skilled in speaking. Then [tell me] what occurred regarding the one who lives by gleaning, concerning the great fruit of the gift of roasted flour."
"O Great Brahmin, this which has been told to me is the truth, without a doubt.
How indeed may the supreme certainty regarding all sacrifices be attained?
You ought to explain this to me in its entirety, O bull among the twice-born."
14,095.004 Vaiśampāyana said: O subduer of enemies, in this connection they cite this ancient history concerning what occurred in the past at the great sacrifice of Agastya.

In ancient times, O great king, the highly effulgent Agastya, devoted to the welfare of all beings, entered upon a twelve-year initiation. At that sacrificial session (*sattra*) of that high-souled one, there were officiating priests (*hotṛ*) who were like fire itself.

There were ascetics and mendicants established therein who subsisted on roots, who took no food at all, who ground their food with stones, and who drank only rays of light; likewise, there were those who lived on what was rubbed [from rocks], those who ate only leftovers, and those who washed away [their impurities].
All of them had direct perception of Dharma; they had conquered anger and mastered their senses.
They were all established in self-restraint and were entirely free from hypocrisy and delusion. They remained constantly fixed in pure conduct and were never led astray by their senses.
Those great ṛṣis attended that sacrifice,
partaking of the food which had been acquired by the Blessed One according to his capacity; indeed,
in that sacrificial session, there was nothing whatsoever that was unfit.
14,095.010 For indeed, many great sacrifices have been performed by numerous sages.
14,095.011 While such a great sacrifice of Agastya was thus proceeding, O best of the Bharatas, the thousand-eyed Indra did not send rain at that time.
Then, O King,
during an interval between rituals, this conversation took place among the high-souled sages of purified minds:
"This Agastya, performing a sacrifice, gives away food free from any sense of possessiveness."
The rain-god does not send down rain; how will there be food?
O Brahmins, this great sacrificial session of the sage is for twelve years, yet the god will not rain during these twelve years.
"O sirs, having reflected upon this, you ought to show favor to this wise great seer Agastya, who is possessed of extreme ascetic power. When these words had been spoken, the powerful Agastya then—
Having propitiated the sages by bowing his head, that eloquent one spoke these words:
"If Vāsava does not send rain for twelve years, I shall perform a sacrifice of meditation; this is the eternal ordinance."
"If Vāsava does not rain for twelve years, I shall perform the sacrifice of touch; this is the eternal rule. If Vāsava does not rain for twelve years..."
Through physical exertion, I shall offer other sacrifices that surpass all vows;
with a meditative soul and restrained observance of vows, I shall take away these [other] sacrifices. Indeed, this seed-sacrifice has been accumulated by me over many years.
"Once the seeds have been sown, I shall perform [the rite], and no obstacle shall arise here. It is not possible for this sacrifice of mine to be rendered fruitless in any way.
Whether the god rains here or whether the god does not rain, it shall come to pass."
"Or rather, Indra might grant my request, yet not out of his own desire;
I myself shall become Indra and I shall sustain the subjects. Whatever kind of food each being requires, that shall be exactly so for them."
"I shall indeed create a distinction again and again, for it is truly extraordinary.
Let gold come here today, as well as whatever other wealth is difficult to obtain;
let whatever exists in the three worlds come here of its own accord."
May the divine hosts of Apsarases, along with the Gandharvas and Kinnaras,
and Viśvāvasu and whoever else there may be, always attend upon you. And whatever wealth exists in the Northern Kurus, may that also be yours.

"May all of that, as well as heaven, those who dwell in heaven, and Dharma itself, present themselves here at my sacrifice of their own accord. When this was said, everything came to pass exactly so for that wise man.

Then, having beheld the power of that sage’s asceticism— the Agastya of blazing fire-like luster and exceeding splendor— all those sages were struck with wonder and spoke these words of great significance.

"We are pleased by your words, yet we do not desire the depletion of your ascetic merit. We are satisfied by our own sacrifices; we desire that you perform them according to the rules. We seek for you sacrifices, initiations, oblations, and whatever else you may require."
"May that [merit] be ours through our own performed sacrifices; we do not seek it from any other source.
Sustaining ourselves with food acquired through righteous means and devoted to our own duties, we seek the Vedas through the practice of celibacy in accordance with the law."

"In due time, having departed from our homes according to the right method, we shall perform austerities through the gateways of ritual prescribed by the Dharma. For this understanding of yours is indeed perfectly free from violence."
"O Lord, you should constantly proclaim this non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) in sacrifices;
then, O best among the foremost of the twice-born, we shall be pleased. Once dismissed at the conclusion of this sacrificial session (*satra*), we shall depart."
14,095.033 Vaiśampāyana said: 14,095.033a While they were thus conversing, Purandara, the king of the gods, possessed of great majesty, sent down rain upon seeing the power of his asceticism.
And while that sacrifice was still unfinished,
O Janamejaya, the lord of the gods, whose prowess is immeasurable, became a rain-giver at will;
and the lord of the thirty deities propitiated Agastya.
Having approached him in person, O royal sage, and placing Bṛhaspati at the forefront,
he then dismissed those great sages upon the completion of the sacrifice. At that moment, Nakula vanished there in the forest.
Agastya, being exceedingly pleased, honored him according to the prescribed rites.
Janamejaya said:
"Who was that person in the form of a mongoose with a head indeed made of gold?"
14,096.001c He spoke these words like a human; being thus questioned, speak this to me.
14,096.002 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,096.002a "I have not been asked about this before, nor has it been spoken by us."

Listen to who this Nakula was and how his speech became human. It is said that in ancient times Jamadagni resolved to perform a *śrāddha* ceremony; the sacrificial cow came to him, and he milked her himself.
He placed that milk in a new, sturdy, and pure vessel; however, Krodha, in his own physical form, overturned the pot,
wishing to test what that best of sages would do when an unpleasant act was committed.
Having thought thus, the dull-witted one assailed that milk.
Recognizing his anger, the sage did not become angry with him at all.
But Krodha, standing before him in embodied form with palms joined in reverence, spoke this to him.
When he had been defeated, the indignant one addressed the best of the Bhṛgus:
"O best of the Bhṛgus, I am indeed defeated; for the Bhṛgus are exceedingly prone to anger. This is a false report in the world, that I have been vanquished by you."
"O virtuous one, I who now stand before you, a high-souled being endowed with forgiveness, am afraid of your ascetic power; O Lord, show me your grace.
Janamejaya said:
"O Krodha, you have been seen by me face to face; go now, free from your fever.
No harm has been done to me by you today, nor does any anger remain within me. However, regarding those for whose sake this resolve concerning the milk was made by me—"
"Those ancestors of yours are highly fortunate; learn from them and depart.
Having been addressed thus, he was seized with fear and vanished on the spot;
yet, due to the curse of the ancestors, he had already attained the state of a mongoose.
He sought to appease them so that there might be an end to the curse.
Then, O Great King, he was told by them: "At the horse sacrifice of Dharmarāja, he shall come and be released from the curse."

And when they said to him, "When you cast aside dharma, then you shall be released," he was told by them to go to the lands fit for sacrifice and the forests of dharma; wandering about in contempt [for them], he approached that sacrifice.

Then, having cast his son Dharmaputra aside with that measure of barley-meal, Krodha was released from the curse; for Yudhiṣṭhira was indeed Dharma himself. Thus did this event occur at the sacrifice of that high-souled one.
Even as we were looking on there, Nakula then vanished;
and that Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace—
the one worthy of sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, the lotus-eyed Janārdana— [also disappeared].
Vāsudeva, Hari, Viṣṇu, Ananta, who is kind to his devotees—
the Lord of the World, Hari— protected the sacrifice until its conclusion. Having protected it, that mighty-armed one went to the city of Dvārakā.
O Great King, this merit bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who hear it. Both the listener and the one who causes others to hear it go to the supreme goal—
Janamejaya.
In the past, when the horse sacrifice had been performed, what did the Grandfather ask Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, regarding a doubt concerning dharma? Vaiśampāyana said: [He asked this].
O King, when Yudhiṣṭhira had bathed after the western horse-sacrifice,
he then paid homage to Keśava and spoke again:
"O Blessed One, what are the fruits of the Vaiṣṇava duties, and what is their ultimate goal?"
With reference to what dharma were you produced in the past?
O Madhusūdana, if I am worthy of your grace and am dear to you;
and if it is something I may hear, O Kṛṣṇa, then tell it to me, O you of noble vows.
"O Blessed One, those dharmas which have issued from your mouth are indeed pure, the destroyers of all sins, the most excellent of all dharmas, and meritorious;
having heard them, even a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a killer of a mother, or one who violates the teacher's bed [is purified]."
One who ruins what has been cooked, an ungrateful person, a drinker of liquor, a seller of the Veda,
one who betrays the trust of a friend, a slayer of heroes, a destroyer of embryos,
as well as a seller of asceticism and a seller of gifts— [these go to the Raurava hell].
The foolish who sell themselves, those who live by forbidden occupations,
the sinful, the deceitful, the dishonest, the hypocritical, as well as the slanderers,
those who corrupt flavors, and those who are slayers of Brahmins— [these are excluded].
Those Śūdras who perform menial service, thieves, those Brahmins who act as domestic priests,
those who misappropriate deposits, those who kill women, and likewise those who commit adultery—
these and other such sinners are also liberated from their transgressions.
"Tell them to me, O best of gods, for I am your devotee, O Acyuta. When the god had been thus addressed by the son of Dharma in that assembly,
Vasiṣṭha and the other sages, endowed with ascetic power and perceivers of truth, [spoke].
Desirous of hearing the supreme secret, the highest Vaiṣṇava dharma,
Yudhiṣṭhira as well as the Bhāgavatas then surrounded him.
But in truth, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, if you know me to be a devoted and loving follower who has come to the soles of your feet,
I wish to know all the secrets of dharma according to their true nature.
"O Lord of Gods, if I am worthy of your favor, please speak to me of the dharmas.
I have already heard the dharmas of Manu, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa,
Gārgya, Gautama, and Gopālaka."

Formerly, those composed by Parāśara and by the wise Maitreya were heard by me; likewise, the Āumā, the Māheśvara, the Nandidharma, and the purifying Brahma-kathita and Kaumāra [texts] were heard by me.
The *dharmas* composed by Dhūmrāyaṇa, as well as those by Kāṇḍavaiśvānara;
likewise those by Bhārgavi and Yājñavalkya, and those composed by Mārkaṇḍeya;
and those composed by Bhāradvāja and those composed by Bṛhaspati.
Those composed by Kuṇa and Kuṇibāhu, those by Viśvāmitra, those composed by Sumantu and Jaimini, likewise those by Śākuneya,
and those sung by Pulastya, Pulaha, and Pāvaki.
The *Agastyagītā*, the purifying hymns of Maudgalya and Śāṇḍilya,
those composed by the Vālakhilyas and those composed by the Seven Sages,
as well as the *Dharma* treatises composed by Āpastamba, Śaṅkha, and Likhita.

I have heard the *Prājāpatya*, the *Yāmya*, and the *Māhendra* [dharmas]; the *Vaiyyāghra*, those sung by Vyāsa, and those composed by Vibhāṇḍaka; the *Nāradīya* dharmas have been heard, and the *Kāpota* have also been heard by me.
Likewise, there were the words of Vidura, as well as those of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras;
the Krauñcas, Mṛdaṅgas, Gītās, Sauryas, and Hārītakas;
and those composed by the Piśaṅgas, the Kautupas, and the Haṃsapālakas.
The *dharmas* composed by Uddālaka, as well as those of Uśanas,
those sung by Vaiśampāyana, and whatever others of this kind there may be—
from all these *dharmas*, O Lord, you have emerged from your own mouth.
Because they are purifying and holy, it is my opinion that they are distinguished. Therefore, for one who has sought refuge in you and is devoted to you with sincere intent— Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Acyuta, tell me of your own excellent and meritorious duties.
Thus questioned by the son of Dharma, Keśava, the knower of dharma,
being delighted, spoke of the duties whose meaning is subtle to the son of Dharma.
O son of Kuntī, O you of noble vows, since you thus exert yourself in these duties,
there is no one in this world to be found who is your equal;
for whether it be dharma heard, seen, spoken of, or even practiced—
O Indra among kings, even if merely rejoiced in, Dharma always purifies a person here in this world.
Dharma is father and mother; likewise, Dharma is protector and friend. O scorcher of foes, Dharma is brother and companion; Dharma is master and lord.
From dharma come wealth and pleasure; from dharma come enjoyments and happiness.
From dharma comes supreme sovereignty, and from dharma comes the highest state of heaven. Dharma, when practiced with purity, protects one from great fear.

Through dharma, a man attains the status of the twice-born and even divinity; dharma leads a person to these states. And when a man's evil is exhausted by the passage of time, O Yudhiṣṭhira, then the intelligence arises to practice dharma.

Human birth is indeed difficult to attain even after thousands of other lifetimes; having attained it here, he who does not practice the Dharma is a fool. Those who are contemptible, poor, deformed, and likewise afflicted by disease—[these are the fruits of such neglect].
Those who were servants of others and fools did not practice the Dharma in the past;
whereas those who were long-lived, heroic, wise, and possessed of enjoyments,
as well as those who were free from disease and endowed with beauty, had practiced the Dharma well in the past.
Thus, when dharma is practiced purely, it leads to the highest state;
but he who practices adharma falls into the womb of an animal.
O son of Kuntī, hear this secret, the unsurpassed dharma.
O Pāṇḍava, I shall declare the supreme dharma to you, my devotee. You are exceedingly dear to me, and you have always sought refuge in me;
I shall speak even of the ultimate truth, let alone that which is consistent with dharma.
This human birth of mine was brought about by my own power of illusion for the purpose of establishing righteousness and for the punishment of the wicked;
yet those who have fallen into this human state perceive me with contempt.
Those fools who wander here through various animal births many times over,
and those who behold Me dwelling in all beings with the eye of knowledge— I lead those My devotees, who are ever-disciplined, into My presence.
My devotees do not perish; my devotees are freed from all taint. O Pāṇḍava, for those devoted to me, birth in the human state is fruitful.
Even if they are intent upon sinful deeds, O son of Pāṇḍu, they remain my devotees.

They are liberated from all sins, like a lotus leaf by water. Devotion arises, O dear one, for those whose selves have been purified by austerity over thousands of previous births; of this there is no doubt.
That supreme form of mine, which is most secret, immutable, immovable, and eternal,
is not seen by the gods in the same way that it is seen by my devotees;
yet another form of mine is seen during my manifestations.
O Pāṇḍava, all beings worship that [form] with all their aims,
as thousands of millions of kalpas pass away and come again. I manifest that form here, and the gods behold it.
He who, having known me as the cause of persistence, origination, and dissolution, takes refuge in me—
him indeed I favor and I liberate from saṃsāra;
for I am the origin of the gods, and Brahmā and the others were created by me.
Supporting my own nature, I create this entire world. I am rooted in *tamas*, unmanifest; I am established in *rajas* at the middle;
and I am expansive with *sattva* above, designated as everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

Know the sky to be my head, and the moon and sun to be my eyes; the divine fire and the Brahmins are my mouth, and the wind is my breath. The eight directions are my arms, and the stars are my ornaments.

Know the atmosphere to be my vast chest, providing space for all beings; know that the path of the clouds and the wind is my imperishable belly; and the circle of the earth, with its continents, oceans, and mountains, is likewise my body.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, my feet are endowed with the power to sustain everything. For I abide in space with a single quality, and I am twofold in the wind; I abide in fire as threefold, and indeed fourfold in water.
The five qualities, beginning with sound, which reside in the five great elements— I, who am established in those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), abide in the earth in five ways.
I, moreover, possess a thousand heads, a thousand mouths, and a thousand eyes.
With a thousand arms, bellies, and eyes, a thousand thighs, and a thousand feet,
he stood firmly supporting the earth on all sides, towering above it by ten finger-breadths;
for I am the one who dwells as the self of all beings and am all-pervading.
I am inconceivable, I am infinite, I am ageless, and indeed I am unborn; I am without beginning, I am invincible, I am immeasurable, and I am imperishable.
I am devoid of qualities, my self is unrevealed, and I am free from dualities and free from possessiveness, O King.
I am partless and changeless, the very source of immortality.
O lord of men, I am the *sudhā*, I am the *svadhā*, and I am the *svāhā*.
By my splendor and my ascetic power, I sustain the fourfold collection of beings.

Bound by the cords of the snares of affection, I sustain [the world] through my own *māyā*. I am the dharma of the four stages of life (*āśrama*), the consumer of the fruits of the four sacrificial offices (*cāturhotra*).
