I possess four forms, four manifestations (*vyūha*), and I am the source of the contemplation of the four stages of life.
Having withdrawn the entire universe and made it my own womb,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I lie within the great ocean during the periods of dissolution by means of divine yoga for the duration of a night of Brahmā, which consists of a thousand yugas.
Abiding therein, I create all beings, both moving and stationary;
and in every kalpa, I withdraw and create all beings. Yet they do not know me, deluded as they are by my māyā.
O King, for me— who am darkness itself and must always be sought—
the course is not perceived at all, like that of an extinguished lamp;
there is no place anywhere, O King, where I am not established.

There is no being that exists which is not established within me. Whatever being there may be— whether gross or subtle, this entire world— I am its very life-force, for I am established in it to that same extent.
What is the use of saying more here? I tell you the truth:
whatever has been and whatever will be, all that is indeed myself alone.
O Bhārata, all beings have been created by me and consist of me.
Deluded by my *māyā*, they do not recognize me alone;
even so, O King, this entire world— including gods, asuras, and humans—
proceeds from me and dissolves back into me alone.
14,096.015d@004_0147 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,096.015d@004_0148 Having thus pointed out that the entire world originates from himself, 14,096.015d@004_0149 the Blessed Lord Keśava spoke.
Then the Lord recounted the meritorious duties of the Son of Dharma:
"Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to this truthfully, for it is purifying, destructive of sin,
meritorious, and the great fruit of the treatises on dharma as it is being told by me."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who, having become pure, with a single-minded focus and endowed with austerity, listens to this— which leads to heaven, brings fame, longevity, and righteousness, and is worthy of being known— for him,
who possesses faith, whatever sin was previously accumulated in this world [is destroyed].
Vaiśampāyana said:
"All that perishes quickly, especially for one who is devoted to me.
Having heard these meritorious and true words spoken by Keśava, [he was filled with joy].
With hearts full of joy, reflecting upon that supreme wonder—
All the gods, the celestial sages (brahmarṣis), as well as the gandharvas and apsarases, And likewise the bhūtas, yakṣas, grahas, guhyakas, and serpents (bhujaṅgas).
The high-souled Vālakhilyas, yogins who perceive the ultimate reality,
as well as the Bhāgavatas who observe the fivefold ritual at the appointed times,
were filled with curiosity, their senses and minds overflowing with joy.

Desirous of hearing the supreme Dharma from the teaching of the Dharma concerning Vaiṣṇava, and wishing to take those words to heart, they bowed their heads in prostration. Then they were beheld by Vāsudeva with a gentle eye.
Having beheld those freed from sin and having bowed his head to Hari,
the powerful son of Dharma questioned Keśava regarding righteousness:
"What is the nature of the duty for a Brāhmaṇa, and what is it for a Kṣatriya?"
"O Lord, what is the destiny of a Vaiśya, and what is the destiny of a Śūdra?
How is a Brāhmaṇa bound by the noose in the abode of Yama?
Or how is it that a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra is bound?"
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Lord of the World, tell me this fruit of action; salutations be unto you!
Thus was Keśava questioned by the wise son of Dharma.
The Blessed One spoke concerning the course of worldly existence for the four social orders born of their actions.
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O best among the upholders of dharma, to the dharma according to the sequence of the castes."
O best of men, there is no evil deed whatsoever for a Brāhmaṇa who remains constantly established in the inner self, who performs the twilight devotions,
who has attained the final oblation, and who offers sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
Those who perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, those who honor guests,
those who are constantly devoted to Vedic study, those intent on the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña),
those who offer oblations in the evening and morning, and those who abstain from feeding Śūdras— [they go to that world].
Those who are free from hypocrisy and falsehood, who are devoted to their own wives,
who are intent upon the five great sacrifices, and who attend to the *agnihotra*— for them,
the three fires, when being offered into, burn away all evil deeds.
Having destroyed their evil deeds, they go to the world of Brahmā;
in the world of Brahmā, they are sung to at will by the Gandharvas who sing to Brahmā, while they themselves are honored with devotion by the Self-Existent One.
They rejoice in the world of Brahmā until the dissolution of all beings;
likewise, a Kṣatriya established in his kingdom, a protector of his own dharma,
who properly guards his subjects and is always intent upon receiving the sixth part [of their produce].
Devoted to sacrifice and charity, steadfast, always intent upon his own wife, following the scriptures, knowing the truth, dedicated to the welfare of his subjects,
he was a constant granter of desires to the Brahmins and devoted to the maintenance of his dependents.
One who is true to his word, ever pure, and free from greed and hypocrisy— even a Kṣatriya— attains the supreme goal frequented by the gods; there,
he is honored especially by divine Apsarases and Gandharvas.
Being served and honored by Śakra, he of great splendor sports there for thirty-four yugas like a god; then,
in this world of men, he becomes a twice-born master of the four Vedas.
Devoted to agriculture and cattle-rearing, intent upon the pursuit of Dharma, likewise engaged in the duty of giving and devoted to the service of Brahmins;
he was true to his word, ever pure, and free from greed and hypocrisy.
Upright, devoted to his own wife, free from violence and malice, not abandoning the duties of a merchant, and honoring the gods and Brahmins—
the Vaiśya attains the heavenly realm, where he is honored by hosts of Apsarases.
Having sported for thirty-five *caturyugas*,
he becomes a powerful king here in the human world,
possessing fifty crores of gold and likewise a hundred of jewels.
He enjoys great wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots; he is always devoted to serving the three social classes,
and especially toward the Brahmins, he stands like a servant.
One who gives without being asked, who is endowed with truthfulness and purity, who is devoted to the worship of gurus and deities, who avoids the wives of others,
and who supports his circle of dependents without causing pain to others.
Even a Śūdra who grants fearlessness to living beings attains heaven;
having sported in the heavenly world for ten million years,
that one of great austerity shall become a lord of wealth as a Vaiśya in this human world.
Thus, there is nothing greater than the Dharma for liberation from saṃsāra;
nor is there anything superior to the Dharma for the removal of evil deeds.
Therefore, having attained this human state which is so difficult to find, one should always practice the Dharma.
For those who are devoted to righteousness, nothing in this world is difficult to obtain.
O Lord of Men, whatever dharma has been ordained for each person here by the Self-Existent One,
that one shall destroy their evil through its correct practice.

Whatever action is innate, that indeed cannot be abandoned by anyone; for that alone is his dharma, and through it he attains perfection. Even an imperfect performance of one's own duty dispels sinful action.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In this very way, even dharma is diminished by the increase of sin.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of Gods, I have indeed a great curiosity to hear [more about this]."
The Blessed One said:
"O King, listen to all that regarding the subtle and eternal Dharma: the destruction and increase of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, each in its proper order."
This is eternally most difficult to comprehend; here, great multitudes have been defeated.
Just as cold water, when covered by a great deal of heat, would instantly become hot and its coldness perish.
Just as when a small amount of heat is covered by a great deal of cold,
all that becomes cold and the state of heat perishes;
even so, whether it be a vast amount of merit or evil, [it is overwhelmed by the greater].
One should quickly exhaust that small amount; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Indra among kings, when those two—merit and demerit—are equal, that which is concealed increases, while that which is proclaimed undergoes diminution.

O King, O giver of honor, sin is generally destroyed through confession and remorse; however, dharma performed in such a manner is destroyed. Both of these, when properly concealed, undoubtedly attain growth.
Therefore, with every effort, a wise person should not conceal a sin;
therefore, one should proclaim it with diligence for the sake of its destruction.
Thus, one should confess one's evil and keep truth and righteousness concealed.
14,096.015d@004_0245 Vaiśampāyana said:
14,096.015d@004_0246 Having thus heard those words of Acyuta, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, spoke.
14,096.015d@004_0247 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The son of Dharma again questioned Hari regarding other matters: "O Puruṣottama,
how many births are in vain, what gifts are in vain,
and for which men is life in vain?"

In what circumstances, O Janārdana, is a gift given such that a person experiences its fruit in this world, O Puruṣottama? What does one experience while still in the womb, or even in childhood, O Keśava?
O Kṛṣṇa, what occurs in youth, and what might occur even in old age?
What kind of gift is characterized by goodness (sāttvika), and what kind is characterized by passion (rājasa)?
O Lord, what kind is characterized by darkness (tāmasa), and what, O Master, will satisfy the gods?
What kind of gift is supreme? What kind would be middling? What kind of gift is inferior? Tell me what the fruit of these is.
Indeed, what gift leads upward, and what would lead to a middling rebirth?
"O God of gods, tell me now of the lowest state;
I desire to understand this, for my curiosity is great. Your word, O Madhusūdana, is both true and meritorious."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus questioned with great effort regarding dharma by the son of Pāṇḍu,
Vāsudeva then spoke of the duties to the son of Dharma.
Listen, O King, to these words according to the proper method— words that are true, supreme,
meritorious, and which dispel all sins— as they are being told by me.
And [otherwise], O lord of men, ten and four births are spent in vain.
O King, I shall describe in due order all those fifty-five types of futile gifts and those six whose lives are likewise declared to be in vain.

The birth of those who destroy the Dharma, of the greedy, and likewise of the sinful, is in vain; so too is the cooking of those who eat it in vain, of those who take pleasure in the wives of others, of those who cause discord in the kitchen,
and of those who are devoid of truth.

If one eats delicacies alone while being watched by his kinsmen, or if he should strike or revile his father, mother, preceptor, teacher, maternal uncle, or paternal aunt; 14,096.015d@004_0273 He who eats choice food alone while being watched by his kinsmen,
14,096.015d@004_0274 Or likewise strikes or reviles his father, mother, preceptor, and teacher, 14,096.015d@004_0275 As well as his maternal uncle and paternal aunt— [he incurs great sin].

O Yudhiṣṭhira, that twice-born man who, having been a Brāhmaṇa, has abandoned the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana), is devoid of the Veda and the ancestral offerings (svadhā); he is a consumer of the food of Śūdras,
whether he belongs to me, to Śaṅkara, or even to Brahmā.

Furthermore, O Pāṇḍava, know that those lowest of men who are not devoted to the Brāhmaṇas have lived their lives in vain; for they are sinners. And whatever is given without faith, or even with contempt, [is likewise fruitless].
O King, that which is given even for the sake of hypocrisy, that which is taken by heretics,
that which is given for the conduct of Śūdras, that which is given and then publicly proclaimed,
that which is given with anger, and that which is given and subsequently regretted— [these do not yield fruit].
That which is given as earned through hypocrisy, or that which is acquired through falsehood; that which is given as the property of a Brāhmaṇa, or that which is acquired through theft;
that which is taken from one accused of a crime, or that which is given to a fallen twice-born man.

That which is taken away by those who have abandoned the Veda, that which is held by all types of beggars, that gift which is held by outcasts (vrātyas) and by those who have fallen from their status after having ascended [to it],
and that which is given to the husband of an unchaste woman or to one who follows after his father-in-law.

That which is taken by a village beggar, and likewise that which is taken by an ungrateful person; that which is given to one who has committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*), and that which is given to a seller of the Vedas;
and that which is given to one conquered by women, and that which is taken by a snake-catcher.

Whatever is given to a domestic priest, whatever is taken by a physician, whatever is given to a merchant, to one who lives by low mantras, to one who lives as a *śūdra*, and to a temple-priest (*devalaka*).

Whatever has been given to one who consumes the property of the gods, and whatever has been given to a painter; whatever has been given to one who lives by dyestuffs, and whatever has been given to one who lives by meat;
whatever has been given to a servant, and whatever has been given to one who is a Brahmin in name only.
That which is given to one who has abandoned the sacred fire, or that which is given to a usurer;

that which is given to one who lacks proper conduct, or that which is given to one who maintains no sacred fires; that which is given to one who does not perform the twilight devotions, or to one who dwells in a village of Śūdras.
Whatever is given to one who bears false marks, and whatever is given to a glutton;
whatever is given to an atheist, and whatever is given to a seller of dharma; whatever is given to a jailer, and whatever is given to a false witness.

O bull among kings, whatever gift is given to a village headman becomes entirely fruitless; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. For these lowest of Brahmins merely bear the name of a Brahmin while being greedy.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, these do not save themselves, nor do they save the donor;
O Indra among kings, even many gifts given to them become as useless as an oblation of clarified butter poured onto ashes.
Whatever fruit may arise from these in any way whatsoever,
the *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*, being delighted, shall plunder it;
for, in brief, these things have been given and spoken of in vain.
Listen, Yudhiṣṭhira, to those whose lives are in vain:
those lowest of men who do not take refuge in me, nor in Śaṅkara, nor in the Brāhmaṇas, the gods upon earth; those men live in vain.
Those who are attached to the treatises on logic (*hetuśāstra*), who have taken refuge in the path of false views,
who revile the Vedas, and who live immorally— those men live in vain. Those lowest of men who, having studied the scriptures composed by the wise, [act otherwise].
Those men who revile the Brahmins and the sacrifices live in vain;
and those who [revile] Durgā, Kumāra, Vāyu, Agni, Jala, Ravi,
the father, the mother, the guru, Indra, and the Moon.
Those fools who revile [the virtuous] and act without proper conduct live their lives in vain; likewise,
that man who, despite possessing wealth, is devoid of the practice of giving and righteousness,
and who eats choice food all alone— he too lives in vain.

Life is declared to be in vain; I shall now tell you about the proper time for giving. O King, whatever gift may be given by one whose mind is immersed in darkness, that man experiences the fruit of it while still within the womb.

That mortal who, joined with envy and stinginess, gives a gift for the sake of hypocrisy or for the sake of wealth, experiences that [result] in his state as a fool; though he desires to enjoy, he is unable to enjoy because he is severely tormented by diseases.
Whatever gift a mortal gives in his old age, he enjoys that in his old age;
whatever gift a mortal gives in his youth— endowed with faith, pure, bathed, and with senses and mind serene— he enjoys that in his youth.

That gift which is given with devotion to a worthy recipient after one has personally brought it oneself— know that, O Yudhiṣṭhira, such a gift is eternal, lasting until the end of one's life; it may be characterized as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or even *tāmasa*.
Listen to the nature of giving, the fruit of giving, and the threefold destiny.
When one forms the resolve, "Giving must indeed be performed," and bestows a gift upon a twice-born man who is free from any expectation of personal benefit— that is indeed *sāttvika* (pure) giving.

O Pāṇḍava, that which is given with joy to a learned Vedic scholar who is poor and has many dependents is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). But that which is given to one who is devoid of Vedic learning, even if he was formerly a benefactor—
That gift which is given to one who is prosperous is considered *rājasa*.
O Pāṇḍava, that gift which is given to a relative, to one who is intoxicated,
or to an unworthy recipient by those seeking rewards— that gift is considered *rājasa*.
A gift given to one who is devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, to one who is not learned in the Vedas,
or even to a thief— that gift is remembered as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). It is given with anger, with contempt, with affliction, and with disdain.
And that which is given to a servant is declared to be *tāmasa*.
O Lord of Men, the gods, the hosts of ancestors, the sages, and likewise the fires,
partake of and are satisfied by *sāttvika* gifts.
The Dānavas, the hosts of Daityas, the planets, the Yakṣas, along with the Rākṣasas,
and the Piśācas, the throngs of Pretas, and those who are dejected and defiled, consume the *rājasa* gift, which is devoid of the ancestors and the gods.

They consume the fruit of tamasic gifts; now hear of the threefold destination [of those who give]. The highest fruit is said to belong to sattvic gifts, the middling to rajasic, and the lowest to tamasic.
The highest fruit belongs to gifts brought and offered after approaching [the recipient];
the middling fruit belongs to those invited; and the lowest fruit belongs to those who ask. But he who gives without being asked attains the supreme goal.
He who gives after having been summoned shall go to the middling state;
he who gives when asked shall go to the lowest state. The divine state is to be known as the highest, and the human state is the middling one.
The lowest state of rebirth is among the animals; this destiny is said to be threefold.
However, whatever gift is bestowed upon Brahmins who are worthy recipients, well-established, and maintainers of the sacred fires, is proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
O King, provide for the maintenance of those learned in the Vedas who are poor;
you should ensure the protection of the prosperous twice-born,
and honor the indigent who lack a livelihood with generous gifts.
A sick person requires medicine; what need has one who is healthy for medicine? Sin reaches the recipient of a gift;
the merit of the recipient goes to the giver.

Therefore, one who desires the welfare of the hereafter should always practice giving. One should diligently establish a treasury consisting of great gifts among those purified by Vedic knowledge, who always abstain from the food of Śūdras.
O Pāṇḍava, invite those whose wives wait for them as if for the arrival of a thousand;
O Bhārata, having invited them, you must not leave them disappointed.
The hopes of those very poor families would be frustrated.
O best of men, one should diligently honor those who are my devotees, who have come to me, who are intent on me, who sacrifice to me, and who observe my rules.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, for their purification, I remain present at both twilights forever; indeed, that vow of mine is never broken. Therefore, the eight-syllable mantra [should be recited] by my devotees who are free from sin.
It should be recited constantly during the two twilights for the sake of self-purification;
indeed, the sins of other Brahmins as well are destroyed thereby. Therefore, a Brahmin should perform the service of both twilights for the sake of purity.
At a rite for the gods and at a *śrāddha*, that Brahmin should be appointed without hesitation;
however, one who is contemptible consumes the *śrāddha* like fire consumes fuel.
The *Bhārata*, the law of Manu, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, and medical science—these are the authorities.
The four [means of success] established by command are not to be refuted by logical arguments. One who knows the Dharma should not examine Brahmins at a rite for the gods;
there would be great censure in the examination of Brahmins.
That lowest of men who utters slander against Brāhmaṇas shall go to the womb of donkeys or dogs; that defiler of men,
by reviling them through slander, attains the state of a dog and becomes a donkey.
Through arrogance one becomes a worm; through envy one becomes an insect.
Whether they are ill-behaved or well-behaved, whether they are commoners or highly refined, Brahmins must not be despised, for they are like fires covered by ashes.
A wise man should never, under any circumstances, show contempt for a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak;
for these three, when treated with disrespect, may utterly consume a person.
Therefore, a wise person should not treat this with contempt through effort;
for just as fire is a great deity in all circumstances,
so too is the Brāhmaṇa a great deity in all circumstances.
Those who are crippled, one-eyed, humpbacked, or likewise have stunted limbs—

all these should be employed in the rites for the gods by those who have mastered the Vedas, provided they are mixed [with others]. One should not provoke their anger, nor should one treat them with inauspiciousness.
The Brahmins have wrath as their weapon; they are not Brahmins who carry swords in their hands. With their wrath, they slay their enemies, just as Indra slays the Asuras with his thunderbolt.
For a Brahmin is indeed a great divinity; he is born by the mere fact of his birth.
The Lord is the protector of all beings for the sake of guarding the treasury of Dharma;
how much more so, O son of Kuntī, those who constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
from whose mouth the dwellers of heaven consume the sacrificial offerings?
And what is the origin of the *kavyas* for the ancestors, and which being is superior? The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
A Brāhmaṇa eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brāhmaṇa’s compassion that other people eat. Therefore, they must never be despised, for these twice-born ones are always my devotees.
In the Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "O twice-born ones, those who behold me hidden in my partless state— honor them with great effort,
whether at home or while traveling abroad, by day or even by night."

O Pāṇḍava, those Brahmins who are my devotees should be honored with faith. There is no deity equal to a Brahmin; there is no teacher equal to a Brahmin. There is no kinsman superior to a Brahmin; there is no treasure superior to a Brahmin.
There is no sacred ford superior to the Brahmin; there is no merit superior to the Brāhmaṇa.
There is nothing more purifying than the Brahmins; there is no purifier greater than the twice-born. There is no dharma higher than the Brahmin; there is no goal higher than the Brahmin.
Even a single gift given to a twice-born man who has become a worthy recipient protects a man cast down by his evil deeds as he falls into hell—
those who maintain the sacred fires from their youth, who are tranquil, and who avoid the food of Śūdras.
My devotees worship me; what is given to them here becomes inexhaustible.
A Brahmin who is honored with gifts, or even saluted, praised, addressed, or merely seen, being a devotee of mine, shall lead one to heaven.

Those who recite [this], pay homage to, and meditate upon the Supreme Person— by touching or even by seeing them, a person is liberated from sins. My devotees, whose life-breaths are absorbed in me, who have gone to me, and for whom I am the supreme goal.
Those who are pure in their seed and origin, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), whose senses are restrained,
and who always abstain from the food of *śūdras*— they purify [others] here by their very sight. Furthermore, one should especially bring gifts to their own homes and offer them personally.
Whatever one causes to be offered with devotion, that gift is equal to ten million;
for whether he is awake or sleeping, whether in travel or at home,
I do not depart from the heart of that Brahmin who possesses such sincere devotion.
O best of the twice-born, whether honored, seen, touched,
or even conversed with, O Indra among kings, such a person always purifies another man.
Thus, O Pāṇḍava, all gifts [are meritorious] in every situation at all times.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard of the Sāttvika gift which bestows the path to heaven when given to my devotees, as well as the Rājasa and Tāmasa gifts, [one should practice the former].

"Each [path] indeed has its own distinct destination and its own distinct fruit. Yudhiṣṭhira, devoted to dharma, his soul filled with joy and still unsated, spoke again to Keśava regarding the nectar of meritorious dharma.
"O Lord of the World, tell me the characteristics of those who are pure in seed and womb;
and how, O Lord of Gods, do men come to be born through defects of the seed? You ought to explain the defect of conduct in its entirety."
O Keśava, [tell me] the distinction among Brāhmaṇas, as well as their virtues and faults;
and how those who abide within the entire system of the four castes in the acceptance of gifts—
by what specific quality do the Brahmins cross over [themselves] and cause others to cross over?
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of Gods, tell these things to your devotee; salutations be unto you!
Listen, O King, to the account of how the seeds and wombs are auspicious or inauspicious."
O Pāṇḍava, by that [means] this world both stands and perishes. But that Brahmin who, having remained steadfast in his celibate vow according to the rule,
possesses a seed— his seed should be known as "good seed" (subīja) and shall be auspicious.
A maiden who is of noble lineage on both her father’s and mother’s side, whose virginity remains intact,
and who has been wed according to the prescribed rites in marriages such as the Brāhma and others—
that woman of beautiful limbs is highly praised, and her womb is likewise extolled.
She who acts according to her own will in thought, deed, or speech should be known as a destroyer of the family; one born of her becomes a dog-cooker (outcaste).
This applies to rites for the gods, rites for the ancestors, as well as in giving gifts, eating together, and conversing.

Those born of a wicked womb are not fit for a bed shared with a husband; therefore, a wise man should not cause conception in a wicked womb. He who, out of delusion, does so destroys his lineage for three generations.
The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son born of a woman pregnant at marriage (*sahoḍha*), as well as both the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*,
and he who is born from one who has fallen from his caste after marrying again (*ārūḍhapatita*), and the son of one who is already fallen—
these six are universal outcasts (*viśvacaṇḍāla*), more degraded even than the dog-cookers (*śvapaca*).
Whether he has discharged his semen here or there, or should he consort with Śūdra women,
that evil-souled man who acts according to his lust— his seed shall become impure;
that impure seed does not deserve a pure womb.
It defiles even that womb, just as an oblation licked by a dog;
the seed would fall into a Śūdra womb while the twice-born man utters cries of "Alas! Alas!
(hāhā), distressed, thinking, "I have fallen into a pit of excrement."
"This evil-souled one, deluded by desire, is casting me down;
he shall quickly go to a downward state. Having thus cursed him, he fell.
For the self is declared to be pure, the supreme and great deity.
Therefore, with every effort, one should restrain the white [semen] of oneself.
Through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one obtains longevity, splendor, strength, vigor, wisdom, prosperity, great fame, merit, and being dear to me.
By those who have not violated their vow of celibacy, who have entered the stage of the householder,
and who are devoted to the five sacrifices, righteousness is established upon the surface of the earth;
for they regularly perform the twilight devotions perfectly, both evening and morning.
Having fashioned a boat made of the Veda, they cross over and cause others to cross over. Whoever mutters the purifying Goddess Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas,
shall not sink even while accepting the earth together with its oceans.
And whatever malevolent planets, such as the sun and others, are situated in his [astrological] houses in the sky,
they become gentle, auspicious, and bringers of good fortune for him; likewise,
wherever the fierce flesh-eaters may reside, [they become benevolent].
Though they were of terrible form and massive body, they could not overcome that twice-born man.
Furthermore, O King, those men on earth who have performed the Vedic vows are purified;
indeed, she is more venerable than even the four Vedas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even those Brāhmaṇas who have not observed their vows or studied the Vedas, and who have resorted to improper courses of action, are worthy of honor by virtue of their name alone;
how much more so one who constantly performs the two twilight devotions?
Moral conduct, study, charity, purity, gentleness, and uprightness—
Manu Prajāpati declared these to be superior to that Veda.
The twice-born who knows the supreme Brahman as "Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ" [is truly learned].
He who is devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, wise, and a protector of the earth—he is a true Brahmin.
Those best of the twice-born who constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), O tiger among men, go to the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the four Vedas, eats all things, and sells all things.
In ancient times, they weighed the Sāvitrī and the Vedas on a scale.
Together with the hosts of gods and sages, all preceded by Brahmā,
O King, she is indeed more venerable than even the four Vedas;
just as bees gather honey from a blossomed flower.
Having cast aside all flavor that is useless and devoid of essence,
O Pāṇḍava, Sāvitrī is thus grasped within all the Vedas;
therefore, Sāvitrī is said to be the life-breath of all the Vedas.
O King, all other Vedas are lifeless without the Sāvitrī; one who possesses the four Vedas but is unrestrained and fallen from moral conduct is contemptible,
whereas one who is endowed with good character and conduct and recites the Sāvitrī is superior.

"Recite the *Sāvitrī*, O son of Kuntī, which consists of a thousand verses at most, a hundred in the middle, and ten at least; it is the goddess that destroys all sins. Yudhiṣṭhira said: [so he spoke].
"O Lord of the three worlds, O Kṛṣṇa, for you are indeed the self of all beings. O supreme one devoted to various yogas, by what action are you satisfied?
The Blessed One said:
If one were to burn even a thousand loads of guggulu and other incenses,
and if one performs prostrations and offers oblations,
and always praises me with hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
O Bhārata, if I do not find satisfaction when the Brahmins are not satisfied, then neither shall I be satisfied.
When a Brahmin is constantly honored, I am honored as well; of this there is no doubt.
And when he is reviled, O bull of the Bharatas, I too am reviled.
Their supreme refuge is in me, for they indeed worship me when I dwell upon the surface of the earth in the form of a twice-born brahmin;
the wise man who worships them with his inner self absorbed in me [worships me].
O bull among men, I see him in his own true form. The wise should not despise the twice-born who are hunchbacked, one-eyed, dwarfish, poor, or diseased; for those twice-born ones are my very forms.
"O best of the twice-born, whoever [exists] upon this earth bounded by the ocean— when they are thus honored, I am indeed honored among them. However,
many men, excluded from knowledge, do not know this."
14,096.015d@004_0542 Just as I dwell upon the surface of the earth in the form of a twice-born,
14,096.015d@004_0543 those who despise the Brahmins cause them to fall from their own dharma; 14,096.015d@004_0544 they employ them with menial tasks and force them to perform service.
And here, having died, these mighty messengers of Yama cut [the bodies] at will along the lines of the cord, like artisans,
those who take delight in reviling and censuring the twice-born.
Having cast those dead ones, who reside in the world of Yama, down upon the surface of the earth,
that cruel one, with bloodshot eyes, would step upon their chests with his foot; then,
with tongs glowing like fire, Yama would pull out their tongues.
Those sinful men who look upon Brahmins with an evil eye— those who are hostile to the Veda, excluded from the sacred revelation, and eternally haters of Brahman—
for them [there arise] beings of terrible aspect, massive bodies, curved snouts, and great strength.
By the command of Yama, birds extract his eyes in a mere moment.
Whoever should strike a lord of the twice-born, cause him to bleed,
break his bones, or deprive him of his life;
He proceeds in succession through these twenty-one hells;
having gone there, he is impaled upon a stake and cooked in a blazing fire.
For many thousands of years, he remains being cooked with his head hanging downward.

The one of dull intellect shall not be liberated; his destination does not perish. Having approached a Brahmin without reflection, acting indeed with the desire to kill him, he is cooked in the Tāmisra hell for hundreds of thousands of years.
Having intentionally and with fury drawn blood from the body,
he shall go in succession through these twenty-one hells.
Therefore, one should not speak what is unwholesome, nor should one utter harsh words.
One should not speak harsh words, nor should one ever transgress against those best of men who honor the brahmins with faith and speech;
for by them I am honored, of this there is no doubt.
O Bhārata, those who threaten brāhmaṇas and cause them to cry out—
by them I am undoubtedly reviled and threatened.
[Yet] he who [honors them] with sandalwood, agallochum incense, and lamps...
If one should worship an image of me made of wood,
I am not truly worshipped by that;
it is through the worship of the Brahmins that I am fully worshipped.
Through the grace of the brahmins, I am the upholder of the earth;
through the grace of the brahmins, I conquer the asuras; and through the grace of the brahmins, I am possessed of sacrificial fees.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O slayer of Daityas, by the grace of the Brahmins I am invincible; indeed, my curiosity is great."
O Omniscient Keśava, tell this to me, your devotee:
what is the difference between the world of humans and the world of dharma; what is its nature, what is its extent, and what indeed is its foundation?
"O Mādhava, by what means do human beings cross over [to the divine state],
O God? O Mahādeva, tell me completely about pleasure and pain in that which is devoid of skin, bone, and flesh, and free from the five elements."
The living being, bound by means of those terrible snares— his own auspicious and inauspicious deeds— in the worlds of karma,
is led away by the messengers of Death, who are invincible, fierce, and possessed of formidable prowess.
When one who is condemned to death, being dragged away, or fleeing by the command of Yama,
stands before all the fruits of their good and evil deeds— happiness and suffering in their entirety—
how then is such a person led away by the invincible messengers of Yama?
O Lord, what actions do human beings perform when they have gone there?
How do those devoted to dharma, who worship the deities and the twice-born, proceed?
And how do men of evil deeds go to the city of the departed spirits?
"What is its form, what is its measure, or what is its color, O Keśava? Tell me, for the Blessed One, as the *jīva* constantly departs for the world of Yama.
The Blessed One said:
[Tell me] concerning the *jīva* that is perpetually going to the realm of Yama.
"Listen, O King, to what has occurred regarding that which you ask me; I shall relate it to you, O lord of men, for you are my devotee.
It is eighty-six thousand *yojanas*, Yudhiṣṭhira."
The distance between the world of humans and the world of Yama is such that there is no shade of trees there, nor any pond, nor even a lake;
neither are there large pools, oblong ponds, or wells, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Neither a pavilion nor an assembly hall, neither a water-station nor a dwelling;
neither a mountain nor a river, nor any cleft in the earth;
neither a village nor a hermitage, nor a garden nor forests—[nowhere was he found].
O Yudhiṣṭhira, on that path there is no place of refuge whatsoever for a living being who has reached his time, who is intensely afflicted by pain,
whose faculties have abandoned the body, and whose vital breaths have reached the throat.

The living soul is indeed moved from the body by the wind against its will; having emerged from the sixfold sheath of the corpse, it becomes like the wind. Another body then arises, identical in form, color, and dimension.
Having entered that which is invisible, he too is unseen by anyone;
that inner self of embodied beings, which moves about with eight limbs,
is not destroyed by cutting, piercing, burning, or beating.
Being led by the invincible messengers of Yama at the command of Yama— fierce beings who assume various forms, who are terrible, violent, and perform wrathful rites—
he is forcibly bound and rendered helpless by the nooses consisting of his sons and wife.
Followed by his own past actions— both good and evil deeds performed—
and crying out piteously to his kinsmen who are themselves oppressed by grief,
he departs, utterly indifferent, having abandoned all his relatives.
Again, he is abandoned by weeping mothers, fathers, brothers, maternal uncles, wives, sons, and friends;
unseen by those wretched ones, whose faces and eyes are filled with tears.
Having abandoned his own body, he goes forth, become like the wind,
into that boundless darkness, most terrible and enveloped in gloom—
a place that is the end of suffering, difficult to cross, and inaccessible to those of evil deeds.

O best of men, O King, that which is described by the seers through tradition is difficult to endure, difficult to reach its end, difficult to behold, difficult to approach, difficult to attain, and full of extreme suffering for the most wicked.
When heard even in stories, it generally produces terror;
yet that path must certainly be traversed, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
having abandoned kinsmen, enjoyments, and wealth when one's time has come.
Whether born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from a sprout; whether moving or stationary— all must go to the abode of Yama,
including gods, asuras, humans, and others, all subject to the power of Vaivasvata.
Whether by women, men, or those of neutral gender; by all living beings upon this earth; whether by those who are middle-aged, young, children, or likewise the elderly;
or even by those just born or still dwelling in the womb—that great path must be traversed.
Whether in the forenoon or the afternoon, or again at the time of twilight; whether at dusk, at midnight, or when dawn has arrived;
by those dwelling in exile, or in the forest, or on mountains, or situated upon the water—
Whether they are situated in a field, in the sky, or even within the interior of a house;
whether they are eating, drinking, or chewing, O Best of Men; or whether they are sitting, standing, or even lying down on a bed—[they all hear it].
Whether awake or asleep, one must travel the great path by the messengers of Death— invincible, fierce, and of cruel commands— who,
having seized them, lead them helplessly to the abode of Yama.
In some places terrified, in some places trembling, stumbling here and there,
and crying out in the agony of their pain, they must go to the abode of Yama—
being reviled, agitated, shaken, and overwhelmed by fear.
With their bodies being pierced and constantly subjected to threats,
men devoid of merit must travel along paths strewn with thorns and hot sand and dust; they must go while being consumed by fire.
Struck by blows of wood, stones, and rocks, and by staffs, flaming torches, whips,
and goads— those devoid of dharma must go to the city of Yama with their faces and limbs wet with fat, blood, and pus, and covered in wounds.
Those who kill living beings must travel [to their destination] covered in burnt and bloody wounds,
wailing, weeping, and crying out with loud lamentations;
afflicted by agony, they groan and shriek discordantly.
Afflicted by pain and falling along the way, those who have taken life must travel on;
with their feet, thighs, hands, and limbs broken, their teeth and necks shattered,
and their throats, lips, and noses severed, those who have taken life must travel on.
Being pierced by spears, slings, javelins, thunderbolts, and arrows, and being tormented by the tips of pikes, those who have killed living beings must go [to that place],
being devoured on all sides by dogs, tigers, wolves, and crows.
Being tormented by flesh-eating *rākṣasas*, they proceed along that path while being devoured by buffaloes,
deer, boars, and spotted antelopes—
all those who feed on flesh.
Those most wicked men who kill children must travel [to hell], being pricked on all sides by flies with needle-like, extremely sharp beaks—
those men who treacherously kill their master, a friend, or a woman.
Being pierced by those weapons, they must go to the abode of Yama;
and those who cause living beings to be killed and bring them suffering,
they go while being devoured by *rākṣasas* and dogs.
Those who steal garments, beds,
and coverings go along that path naked and fleeing like *piśācas*.
Likewise, those who take by force cattle, grain, gold, fields, or houses [go the same way].
Those evil-minded evildoers who steal the property of others must go to the abode of Yama,
being struck with stones, flaming brands, staffs, blows from wooden clubs, and rattling sticks,
their bodies covered in wounds.
Those men who, fearless of hell, seize the property of Brahmins here,
or who constantly revile and strike the twice-born,
shall have their throats parched and be bound with their tongues, eyes, and noses cut out.
Foul-smelling with pus and blood, they are devoured by crows and jackals;
being tormented on all sides by fierce and terrifying *caṇḍālas*,
they wail piteously and dreadfully as they go to the abode of Yama.
And having gone there as well, those wicked ones fall repeatedly into pits of excrement;
living for tens of millions of years, they suffer, tormented by agony.
Then, after a time, those lowest of men are released from that state into this world.
O King, they go through hundreds of millions of births as worms in excrement— those who,
though possessing wealth, fail to give gifts to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), being possessed by greed, hypocrisy, and falsehood, O bull among the Kurus.
Bound by nooses around their necks and being struck by *rākṣasas*,
those men— afflicted by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion— go to the city of the dead (*pretapura*),
having failed to give gifts; they go with their throats, mouths, and palates parched.
Seeking food together with drink again and again, O Master, we are afflicted by hunger and thirst; we are simply unable to go today.
"O Master, let food be given to me; let drink be given to me."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Speaking thus, they were sent to the abode of Yama by those messengers.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the Pāṇḍava fell to the earth.
Though unconscious, terrified, and overwhelmed by a swoon,
he gradually regained his senses and was comforted by Acyuta;
having washed his eyes with water, he spoke again to Keśava.
"I am afraid, O Mahādeva, having heard the extent of that path.
The Blessed One said:
"By what means do persons cross that path with ease?"
In this world, those who are righteous, who refrain from killing living beings,
who are devoted to serving their teachers, and who worship the gods and Brahmins—
along with their wives and kinsmen— [depart] from this human world.
Now learn from me,
O King, the path upon which those who duly bestow various kinds of gifts upon learned Brāhmaṇas travel— that path of happiness.
Those who provide well-prepared food to Brāhmaṇas—
especially to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya)— endowed with the highest affection,
those great-souled ones travel to the abode of Yama in variegated celestial chariots.

Those who always speak words that are truthful and stainless travel to that abode of Yama in celestial chariots resembling pure clouds, being attended by excellent women who are like *apsarases* upon the great path.
Those men who bestow upon Brāhmaṇas, and especially upon those learned in the Vedas, meritorious gifts such as Kapilā cows and other such offerings,
travel in celestial chariots of pure luster yoked with bulls.
Having reached the city of Vaivasvata, they are attended by celestial nymphs;
those who bestow upon Brahmins sandals, umbrellas, beds, seats, garments, and ornaments [attain this state].
Adorned with horses, bulls, or even elephants, they go to the beautiful city of Dharmarāja, graced by golden parasols;
and those who give food to be chewed, as well as food to be eaten and drunk, [attain that same state].
Those who, endowed with supreme faith, offer even succulent foods to the Brahmins,
go happily to the abode of Vaivasvata in golden vehicles,
being attended by thousands of excellent women according to their desire.
And those who, full of faith and well-prepared, diligently offer milk, ghee, curds, molasses, and honey to the Brāhmaṇas,
[they travel] on beautiful golden vehicles drawn by ruddy geese.
Attended by the musical instruments of the Gandharvas, they go to the abode of Yama;
those men who offer fruits and fragrant flowers travel to the City of Dharma in celestial chariots drawn by swans.

Those who bestow upon the Brahmins various kinds of food soaked in ghee travel in celestial chariots that have the speed of the wind and possess the brilliance of stainless clouds to that city of the Lord of the Dead, which is crowded with diverse people.
Those who bestow water, which sustains all living beings,
go to their happiness fully satisfied in celestial chariots impelled by swans.
Those who give sesame seeds, or a cow made of sesame, or even a cow made of ghee—
Endowed with a gentle disposition, they bestow gifts upon those learned in the Vedas;
O King, they travel by means of pure vehicles resembling the orb of the moon,
while being sung to by Gandharvas, as they proceed to the city of Vaivasvata.
Those for whom there are ponds, wells, tanks, lakes,
oblong pools, lotus-pools, and water-filled reservoirs,
travel by means of vehicles as bright as the moon and resounding with divine bells.
Fanned by chowries and palm-leaf fans, those of great splendor,
eternally satisfied and high-souled, go to the abode of Yama—
those for whom there are here variegated temples and sacred dwellings.
Charming, lovely, beautiful, and radiant,
they travel in aerial chariots that have the speed of the wind and resemble stainless clouds to that city of the Lord of the Dead, which is crowded with various kinds of people.

And they behold Vaivasvata with a joyful mind, established in happiness; honored by Yama, they then proceed to the same world as the gods. Having dedicated [the gift] to the gods in the worlds, [they offer] water drawn from jars at water-stations (*prapā*).
Those who provide cool, delightful water to the thirsty attain supreme satisfaction and proceed happily upon the Great Path;
those who give wooden sandals travel that road with ease.
Having placed their feet upon golden jeweled pedestals in that most excellent chariot,
those men who plant groves and clusters of trees,
and who, with undistracted minds, nurture them until they are adorned with fruits and flowers, [attain this state].
Adorned with fine ornaments, they proceed by means of divine vehicles through delightful and cool tree-shades, being honored again and again and attended with great care by women of supreme beauty.
Together with women of golden complexion, according to their desire and at their pleasure,
those who bestow horse-vehicles, ox-carts, or even elephant-vehicles upon the brahmins [ascend] celestial palaces resembling gold.
Those who bestow gold, silver, coral, or likewise pearls,
travel in celestial chariots radiant with gold;
they proceed at their pleasure, attended by excellent women.
Those who give land go to that world, fully satisfied with all their desires,
traveling in celestial chariots yoked with bulls that resemble the rising sun.
And those who bestow a maiden upon a learned Brahmin who is well-versed in the Vedas [attain the same].

Surrounded by celestial maidens, they travel to the abode of Yama in divine chariots. Endowed with supreme devotion, they offer fragrant perfumes, aromatic blends, and sweet-smelling flowers to the foremost of the twice-born.
Fragrant, well-attired, radiant, adorned with garlands and ornaments, they proceed to the City of Dharma in various decorated vehicles;
those who gave lamps go in vehicles illuminating the ten directions.
Resembling the sun in appearance and blazing like fires,
men who have given houses and dwellings travel to the city of Dharmarāja on celestial vehicles with golden pedestals that shine like the rising sun.
Those who give water vessels, and those who give water-pots (*kuṇḍikā*) and water-jars (*karakā*),
go forth satisfied upon great elephants while being honored by excellent women;
likewise, they receive foot-massage, head-anointing, drink, and water for their feet.
Those who bestow [gifts] upon Brahmins go to the abode of Yama by means of horses. Those who provide rest to Brahmins who are exhausted and worn out on the road,
they too travel by a vehicle drawn by ruddy geese (*cakravāka*).
He who honors Brahmins with a welcome and with a seat travels that path happily, supremely at peace;
he who, upon seeing me, greets me saying, "Homage to the God who is the Friend of Brahman."
He who is ever restrained like one observing a vow travels that path with ease;
he who, day after day, pays homage saying "Salutation to all assemblies" and offers salutations to the cows, travels that path with ease.

He who, rising from his bed each morning, steps upon the ground day after day while uttering the words, "Homage be to Priyadattā," shall have his soul satisfied with all desires and be adorned with every ornament.
They go happily to the abode of Vaivasvata by means of a divine vehicle. But those who eat only what remains [after serving others], being free from hypocrisy and egoism,
they too indeed go happily by a vehicle yoked with cranes.
Those who subsist on eating only once a day and are free from hypocrisy travel happily to the abode of Yama in celestial chariots drawn by swans.
And those who have conquered their senses and subsist on eating only every fourth mealtime [day], [travel likewise].
Those who have conquered their senses and partake [of food] here on the third day go by means of vehicles yoked with peacocks to the City of Dharma;
they also travel that path upon elephant-chariots resplendent with gold.
He who observes this sixth daily fast for one full year—
free from desire and anger, pure, and always having his senses conquered—
goes forth seated upon an elephant, accompanied by the sounds of shouts of victory.
Those who observe the fast for a fortnight go by means of vehicles yoked with tigers to the delightful city of Dharmarāja, which is frequented by hosts of celestial women;
and those who, with their senses restrained, perform the month-long fast.

They too go to the abode of Yama in vehicles that resemble the rising sun. And he who enters the fire with his soul absorbed in me goes to the abode of Yama in a celestial chariot (vimāna) radiant like fire.
That brahmin who, having taken refuge in me, gives up his life through fasting,
shall travel that path by means of a vehicle with the brilliance of the rising sun. Furthermore,
the man who enters into the water and gives up his life there—
He who, with his mind fixed on me, offers his own body to the vultures, travels along that path in a vehicle resembling the orb of the moon;
he goes to the abode of Yama in a preeminent golden chariot.
Those who have been killed for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a woman, or even for the sake of a Brahmin,

go [to heaven] with the splendor of the sun, being served by celestial maidens. And those devotees of mine who, having conquered their senses, undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords (tīrthas), [attain the same state].
Those great-souled ones who,
as the best of the twice-born, perform sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees,
travel along that path in vehicles, perfectly at ease; they go upon that path in vehicles yoked with swans and cranes.
Those men who support their dependents without causing suffering to others travel happily along that path in celestial chariots radiant with gold;
they who are impartial toward all beings and grant fearlessness to living creatures.
Freed from anger and greed, with their senses thus restrained,
those beings of great splendor travel to the city of Vaivasvata in celestial chariots resembling the full moon, attended by gods and gandharvas.
Those who, with single-minded devotion, worship, bow down to, and praise me as well as the three-eyed god Śiva day after day,
go to the city of Dharmarāja in vehicles possessing a radiance equal to the sun.
Having been honored there according to dharma with auspicious garlands and other offerings,
they go indeed to my world or else to the world of Rudra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard about the path to the city of Yama and likewise the departure of living beings,
Dharmaputra, with a joyful heart, spoke again to Keśava:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O slayer of Daityas, you who are praised by the hosts of sages!"
O Blessed One, creator of existence, glorious one, possessing the radiance of a thousand suns; O source of all, omniscient one, promoter of all dharmas;
O gentle one, O Acyuta, tell me the fruit of all giving.
"O Kṛṣṇa, how should a gift be given, and to what kind of twice-born man?
Or, having performed what kind of austerity, where is its fruit enjoyed?
Thus was Hṛṣīkeśa addressed by the wise son of Dharma.
He spoke to the son of Dharma concerning meritorious and highly exalted duties:
"Listen attentively, O King, to this supreme, purifying, and sin-destroying teaching. It yields the fruit of all gifts, O gentle one, yet it must not be heard by those of evil deeds."
Having heard this, whether a man or a woman, one whose sins are destroyed becomes composed;
even one devoted to evil deeds attains purity at that very moment. O son of Kuntī, water produced upon the earth for even a single day [is sacred].
One who gives water liberates seven ancestors from thirst, wherever that cow may be. Water is considered the supreme sustenance for living beings in this world;
O Pāṇḍava, through the gift of water, one attains satisfaction.
The divine qualities of water bring happiness in the next world.
There, O King of kings, is a most purifying river named Puṣpodakī; by giving a gift of water there, one obtains all desires even in the abode of Yama.
Its cool water is inexhaustible and like nectar;
it shall always bring happiness to those who give cold water. And for those who do not give water, pus is ordained as their lot.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, hunger is extinguished by the drinking of water;
yet for one who is thirsty, thirst is not extinguished by food.
Therefore, a wise person should always give water to those who are thirsty.
The form of fire, the womb of the earth, and the source of immortality— therefore,
water is called by the wise the root of all beings. By means of water, all beings live and they come forth.

Therefore, among all gifts, the gift of water is preeminent. Whatever supreme fruit is obtained through all forms of giving, austerity, and sacrifice—all that is obtained by the gift of water; there is no doubt in this.
O bull of the Bharatas, those who bestow well-prepared food upon the Brahmins effectively give their own life-breaths themselves;
for from food come both blood and semen, and in food the living soul is established.

The sense organs and the intellect are constantly nourished by food; deprived of food, O Pāṇḍava, all beings perish. Splendor, strength, valor, vitality, form, luster, and fortitude—[all these depend on food].

Knowledge, intelligence, and likewise life— all are established in food. At all times, among gods, humans, and animals, and in all worlds, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of everyone are indeed established in food.
Food is the form of Prajāpati; food is known as procreation.
Food consists of all beings, and the individual soul (jīva) is known to consist of food. Prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna are presided over by food.
The *udāna* and *samāna* [vital breaths] sustain embodied beings; lying down, rising, walking, grasping, and drawing [objects toward oneself]—
all actions performed by sentient beings proceed from food alone.
O Indra among kings, the four kinds of beings—both mobile and immobile—arise from food; this is the creation of Prajāpati. All branches of knowledge and all sacrifices are purifying.
Since all beings proceed from food, food is therefore remembered as supreme.
Since all the gods, beginning with Rudra, as well as the ancestors and the sacred fires,
are satisfied by food, food is thus distinguished as preeminent.
Since the Lord created all creatures from food in every eon,
therefore there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to that of food.
Since from food proceed both dharma and artha, as well as kāma itself.
Therefore, O Pāṇḍava, there is no gift superior to food, both in the next world and in this one.
Since Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Grahas, Nāgas, Bhūtas, Daityas,
and Dānavas are all satisfied by food, therefore food is the supreme gift.
O Bhārata, when one who subsists on another’s food performs an auspicious deed, only one part of that merit belongs to the doer;
O bull among men, three parts belong to the giver of the food.

Therefore, food should be given to Brahmins, especially so. O King, he who for a year gives food to a poor Brahmin learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), doing so without partiality toward any particular dish, [attains great merit].
But he who is free from hypocrisy and falsehood and has attained supreme devotion—
listen to the fruit of his merit, the reward earned through his own duty:
for a hundred thousand years, moving at will and assuming any form at will, he shall dwell [in heaven].
Abiding in the world of the immortals, he rejoices while being honored by hosts of apsarases. Then, when his time there has passed, he shall become a twice-born man in the world of men.
Furthermore, he who gives the first alms to a poor member of the twice-born caste [attains this same result].

Listen to the meritorious fruit of his annual *śrāddha* performed after six months: a man indeed attains that same merit which is proclaimed to result from the gift of a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.
Now, if one should provide the first alms-food for a year without being asked,
having personally brought it and concealed [the act], hear the fruit of his merit:
that which is said to be the merit of giving thousands of *kapilā* cows.
Having attained all of that in its entirety, he is glorified in the world of Śakra.
O King, for a hundred crores of years in the delightful abode of Śakra,
that one of great splendor sports at will with hosts of apsarases.

O Indra among kings, listen to the fruit of the merit of that man who, being restrained by his vows, gives choice food to a twice-born man for ten years— the same fruit that results from a hundred thousand tawny cows given according to the prescribed ritual.
Having attained the fruit of that merit, one shall go to the city of Indra. In the delightful abode of Śakra, assuming any form at will,
O King, he shall sport for a hundred koṭis of years, honored by the immortals.
Having descended from the world of Śakra, he of great splendor is born here in this world as a glorious twice-born man learned in the four Vedas, honored by kings.
[This occurs] for a Brahmin exhausted by the road, hungry and longing for food.
O son of Pāṇḍu, food is given to one who arrives at the proper place and time; he who does not give food when requested, despite having the means to acquire wealth,
is a greedy man who goes to the Kṛmisaṃjñaka Kālasūtra hell.
There, in that terrible hell, with his mind deluded by greed,
he suffers for ten thousand years, tormented by painful sensations;
and after a long time, he is indeed released from that hell.
A poor man in this world may even be born among the Caṇḍālas;
yet there is the twice-born man whose feet are covered in dust, who is emaciated by the fatigue of a long journey,
exhausted by hunger, thirst, and toil, distressed and with weary gait.
Indeed, one who comes to a house seeking food should be questioned and entreated;
one should honor him with effort, for that guest is a bridge to heaven.
O best of men, when he is satisfied, all the gods are satisfied.
O Pārtha, the sacrificial fires are not so pleased by oblations of clarified butter, nor by flowers, nor by ointments, as they are by the honoring of a guest; indeed,
this is the case when a tawny cow is given according to the rules at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara.
One does not obtain that fruit which is obtained from feeding Brahmins;
for as long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of the twice-born,
for that long the ancestors drink water from a lotus leaf.
Removing the divine garlands, wiping away the remnants of the twice-born’s meal, massaging those who are weary, likewise washing their feet,
providing shelter, as well as beds and seats.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, each one of these [acts] excels the gift of a cow:
those who provide water for the feet, oil for the feet, a lamp, food,
and shelter to the Brahmins do not approach Yama.
O King, when hospitality is rendered to a Brahmin and he is served with devotion,
all thirty-three gods are thereby served by you. For one who has been previously known is called an *abhyāgata* (a guest of honor), while one unknown is called an *atithi* (a guest).
"A twice-born man should perform worship for those two"—such is the scriptural tradition of the Purāṇas.
O Indra among kings, that man who honors a guest with oil for his feet, food, and drink, by him am I honored here; of this there is no doubt.
"Quickly liberated from evil and favored by me,
he shall go to my world in a celestial chariot resembling the moon.
They follow one who has arrived weary."
All the gods, the ancestors, and the sacred fires—
when that twice-born man is honored, they all become honored;
when he departs, the ancestors go away disappointed.
If a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated,
the ancestors do not eat [the offerings] of that person for fifteen years;
abandoned by the ancestors, he is forsaken by the gods along with the sacred fires.
Having gone to the Raurava hell, he is cooked there for ten years;
then, when his time there has expired, he falls away and becomes here a consumer of leavings.
He who does not honor a guest who has arrived near the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering [is likewise reborn as such].

He who expels a Brahmin who has arrived at his home at the proper time and place immediately incurs the state of a Caṇḍāla; of this there is no doubt. At that very moment, he becomes fallen; of this there is no doubt.

He is cooked for ten million years in the terrible Raurava hell. Then, having passed away from there at the end of that time, that lowest of men is born in this world as a dog for twelve lifetimes, tormented by hunger and thirst.

Even if a Caṇḍāla arrives as a guest at the proper time and place seeking food, he must always be welcomed and honored by the householder. He who, devoid of consciousness through greed and delusion, eats without having honored him, [commits a sin].

O Pāṇḍava, he who eats with delight after leaving a guest disappointed incurs the state of a Caṇḍāla for ten births; such a person does not realize that by his own act he has cast himself into a pit of excrement.
In vain indeed he covers [his head], and in vain does his food ripen;
in vain does he always eat food who does not honor a guest—
even if he recites the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs here day after day.
That twice-born man who does not honor a guest lives in vain,
even if he performs *pākayajña* and *mahāyajña* sacrifices, as well as the *soma-saṃsthā* rites;
for those who offer such sacrifices yet do not worship a guest who has arrived at their home.

Whatever is given or offered by those who desire fame becomes entirely in vain; for it is destroyed by that [selfish] intention. One should, however, consider the place and time, as well as the recipient and one's own capacity.
Whether it be small, moderate, or great, a self-possessed man should extend hospitality;
with a cheerful countenance and a tranquil mind, the wise man should honor the guest who has arrived with a welcome, a seat, water, and food.
Whether he is beneficial or dear, whether he is hateful or even a fool or a scholar—

whosoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite is a guest who serves as a bridge to heaven. [One should honor] him who has come at the proper time and place, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue.
One who desires the fruit of sacrifice should give food with due respect;
one should feed the most excellent of men according to the rules for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Food is the life-breath of human beings; therefore, the giver of food is the giver of life.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should especially give food.
The giver of food is fully satisfied with all his desires and is beautifully adorned,
shining in a celestial chariot that possesses the brilliance of the full moon.
Served by excellent women, he goes to my world;
having sported there like an immortal for ten million years,
he eventually falls from that time and becomes one of great renown in this world.

One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras shall become a wealthy Brahmin. Furthermore, he who performs [rites] according to his faith is born among men as a glorious lord of great wealth, having mastered the Vedas and the Vedangas.

A Brāhmaṇa who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures shall become possessed of enjoyments; he who, free from sin, having acquired wealth through righteous means and being devoid of any distinction of evil, should practice hospitality toward all for one year.
Having personally honored the Brahmins as if they were gods, and likewise the ancestors,
listen to the fruit of the merit of that man who eats only after the Brahmins have first eaten. As many rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) as the twice-born eat in one year— [hear the result of that]...
O Indra among kings, for that many years he is honored in my world;
then, when his time there has passed, he falls back to this world as one of great renown,
a Brahmin endowed with enjoyments who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras.
O Lord of Men, he who extends hospitality to all according to his faith—

even without regard for time or fixed rules— and who is truthful in speech, has conquered his senses, is faithful to his word, has subdued his anger, and is free from the sectarianism of the various branches of dharma; [he attains the highest state].
Fearful of unrighteousness, most virtuous, and free from deceit and envy; full of faith, ever pure, and avoiding the distinction between cooked and uncooked food—
he, possessing great renown, assumes a divine form and travels by means of a celestial chariot.
Being sung of by throngs of *apsarases*, he goes to the city of Indra;
having sported there for the duration of a *manvantara*, honored by the gods,
he returns to the world of men and becomes a Brahmin endowed with enjoyments.
For ten births he shall attain the status of a Brahmin, honored by kings;
the Blessed One said:
"And wherever he is born, he becomes one who remembers his past lives."

14,096.015d@004_1031 Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed gift of land. 14,096.015d@004_1032 O Pāṇḍava, he who bestows beautiful land, together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), upon a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas, impoverished, and maintains the sacred fire-offering (agnihotra); 14,096.015d@004_1033 [he attains great merit].
His soul satisfied in all desires, adorned with every kind of jewel,
and liberated from all evil, he shone constantly like the sun,
with the brilliance of the rising sun and graced by various banners.
By means of a divine vehicle, that one of great renown goes to my world;
there, being served by celestial women according to his pleasure, moving at will and assuming forms at will, he sports with hosts of apsarases.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, as long as the earth supports the worlds,
so long is the giver of land exalted in my world according to his desire;
indeed, no other gift excels the gift of land.
Nor is any other sin more distinguished than the seizure of land.
O bull among the Kurus, other gifts may diminish over time,
but the merit of the gift of land never undergoes depletion.
O tiger among men, listen to the fruit of merit for that man who does not harm land that has been given to a poor brahmin—
land bounded by the seven islands and oceans, and filled with jewels and grain.
By him, the earth, rich with mountains and forest fortresses, shall be given away. Seeing land being bestowed upon a *śrotriya* who maintains the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
all beings joyfully think, "He is giving me [a share]."
O King, by giving away the earth, one indeed gives all gifts— gold, gems, jewels, wealth, grain,
and riches— as well as the oceans, rivers, mountains, and both the level and the uneven terrain.
By giving the earth, one gives all fragrances and flavors; by giving the earth, one gives medicinal herbs rich in fruit and endowed with various flowers and fruits,
as well as clusters of lotuses and water-lilies.
By giving land, one bestows dharma, pleasure, and likewise wealth, as well as the Vedas and sacrifices, and even the attainment of the path to heaven;
this is true for those who perform the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees.
O Pāṇḍava, those who, having given land to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), do not cause him harm, do not obtain that fruit which is the fruit of a gift of land;
they shall proclaim that gift for as long as the worlds endure.

O son of Pāṇḍu, for that many years they shall be enjoyers of heavenly pleasures; moreover, for him who bestows a land filled with grain upon one learned in the Vedas, his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.

"O Indra among kings, know that this land has indeed been given to a twice-born for the pleasure of me, Rudra, Savitṛ, and likewise the thirty gods. By that merit, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the giver of land becomes one whose soul is purified."
He attains residence in my same realm; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whatever sin a man afflicted by his livelihood may commit, he is purified by the gift of land even as small as a cow’s ear.
Whatever merit is found in fasting for a month, in the *kṛcchra* penance, and even in the *cāndrāyaṇa*,
that same merit is ordained by [giving] earth the size of a cow’s ear. And whatever merit is proclaimed to come from bathing at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), [that too is obtained].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Even by [giving] a piece of land the size of a cow's ear, that merit is indeed ordained.
O God of gods, obeisance to you, Vāsudeva, Lord of the Suras!"
The Blessed One said:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, you ought to speak truly of the measurement of Gokarṇa. Listen to the measurement of that which is the size of a cow's ear."
O King of kings, measured in all directions by a distance of thirty *daṇḍas*, extending west to east and likewise south to north—
those who know it call that the "Cow's Ear" (*gokarṇa*), O monarch, as the measurement of the earth.

O tiger among the Kurus, where a hundred cows with their bulls and calves dwell happily and without restraint, that place is called Gokarṇa. [Therein are absent] the servants of Yama, the staffs of death, and the terrible Kumbhīpāka hells.
The terrible nooses of Varuṇa do not approach the giver of land;
nor do the hells such as Raurava, nor the river Vaitaraṇī,
nor the intense and painful torments approach the giver of land.
Citragupta, Kali, Kāla, Kṛtānta, and Mṛtyu,
as well as the Lord Yama himself, worship the giver of land;
likewise do Rudra, Prajāpati, Śakra, the gods, and the hosts of ṛṣis.
And I too, O King, am filled with joy as we honor the giver of land.

O best of men, land should be given to one whose servants are emaciated, whose cattle are emaciated, whose horses are emaciated, and whose guests are emaciated; for that is the treasure for the world beyond.
O lord of men, land should be given to a learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, who is observing his vows, and who is destitute, even if his family is sinking into distress;
for just as a nurse herself nourishes her child with milk, so does the earth sustain him.

The earth favors the donor; for once given, the earth is thus like a cow that, while yielding her own milk, nourishes her calf. In the same way, the earth, endowed with all virtues, carries the giver of land.
O Lord of the Earth, just as seeds sprinkled with water sprout,
so do the desires of one who steals land grow day by day;
yet, just as the rising sun dispels all darkness.
In this world, the gift of land likewise dispels a man’s sin.
The giver benefits ten generations, while he who seizes it destroys ten.
O bull among the Kurus, this applies to families both past and future in this world.
But he who, having heard of the gift of land, takes it back after it has been given,
is bound by the nooses of Varuṇa and cast into pus and blood.
He who seizes the earth, whether given by himself or given by another, [is likewise punished].
For him, there is no deliverance anywhere from that terrible hell.
When the field of a Brahmin is destroyed, he destroys twelve ancestors;
he shall go to the womb of a worm and shall never be released from it.
He who, having given land to a preeminent brahmin, lives off that very land himself,
reaps the fruit of one who has killed a hundred thousand cows;
that evil-souled man, with his head hanging downward, is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells.
After emerging from the Kumbhīpāka hell, O Pāṇḍava, he shall remain there for ten thousand divine years; having been released, he will become a dog in this world for a hundred births— he who,
having given land to the best of the twice-born, lives off that very same land himself.

That deluded one of wicked soul goes to the twenty-one hells. Released from the hells, he enters the womb of a dog. Land that has been ploughed by a plow, provided with seed and garlanded with crops, should be given as a gift.
Alternatively, O King, water should be given to a poor twice-born man;
when the earth is thus given with a joyful inner self,
one attains all desires and whatever is conceived by the mind.
The earth has been given by many kings, and it is being given even now. Whosoever possesses the land at any time, his is the fruit thereof.
Indeed, he who bestows a beautiful maiden upon one learned in the Vedas...

O Indra among kings, hear now the fruit of that merit belonging to that god Brahmā: O King, the fruit that one obtains by the gift of a maiden is equal to the fruit obtained by giving thousands of draft-oxen capable of bearing the yoke.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows,
that same fruit one attains who gives away a daughter in marriage.
And as many hairs as there are on that girl, O bull among the Kurus—
For as many thousands of years as there are syllables in that [mantra], he is glorified in my world; then,
having passed away from that time, he is born here in this world as a twice-born man who knows the six Vedāṅgas, is learned in the four Vedas, and is honored by all the world.
O Pāṇḍava, he who bestows gold upon a poor Brāhmaṇa— one learned in the Vedas, destitute, and having many sons—
is liberated from all sins and becomes radiant like the rising sun.
Having ascended a divine celestial palace (*vimāna*), moving at will and enjoying all desires,
he of great majesty rejoices in my world for ten million years.
Then, when his time has passed, he descends and is born again in this world.
A Brahmin who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences shall become a lord of ten million in wealth. Furthermore,
he who gives silver to a poor twice-born man whose livelihood is meager and whose cattle are emaciated is liberated from all sins.
Shining in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the full moon, possessing the power to assume any form at will, he is honored in the heavenly world according to his desire.
Then, in due time, that one of great renown descends from there into this world.
The illustrious and heroic king, honored by all the world,
[attains this]. Now hear what the fruit is for him who gives a mountain of sesame seeds to a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), especially one who is poor.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having attained that merit which is said to result from the release of ten thousand bulls,
one becomes free from passion at that very moment,
just as a snake, having cast off its skin, becomes pure of body.

By the gift of sesame seeds, one indeed abandons sin and becomes purified. One who bestows a grove of sesame seeds ascends a divine celestial chariot adorned with gold and is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
For sixty thousand years, O King, the highly illustrious giver of sesame seeds, able to assume any form at will, rejoices in the world of the ancestors according to his pleasure,
he who bestows a cow made of sesame seeds upon a brahmin.
Listen also to the fruit that belongs to one who gives [sesame] to a learned Brahmin who is poor:
a man who bestows a sesame-cow obtains that same fruit of merit which is proclaimed to result from the gift of a thousand cows.
