O King, he who gives a sesame-cow made from *kuḍava* measures of sesame seeds is honored in the heavenly world for as many millions of years as there are sesame seeds. O lord of men, having fashioned a sesame-cow with eight *āḍhaka* measures of sesame seeds—
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who, with devotion to me and with his soul absorbed in me, gives thirty-two *niṣkas* at the equinox (*viṣuva*):
it is the same fruit as that which comes from the gift of a thousand maidens bestowed according to the prescribed rites.
Having attained that merit, he is honored in my world;
having descended from my world,
he is born in this world as a bull among brahmins, one who has reached the further shore of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

O King, whatever evil deed was previously committed by one who gives a cow— gracious, milking, auspicious, with her calf, and accompanied by a bronze milking vessel— to a poor man learned in the Vedas, [is all destroyed].
All that perishes at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
Mounted upon a divine, self-luminous chariot yoked with bulls, well-adorned and moving according to one's desire, he attains Goloka.
O lord of men, for as many hairs as there are on that cow,
for so many thousands of years he is honored in the world of cows;
having descended from Goloka, he shall become a brahmin in this world.
A performer of long sacrificial sessions (*satra-yājī*) and a generous donor, honored by all kings— O mighty-armed one,
sesame seeds, cows, gold, food, maidens, and land,
when given to Brāhmaṇas here, deliver [the giver] from worldly existence.

O King, one should satisfy according to the rules a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with good conduct, who maintains the sacred fires, and who is free from greed; that is his treasure for the world beyond. [One should likewise satisfy] a poor Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires and is learned in the Vedas, as well as one who has conquered his senses.
One should diligently honor a twice-born man who avoids the food of a Śūdra;
for one who maintains the sacred fires and knows the Veda is always a worthy recipient. Among all recipients, he is the most worthy recipient whose stomach contains no food from a Śūdra.

That vessel which consists of the Veda, that vessel which consists of austerity, and that vessel which is unmixed— such a vessel shall deliver [others]. Those who are constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and whose senses are not scattered [are such vessels].
Those who are constantly devoted to the five sacrifices, when honored, deliver others; those who are patient and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning,
who have conquered their senses, and who abstain from taking life.
Householders who are restrained in receiving gifts—
those Brāhmaṇas are capable of delivering [others];
they are those who constantly offer water and constantly wear the sacred thread.
One who constantly studies the Vedas, avoids the food of a *vṛṣala*, approaches his wife only during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules—
that Brāhmaṇa is capable of delivering others across [the ocean of saṃsāra].

But that Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to me, who sacrifices to me, who has me as his supreme goal, and who has surrendered all actions to me— that sage will certainly effect deliverance. He is a knower of the reality of the twelve syllables and a knower of the division of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
Vaiśampāyana said:
"That Brahmin, who knows the five periods of time without omission, will deliver you,
once Vāsudeva has explained the various gifts in their proper order."
Still unsatiated with the teachings, he spoke again to Keśava:
"O Lord, O scorcher of foes, even as I listen to this nectar of dharma,
O best of gods, O Mādhava, I find no satiety."
"O Acyuta, tell me here the fruit that is ordained for the gift of a bull, for I am your devotee. And what other gifts have not been mentioned by you?"
"O best of gods, tell me of those [mantras] and their fruits in due order.
The Blessed One said:
"Because of their purity, their great merit, and likewise because of their sanctifying power..."
Listen to the supreme nectar of Dharma, the fruit of giving a bull: O bull among the Kurus, even a single bull is equal to ten cows;
it has limbs nourished by fat and flesh, is free from disease, and is devoid of anger.

O Pāṇḍava, Yudhiṣṭhira, that youth was auspicious, well-behaved, and free from all faults; he quickly bore the burden when given to the brāhmaṇa. By virtue of that meritorious gift, for ten million years— 14,096.015d@004_1219 He was young, auspicious, and of good character, entirely free from all defects. 14,096.015d@004_1220 O Pāṇḍava, he quickly bore the burden when given to the brāhmaṇa. 14,096.015d@004_1221 By means of that gift of merit, O Yudhiṣṭhira, for ten million years—
Possessing great splendor, he is honored in the world of cows according to his desire.
Furthermore, he who gives two oxen, yoked and capable of bearing the burden—
especially to a poor man of good conduct who is learned in the Vedas— [attains the same merit].
Listen, Yudhiṣṭhira, to that merit which has been declared for him:
he obtains the supreme fruit that is said to result from the gift of a thousand cows;
he attains that meritorious reward and goes to my worlds.
O King, as many hairs as there are on those two oxen,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in my world.
O Pāṇḍava, a gift should be given only to the poor, not to the wealthy.

Indeed, the fruit [of merit] for those who give in tanks is not found in the oceans. O bull among the Kurus, he who gives an ox to a poor twice-born man becomes purified in soul by that gift of merit.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*), possessing a divine form, he dwells at his pleasure in my worlds until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*).
His home is endowed with the light of lamps and adorned with beds and seats.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, [one should give] to a poor Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas a house equipped with utensils, filled with grain, and adorned; provided with female slaves, cattle, and land, and complete with all means of success.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives [this] along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā):
the gods, the hosts of ancestors, the fires, and likewise the sages,
being truly delighted, bestow upon him a vehicle resplendent like the sun.
Endowed with such glory, he shall go to the unsurpassed world of Brahmā;
there, in a divine golden palace surrounded by thousands of women,
he rejoices while dwelling in the world of Brahmā until the dissolution of all beings.
O Pāṇḍava, listen to the fruit of merit for him who provides a bed equipped with a mattress,
having honored a twice-born man with devotion through garments, garlands, and ointments,
and having fed him various kinds of food.

O Pāṇḍava, having attained that merit which belongs to the gift of a cow given according to the prescribed rites, one is glorified in the world of the ancestors. [Likewise,] craftsmanship, study, as well as knowledge, mantras, and medicinal herbs—
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who bestows [knowledge] upon a Brahmin:
he who imparts learning obtains that same fruit of merit which belongs to one who has honored a thousand *āhitāgni* priests.
In a radiant celestial chariot (*vimāna*) adorned with meters (*chandobhiḥ*),
he travels to the world of the Seven Sages (*saptarṣiloka*) and is honored by those who discourse on Brahman. Having sported there like a god for thirty *caturyugas*, he remains.
In this world of mortals, O King, that brahmin who knows the Vedas and provides rest to a weary and emaciated brahmin on the road destroys all the sin he has committed during that year.
Then, one who is full of devotion should wash his feet with water;
there is no doubt that he removes the sin committed over ten years.
Or else, one should honor his feet with ghee or oil.
That [merit], when practiced twelvefold, quickly dispels evil.
One obtains that same fruit of merit which is proclaimed for one who has given a milch cow and gold, who honors a Brahmin in this manner.
O King, he who honors a Brahmin with a welcome, with a seat,
or by rising to meet him, shall become dear to the gods. O King, through a welcome the sacrificial fires are pleased, and through a seat, Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
By rising to greet them, ancestors who are fond of guests attain satisfaction;
O lord of men, through that gratification of Agni, Śakra, and the ancestors,
the sin committed by one in a year is instantly destroyed.
He who bestows upon a brahmin a seat adorned with garlands goes by means of a chariot variegated with jewels to the abode of Indra;
there, in the city of Purandara, he is adorned by celestial women.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who gives a vehicle to a Brāhmaṇa sports for sixty thousand years with hosts of Apsarases;
he goes to the abode of the gods by means of a vehicle variegated with jewels.

Having sported there at will, served by throngs of apsarases, he shall become a king here on earth, O King; there is no need for deliberation on this point. [He sees] a tree covered with sprouts, likewise in bloom and laden with fruit.
Having honored him with perfumes and garlands, and having adorned him with garments and ornaments,
he who gives [this] to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas along with a sacrificial fee,
after having fed him according to his desire— listen now to the fruit of his merit.
Shining in a celestial palace variegated with Jāmbūnada gold,
he proceeds to the city of Indra accompanied by the sound of shouts of victory;
thereafter, in that delightful city of Śakra, there is for him the wish-fulfilling tree.
It bestows everything desired, whatever one wishes for in one's mind; for as many leaves, flowers, and fruits as it has,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
Having descended from the world of Śakra and come to the world of humans,
he protects a kingdom and a city filled with chariots, horses, and elephants— any man who, out of devotion to me, establishes an image of me.
Having constructed an *ālaya* according to the rules, one should cause the rites of worship to be performed;
or one may worship it oneself with devotion—listen now to the fruit of that merit. It is said to be equal to the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*).
One attains that fruit and reaches the same world as mine;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I do not know of anyone’s departure from my world who has performed this in a temple of the gods, the house of a Brahmin, a cow-pen, or even at a crossroads.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who kindles a lamp:
having ascended a golden vehicle that illuminates all directions,
he shall go to the world of the Sun, served by the most excellent gods.
Having sported there at will for ten million years,
O King, that great ascetic shall become a Brahmin in this world, one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
whether he dwells in temples or in the dwellings of Brahmins.
Whether at a crossroads or a square, by night or by day,
whoever with devotion and a heart absorbed in me causes various musical instruments of the gandharvas to be played for the purpose of proclaiming the Dharma—

O best of men, the gods and the ancestors are likewise delighted; being well-pleased, they grant him a beautiful celestial chariot that moves at will. And by means of that chariot, that man travels to the city of the gods.

There, being served by divine apsarases, he rejoices. Having descended from the world of the gods, O lord of men, he shall become a Brahmin in this world, possessing enjoyments and knowing the truth of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, whether at a crossroads, in an assembly hall, or in a spacious courtyard of the hall,
one who is devoted should construct a large fire-pit or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and kindle the fire there for four months.
When the months beginning with Pauṣa have been completed, one should then feed the twice-born with refined milk-rice (pāyasa) with an inner self absorbed in me,
and one should present sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen now to the fruit of the merit belonging to one who thus establishes the fire and constantly worships me;
by him I am worshipped, as well as Śaṅkara, the ancestors, and likewise the sacrificial fires.
We shall attain supreme joy; there is no need for deliberation on this point. For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years, that glorious one, who brings us delight, is honored in my world.

And he, O best of men, who provides maintenance for a Brāhmaṇa, becomes one of great fame who has descended into this world; he is born as a learned Brahmin, a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, honored by kings.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn now the fruit of the merit of that learned and well-born man who is especially poor; indeed,
it is equal to the merit that is proclaimed to come from the gift of ten million cows.
O Pāṇḍava, by means of a wonderful golden vehicle that adorns the sky, he attains the fruit of that merit within a single year and goes to my world, served by hosts of divine women.
Being sung of by excellent women for twenty million years while sporting in my world, and being praised there by the gods,
he shall descend to the human realm and become a Brahmin learned in the Vedas.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who gives a water-pot, a *kuṇḍikā*, or even a large water-vessel to a Brahmin;
it is equal to the fruit that is declared for drinking the *brahmakūrca* according to the prescribed rule.
The man who gives a water vessel obtains that fruit of merit:
well-satisfied, radiant, gentle, with his senses and mind delighted,
he travels in a resplendent celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes.
He goes to the world of Varuṇa, served by divine Gandharvas— he who bestows water, the supreme sustenance for living beings. Hear now the fruit of his merit during the months of summer.
Whatever merit is prescribed for the gift of ten million tawny cows,
that fruit of merit one obtains by providing water,
shining upon a celestial chariot (vimāna) resplendent with the brilliance of the full moon.
He shall go to the abode of Indra, being served by throngs of apsarases;
there, attended by divine gandharvas for thirty koṭis of yugas,
he shall sport, and upon returning to the world of men, he shall become a twice-born master of the four Vedas.
By the gift of oil for anointing the head, a twice-born man becomes radiant, pleasing to behold, fortunate, handsome, heroic,
and wise. Moreover, the giver of clothing becomes radiant and pleasing to behold everywhere.
The illustrious lord of pleasure and enjoyment, ever delightful to women—
such becomes that best of men who gives shoes and an umbrella.
He travels, resplendent upon a golden vehicle, the foremost among men.
Possessing great majesty and attended by hosts of apsarases,

the giver of wooden sandals goes to the world of Śakra; he travels in celestial chariots fashioned by the Bull (Indra) to the delightful city of Dharmarāja, where he is served by the most excellent apsarases.
By the gift of a tooth-stick, a man shall become one who speaks kindly;
he shall have a fragrant mouth, be endowed with splendor, intelligence, and good fortune.
Likewise, [the gift of] milk, curd, ghee, or molasses and sweet juices [yields these fruits].
Those men who, having attained supreme devotion, bestow [gifts] upon the Brahmins,
travel to the city of the Lord while being sung to by Gandharvas, adorned with white garlands and wreaths, and riding upon bulls and horse-drawn chariots.
There, attended by divine apsarases according to their pleasure,
they rejoice for sixty thousand years like unto gods; thereafter,
when their time has passed, they descend and are born here as human beings.
Possessing abundant wealth and grain, those best of men were enjoyers of prosperity;
O son of Pāṇḍu, on this day of the month of Vaiśākha,
they have attained supreme devotion directed toward Vaivasvata.

O son of Pāṇḍu, listen to the meritorious fruit for those who, having duly honored the Brahmins, offer sesame seeds mixed with jaggery; hear the merit that comes from the gift of a cow according to the prescribed rites.
Having attained that merit, he is honored in the world of Yama;
then, when his time there has passed, he shall become a king here on earth. On that very day, having fed the Brahmins with appropriate ritual gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), [he attains this].
Those who give divine vessels filled with water go to the abode of Varuṇa in celestial chariots radiant as the sun;
there, they who desire pleasure enjoy themselves with divine women.
Then, in due time, they shall descend again into this human world;
O best of the twice-born, there is no doubt that they will become possessors of enjoyments.
Furthermore, he who eats only after others have been fed and always conducts himself according to his vows—
Truthful in speech, free from anger, pure, and always devoted to bathing—
that man travels by means of a divine celestial chariot to the city of Śakra. There,
that one of great austerity dwells for ten million years among the divine apsarases.
Having sported in the world of men, he is born as a twice-born who is learned in the Vedas;
likewise, he who subsists on a single meal for one year,
remaining celibate, having conquered anger, and endowed with truthfulness and purity.
That man travels by means of a divine celestial chariot to the city of Śakra;
having sported for ten thousand times ten million years with hosts of apsarases,
he shall become a Brahmin learned in the Vedas in this human world.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who, as a celibate with senses conquered, eats only at every fourth mealtime and maintains this practice for one full year:
[he travels] in a vehicle yoked with peacocks of variegated plumage, adorned with many-colored banners.
That man travels by means of a divine vehicle to the city of Mahendra,
being served at his pleasure by beautiful women who are not emaciated;
thereafter, he rejoices perfectly for twelve koṭis of years.
And having descended from the world of Śakra to this world, O lord of men,
he shall indeed become a learned Brāhmaṇa, patient, and one who has mastered the Vedas;
he who, free from sin, eats only at the sixth meal-time for one year.
Endowed with the vows of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), pure and free from anger—
now hear of the supreme fruit for him who is thus engaged in austerity.
Resembling the sun, he travels in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that possesses a brilliance surpassing even the sun.
He indeed goes to my worlds, attended by divine women;
there, being honored by the Sādhyas and the Maruts as he pleases,
he constantly beholds me and sports with hosts of Apsarases.
And whoever, with their soul devoted to me, observes a fast for a fortnight,
when that vow is completed, he should gratify Vedic scholars and twice-born men;
that one of great austerity also goes by means of a divine celestial chariot.
Illuminating the sky with his radiance, he enters my world. There he rejoices at will, assuming any form he desires according to his pleasure.
Having sported there like a god for thirty crores of years, O King, he remains.
In this world of mortals, such a twice-born man shall be worthy of worship;
he shall become one who has mastered all three Vedas along with their auxiliary branches,
and he who, with his soul absorbed in me, observes the month-long fast.
Having conquered the senses, conquered anger, and mastered the intellect, he should be intent upon bathing. When that observance is completed, having fed the best of the twice-born there,
he should then give a sacrificial fee with a joyful inner soul.
Possessing great majesty, he goes to the unsurpassed world of Brahmā,
served by hosts of celestial women, traveling in a vehicle yoked with lions;
there, in the world of Brahmā, he is attended by hosts of divine sages.
O King, for fourteen thousand nine hundred and sixteen billion years, he rejoices according to his desire;
then, having descended from that time, he becomes a twice-born man in this world,
learned in the six auxiliary sciences and the four Vedas, remaining free from disease for thirty lifetimes.
He who, having renounced all actions, pure and free from anger,
sets out upon the Great Journey with one-pointed mind and his thoughts fixed on Me—
that man of great austerity shall go to the abode of Indra by means of a celestial chariot.
Adorned with a magnificent golden crown variegated with great jewels,
and honored there by the lords of the gods, he dwells upon the surface of the celestial realm, attended by hosts of divine women. He possesses a hundred million [attendants].
Descending from the world of Śakra, he is born among human beings as a king of kings, possessed of great splendor, a lord honored by all the world. And he who,
with his soul dedicated to me, undertakes a fast unto death—
Having uttered the mantra "Namo brahmaṇyadevāya" with a concentrated mind,
established in his inner self and having conquered anger— listen now to the fruit of his merit: he shall travel at will, assume any form at will, and possess a radiance equal to the rising sun.
In a divine celestial chariot, he travels to the worlds free from affliction;
having gone from heaven to heaven at his pleasure, that one of great splendor rejoices in my worlds until the dissolution of all beings.
And whoever, with his mind absorbed in me, enters the fire,
he too attains my world by means of a divine vehicle;
thereafter, endowed with all virtues, he shall behold me forever.
O King, for thirty crores of years he rejoices in my presence;
then, descending in due time, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, one who,
with a serene mind and pure vows, practices agriculture while propitiating me.
Uttering this mantra, "Namo brahmaṇyadevāya," he shall reach my world and rejoice for sixty million years, traveling in a resplendent celestial chariot with the brilliance of the rising sun.
And having descended into my world, he shall become a king in this world;
devoted to me and pure, he shall establish himself through my form,
especially on the fourteenth day, in the southern form of Rudra.
Worshipped by the Siddhas, the Brahman-sages, and the denizens of the divine worlds,
and being praised in song by Gandharvas and hosts of spirits,
that one of great ascetic power and immense splendor might enter either me or Śaṅkara.
O King, there should be no doubt in this matter that for him there is no further rebirth—
whether it be for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a woman, or even for the sake of a teacher or a Brahmin.
O Indra among kings, those who are slain go to the world of Śakra;
there, in celestial palaces made of Jāmbūnada gold that move at will,
they rejoice for the duration of a Manvantara, attended by divine women.
By failing to give what has been promised and by seizing what has been given,
O Bhārata, everything that was given since birth is destroyed;
there, those who do not give cows drink nothing but milk.
Those who do not give land do not attain land;
whatever desires one gives to the brahmins,
those very same desires one enjoys in the heavenly world.
Whatever object is most beloved and has been acquired through righteous means—
that very thing should be given to one possessed of virtue by him who desires that it become inexhaustible;
for this cannot be achieved without fasting for three nights and without visiting sacred fords.
If one does not give gold and a cow, he is born as one known as "the poor. That gift which is not given to a *śrotriya* fails to yield its fruit.
Where the *śrotriyas* do not eat, there the gods do not partake.

There is nothing greater than those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*); there is no higher, supreme deity. And furthermore, O Indra among kings, there is no greater treasure than the feeding of those learned in the Vedas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Especially at the time of the separation from the body along with its senses,
the Blessed One said:
"What is the nature of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as it exists in the intermediate state?"
A person here obtains the fruit of everything done, whether good or evil;
yet for no being does the state of the five elements (death) truly exist.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, this state of the five elements brings about great prosperity for men.

Those best of the twice-born who perform these five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) are said to undergo "fivefoldness," which is the separation from the five elements. The eternal person is never born and never dies.
O Pāṇḍava, death generally belongs only to the sinful;
for those who possess no meritorious destiny, it is called "death.
Generally, people who have not accomplished their duties tremble before death.
Having accomplished their purpose, they await death as if it were a beloved guest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, how are the five sacrifices performed here by the twice-born?"
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to state their names in their entirety.
"Listen, Yudhiṣṭhira, as I proclaim the five great sacrifices."
O King, by these very acts a householder attains the same world as Brahman;

they declare the five sacrifices to be the sacrifice to the sages (*ṛṣiyajña*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*), and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*).

The libation (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the sages (ṛṣiyajña); self-study of the Vedas (svādhyāya) is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña). The offering of bali is the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūtayajña), and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).
That rite which is performed with reference to the ancestors is proclaimed as the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
The *huta*, the *ahuta*, as well as the *prahuta*, the *prāśita*,
and the offering of the *bali*— these are declared by the wise to be the *pākayajñas*. The oblations beginning with the *vaiśvadeva* are called *huta*.
That which is offered as an *ahuta* sacrifice becomes the gift; that which is offered as a *prahuta* sacrifice is the food eaten by Brahmins.
The wise know that the ritual consumption [of the remains] is the *prāṇāgnihotra* oblation. And the *balikarma*, O King of kings, is proclaimed as the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
Some declare the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*) to be the *pākayajñas*;
others, who know the great sacrifices, understand them to be the *brahmayajña* and the rest.
All these are proclaimed as the great sacrifices in every respect.
One should not, according to one's ability, neglect to feed hungry Brāhmaṇas.
Those men who eat for themselves day after day without having first provided for them,
undoubtedly consume nothing but impurity.
Therefore, having bathed, a learned twice-born man should perform these rites day after day.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"But if a twice-born man eats otherwise than this, he indeed becomes liable for penance."
"O God of gods, salutations be unto you; O Janārdana, [speak] for the sake of your devotee.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of gods, you ought to tell me the ritual procedure for bathing."
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to all that which is purifying and destructive of sin—
by which rite of bathing the twice-born are liberated from evil.
[One should take] earth, cow dung, sesame seeds, and likewise *darbha* grass.
Having taken flowers according to the prescribed rule, one should go toward the water;
O best of the twice-born, one should not bathe elsewhere when a river is available.
When abundant water is present, one should never bathe in a small amount.
Having gone near water to a pure and pleasing place,
one should then sprinkle earth, cow dung, and other materials there and cast them down;
having washed one's feet outside and sipped water twice with diligence.
Having circumambulated it clockwise, one should pay homage to that water;
however, a wise person should never wash away the sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*) with water,
nor should he strike that water with his foot or with any other hand.
O son of Pāṇḍu, for water consists of all the gods and is composed of me;
therefore, it must not be destroyed, but one should wash the ground with water. A wise person should first immerse himself entirely and should not rub his limbs [against the ground].

Having reached that sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) once again: having formed the hand in the shape of a cow’s ear, one should drink water three times;
then one should wipe the mouth twice and sprinkle water upon one's own feet.
Then he should touch the vital breaths located in the head only once;
then, having touched both arms, the heart, and the navel,
and having touched water for each limb, he should touch his head again.
Having recited, "May the waters purify," one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again;

likewise, having recited the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, or the verse beginning with "sadasaspatim," and having performed the sipping of water, one should subsequently apply the earth-clods after dividing them into three parts.
With the verse "idaṃ viṣṇur," one should touch the highest, lowest, and middle parts of the body; then, having offered salutations with the hymns dedicated to Varuṇa, one should [offer] water.
If at a flowing stream, one should offer against the current; in other waters, one should face the sun.
Having uttered "Oṃ," one should immerse oneself and must not agitate the water.
Having divided the cow dung into three parts, one should first apply it to the body while in the water.
Then, one should again recite the Gāyatrī mantra together with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) once more with a heart absorbed in Me,
one should sprinkle oneself in due order with water purified by *darbha* grass using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and likewise with the four verses beginning with "tarat sa mandī."
Then, with the *gosūkta*, the *aśvasūkta*, and the *śuddhavarga*,
as well as with the hymns (*sūkta*) dedicated to Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, Savitṛ, and Indra,
and with the *vāmadevya* and other Sāmans composed by me, he [purified] himself.
Standing within the water, one should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn with speech;
or then, one should mutter the *gāyatrī* together with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*;
or, recollecting Me, one should mutter the *praṇava* until the release of the breath.
Having leaped up and reached the bathing place, one should put on two washed white garments;
one should fasten the girdle around the pure [waist] and not make it hang down to the ankles.
For whatever Vedic rite one performs while the girdle is tied at the ankle...
The *rākṣasas*, *dānavas*, and *daityas* will joyfully plunder that [place].
Therefore, with every effort, one should not fasten a rope around the waist.
Then, having slowly washed both feet and hands with clay, [one should proceed].
Having sipped water once, the twice-born should sip again with the Sāvitrī mantra;
being pure while standing in water, he should do so while remaining in the water, and while standing on dry land, he should do so while remaining on dry land.
Therefore, standing in both places, he should sip water for the sake of self-purification.
Seated upon *darbha* grass with *darbha* grass in hand, facing east and well-composed,
he should then perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with his inner self absorbed in me;
he should mutter the *Sāvitrī* mantra a thousand times, or indeed a hundred times.
When that recitation of the Sāvitrī is completed and has been consecrated with mantras,
one should sprinkle water for the destruction of the Mandehas and the Rākṣasas. Then, having sipped water with the mantra "udvargo 'si," one should pour out the water for expiation.
Then, taking water together with flowers in his joined palms, the twice-born man should cast it toward the sun and form the *vyomamudrā* (the sky-gesture). Thereafter,
he should mutter the single-syllable mantra of the Sun twelve times.
Then one should recite the six-syllable mantra and others six times;
having performed a circumambulation and touched one's own face with that mudrā,
one should then stand with arms raised and gaze at the sun with a concentrated mind.
One should meditate upon me situated within that maṇḍala, as a form of light with four arms;
one should recite the mantra "ud u tyam" and also "citraṃ taccakṣuḥ," and having recited the Sāvitrī and my own hymn according to one's ability.
He should recite the Sāmans dedicated to Manu and the Puruṣavrata;
then he should look at the sun with the verse, "The swan dwelling in purity. Having circumambulated him clockwise and paid homage to the Maker of Day, he should proceed.
Then one should offer libations with water to Brahmā, to me, and to Śaṅkara;
likewise to Prajāpati, to the gods, and also to the divine sages;
as well as to the Vedas along with their limbs, to the Itihāsas, and to the sacrificial rites.
The ancient and divine lineages of the Apsarases,
as well as the seasons, the years, and the divisions of time down to the smallest units; the hosts of beings, all created things, the rivers, and the oceans.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), one should satisfy the mountains, the deities dwelling upon the mountains, the medicinal herbs, and the forest trees, saying for each: "May they be satisfied.
Then, having taken hold [of the vessel] with the left hand, [one should offer] with the right hand.
Wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītin), he should thereafter offer libations to the seers who composed the mantras;
with a concentrated mind, he should likewise offer to the seers beginning with Marīci and ending with Nārada.
Then, wearing the sacred thread over his right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), he should offer libations to these deities and the ancestors.
Then, however, [he should offer] to Kavyavāhana Agni, to Soma, and likewise to Vaivasvata;
then also to Aryaman and likewise to the Agniṣvātta ancestors,
and to the Somapās, with darbha grass, sesame seeds, and water.
Having said "Be satisfied," he should thereafter offer libations to his own ancestors:
first to the fathers, then to the grandfathers, and likewise to the great-grandfathers;
and likewise to the paternal grandmother and the great-grandmother.
Likewise, one should likewise [behave toward] paternal aunts and maternal aunts,
as well as one's own mother and even one's maternal grandmother; likewise,
one's mother’s maternal grandmother, as well as the guru and the teacher.
Out of compassion and free from envy, he should offer libations to his deceased preceptors, friends, kinsmen, disciples, officiating priests, paternal relatives,
and sons; having thus offered the libations and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), he should wring out the bathing garment.

Those who know the tradition say that one should first provide an increase for one's servants and for those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas). Without having first satisfied them, one should not wring out the bathing garment;
for if one should wring it out out of delusion beforehand, the gods along with the hosts of sages [would be offended].
But the ancestors, having departed in despair after pronouncing a curse, go back the way they came. Having washed his feet with earth and sipped water again, being purified,
he should then begin his private Vedic recitation (svādhyāya) while seated upon *darbha* grass with *darbha* blades in hand.

Beginning with the Veda at the outset, and thereafter [reciting] the word-for-word (pada) and sequential (krama) arrangements according to one's own ability— whatever one studies in this manner is declared to be *svādhyāya*.
Whether it be a *ṛc*, or a *yajus*, or even a *sāman* verse.
One should not neglect the study of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* according to one’s ability. Having risen and paid homage to the cardinal directions and their presiding deities,
as well as to Brahmā, Agni, the Earth, and likewise the medicinal herbs;
Having likewise paid homage to Vāc, Vācaspati, myself, and the rivers, one should worship with water, beginning with the syllable *praṇava*. Then,
having said "Obeisance to the waters," one should pay homage to that water.
Having bowed his head to those— the radiant one, Sūrya, and likewise Āditya—
he then, being composed, gazed at the sun with the *praṇava*.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Then one should constantly worship me with flowers that are dear to me alone.
O Mādhava, those flowers which are dear to you have you as their presiding deity.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Acyuta, tell me everything concerning my devotion to you. "Listen attentively, O King; these flowers bring me great pleasure:
the kumuda, the karavīra, the caṇaka, and likewise the campaka."
O King of kings, the *mallikā* flower, the *jāti* flower, the *nandyāvarta*, the *nandika*,
the petals of the *palāśa* flower, *dūrvā* grass,
and the *bhṛṅgaka* are especially dear to me; so too is the forest garland (*vanamālā*).
Of all flowers, the *utpala* is a thousand times more meritorious;
from that, O King, is the *padma*, and from the *padma* comes the *śatapatraka*. Beyond that is the *sahasrapatra*, and after that, the *puṇḍarīka*.

A single *tulasī* leaf is superior in merit to a thousand *puṇḍarīka* lotuses; a *baka* flower is superior to that, and a golden flower is even more excellent than that. O Pāṇḍava, there is nothing dearer to me than a golden flower.
In the absence of flowers, a wise person should worship me with *tulasī* leaves;
in the absence of leaves, with branches; in the absence of branches, with roots and fruits;
and in the absence of roots, a wise person full of devotion should worship me there with earth.
"O King, listen with a concentrated mind to the flowers that are to be avoided:
the *kiṅkiṇī*, the *munipuṣpa*, the *dhattūra*, the *pāṭala*, as well as the *atimuktaka*, the *puṃnāga*, and the *naktamālikā*."
Yaudhika, kṣīrikā flowers, nirguṇḍī, lāṅgalī, and japā;
likewise karṇikāra, aśoka, and śalmalī flowers;
as well as kakubha, kovidāra, or even vaibhītaka.
One should entirely avoid the *kuraṇṭaka* flower, as well as the *tilvaka*, *lāṅgalī*,
*aṅkola*, and *girikarṇī*; likewise, one should avoid all those that are exclusively blue in color,
as well as any others that are of a single uniform hue.

The flowers of the *arka* tree should be avoided, as should those placed upon *arka* leaves; one should avoid all *vyāghāta* and *picumanda* [leaves] as well. However, O Lord of Men, one may use other fragrant leaves that are white in color.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"My devotee should worship me with those things that are not forbidden, according to what is available. But how are you to be worshipped, and what are your forms?"
"How should the Vaikhānasas speak, or how should the Pāñcarātrikas speak?
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to all that regarding the sequence of one's own worship."
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila),
one should perform the rite according to the procedure for the eight-syllable mantra, or else with twelve-syllable [mantras],
or again with Vedic mantras, or with my own hymn (sūkta).
Having then installed me there, the wise man,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, worships me as Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aniruddha; so say the people who know the Vaikhānasa scriptures.
But others, O King, the followers of the Pañcarātra, understand me thus:
as Vāsudeva, O Indra among kings, and also as Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; they declare me to be fourfold in form.
"O Indra among kings, these and other forms exist through various designations.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Know that they are indeed not different from me; thus should the wise man worship me."
"O Lord, what are your devotees like, and what are their vows? O Blessed One, tell me this, O Lord of Gods, for I am your devotee, O Acyuta. The Blessed One said:
"Tell me this, O Lord of Gods, for I am your devotee, O Acyuta."
Those who do not worship other deities, who are dear to my devotees,
and who have come to me alone for refuge— they are proclaimed as my true devotees. Even the heavens, which bring glory and are especially dear to me, [are attained by them].
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, my devotee should observe these vows:
my devotee should not wear any other garment while crossing water;
being healthy, he should not sleep during the day, and he should avoid honey and meat.
One should circumambulate Brahmins, a cow, an *aśvattha* tree, and the sacrificial fire from left to right.
One should not run when it rains, nor should one omit the first alms received. One should not eat salt that is not processed, nor the *saubhañjanaka* or *gṛñjana* plants.

One should give a handful of grain to a cow and avoid fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla). Likewise, one should carefully avoid food that has been stale, cooked food brought from another's house, and any substance that has not been offered.
One should avoid from afar the shade of the *vibhītaka* and *karañja* trees. Even when afflicted, one should not utter slander against Brahmins or the gods,
O Pāṇḍava, whether they be of the nature of goodness (*sāttvika*), passion (*rājasa*), or darkness (*tāmasa*).
My devotees worship me; such is their destination. Those characterized by darkness (tāmasas) go to darkness; those characterized by passion (rājasas) go to that very passion;
those characterized by goodness (sāttvikas), being endowed with purity, go to that very purity.

Those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya and the power of the essence of Yoga behold the expanse of the path from the sky, the sun, and the moon. [They see it] within that which has a single pillar, nine gates, three posts, and five elements.
In this city of the body, the king should always be present.
When the sun has risen for this wise man engaged in his duties,
even though he knows the four Vedas, six types of śūdras are said to reside within his body.
Seven classes of Kṣatriyas are to be known, and eight of Vaiśyas are proclaimed;
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, twenty-one classes of Śūdras are fixed.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, and pride—these [are their characteristics].
Great delusion— these six are known as the *vṛṣalas* (outcasts) within the body. Arrogance, stiffness, egoism, envy,
malice, harshness, and cruelty— these seven are known as the *kṣatriyas*.
Sharpness, deceit, guile, crookedness, hypocrisy, and indeed lack of uprightness,
backbiting, and falsehood— these eight are proclaimed as the qualities of Vaiśyas.
Greed, hunger, sleep, laziness, lack of shame, and lack of compassion [are likewise their traits].
Debt and dispute, negligence and a lack of fortitude; fear, timidity, dullness, evil, and resentment; hope, lack of faith, instability, and lack of restraint.
Impurity and defilement—these, indeed, are proclaimed as the characteristics of Śūdras.
He in whom these are not seen is truly called a Brāhmaṇa. For in whatever states a twice-born man may exist at any given time, [he remains such].
At that specific time, he should be known as a Brāhmaṇa, though weak in knowledge;
at whatever time one restrains the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and meditates upon me,
at that time indeed he is to be known as a twice-born (*dvija*), for at all other times he is otherwise.
Therefore, becoming sattvic, pure, and free from anger,
one who desires to be dear to me should constantly worship me; with tongue not fickle, established in steadfastness.
Casting the gaze only a yoke’s length ahead,
restraining the flickering mind and speech,
and turning away from fear— one is called my devotee.
Those Brāhmaṇas who are such spiritual practitioners with their senses restrained—
when they are fed at Śrāddha rites, the ancestors are satisfied by that;
for righteousness triumphs, not unrighteousness, and truth triumphs, not falsehood.
Forgiveness triumphs; anger does not. One who possesses forgiveness becomes a true Brahmin.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the fruit of the merit of giving and the fruits of the merit of austerity...
With a joyful heart, Dharmaputra spoke again to Keśava:
"O Lord, O Mādhava, this Kapilā cow who was previously produced by the four-faced one [Brahmā] as a sacrificial cow is eternally meritorious, O All-pervading One."
How indeed should she be given to the Brahmins, or on what day?
To what kind of Brahmin should she, who possesses auspicious marks, be given?
And how many types of Kapila cows have been described by the Self-Existent One himself?
"O Lord, by whom should those cows be given? I wish to hear this in its true essence.
Thus addressed in the assembly by the son of Dharma, Hṛṣīkeśa spoke of the number of Kapilā cows and their very greatness.
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to this supreme, purifying, and sacred truth,
by hearing which even a man of sinful deeds is liberated from his sins—
[the goddess] who was born from the midst of fire, divine, and possessing a splendor equal to the flames of fire.

With horns blazing like flames of fire, with eyes like glowing embers, with a tail of fire and hooves of fire, endowed with the luster of fiery hair— she was that one of the nature of fire, with a tongue of fire, a neck of fire, and a flaming radiance.
Those Śūdras who, deluded by greed, consume the milk of a Kapilā cow—
one should know them to be fallen, for they are indeed like Caṇḍālas;
no Brāhmaṇa whatsoever should accept anything from their house.
Even those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) must be avoided from afar;
for at all times they are shunned by all ancestors and deities. Indeed, those sinners are always unworthy of receiving gifts and unfit for conversation.

As long as they drink from a *kapilā* cow, their ancestors continue to consume impure substances upon the earth like dogs and jackals. This applies whether it be the ghee, milk, curd, or even the buttermilk of a *kapilā*.

Listen to this destination of those Śūdras who subsist upon [the teachings of] Kapila: A Śūdra who lives by the teachings of Kapila, having died, goes to the Raurava hell. Dwelling in that terrible Raurava, he suffers for a hundred million years.
Falling away from Raurava, he is born as a worm in excrement;
lying by the thousands in foul-smelling pits of filth,
being born right there, he finds no means of escape.
And if a Brāhmaṇa should accept a gift from those [outcastes] in their house,
from that time forward his ancestors, too, shall drink impure substances. One should not converse with him, nor should one share a seat with him.
That lowest of Brahmins must always be avoided from afar. Whoever converses with him or shares a bed with him must perform the Prājāpatya penance; by that alone is he purified.
If a Brāhmaṇa accepts a gift from a Śūdra who lives off the wealth of a Kapila cow, he must undoubtedly perform an expiation;
he should either perform the Brahmakūrca penance or the Cāndrāyaṇa.

He is released from that sin; therefore, he is indeed a Brāhmaṇa by this [act]. For the Kapilā cow was created of old by the Self-born Brahmā for the sake of the Agnihotra and for the sake of sacrifice, having extracted the splendor from every source.
O son of Pāṇḍu, the Kapilā cow is the most sacred of all sacred things, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the highest merit among merits,
the foremost austerity among austerities, and the supreme vow among vows.
Among all gifts, this gift is supreme; for it is the inexhaustible source.
O Pāṇḍava, whatever holy fords, sacred shrines, purifying sites, and delightful places exist upon the earth throughout all the worlds— [all these are encompassed by this].
Having extracted the essence of light from them, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds,
himself fashioned the Kapila cows for the very purpose of delivering the world.
For this Kapila cow, O son of Pāṇḍu, consists of all forms of splendor.
Consisting of eternal nectar, pure, holy, and the supreme purifier—
twice-born men should offer the Agnihotra oblations with the milk, curd, or ghee of a Kapila cow, both morning and evening.
O Lord, those Brahmins who, having attained supreme devotion, duly perform the *agnihotra* sacrifices with the ghee, curds, or milk of a tawny cow (*kapilā*), and likewise honor their guests;
Those best of the twice-born who constantly abstain from the food of Śūdras and are free from hypocrisy and falsehood go, in celestial chariots radiant as the sun,
through the center of the solar disc to the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
In the divine abode of Brahmā, moving at will and assuming forms at will,
they rejoice for an imperishable kalpa while being honored by Brahmā himself.
Thus indeed, O King, is the Kapilā cow holy, a source of the nectar of mantras.
Maitreyī was created by Brahmā from the very midst of fire at the very beginning;
O Pāṇḍava, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell upon the tip of the horn of Kapilā day after day, by the command of Brahmā.

That mortal who, having risen early in the morning, being self-restrained and pure, holds upon his head the water dripping from the tip of a tawny cow's horn— that man is instantly cleansed of all sin by that sacred water.

It burns away the sin committed over three years like fire consumes grass. That man who performs the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) in the morning with the urine of a *kapilā* cow becomes free from sin through that meritorious bath.
One is liberated from the sins committed over thirty years; there is no doubt about this.
O King, for one who rises in the morning and with devotion offers a handful of grass, even the sin committed during thirty nights is destroyed.

O Pāṇḍava, whoever rises early in the morning and, out of devotion to me, performs that circumambulation— with a single circumambulation by one endowed with faith— the entire earth has been circumambulated by him; of this there is no doubt.

The sin committed during the ten-night period is certainly destroyed for him. O Pāṇḍava, that pure man who bathes with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords (tīrthas).
O Pāṇḍava, by that bath, even for one endowed with faith,
the sin committed over ten nights perishes at that very moment; likewise,
by seeing a Kapilā cow with devotion and hearing her lowing sound.

O King, a man who, being pure, touches a *kapilā* cow on any part of her body whatsoever, whether here or there, destroys the sin committed during a year, O Pāṇḍava. He removes the evil done throughout a day and night.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) declared that the fruit for a man who gives a thousand cows and one tawny cow (*kapilā*) is equal in the world of Brahmā;
yet, if a man should by some negligence kill even one tawny cow, [his merit is lost].

By him, ten thousand cows would have been slain; there is no doubt about this. But he who gives even a single tawny cow to a *śrotriya* who maintains the sacred fires, O Pāṇḍava, it is as if a hundred thousand cows have been given by him.
The Self-Existent One himself has declared that there are exactly ten types of tawny cows (*kapilā*).
Listen to what happens when one gives these to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*): such a person goes to heaven. The first is the golden-tawny cow; the second is the light-brown cow.
The third has reddish-brown eyes; the fourth has a reddish-brown neck;
the fifth has the luster of a brown color; the sixth is white and reddish-brown;
the seventh has reddish-brown eyes; and the eighth has reddish-brown hooves.
The ninth is to be known as Pāṭalā, and the tenth is Pucchapiṅgalā.
These ten are declared to be Kapilā cows; they always deliver men, being auspicious, purifying, and destroyers of all sins.
"O Lord of Men, ten oxen have been described in this very way;
a Brāhmaṇa may make them work, but no other caste under any circumstances. Furthermore, a twice-born man must not strike them with a stick, whether in a field or on the road."
One should drive [the oxen] with a mere "hum" sound, or with a branch bearing leaves;
never with a staff, nor with a stick, nor again with a rope. One should not drive those who are exhausted by hunger, thirst, or fatigue, nor those whose senses are impaired.
One should not eat while those who have not yet eaten remain unsatisfied, nor should one drink water before they have drunk theirs.
These mothers are declared to be the ones for whom service is due; they are proclaimed as one's fathers.
Furthermore, it is ordained that the yoking of draft animals shall take place during the first third of the day.
One should rest at the middle stage, at the final stage, or wherever it is convenient; or where there is urgent business on the road, or where there is danger on the way,
one may drive the draft animals there, and he is not tainted by sin.
O King, he who drives [the oxen] otherwise goes to the Raurava hell;
O lord of men, O son of Pāṇḍu, he who out of delusion causes their blood to flow incurs a sin equal to that of killing a Brahmin.
By that sin, the evil-souled one goes to hell without a doubt;
having remained in all the hells for hundreds upon hundreds [of years],
he will become an ox in this world of human beings.
Therefore, a man seeking liberation should indeed give away a *kapilā* cow. But that *vṛṣala*, deluded by greed, who would drive a *kapilā*—
by him the thirty-three gods and the ancestors as well have been driven.
O King, that evil-minded man, being constantly tormented by the gods and the ancestors,
shall go from one hell to a more terrible hell until the dissolution of the universe.
Brahmā, Rudra, and likewise Agni have all attained the destination of the Kapilas.
Therefore, they must not be killed; rather, they should be especially honored.
When, exhausted, they sigh, then they may destroy that entire lineage.
O King, for as many hairs as they possess, for that many hundreds of years [the sin remains].
In that hell, those men who carry them are cooked;
therefore, a tawny cow is prescribed for the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in all sacrifices.
Consequently, those fees should be given in sacrifices by the twice-born.
And for the purpose of the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
he who should diligently bestow [a cow] upon a learned *śrotriya* who is poor, weary, and of immeasurable splendor—
purified by that gift, his soul is glorified in the world of Agni.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for as many hairs as there are on the body of a tawny cow (kapilā),
for that many thousands of years does a man dwell in heaven;
so it is for one who gives away a tawny cow with golden horns and hooves.
On either the equinox or the solstice, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
by that merit equal to an Aśvamedha, he goes to my world.
[One should give] a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, accompanied by her calf, and a bronze milking vessel.

Adorned with garments, well-nourished, and beautified with perfumes and garlands—indeed, gold is the most sacred of all purifying things; this is my conviction. Therefore, she who is adorned with golden ornaments should be given to the maintainer of the *agnihotra* fire.
O Indra among kings, having given in this manner, one shall deliver seven ancestors and seven descendants;
O Indra among kings, there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
It would be equal to a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices and the Vājapeya sacrifice.
A thousand *vājapeya* sacrifices are equal to one *aśvamedha*;
a thousand *aśvamedhas* are equal to one *rājasūya*. O Pāṇḍava, [this is equal] to a thousand tawny cows (*kapilā*) given according to the prescribed rite.
Having obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, he is glorified in my world; for him,
O bull among the Kurus, there is no returning again,
he who bestows a tawny cow with her calf and a bronze milking vessel.
Having become a cow of plenty through those various virtues,
that cow approaches the man who gave her away,
even as he is bound by his own past actions.
Like a boat driven by the wind upon the great ocean, [a gift] saves a person falling into the hell of intense darkness; for indeed,
a cow that has been given delivers a human being.
It delivers one's sons, grandsons, and the entire family up to the seventh generation in the hereafter,
for as long as men support the earth.
Just as medicine prepared with mantras, when administered to a person, destroys diseases immediately, so too does [the gift] from this world to the next destroy the giver's misfortunes.
In the same way, a tawny cow given to a worthy recipient quickly destroys all the sins of a man,
just as serpents flee upon seeing Garuda.
Just as those who are helpless and afflicted by fear flee from afar,
even so, upon seeing the gift of a Kapila cow,
a person's sins quickly perish.
Just as a serpent, having cast off its own skin,
assumes a new and auspicious form,
even so does the liberated person [shed] his own sins.
Indeed, one shines through the gift of a tawny cow (*kapilā*),
just as a blazing lamp dispels the darkness clinging within a house.
In the same way, a man may indeed expel even long-subsided sin by the gift of a *kapilā* cow;
for as many hairs as there are upon her, [so many sins are removed].
And for as many millions of ages of the Yuga as there are hairs on the body of a cow with its calf,
that man rejoices in the world of Brahmā.
Of that man who maintains the sacred fires, who is fond of guests, who keeps far from the food of Śūdras, who has conquered his senses, who is devoted to truth, and who is engaged in Vedic study—
"For a cow given away indeed delivers one in the hereafter.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having thus heard of this supreme merit of the excellent gift of a Kapila cow..."
With a joyful heart, the son of Dharma spoke again to Keśava:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, when a Kapilā cow is given to a Brahmin,
how is it that the deities abide within all her limbs?"

"O best of gods, among these ten types of *kapilā* cows that you have described to me, how many possess the marks of merit? And by what means were they favored by the gods and the hosts of ancestors?"
"By whom was it joined with color? For I have a great curiosity to hear this.
When Yudhiṣṭhira had spoken thus, Keśava, whose word is truth, then began to speak that which is the supreme secret among all secrets.
"Listen, O King, to this purifying secret, the supreme dharma. This truth is to be grasped; it must not be proclaimed to those who argue from mere logic.
When, at birth, the two feet of the calf emerge along with its head—"
Those who know the proper time declare that when these two are seen together, it is the time for giving.
As long as the calf, though situated in the atmosphere, has not yet descended to the earth, so long is the cow to be known as the Earth herself; therefore, such a cow should be given.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for as many hairs as there are on a cow with her calf,
and as many grains of sand as there are submerged in the waters of the womb,
for that many thousands of years is the donor glorified in heaven.
Having adorned a tawny cow (*kapilā*) along with her calf with golden ornaments and covering her with sesame seeds,
one should indeed give her away, fully decorated with all kinds of jewels; by that act, the entire earth— with its oceans, mountains, forests, and groves— is gifted.

The four oceans shall be given; there is no need for deliberation on this point. By that gift, which is equal to the gift of the entire earth, a human being crosses over the ocean of *saṃsāra* and goes to the world of Prajāpati.
Whether one is a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a destroyer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
even if burdened by such great sins (mahāpātaka), one is purified by this gift.
Whoever recites this meritorious and supreme gift of a Kapilā cow [attains the highest state].

Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who, having risen in the morning with devotion to me, recites this chapter, O Yudhiṣṭhira: by mind, deed, or speech, and with full awareness, such a reciter shall destroy the sin committed during the night.
But he who, while performing the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*), gratifies the twice-born with this [text],
his ancestors, exceedingly delighted, partake of nectar (*amṛta*).
And he who should listen to this with devotion, with his inner self absorbed in me—
All the evil committed by him during the night is quickly destroyed. Beyond this, O King, I shall tell you the specific qualities of the *kapilā* cows that I have described to you as tenfold.
Among them, four are preeminent, pure, and destroyers of sin:
the auspicious Suvarṇakapilā, as well as Raktākṣipiṅgalā,
the cow Piṅgalākṣī, and she who is Piṅgalapiṅgalā.
These four excellent cows are meritorious and destroyers of sin;
whether saluted or merely touched, they destroy the sins of a man. He in whose house these tawny cows, which destroy all evil, reside, [is freed from sin].
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there Śrī, Vijaya, and Kīrti abide eternally;
the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) finds pleasure in these through milk,
all the gods through curds, and the Fire-god through clarified butter.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the fathers, grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers are satisfied for ten million years by even a single gift of ghee,
milk, curds, or milk-rice from a Kapilā cow.
Having given [this] once to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one is liberated from all sins. Furthermore, having observed a fast for a day and night with the senses subdued,
and having drunk the five products of a tawny cow (*kapilā-pañcagavya*), it is superior even to the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Having consumed that during an auspicious moment in the bright fortnight, he— purified in soul and pure in mind,
liberated from anger and falsehood, with his inner self absorbed in me—
[should do so] with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya), each applied separately according to the mantras.

Whoever bathes either my image or an image of Śaṅkara at the equinox (viṣuva) shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). Purified of sin and pure in soul, he shall travel by a celestial vehicle that illuminates the sky.
A mortal who goes to my world, or even to the world of Rudra, [is purified];
for in ancient times, Kapilā, possessing a golden luster, was created by Brahmā from the sacrificial fire-pit as a highly radiant *homa*-cow through supreme mantras.
But as soon as she was created, the gods led by Rudra in heaven,
the Siddhas, the Brahman-sages, the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and sacrifices,
the oceans, the rivers, and the mountains together with the clouds beheld her.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and Pannagas also arrived;
they were all filled with wonder at the one of great splendor in the midst of the fire,
and they praised her many times with all kinds of various mantras.

With palms joined in reverence, they all prostrated themselves on the ground with their heads before Tāmraśṛṅgī, the three-eyed one, who was accompanied by her calf and was the source of the nectar of immortality; then,
with hands folded, they all spoke to the four-faced Grandfather.
"Command us, O Great God; what dear service may we perform for you, O All-pervading Lord?
When thus addressed by all the gods, Brahmā spoke these words:
"May you also show favor toward this milch-cow, who yields such abundance."
This sacrificial cow (homadhenu) should be known as one who will satisfy the fire;
then the fire, being satisfied, will satisfy all of you. Satisfied by her nectar-like milk, you shall become endowed with vigor and prowess.
All of you shall indeed conquer the Dānavas according to your desire; having attained vigor, strength, and sovereignty, being full of courage and having vanquished your enemies,
and possessing all of you an incalculable power, you shall surely protect the subjects.
"And all subjects here shall be protected by you in accordance with Dharma;
they shall always honor you with sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees.
Thus were all the gods addressed by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Then, with delighted minds, they granted a boon to Kapilā:
"Since you have been created today by Brahmā for the welfare of the world,
therefore become pure, sanctifying, and the remover of sin."
Those men who, having seen you, bow down to you, and even touch you with their hands—
the sin committed by them over a year perishes for those devoted to you.
This includes whatever sin was committed unintentionally, unknown, or unseen.

"Those men who, upon seeing you, bow down and address you as 'All-Enduring' (Sarvasaha)— their darkness shall dissolve like the gloom at the rising of the sun. Having spoken thus and granted her this boon, they departed as they had come.
For the sake of delivering the world, she indeed wandered through the worlds;
O sinless Kapila, these [goddesses] were born from her very self and wander this earth for the purpose of showing grace to the world.
Therefore, one who desires welfare in the hereafter should give away a *kapilā* cow.
And just as a *kapilā* cow is given, O King, to an *agnihotrī*,
so too do Viṣṇu and Indra abide upon its two foremost horns.
Candravajradhara also resides at the two bases of the horns;
likewise, Brahmā is in the middle of the horns, and the one whose banner is a bull (Śiva) is on the forehead.
The two Aśvin gods are in the ears, and the Moon and Sun are in the eyes.
In his teeth dwell the Maruts, the gods; in his tongue is Vāk Sarasvatī.
On the tips of his body hair reside all the sages, and on his skin alone is Prajāpati.
In his breaths abide the Vedas, together with the six auxiliary limbs, the Pada-pāṭha, and the Krama-pāṭha.
In the nostrils reside fragrances and sweet-smelling flowers;
all the Vasus dwell in the lower lip, and Agni is established in the mouth. The Sādhyas gods abide in the armpits, and Pārvatī resides in the neck.
On his back are the hosts of stars, and on the hump is the vault of heaven;
in his anus are all the sacred fords, and in his urine is the Ganges herself;
in his dung dwells forever Lakṣmī, consisting of desire and contentment.
At that time, the beautiful goddess Jyeṣṭhā dwells in the nose;
the Pitṛs reside on the surface of the hips, and Ramā rests upon the tail;
all the Viśvedevas are established on both sides.
Guha, the wielder of the spear, stands upon their chest, delighted. Five winds abide in the regions of their knees, shanks, and thighs;
the Gandharvas are in the middle of their hooves, and the Pannagas are at the tips of their hooves.
The four oceans are her very breasts.
She is Rati, Medhā, Kṣamā, Svāhā, Śraddhā, Śānti, Dhṛti, Smṛti,
Kīrti, Dīpti, Kriyā, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Saṃtati.
The cardinal directions and the intermediate directions always attend upon Kapilā;
so too do the gods, the hosts of ancestors, and the throngs of Gandharvas and Apsarases;
as well as the worlds, the islands, the oceans, and the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā.

The planets, the hosts of ancestors, and the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and sacrifices likewise praise him joyfully with various mantras declared in the Vedas; as do the Vidyādharas, the Siddhas, the Bhūtas, and the hosts of stars.
They shower down a rain of flowers and dance with joy.
The goddess of great splendor was produced by Brahmā from the sacrificial fire-pit:
"Obeisance to you, O auspicious Kapilā, who are saluted by all the gods."
"O Kapila, you who are a great being and the embodiment of all sacred fords, auspicious one,
lead this donor, together with his kinsmen, yourself to the world of Brahmā!
Oh, what a meritorious jewel this is— supreme and the destroyer of all suffering!"
"Aha! This pure wealth, acquired through righteousness, is supreme and great!"—
thus do the gods stationed in the sky speak and bow down,
as long as that best of the twice-born accepts and consumes her [gift].
For that long, all the hosts of gods worship Kapilā;
she, with golden horns and silver hooves, is honored with perfumes and flowers,
adorned with two unwashed garments as long as she remains decorated.
To that extent, a tawny cow (*kapilā*), purified by mantras and well-consecrated,
may herself lead all the inhabitants of the earthly realm to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Earth, horses, gold, cows, silver, food, sesame seeds, and barley— these are the gifts.
Day after day, these things being given to a Brahmin, they rejoice;
but when, O Pāṇḍava, they are given to those who are not learned in the Vedas,
they then reproach themselves, saying, "What evil have we done?"
"Alas! Being plundered on all sides by *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*, we shall quickly go to hell"—thus indeed do they grieve.
These [gifts] should also be given to the twice-born, especially to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O Lord of the gods of gods, O slayer of Daityas, as gifts are being given, they increase and deliver the donor; what, then, is the proper time for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*)?"
The Blessed One said:
"Which twice-born (dvijas) are worthy of worship there, and which are to be avoided?
It should be known that the rite for the gods (daiva) belongs to the forenoon, while that for the ancestors (paitṛka) belongs to the afternoon."

They know that gift which is given at an improper time to be the portion of a *rākṣasa*. O Bhārata, they know that food which is eaten while it is being publicly proclaimed, or that which is touched by a dog, to be the portion of a *rākṣasa*.

O King, as many Brahmins as have fallen from their status, as well as those who are dull-witted, insane, and so forth, and those who do not deserve the rites of honor at ceremonies for the gods or the ancestors— such as one who is impotent, one with an enlarged spleen, one afflicted with leprosy, and one suffering from pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman)— [these are excluded].
One who suffers from epilepsy, one who does not deserve honor at ancestral rites, physicians, temple-priests, those who observe religious vows in vain,
and sellers of Soma— these do not deserve hospitality at a *śrāddha*.
Those twice-born ones who eat the food of an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite according to the prescribed rules,
yet have not performed the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, do not deserve to receive honor again. This applies likewise to singers, dancers, acrobats, and musicians.
Those who are professional storytellers and those who are professional soldiers do not deserve hospitality at a *śrāddha* feast. Likewise, O King,
those Brahmins who maintain no sacred fires, those who serve as funeral carriers for the deceased,
thieves, and those who follow improper occupations do not deserve hospitality.
Those twice-born who have not previously been fully known, those who are members of a *gaṇa*,
and even the sons of appointed daughters (*putrikā*), do not deserve hospitality at a *śrāddha*. Likewise, a Brahmin who is a debtor and a twice-born man who is a merchant [are also excluded].

Those who subsist by the sale of living beings do not deserve hospitality at a *śrāddha*. However, those who have observed their vows, who are endowed with virtues, who are constantly devoted to Vedic study,
who know the *Sāvitrī*, and who are observant of ritual duties— they are worthy of hospitality at a *śrāddha*.

The time for the *śrāddha* has arrived; at that time, there were Brahmins with curds and ghee, as well as *darbha* grass, flowers, and a sacred field. O King, those who were restrained in their conduct, though emaciated, were of meager means.
Those who come as supplicants— giving to them yields great fruit. As for those Brahmins who are ascetics, as well as those who live by begging,
and whoever else comes seeking, giving to them yields great fruit.
O best among those who know the Dharma, having understood this with your whole being at that time,
give whatever gift is dear to you and whatever is dear to the learned (śrotriya) to a learned man who is poor and provides no service in return.
O knower of dharma, grant that which you desire as inexhaustible.
Now hear from me, Yudhiṣṭhira, about those who go to hell—
unless, O Pāṇḍava, it was for the sake of a guru or for the sake of fear, and not otherwise.
Those Brahmins who speak falsehoods are indeed destined for hell;
those who carry off another's wife, those who violate another's wife, and those who incite others to do so— they too are indeed destined for hell.
Those who are informers, those who break alliances, those who subsist on the wealth of others, those who are ungrateful toward their friends— they indeed go to hell.
O Pāṇḍava, so too do those who stand outside the system of castes and stages of life, and those who adhere to heretical doctrines.
And those who wait upon such [teachers] are all destined for the abode of hell;
likewise, those who sell the Vedas, those who defile the Vedas,
and those who write down the Vedas— these indeed go to hell.
O King, those who sell liquids, those who sell poison,
and even those who sell milk, go indeed to hell;
for they are the lowest of men who give milk to Caṇḍālas.
Those who act for the sake of wealth or out of affection [toward others] are indeed destined for hell; likewise, those who tame cattle and those who pierce their nostrils,
as well as those who destroy virility, are indeed destined for hell.
Those capable givers who, out of greed for wealth, do not look upon the poor and the helpless, are indeed destined for hell. [Likewise,
those who do not honor] the patient, the self-controlled, the emaciated, the wise, and those who have resided with them for a long time.
Those who, having fulfilled their duties, abandon [others] are indeed destined for hell. Furthermore,
those men who eat delicacies without giving any to the young, the old, or even the weary are indeed destined for hell.
These men, O Yudhiṣṭhira, who go to hell have been described by the ancient seers;
now hear from me about those who have attained heaven—
those who are distinguished by generosity, austerity, truthfulness, and self-restraint.

Those men who follow the Dharma go to heaven. O Pāṇḍava, those men who, having received the sacred learning from their preceptor through service, remain free from attachment to receiving gifts, go to heaven.
Those men who abstain from honey, meat, and wine, who live according to righteous conduct, who refrain from the wives of others, and who serve their mother and father— they go to heaven.
Those men who are affectionate even toward their brothers go to heaven;
those who are self-restrained at the time of eating and are fond of guests,
and who do not block the door, those men go to heaven.
Those men who cause the marriage ceremonies of maidens to be performed, and those men who perform them themselves— even for the poor— go to heaven. Furthermore,
[those who provide] juices, seeds, and likewise medicinal herbs...
Those men who are endowed with faith and are givers go to heaven.
Those men who, for the sake of those in need, speak of safety and danger on the roads, and of even and uneven terrain, go to heaven.
On both lunar festival days (parvan), on the fourteenth and eighth days of the fortnight, during the two twilights,
under the constellation Ārdrā, on one’s own birth star, at the equinoxes, and likewise under Śravaṇā—
those men who abstain from sexual intercourse go to heaven.
The rules for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and those who go to hell or heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Dharma and adharma have been explained; what more do you wish to hear?"
"O Lord, you ought to tell me this in its true nature and in its entirety:
how a mortal might incur the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) without having committed an act of violence.
The Blessed One said:
O Bhārata, he who, having personally summoned a Brāhmaṇa of meager means for the sake of alms,
subsequently says "there is nothing," is called a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
as is he who [acts similarly] toward a neutral Brāhmaṇa here who is well-versed in the Vedas.
The evil-minded one who seizes the livelihood [of others], them they call a slayer of Brahmins.
O lord of the earth, he who creates an obstacle for a herd of cows afflicted by thirst at the edge of water, them they call a slayer of Brahmins.

One who, being ignorant, reviles the true revealed scripture (*śruti*) that has come forth, or the treatise (*śāstra*) composed by the sages— whether in a hermitage, a forest, a village, or even a city— one should know him to be a slayer of Brahman (*brahmaghātaka*).
They call him a slayer of a Brahmin who, out of anger, should cast fire [upon one]; likewise,
one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin who seizes all the property of one who is blind, or lame, or even mute.
Whether out of anger or out of hatred, if one reviles or threatens [his teacher], or fails to approach his wife during her fertile season, they call him a slayer of a Brahmin.
As long as a man remains firm in his essence, so long is he stable; but upon its destruction, he falls into a state of misery.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"They say that he who seizes all one's possessions is a slayer of a Brahmin.
Among all gifts, however, there is one gift that is distinguished above all others."
The Blessed One said:
"O best of gods, tell me who those Brahmins are whose food should not be eaten;
for the gods, with Brahmā at their head, praise food alone."
A gift equal to that of food has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
Food provides vigor in this world; from food, the life-breaths are established.
O King, learn from me these persons whose food must not be eaten, as they shall be described.
[The food] of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice, of a miser, of one who is bound, and of one who has been humiliated;

of one who is accused of a crime, of a eunuch, and of one who causes dissension among those cooking; of a physician, of everyone [of such types], and likewise of one who eats the remnants of another's meal.
One must not eat the food of a fierce person, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), nor the leavings of a *śūdra*,

nor the food of an enemy, nor as it has been heard, the food of an outcast (*patita*). Likewise, one must not eat the food of a slanderer, nor the food of one who sells the sacrifice (*yajña-vikrayin*).
The food of an actor, a weaver, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person;
the food of an Ambaṣṭha, a Niṣāda, and a stage-player;
as well as that of a goldsmith, a flute-maker, and a seller of weapons.
[The impurity lasts for ten days] for charioteers, liquor-sellers, physicians, and washermen;
likewise for those ruled by their wives, the cruel, and buffalo-herders; and similarly for those who have died within ten days of birth, and for prostitutes.

The food of a panegyrist, of a gambler, and likewise of those who know the art of gambling; the food of one whose younger brother has married before him (parivitta), and likewise of the one who marries before his elder brother (parivettṛ); and that of a Brahmin who marries before his elder sister whose husband is living (agredidhiṣu), as well as of one who has taken a younger sister as a wife while the elder remains unmarried (didhiṣūpati).
One should avoid the food of both of these as well as that of a king.

A king’s food takes away one's *tejas* (vital energy), while a Śūdra’s food takes away one's *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster). The food of a goldsmith takes away one's lifespan, and that of a leather-cutter takes away one's fame.
