The food of a group and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the worlds;
the food of a physician shortens one's life, while the food of the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) is pure only in appearance.
The food of a usurer is excrement; therefore, one should avoid it.

He who eats the food of those [outcastes] consumes their skin, bones, and hair. Having eaten the food of these ministers, one should fast for three days. If a twice-born man eats even once intentionally, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
O Pāṇḍava, hear now in truth the fruit of various gifts: the giver of water obtains satisfaction, the giver of food obtains inexhaustible happiness,
the giver of sesame seeds obtains desired offspring, and the giver of lamps obtains excellent vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold obtains long life; the giver of a house obtains the finest dwellings; the giver of silver obtains supreme beauty;
the giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; and the giver of a horse attains the same world as the Aśvins.
The giver of oxen gains cherished prosperity; the giver of a cow attains the world of the Sun. The giver of a vehicle or a bed obtains a wife; the giver of freedom from fear obtains sovereignty.
The giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Among all gifts, the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*) is preeminent.
Among gold, land, cattle, horses, goats, clothing, beds, seats, and so forth,
he who receives what is honored and gives only that which is honored [is truly a giver].
Both of them go to heaven; in the opposite case, they go to hell. One should not speak untruth even after performing a sacrifice, nor should one feel pride after practicing austerities.
Even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift.

Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; life perishes through reviling Brahmins; and giving perishes through boasting. A creature is born alone, and alone indeed it dies.
One alone experiences the fruit of good deeds, and one alone reaps the result of evil deeds.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of clay, the kinsmen depart with averted faces; only *dharma* follows after him.
The mind calculates how to perform future deeds;
surely Death smiles, aiming at this fragile body.
Therefore, let Dharma be one’s companion; one should always accumulate merit.
For with Dharma as one’s companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to cross— those who possess ponds with abundant water,
assembly halls, wells, and shelters.
The giving of food and sweet speech—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By these, they become beyond the domain of Yama."
The wise have said that the Dharma is non-absolute and possesses many doors.
The Blessed One said:
"O Janārdana, tell me, what are its characteristics?"
"Listen, O King, in brief, to the sequence of rules for the purification of dharma:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, compassion, self-restraint, tranquility, and straightforwardness— these, O Indra among kings, are the established characteristics of dharma."
Celibacy, austerity, forbearance, and the avoidance of honey and meat;
remaining within the bounds of propriety and tranquility—these are the characteristics of purity.
One should pursue learning in childhood and take a wife in youth.
In old age, one should observe silence and always practice righteousness;
one should not despise Brahmins nor speak ill of one's teachers; one should be favorable toward ascetics—this is the eternal dharma.
The teacher is the preceptor of the twice-born; among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor.
The husband alone is the preceptor of women; the king is the preceptor of all.
Whatever sin has been committed by a householder, whether knowingly or unknowingly—
A mendicant who has stayed for even a single night will consume all that [evil],
whether they be of bad conduct or good conduct, or whether they be wise or ignorant.
Those who desire their own welfare in the next world should honor mendicants, even if they are householders.
Whether he carries a single staff or three, whether he has a topknot or is shaven, and even if he merely bears the saffron robe and staff— a *yati* is worthy of honor, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
even if he is unhonored or likewise insulted by householders.
Whether they be ascetics or guests, both shall cause one to fall into hell;
therefore, those who have dedicated their actions to me, who are devoted to me and intent on me, must be honored with effort by those desiring their own welfare in the hereafter.
A wise man should not strike the twice-born, nor should he ever kill a cow;
for he who practices either of these two acts incurs a sin equal to that of killing an embryo.
He should not blow upon fire with his mouth, nor should he warm his feet over it.
One should never place [the fire] below, nor cause the back to suffer heat;

one should not enter between [the fire and the teacher], nor cast impure things [into it]; while impure from eating, one should never touch the fire, nor ever do so while in a state of ritual impurity.
If one has been touched by a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, or others, one should not warm one's limbs over the fire. Since fire embodies all the gods, one should always touch it when pure;
however, a self-controlled person who has discharged urine or feces must not touch the fire.
As long as one restrains the flow [of semen], for that long one remains uncontrolled.
One should never take up the cooking fire in another's house; whatever auspicious rite one performs with food cooked by that fire, [it becomes fruitless].
O King, half of that auspicious fruit shall belong to the one who set fire to it;
therefore, one should perform even more auspicious deeds so that they are not destroyed.
Should their destruction occur through negligence or ignorance, [it will be so].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Should one take [the gift] by churning [the fire] oneself, or even from the house of a *śrotriya*? What kind of brahmins are virtuous, and to whom does a gift given yield great fruit?
The Blessed One said:
"O Janārdana, tell me: to what kind of people should gifts be given?
Those who are free from anger, devoted to truth, constant in righteousness, and have conquered their senses."
To such virtuous Brahmins as these, a gift yields great fruit;
they are free from pride, all-enduring, perceptive of the ultimate truth, and have conquered their senses.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings and full of loving-kindness, a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Those who are free from greed, pure, learned in the Vedas, modest, truthful,
and devoted to their own duty— to them, what is given yields great fruit. Furthermore, he who studies the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs day after day [attains the same].

The sages know that he in whose body the food of a Śūdra has not entered is a worthy recipient. O Yudhiṣṭhira, even a single person here who is endowed with wisdom, learning, conduct, and character can deliver his entire family.
One should bestow a cow, a horse, food, or wealth upon such a person.
Having heard that a Brāhmaṇa was endowed with virtues and esteemed by the virtuous,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having brought [the image] from afar and having honored it, one should worship it with great effort.
O God, the rule regarding dharma and adharma was spoken by Bhīṣma to me;
O Lord of the Gods, speak the dharma that is the very essence of Bhīṣma’s words.
The Blessed One said:
By food is this entire world, both moving and unmoving, sustained.
From food life-force arises; this is perceptible, there is no doubt.

Even by causing distress to one's wife, food should be given to a mendicant at the proper place and time according to one's ability by one who desires his own prosperity; likewise, [food should be given] to a Brahmin exhausted by travel, or even to a child or an old man.
A householder, being joyful, well-behaved, and free from envy, should honor a guest who has come to his home like a guru, casting aside any rising anger,
for the sake of attaining welfare in the next world.
One should not treat a guest with contempt, nor should one utter untruthful speech. One should never inquire about his lineage, his Vedic school, or what he has studied.
Whether he be a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapāka, whoever arrives at the proper time [is a guest].
He who desires his own welfare in the hereafter should honor him with food.
But he who closes the door of his house and eats alone, as if full of joy,
has indeed closed the gate of heaven for himself, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

That man who gratifies with food the ancestors, the gods, the sages, the learned brahmins, guests, and those who are destitute, gains a great fruit of merit. Even if he has committed many sins, he who gives food to one in need [is purified].
Especially by giving to a Brāhmaṇa, one is liberated from all sins. In this world, the giver of food is a giver of life; the giver of life is a giver of everything.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should especially give food.
For they say that food is indeed immortality; food is remembered as the source of procreation. When food is destroyed, the five elements in the body perish;
the strength of even a strong person perishes when he is deprived of food.
Therefore, food should be given, whether with faith or even without faith;
for the sun takes up all essence with its own rays,
and the wind, having taken that essence from there, holds it within the clouds.
Śakra rains down that very same [water] from the clouds upon the earth;
by it, O Pāṇḍava, the goddess Earth becomes drenched and delighted.
Upon her, the crops grow, by which all living beings subsist.
For the production of flesh, fat, bone, and marrow arises from those very [elements] alone. In this same way, the sun, the wind, the cloud,
and likewise Śakra are known as a single aggregate, from which all beings were born.
And the divine palaces of those great-souled ones in heaven possess various forms and structures, are filled with diverse beings,
are as brilliant as the lunar orb, and are adorned with networks of tinkling bells.
There are stationary and moving beings with the color of the rising sun,
numbering many hundreds, along with forests within the waters;
there, the celestial trees (surapādapa) are laden with flowers and fruit, granting all desires.
There were thousands of ponds, walkways, assembly halls, wells, and oblong lakes;
there were also thousands of resonant vehicles yoked for travel,
as well as mountains consisting of various kinds of food and drink, along with garments and ornaments.
There are rivers flowing with milk as well as mountains of food;
there are white, radiant palaces and couches resplendent with gold.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Fourteen thousand, nine hundred and sixteen [deities] dwell there; therefore, one should be a giver of food. Having heard the fruit of the gift of food, O Madhusūdana, I am pleased.
The Blessed One said:
"O God of gods, you ought to explain the rules for eating.
O Pāṇḍava, listen to the ordinance for the twice-born regarding food:
having bathed, being pure, in a clean and secluded place where the fire has been offered."
Having caused a square mandala to be made, O best of the twice-born, a Kṣatriya should have it circular,
and a Vaiśya should have it in the shape of a half-moon;
then, with wet feet, he should eat while facing eastward on a pure seat.

A twice-born man should not eat while touching the ground with both feet, nor again with only one foot; he should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor with an intermediate cloth (lower garment) removed;
he should not eat from a broken vessel, nor likewise from the back of a leaf.
One should first pay homage to the food with a joyful inner self;
one should not look at anything other than the food, nor should one be contemptuous of it, being intent upon it. And as for that food which is held in contempt, only Rākṣasas eat it.

Having drawn up water with the hand, one should circumambulate the food from left to right. One should know that such water is unfit for drinking; if one drinks it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Water other than that used for serving may be drunk, provided it is consecrated with mantras.
One should perform the five *prāṇāhuti* offerings equally, yet individually.
O King, just as the tongue does not perceive the taste during the *prāṇāhuti*,
so too should one perform the *prāṇāhuti* with a concentrated mind and without sloth.

O Pāṇḍava, having understood the food, the eater of the food, and the five vital breaths, he who performs these five oblations has thereby worshipped the five winds. But a Brāhmaṇa who eats otherwise, being weak in knowledge, [does not attain this].
With that food, he will satisfy the asuras, pretas, and rākṣasas;
furthermore, he shall swallow balls of food, each the size of his own mouth.
However, any ball of food that exceeds the size of his mouth is said to be his own leavings.
One should know that food remaining from a meal, as well as that which has issued from the mouth, is unfit for consumption; having eaten such, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Likewise, he who eats his own leavings, or he who eats food left over by another, [is guilty].
If one drinks water that has fallen [on the ground] or food that has come out of the mouth,
one should know that it is unfit to be eaten; having consumed it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra.
O son of Pāṇḍu, that which remains after being drunk by another must not be drunk;
for if one should drink it out of delusion, a twice-born man must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
O best of the twice-born, he who drinks water from that same vessel [must likewise undergo penance].
It remains untouchable (anucchiṣṭa) as long as it has not been placed upon the ground;

whether observing silence or not, the Brahmin, being joyful and with senses restrained, should eat according to the rule and must not cause any food to be given away while he is still impure from eating.

One should never eat excessively, nor ever eat too little; one should always eat in such a way that no distress arises from food. One should avoid a woman in her courses, a Caṇḍāla, a dog, or even a Ruru deer.
While eating, if he should see [an impurity], he should discard that food;
for a twice-born man who eats while failing to discard it out of delusion must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
[Likewise, food] contaminated by hair or insects, or blown upon by the breath from the mouth, [must be discarded].
One should know that to be unfit for consumption; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Food that has been touched after [the owner] has risen, touched by the feet, or stepped over, one should know to be demonic (rākṣasa); therefore, one should avoid it.
A Brahmin who eats the leftovers of a Rākṣasa will cause seven ancestors before him and seven descendants after him to fall into the terrible Raurava hell;
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) from the same vessel in which he has eaten.
If one has risen from his seat after eating without having sipped water for purification, Yudhiṣṭhira said: "He should immediately perform a bath; otherwise, he would remain impure."
O giver of honor, you ought to tell me about the ritual for the handful of grass, the majesty of that very grass, and the origin of *ikṣu* (sugarcane) from the *soma*. The Blessed One said:

The bulls should be known as the fathers, and the cows as the mothers of the world. By honoring them, O King, one honors both fathers and mothers. [One should also establish] assembly halls, water-stations, houses, and temples for the deities.
If even those [cows] that are purified by dung become pure, what could be more sacred than them? He who,
for an entire year, gives a handful of fodder to another’s cow while abstaining from food himself, fulfills a perpetual vow.
"All cows are my mothers, and the bulls are my fathers; may the mothers accept this handful of fodder given by me. Having spoken thus with this mantra, or with the Sāvitrī, he should remain composed.
Having consecrated a handful of food with this mantra, hear now the fruit of its merit:
whatever evil deed has been committed by that person, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
all of it is destroyed, and even bad dreams perish.
Sesame seeds are pure, destroyers of sin, and originated from Nārāyaṇa. They praise sesame seeds at a *śrāddha* ceremony; this gift is unsurpassed.
One should give sesame seeds, eat sesame seeds, and touch sesame seeds while performing the morning ablutions.
One should say, "sesame by the sesame," for these sesame seeds indeed remove sin.
Whether purchased or received as a gift, they must not be sold by the twice-born. If one uses sesame seeds for anything other than eating, anointing, or giving as a gift, [he incurs a fault].
Having become a worm in a dog’s excrement, he sinks there together with his ancestors.
O King, a Brahmin should not himself press sesame seeds in an oil-press;
for by pressing them out of delusion, a twice-born man goes to the Raurava hell.

Soma was born from the Ikṣu lineage, and the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas) were born from the Soma lineage. Therefore, one should not crush the sugarcane; for he who destroys sugarcane is a destroyer of himself.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [the merit of] each single stalk of thousands of sugarcane [stalks...]
A Brāhmaṇa who operates a sugar-press incurs the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, a Brāhmaṇa should not press sugarcane in a mechanical press.
The Blessed One spoke concerning the collection of dharmas, as well as what is fit and unfit to be eaten: "By your grace, I have heard [all this]; now tell me the dharma for times of distress."

During a famine, in times of national distress, during periods of ritual impurity following death or birth, at a time of religious duty, or while traveling on a journey— the observance of the rules is not violated. One who is exhausted from a long journey, or in the absence of a twice-born man, may accept food from a Śūdra.
Whatever unprepared food he may take for his own sustenance—
whether he be afflicted by illness, suffering from pain, overcome by fear, or tormented by hunger—
a Brahmin who eats it contrary to the prescribed rule does not incur the need for expiation.
But a Brahmin who has been duly invited to the offerings for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*), even if he eats meat, does not incur the need for penance.
These eight do not destroy one's vows: water, roots, ghee, milk, [curd, honey, sesame, and sacrificial food].

The sacrificial oblation is for one who desires the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and the word of the Guru is medicine. That man who is unable to perform the expiations according to the rules is purified by the word of the learned as well as by giving gifts.
Whether out of season or during the fertile period, by day or likewise by night—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If a man who has gone abroad should approach his wife, does he not incur the need for penance?"
"O Lord of the Gods, what kind of brahmins are praiseworthy, and what kind are censurable?
O you of noble vows, tell me also what the proper time for the *aṣṭakā* rites is. The Blessed One said: "Tell me that, O you of noble vows."
Seeing that twice-born man who is true to his word, the Sun trembles from his station. Piercing through my orb, he goes to the eternal Brahman—
he who is of noble birth, a performer of rites, a physician, and likewise compassionate.
One who is modest, upright, and truthful—a vessel worthy of honor—all these twice-born ones are such.
These twice-born ones, seated at the head of the row, eat first;
and all others in that same row are indeed purified by the mere sight of them.
O best of the twice-born, know those who are my devotees— those who have gone to me and for whom I am the supreme goal— to be purifiers of the assembly and especially worthy of worship.
O King, hear now about those twice-born who are censurable, even if they have mastered the Vedas.
One who wanders in the world under the guise of a Brahmin while committing evil deeds; one who maintains no sacred fire, does not study the Vedas, yet delights in receiving gifts;
and one who eats at any place whatsoever—one should know him to be a defiler of the assembly.
O lord of men, I do not know the destination of that twice-born man whose body is nourished by the impurity of death or birth, who eats the food of a Śūdra,
and whose limbs are sustained by the essence of a Śūdra’s food— even if he studies the Vedas constantly.

Even for one who recites the mantra or performs oblations, no higher destination is found; and that Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires but does not refrain from the food of a Śūdra—five things perish for him: his self, the Veda, and the three sacrificial fires.
And especially for a Brāhmaṇa who performs service for a Śūdra,
food should be given to him upon the ground, for he is equal to a dog or a jackal;
likewise for a Brāhmaṇa weak in knowledge who [serves] a Śūdra as if he were a deceased person.

If one follows a corpse being carried out, one remains impure for three nights. When those three nights have passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one becomes pure after consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Those best of the twice-born who carry a deceased Brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
at every step, the fruit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice;
indeed, there is no inauspiciousness or sin for them, even if they were performers of unwholesome deeds.
Immediate purification is ordained simply by immersion in water.
If a Brahmin, having accepted milk or curd in the house of a Śūdra,
should eat it with a sense of complacency, know that to be the very food of a Śūdra.
There is no other evildoer than that mortal who creates an obstacle for Brahmins desiring to eat and longing intensely for food;
[for him], all the Vedas along with the six auxiliary limbs [are lost].
O King, for a twice-born man who is devoid of virtuous conduct, neither knowledge of the Sāṃkhya, nor the Purāṇas, nor birth in a noble family— none of these lead to a higher destination.

O son of Pāṇḍu, during an eclipse of the planets, at the equinoxes, at the end of the solstices, on the day sacred to the ancestors (the Pitṛpakṣa), under the Maghā asterism, when a son is born to one's own daughter, and at the offerings of rice-balls (piṇḍas) at Gayā— these are the times for ancestral rites.
A gift given on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika would be equal to a thousand gold coins (niṣka).
On the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and on the [same] days of the month of Māgha during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.

For the time for the *śrāddha* is indeed during the two solstices; yet he who, out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth, serves worldly objects to one person in a single row [of guests], [incurs sin].
The sages call him a slayer of a Brahmin who is cruel, of evil conduct, and lacking self-control;
for one [suffers] only here and not in the hereafter, while for another [it is suffered] only there and not here.

Those who possess vast wealth find delight in this world and the next; yet others find it only in the next world, and still others find it neither here nor there— these are those who are perpetually deluded regarding the world beyond.
This world belongs to those who destroy the foremost of enemies,
and not to others who are always devoted to the pleasures of the body; it belongs to those who are disciplined in yoga and intent upon austerity.
Those who are devoted to the practice of sacred study, who wear away their bodies through austerity,
who have conquered their senses, and who are intent on the welfare of all beings— for them,
this world of the slayers of enemies does not exist.
Those who first practice the Dharma itself,
having acquired wealth through righteousness at the proper time,
obtain wives and win [merit] through sacrifices.
For those who possess neither knowledge, nor austerity, nor charity, and who, being deluded, do not even strive for procreation, this world as well as the next are lost.
Nor do they attain happiness or enjoyments;
for them, neither this world nor the next exists.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Purāṇas, Abode of Yoga, homage be to you!
I wish to hear in its entirety the compendium of the essence of Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
"O Great King, the essence of Dharma was proclaimed by Manu from the beginning.
I shall now declare that ancient teaching of Manu, which is consistent with the Vedas:
the maintainer of the sacred fire, the tawny cow, the performer of a long sacrificial session, the king, the mendicant, and the great ocean."
These purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should always look upon them.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, a cow should be given to only one person, not to many;
for if that cow is sold, it consumes the family unto the seventh generation.
A cow, clothing, a bed, or women should not be given to many people;
such a gift does not benefit the donor. It is like food that has been stepped over by Brahmins while being eaten in the house of the ignoble.
The merit derived from those cows is superior even to the Rājasūya sacrifice. He who says "Do not give" regarding cows, fire, or Brahmins,
having passed through a hundred births as animals, is reborn among the Caṇḍālas.

O King, the property of a Brahmin, the property of a deity, the wealth of a poor man, and even that of a preceptor— if these are seized, they cause one to fall even from the heavenly realm. For those who desire to know the Dharma, the Veda is the supreme authority.
The second is the treatises on Dharma (Dharmaśāstra), and the third is the welfare of the world. That which lies between the eastern ocean and the western ocean,
and between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, is declared to be Āryāvarta.

The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta. Whatever conduct has been handed down through tradition in that region [is authoritative].
That which consists of the castes together with the intermediate classes is called *sadācāra* (the land of virtuous conduct).
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and the Śūrasenas—
these are the regions of the Brahmanical seers (*brahmarṣideśa*), situated immediately adjacent to Brahmāvarta.
From the presence of one born in this region who is of the highest birth,
all human beings on earth should adopt their own proper conduct;
[this applies to] the land between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, extending as far east as Viśasana.
The region extending from Prayāga to Pratyag is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country).
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice (*yajñiya*); beyond that is the land of the barbarians (*mleccha*).
Having recognized these regions, the twice-born should take refuge in them;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
For dharma originates from right conduct, as do non-violence and truthfulness.
One should practice charity according to one's ability, as well as observances together with restraints;

and for the twice-born, the purifying rites of the body, beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception), should be performed through meritorious Vedic rituals, both for the sake of this world and for the life hereafter.
Through the fire-oblations at conception, the birth-rite, naming, tonsure, and initiation;
through Vedic study and its observances, as well as the vows of marriage and the snātaka;
and through the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.
Where neither dharma nor artha are found, nor even a corresponding desire to listen— to such a person knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil.
This applies whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge.
One should first salute that person from whom this knowledge was obtained;
grasping the left foot with the left hand and the right foot with the right hand,
one should not perform the salutation of the teacher’s feet with only one hand.
He who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the prescribed rule,
and also teaches him, is called a *vipra* and a *guru*. He who, having performed the initiation (*upanayana*), constantly teaches the Vedas [is likewise a guru].

He who [teaches] the ritual manuals along with their secret doctrines is called an *upādhyāya*. Having taught the Vedas together with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and having instructed [the student] in the vows,
he who explains the meaning of the mantras is designated an *ācārya*.
Ten teachers are equal to one preceptor (upādhyāya), and a hundred teachers are equal to one father. A mother exceeds the father a hundredfold in terms of venerability;
therefore, one should remain under their authority and be intent upon serving them.
For by insulting them, one would undoubtedly fall into hell.
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.
The merit that was performed by one who curses goes to the one being cursed;
the sin of the one being cursed follows after the one who curses. [One should avoid] atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities.
One should avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, dear to the people of Dharma, [be gracious] to me, your devotee.
The Blessed One said:
"O God, tell me, who am asking you, about that most meritorious dharma which is this Agnihotra sacrifice created for the three social orders."
That which is offered as an oblation according to the mantra and properly worshipped according to the rite—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Does it lead the maintainer of the sacred fires (āhitāgni), together with his wife and kinsmen, to the higher world?"

O God, Lord of the Gods of gods, how should that sacrifice be offered by Brāhmaṇas, and how by Kṣatriyas? Or how, O best of deities, should it be well-offered by Vaiśyas? Furthermore, at what time and for whom should the fire be established?
How can one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) practice correctly?
O Lord, how many are the fires, what is their nature, what is their location, and to whom does each belong?
Upon the offering being made in which location does the performer of the Agnihotra go?
O sinless one, what was the original cause for the *agnihotra* sacrifice?
How indeed are the oblations offered, and how are the gods gratified? And how are the fires worshipped according to the rules, with mantras, and with devotion?

O best among those who speak, what destination do the performers of the *agnihotra* sacrifice reach? O Blessed One, what happens when the three fires are not properly offered into, or are not recognized?
And what do they do for the one who has maintained the sacred fires if they are poorly performed, O Keśava?
"O Lord, what kind of womb does that evil-souled person enter who has extinguished the sacred fire?
Please explain all this in brief to me, for I have approached you with devotion.
The Blessed One said:
O Omniscient One, O Abode of All, you ought to speak; homage be unto you!
Listen, O King, to this supreme nectar of Dharma, which possesses great merit and delivers those disciplined Brahmins who maintain the sacred fire.
O one of great splendor, in the beginning I created the worlds in the capacity of Brahmā. Desiring the welfare of the worlds, Agni was first created from my mouth;
because he was fashioned by me at the very beginning of all beings.
Therefore, O wise ones, he is called "Agni" by those who know the ancient lore;
because in all ritual acts, the blazing oblation is first offered to him,
he is thus celebrated as Agni.
And because, when well-honored, he leads the Brahmins to the highest state, O King, he is therefore celebrated as "Agni" (the Leader) in the Vedas due to that act of leading. And because,
when poorly offered, he is capable of consuming [the offerer] in an instant—

O best of men, because he consumes the sacrificer [as his food], he is therefore known as the "flesh-eating" fire (*kravyād-agni*). O King, he is the self of all beings and is indeed the mouth of the gods;
for the sake of the world, this powerful consumer was first created from my own mouth.

Long ago, as soon as it was created, that fire indeed desired to devour the entire world; therefore, it was pacified by me through worship. Because of this constant worship, it is remembered as the *aupāsana* (the domestic sacrificial fire).

All oblations are said to be contained therein; that fire dwells within it, and for this reason it is designated as the *āvasathya* by those who discourse on Brahman. Within it, the five great sacrifices proceed according to dharma.
The movement of that twice-born one was through the center of the lunar orb;
those seven sages, perfected ones whose senses and intellects were restrained,
having been devoted to the worship of the single fire, indeed attained union with the immortals.
Others, moreover, designate the *āvasathya* fire as the cooking fire (*pacanāgni*).
In it, the five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*) and the *vaiśvadeva* offering take place; both the *sthālīpāka* and the domestic rites (*gārha*) are indeed established in this fire.

Because he carries out the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*), he is therefore called the *gṛhapati* (householder). Some knowers of Brahman call the *aupāsana*, the *āvasathya*, the *sabhya*, and the *pacanapāvaka* [fires]; this is also my own opinion.
O King, listen with a concentrated mind to the manner of the *agnihotra* sacrifice. I shall now state the names of the three fires;
for the lordship over the household is indeed remembered as *gārhapatya*.
That which belonged to the householder (gṛhapati) became the Gārhapatya fire;
because it leads the sacrificer to the southern path (dakṣiṇā-gati),
the twice-born call that the Dakṣiṇāgni, whose seat is the south.
The *āhuti* has been fully explained, as well as the *havana*, the *havyavāhana*, and Vahni, the carrier of all oblations,
who attained the state of the *āhavanīya*. Furthermore,
that twice-born man who should duly offer oblations into the *āvasathya* fire, which is the root-fire (*mūlāgni*), [attains the highest goal].
Those who designate the *āvasathya* fire as the *pacanāgni* (the cooking fire),
for them that fire is called the *sabhya* by way of its portion.
However, the *āvasathya* fire which is the first is Prajāpati himself.
Brahmā is the Gārhapatya fire; from him alone that [fire] arises.
This Dakṣiṇāgni, however, is Rudra; he is the very essence of wrath and is fierce. I am the Āhavanīya fire, into whose mouth indeed the oblation is poured.
O lord of men, the fifth fire is Skanda himself, who is the fire of the assembly hall (*sabhya*); the earth is the *gārhapatya* fire, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is the *dakṣiṇa* fire,
and heaven is the *āhavanīya* fire— thus is the triad of fires traditionally remembered.
For the Gārhapatya fire is circular, and because the earth is circular; the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is indeed of the shape of a half-moon, and from that,
heaven is square— pure and free from affliction.
Therefore, O King, the Āhavanīya fire should be square;
that twice-born man who offers oblations into the Gārhapatya fire conquers the earth,
and he who offers into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire conquers the intermediate space.
The twice-born who, full of devotion, offers oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire, conquers the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven along with the hosts of seers;
for in his sacrifices, the offering proceeds directly toward [the deity].
By that [act], the fire of great splendor attained the status of the *āhavanīya*;
for it is from this [fire] that all the *agnihotra* offerings and sacrifices proceed until the completion of the oblation. Therefore, indeed, it possesses the nature of the *āhavanīya*.
That twice-born man who offers oblations into the *āvasathya* fire— the root fire— according to the rule,
rejoices together with his wife in the worlds of the Seven Sages. And he who, self-restrained, duly attends upon the *sabhya* fire, [attains the same].

He would conquer all that consists of speech, as well as the assembly of sages. Furthermore, for one to whom the oblation is offered into the fire of speech rather than into the [physical] fires, it becomes an offering to all fires, and that indeed constitutes the *agnihotra*.
The *cāturhotra* is traditionally taught as belonging to the three [fires] and the sacrificer. "Ho" is indeed dejection; dejection is said to be suffering.
Suffering is declared to be the threefold affliction (*tāpatraya*), for they know affliction to be hell.
Therefore, the fire, when offered as a sacrifice, truly protects the sacrificer from suffering;
for this reason, it is declared according to rule in the Śruti as "Agnihotra. That Agnihotra was indeed created by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
The Vedas themselves were born for the purpose of the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
the Vedas have the *agnihotra* as their fruit, sacred learning has virtuous conduct as its fruit,
wives have pleasure and offspring as their fruit, and wealth has giving and enjoyment as its fruit.
Through the conjunction of the threefold mantras, the *agnihotra* sacrifice proceeds;
it is established by means of the meritorious *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* verses joined with the ritual threads.
O lord of men, in the spring, the fire should be installed for the Brāhmaṇa.

The Brāhmaṇa is said to be springtime; he is called the source of the Vedas. O King, for that Brāhmaṇa by whom the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is performed in spring, his prosperity and the increase of his Vedic knowledge flourish.
O King, for a Kṣatriya, the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is most excellent when performed in the summer;
for him by whom the installation is indeed carried out in the summer, his prosperity,
progeny, cattle, wealth, splendor, strength, and fame increase.
On the night of autumn, O Pāṇḍava, the fire is to be established for the Vaiśya; indeed,
that autumnal night is called the "Vaiśya-womb" by the Vaiśya himself,
and it is in this way that the establishment of the fire is performed by him, O son of Pāṇḍu.
For him as well, prosperity, progeny, longevity, cattle, and wealth increase.
All these cattle are adorned by the three Vedas;
from the Agnihotra they proceed, by which this world is sustained.
Domestic and wild animals, as well as trees and grasses,
fruits and medicinal herbs— these indeed exist for the sake of the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
likewise, juices, oils, fragrances, gems, and jewels [are provided].
There were indeed golden vessels for the sake of the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
the science of medicine (*āyurveda*), the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), *mīmāṃsā*, the expansion of logic (*nyāyavistara*),
and the treatises on dharma— all that was created for the sake of the *agnihotra*.
O King, the Chandas, Śikṣā, Kalpas, and likewise Vyākaraṇa;
the Śāstra, Jyotiṣa, and Nirukta were also composed for the sake of the Agnihotra sacrifice;
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Gāthās, and the Upaniṣads.
The ritual acts of the Atharvans were performed for the sake of the Agnihotra; whatever exists here on this earth, whether moving or stationary,
all that was created by the Self-existent One for the sake of the Agnihotra.
Furthermore, [he knows] the Agnihotra, the Darśa, and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifices;
the rites of the sacrificial posts, the Ishtis, and the animal sacrifices accompanied by the drinking of Soma;
and the conjunctions of lunar days and constellations, consisting of auspicious moments (muhūrta) and astrological configurations (karaṇa).
In ancient times, the science of astrology was established for the purpose of knowing time;

the science of prosody was devised from the contemplation of the true meaning and principles of the verses of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* mantras, as well as from the analysis of their restorations and variations.

The intended mark of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) among phonemes, syllables, and words has been explained. Grammar was composed in the past for the purpose of distinguishing between nouns and verbal roots,
as well as for the sake of hearing the sprinkling of water for the sacrificial post and the altar during a sacrifice.

The knowledge of phonetics (*śikṣā*) was established for the purpose of the application of the deities of sacrifice; the ancient ritual manual (*purākalpa*) was established for the preparation of sacrificial vessels, for the purification [of materials], for the gathering of substances, and for the various forms of all sacrifices.
And for the sake of establishing the true meaning and rules of names, verbal roots, and case endings,
the seers composed a Nirukta for all Vedic etymologies. Furthermore, the earth was created for the purpose of being known, and likewise for the purpose of providing the necessary materials.
Then, for the sake of the sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial post, Brahmā fashioned a tree. For the purpose of the sacrifice, both domestic and wild animals are produced;
likewise, there is the application of the mantras and the proclamation for those who have gone abroad.
The after-offerings (*anūyāja*) and the fore-offerings (*prayāja*), as well as those who praise the Maruts;
the chanters (*udgātṛ*) of the *sāmans*, and indeed the *baliprasthāna*;
the stepping of the Viṣṇu-strides (*viṣṇukrama*), and likewise the southern purificatory bath (*dakṣiṇāvabhṛtha*).

Those Brahmins who do not understand that worship performed at the three times of day, as well as offerings presented in sacred places, the invocation of the deities, the release [of animals], and likewise the hearing of the mantras regarding oblations, and who instead censure the slaughter of sacrificial animals— [they are ignorant].
They go to the terrible Raurava hell, shrouded in darkness;
having remained there for hundreds of thousands of years, those lowest of men shall stay amidst pus and blood, being devoured by worms.
O Lord of Men, through the purificatory rites of the mantras, these sacrificial posts and likewise the animals,
together with the sacrificer, go to heaven;
for as long as time permits, the performer of the sacrifice is indeed glorified in the world of heaven.
For that long, indeed, do the animals slaughtered at the sacrifice rejoice;
likewise, trees desire the state of sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), animals desire the state of sacrificial victims,
grasses desire the state of *darbha* grass, and plants desire the state of being oblation-materials (*havis*).
All creepers possess the nature of Soma, and the earth indeed possesses the nature of the Vedas;
since animals desire the state of being sacrificial victims out of a longing for heaven,
therefore, O Pāṇḍava, there is no violence in the slaughter of animals during sacrifices.

Non-violence is Vedic action; that is remembered as the "action of Brahman. Those twice-born ones who, with a mind intent on violence, do not perform the sacrifice prescribed in the Vedas, immediately attain the status of a Śūdra and, after death, even the state of a Caṇḍāla.
Cows were produced for the sake of sacrifice and likewise for the purpose of sacrificial fees;
gold and silver for the sake of vessels and water-jars;
and *darbha* grass for the purpose of spreading as a seat and for protection against the *rakṣasas*.

The twice-born were created for the purpose of sacrifice; the stars in the sky are the deities. The Kṣatriyas were created for the purpose of protection, while the Vaiśyas were created for the sake of livelihood.
And the Śūdras were created by the Self-existent One for the purpose of serving the other three castes.
In this way, this entire world has been created for the sake of the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
yet those men who do not understand this are shrouded in darkness,
and they go to the terrible hell well-known by the name Raurava.
But those who are released from the Raurava hell go to the womb of worms. Those twice-born ones who serve the Agnihotra fires as prescribed—
by them, what is well-sacrificed, well-performed, given, and taught becomes [meritorious].
O King, whatever *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works) are performed by the Brahmins,
I gather all of that together and establish it in the Sun;
for that merit of the world is indeed established by me within the Sun.
The thousand-rayed sun indeed sustains the merit of those who maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice for as long as those *agnihotrin*s remain in this world;
by that merit, they shine with the sun in the sky.
In heaven, for those who have gone to heaven, there arises through their own prowess one who is powerful;
there they indeed enjoy the fruit of the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
remaining in forms identical to the gods until the dissolution of all beings.
And those Agnihotrin priests who are burned by a useless fire do not go to the world of the Agnihotrin priests even in thought;
they are slayers of heroes, of evil conduct, utterly destitute, and the lowest of men.
They are born deficient and afflicted by disease even among the *śūdra* wombs.
Therefore, O King, the twice-born who desire the higher goal must always perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice according to the rules while remaining at home.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Agnihotra sacrifice should be regarded there as being like one's own self;
it must not be abandoned even for a moment, and it should be undertaken by the twice-born. Indeed, even in old age, the twice-born perform the Agnihotra according to the prescribed rules.
Abstaining from the food of Śūdras, self-controlled, with their senses and intellect restrained,
constantly devoted to the five great sacrifices, and free from anger and greed,
they honor guests twice a day with devotion.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, those best of the twice-born also rejoice in my world upon seeing me, traveling in aerial chariots that possess the speed of the wind and resemble the rising sun; having rejoiced there for one *manvantara*, they [depart].
In this world of mortals, O best of the twice-born,
there are born those who maintain the sacred fires from their youth, who always abstain from the food of Śūdras,
who are entirely free from anger and greed, and who are devoted to bathing at dawn.
As it has been said: "Those who offer the Agnihotra sacrifice, having conquered their senses,
who are hospitable, ever gentle, and devoted to Me as their supreme goal— performing this twice a day—
they go, having pierced the solar orb, to the state from which there is no return."
Together with my wife, we shall go to my world by means of vehicles radiant as the rising sun;
there, resembling the morning sun, moving at will and assuming forms at will,
endowed with the qualities of sovereignty, we shall sport according to our pleasure.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, such indeed is the glory of those who maintain the sacred fires.
But those of little intelligence who revile the Vedic revelation and do not accept it as authoritative go to imperishable darkness."
Those twice-born ones who treat the *itihāsas* and the *purāṇas* as authoritative alongside the Vedas—
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Those whose intellects are constantly fixed on faith attain union with the immortals."
"O wielder of the discus, obeisance be to you, O Lord of Gods, whose banner is Garuḍa!
O Blessed One, tell me the meritorious procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to that which truly destroys all sins; I shall tell you everything by which sinners are purified. Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who has observed his vows—
For one who desires to perform [the rite] correctly, this is the first action:
he should, with self-restraint, purify his own body with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
thereafter, he should purify his body up to the armpits and the sides.

Having become pure, the one dwelling in the Pure Abodes (Śuddhavāsa) should tie on a girdle made of Muñja grass; taking up a staff of Pālāśa wood and remaining firm in the vow of a religious student (brahmacārī),
the twice-born man should first observe a fast on the first day of the bright fortnight.
At the confluences of rivers, at sacred bathing places, in a pure location, or even in the home—

having smeared the ground with cow dung— one should then have the fire established upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). One should likewise perform the two *āghāra* libations, the two *ājyabhāga* portions, the *praṇava*, and the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having also offered five oblations to the deities of Varuṇa in their proper order—
to Satya, to Viṣṇu, to the Brahman-sages, then to Brahmā,
Afterwards, the twice-born should offer six oblations for atonement;
then, having performed the rites of pacification (śānti) and prosperity (pauṣṭika), he should conclude the fire-ritual.
Having bowed to Agni and Soma, he should likewise place the sacred ashes upon his own body.

Having gone to a river, with a secluded mind, having paid homage to Soma, Varuṇa, and Āditya, he should then bathe with a concentrated mind. Having emerged from the water and sipped water for purification, he should sit facing the east.

Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and consecration with purifying substances, and having sipped water for purification (ācamana), he should gaze at the sun with his arms raised. Then, with palms joined in reverence (añjali), he should perform a circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa).
Either Nārāyaṇa or Rudra, or even Brahmā;
or the Vāruṇa mantra-sūkta before eating;
or likewise the Vīraghna, the Ṛṣabha, and the Aghamarṣaṇa.
Then he should mutter either the Gāyatrī or the divine Sāvitrī; thereafter, he should recite it eighteen times or even another thousand times.
Then, at the time of midday, he should indeed consume milk-rice or barley-gruel.
Having cooked [the food] with great effort, being pure and well-composed,
he should take up a vessel— whether it be made of gold, silver,
copper, clay, or even udumbara wood.
With fresh, unblemished leaves from trees fit for sacrifice,
he should go about for alms with a concealed bowl, composed in mind;
he should not go beyond seven houses of Brāhmaṇas.
He should stand for as long as it takes to milk a cow, maintaining silence and restraining his senses;
he should not laugh, nor look at, nor speak to a woman;
and upon seeing urine, feces, a *caṇḍāla*, or a menstruating woman, [he should likewise remain silent].
And likewise, one should look at the sun upon seeing a dog that has fallen [into food]. Indeed, seeing a twice-born man who always moves about while mounted on sandals—
a man of sinful deeds— one should look at the sun.
Then, having arrived at his dwelling and set aside his alms on the ground,
he should wash his feet up to the knees and his hands up to the elbows; then,
sipping water, he should worship the fire and the Brahmins with that same water.
One should divide that alms-food into five or seven portions;
from among these, one should offer one morsel to Āditya,
and likewise to Brahmā, Agni, Soma, and Varuṇa.
One should offer food in due order to all the gods; then, one should set aside a single remaining morsel, the size of a mouthful,
and consecrate the ball of food resting on the tips of the fingers with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Facing east and purified, one should eat the ball of food with three fingers.
Just as the moon waxes and wanes again,
so do the balls of food increase and decrease day by day.

Bathing three times a day is prescribed for him, or else twice, or even once; he should always remain celibate and must not wring out his garment. He should not remain standing during the day, and at night he should adopt the *vīrāsana* posture.
He may sleep on the bare ground or at the foot of a tree; his covering for the sake of clothing, O son of Pāṇḍu, may be made of bark, linen, hemp, or cotton.

Thus, when the Cāndrāyaṇa is completed at the end of the month, the diligent practitioner should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas and likewise give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Whatever evil deed has been committed by one who has performed the Cāndrāyaṇa [is thereby purified].
All that is reduced to ashes in that very instant, like wood.
Even the killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a cow, the theft of gold,
the destruction of an embryo, the drinking of liquor, and the violation of the teacher’s wife [are thus destroyed].

In this way, other sins and those that constitute mortal transgressions (pātaka) are destroyed by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, just as dust is blown away by the wind. [The same applies to] the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, as well as the milk of camels and sheep.
Having eaten food from those in a state of birth-impurity or death-impurity, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, having eaten the food of those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), the food of outcasts (patita),
or even the leavings of a Śūdra, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten food that is situated in the air, in one's own hand, or likewise on a seat,
or even food held in the hand of another, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Furthermore,
one should likewise [perform this] for the food of an Agredidhiṣū or of a Didhiṣūpati.
Having eaten the food of one who marries before his elder brother (parivettṛ), as well as the food of the elder brother whose younger brother has married first (parivitti),
the food of a *kuṇḍa*, the food of a *golaka*, and likewise the food of a temple-priest (*devala*),
as well as the food of a family priest (*purohita*), one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
A twice-born man who sells liquor, fermented spirits, poison, clarified butter, lac, salt,
or even oil, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Furthermore,
he who eats at an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, or he who eats while the sun is at its zenith, [shall likewise perform it].
A twice-born man who eats from a broken vessel shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who eats with one who has not been initiated, he who eats together with a woman,
and he who eats together with a maiden, that twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, should place leavings [of food] within his meal,
or if he should give them away out of confusion, that twice-born man must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Likewise, [he must avoid] the bottle-gourd, the eggplant, the onion, and the garlic.
Having eaten mushrooms and light food, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, having eaten stale food, cooked food brought from another's house,
or meat that has been kept overnight, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

O best of the twice-born, if a twice-born man eats food that has been seen by a menstruating woman, a dog, or even a *caṇḍāla*, he should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. This vow was practiced in ancient times by the seers for the sake of purification.
O Pāṇḍava, this which has been proclaimed is meritorious, the purifier of all sins.
By means of this, the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas went to heaven.
This is remembered as the primordial, supreme secret, the purifier, and the sanctifier.
"Whoever among the twice-born should perform this act as described, it shall destroy his sins.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having purified his soul, he goes to heaven, resembling the stainless sun."
When Keśava had thus spoken regarding the sequence of rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow,
Yudhiṣṭhira,
the son of Dharma, O King, asked again about other duties.
"O glorious Lord of all beings, you who are saluted by all beings, O Omniscient One, tell me the Dharma that is for the welfare of all beings. The Blessed One said:

Listen, O Yudhiṣṭhira, to that which brings about heaven even for a poor person, which bestows happiness, and which pacifies all sins. These twelve months, beginning with Kārttika, have indeed been proclaimed.

I declare that for all of them, the rule of eating only once a day is prescribed. He who, devoted to me, with his senses restrained, observes the practice of eating only one meal a day during the month of Kārttika on the Nandā days for the duration of one month—
For one month, he should not drink water between meals;
always worshipping me in the form of the Sun with a well-concentrated mind,
he should, at the conclusion of the vow, feed the Brahmins and bestow sacrificial fees upon them.

Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who is completely free from anger and greed: having attained that merit which is proclaimed as resulting from the ritual gift of a Kapila cow, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Then, having passed away from that state at the end of his time, he is reborn among human beings.
Furthermore, he who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa eating but one meal a day,
having duly abandoned desire, anger, and greed—
Having bathed, one with senses restrained should worship me in the form of the Sun;
reciting the Gāyatrī dedicated to me, pure in speech and mind;
and when the month has been completed, having fed pure brahmins.

Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who honors them with devotion to me: having attained that fruit of merit, he travels by a vehicle that adorns the sky, which is the very merit that would accrue to one who maintains the sacred fires when the *agnihotra* sacrifice has been performed.

He wanders through the world of the seven ṛṣis at will and according to his pleasure. Then, when his time there has passed, he is reborn in the region of Harivarṣa. Having played there to his heart's content, he shall later become a king.
The man who thus passes the month of Pauṣa by eating only one meal a day,
constantly worshipping me with his inner self absorbed in me,
practicing non-violence and truthfulness, and remaining free from anger and joy— [attains this].
O Indra among kings, hear now the supreme fruit that belongs to one who is thus disciplined:
having attained that merit which is proclaimed to result from a thousand acts of hospitality toward Brahmins, he is glorified in the world of Śakra.
After that time, having fallen away, he is born among the inhabitants of Ilāvṛta;
remaining there for a long period, he will become a Brahmin in this world.
Likewise, he who observes eating only once a day during the month of Māgha [attains the same].
Becoming intent upon my worship, free from hypocrisy and anger,
the wise man should recite my Gāyatrī during the twilight;
having given a sacrificial fee at the conclusion, he should also feed the twice-born.
He pays homage to them with devotion, his inner self absorbed in me.
Hear now the fruit of the merit of one who is engaged in bathing at the three periods of the day:
he travels by a vehicle employed by Nīlakaṇṭha that shines in the sky.
The illustrious one shall go to the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), being attended by throngs of *apsarases*. Having sported there at will, he is reborn among the *Bhadrāśvas*.
Falling from there, he becomes a Brahmin learned in the four Vedas on this earth.

He who, having conquered his senses, fasts on a single meal for the month of Phālguna, should constantly mutter this mantra: "Obeisance to the God who is the Friend of Brahman. At the conclusion of the vow, he, with senses restrained, should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who is devoted to my worship and free from anger:
having ascended a celestial chariot drawn by cranes that moves at will,
he rejoices in the world of the stars, possessing a form like a star.
Then, having passed away from that time, he is born among the Ketumālas;
having sported there to his heart's content, he becomes a sage among humans.
O King, he who subsists on a single meal during the month of Caitra—
Listen to the fruit of the merit of that celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who possesses devotion to me:
having attained that fruit of merit which belongs to one who maintains the sacred fire (*agnihotrī*) and practices the prescribed vows, he is glorified in the world of the Moon.
Then, descending from there, he shall be born again in the Ramanaka continent;
having enjoyed sensual pleasures there, he will subsequently become a king here in this world.
This applies to one who observes the month of Vaiśākha by eating only once a day.
Having seated a twice-born man on the seat of honor and eating himself upon the ground while maintaining silence,
and having worshipped the Sun with the mantra "Obeisance to the God who is the friend of Brahman," one should feed the Brahmins at the conclusion of the vow; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof.
Having attained that meritorious fruit which is declared according to rule as the result of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices, one is glorified in the world of the gods; thereafter,
by the turn of time, one is born in the region of Haimavata.

Having sported there to his heart's content, the Brahmin shall afterwards attain [the highest state]. O King, he who passes the month of Jyeṣṭha eating but one meal a day, having placed a Brahmin at the head of the seat, eats upon the ground according to the prescribed rule.
"Chanting with a concentrated mind, 'Salutation to the God who is the Friend of Brahman,' while being free from hypocrisy and falsehood— listen to the fruit of his merit.
It is equal to the merit that is declared to be fully attained by one who has correctly performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Having attained the fruit of that merit, he is honored in the world of the gods;
then, having departed from there, he is born among the people of Uttarakuru;
and when his time there has passed, he becomes a twice-born man in this world.
O King, he who passes the month of Āṣāḍha eating but one meal a day,
remaining celibate, having conquered anger, and being devoted to my worship; who places a Brahmin on the seat of honor and eats upon the ground with his senses subdued— [he attains this merit].
Having performed the ritual bath at the three sessions of the day according to the procedure for the eight-syllable mantra,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) at the conclusion of the vow,
or with rice and jaggery, O King; hear now the fruit of his merit.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having attained that fruit of merit which belongs to the gift of a hundred tawny cows, one is glorified in the world of the gods; then,
descending at the proper time, one is born in Śākadvīpa.
Then, having passed away at that time, he will become a Brahmin here;
he who passes the month of Śrāvaṇa subsisting on a single meal a day,
and always worships me after saying, "Homage to the God who is Benevolent to Brahmins."
Having seated a Brahmin on the seat of honor and eating upon the ground according to the rule,
one who has conquered anger and subdued the senses should honor the Brahmins with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Listen to the fruit of his merit, being entirely free from greed and delusion.
O Pāṇḍava, having attained that merit which belongs to the gift of a tawny cow (kapilā) given according to the prescribed rite, one is glorified in the world of Śakra;
and when he eventually falls from there at the end of his time, he is reborn in Kuśadvīpa.
Having sported there to his heart's content, he becomes a Brahmin among humans. He who passes the month of Bhādrapada eating only one meal a day,
remaining celibate, conquering anger, true to his word, and having subdued his senses—
Having seated the Brahmin on the seat of honor and remaining free from partiality regarding the food,
one should say, "Obeisance to the God who is the friend of Brahman," and touch his feet;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give sesame seeds or ghee as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
O best of men, hear the fruit of the merit belonging to my devotee:
having attained that same fruit of merit which is declared according to rule for the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, he is glorified in the world of Śakra.
Then, having passed away from that state in due time, he is born in the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Having sported there to his heart's content, he becomes a king among humans.
Furthermore, he who subsists on a single meal during the month of Āśvayuja—
One should recite my *gāyatrī* with devotion, with one's inner self absorbed in me,
at two or three junctions of the day, or a hundred and eight times,
having seated a Brahmin of restrained senses and mind upon the seat of honor.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should feed the Brahmins; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having attained that same meritorious fruit which belongs to a horse-sacrifice performed according to the rules, one is glorified in my world.
Then, having passed away from that time, one is born in Śvetadvīpa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having enjoyed great pleasures there, one shall become devoted to Brahmins here [on earth].
"Whoever should pass a full year eating but one meal a day—
O Keśava, tell me truly what the fruit of his merit shall be," said the Blessed One.

"Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to my truthful, meritorious, and supreme words— those by which a man is liberated from sins, whether he has failed to perform them or has performed them. That man who subsists on a single meal for a full year,"
For a celibate student (brahmacārī) who sleeps on the ground, has conquered anger, and has mastered his senses;
who is pure, devoted to bathing, diligent, truthful in speech, and free from malice; who constantly worships me with an inner self absorbed in me—[he attains success].
One should always recite my *gāyatrī* with a concentrated mind during the two twilights;
and having bowed down to me repeatedly with the mantra "Obeisance to the God who is Benevolent to Brahman," one should place a Brahmin on the seat of honor and [offer] barley-gruel and alms-food.
Having eaten, the twice-born man, restrained in speech, should rinse his mouth on the ground;
then, having said, "Salutation to Vāsudeva," he should touch [the teacher's] feet.
At the conclusion of every month, having fed pure brahmins...
When that year has been completed, one should then give the sacrificial fee (*vrata-dakṣiṇā*) consisting of either a cow made of fresh butter or a cow made of sesame seeds;
having been sprinkled with water accompanied by gold that has passed through the hands of a Brahmin.
"O King, listen as I describe the fruit of his merit:
whatever sin has been committed in ten lifetimes, whether knowingly or unknowingly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
That perishes for him instantly; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whatever great fruit is the most excellent among all fasts—the Blessed One said:
"O King Yudhiṣṭhira, you ought to speak of that which is the highest good in this world; listen, O King, as it was sung of old by Nārada,
and I shall relate it to you, my devotee, exactly as it was."
"O lord of men, he who, having become pure through devotion, observes the vow of fasting on my fifth [lunar day] and worships me at the three times of day," Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is glorified in my world.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, what is this [vow] of yours called 'the fifth'?
The Blessed One said:
I desire to hear that; tell it to me, O Acyuta. O Lord of Men, the two *parvan*s on the twelfth lunar day and the *śravaṇa* [nakṣatra]—that is renowned as the fifth, and it is especially dear to me.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of Brahmins whose intellects are established in me should observe a fast for the sake of my pleasure; or,
if they are unable [to fast the entire day], they should observe the fast on the twelfth lunar day alone.

"By that, O bull among men, I shall attain supreme joy. He who, having fasted for a day and night on the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, worships me as Keśava, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."

On the twelfth day of the month of Puṣya, however, he who fasts and worships me by the name Nārāyaṇa shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. On the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, having fasted and worshipped me as Mādhava...
He who worships me on the twelfth day of the month of Phālguna, fasting and honoring me under the name Govinda,
O King, obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and attains the merit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
He who, having fasted on the twelfth day of the month of Caitra, worships me as Viṣṇu,
obtains that fruit which belongs to the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha, [one should worship] the one known as Madhusūdana.
O Pāṇḍava,
he who fasts and worships me on the twelfth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha as Trivikrama obtains the fruit of a Gavāmedha sacrifice, O King.

O bull among the Bharatas, by fasting on the twelfth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice when worshipping me under the name Vāmana. By fasting on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one obtains the same fruit by worshipping me under the name Śrīdhara.
O King,
he who worships me during the month of Bhādrapada, calling me by the name Hṛṣīkeśa, and observes a fast,
attains the fruit of the five great sacrifices and the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice.
O King, he who fasts on the twelfth day of the month of Āśvayuja and worships me as Padmanābha attains the fruit of giving a thousand cows; likewise,
on the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship me under the name Dāmodara.
Whoever, having fasted, should worship [on this day], shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
O son of Pāṇḍu, by fasting alone on the twelfth day,
one obtains half of that fruit which was previously described.

In the same way, whatever man with devotion should worship me even during the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra], he attains my *sālokya* (residence in the same world as I); there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By worshipping me diligently month after month in due order, [he shall attain the same].

When a full year has passed, one should perform the worship again for another year. Thus, he who is my devotee, who is intent on me, and who performs this worship without obstacle for twelve years, shall attain my *sālokya* (residence in the same world as I).

O King, he who with devotion worships me on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) through the Vedic collection (vedasaṃhitā) obtains the fruit previously described; of this there is no doubt. [One should offer] perfume, flowers, fruit, water, leaves, or even just fruit.
On the twelfth day, whoever would give [this] to me—there is no one dearer to me than that person.
By this rite, all the gods, headed by Śakra, [are pleased].
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O tiger among men, my devotees enjoy the pleasures of heaven. While Keśava, the lord of gods, was speaking thus, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, said:
With palms joined in reverence, the son of Dharma spoke this hymn with devotion:
"O Lord of all worlds, O Lord of gods, O Hṛṣīkeśa, homage be unto you!
Homage, repeated homage, to you who possess a thousand heads and a thousand eyes!"

O you who consist of the three Vedas, O Lord of the three Vedas, O you who are praised by the three Vedas, salutations, salutations! O Soul of sacrifice, O born of sacrifice, O Lord of sacrifice, salutations, salutations! O fourfold form, O four-armed one, O fourfold manifestation, salutations, salutations!
O Soul of the world, Creator of the world, Refuge of the world, homage, homage!
O Narasiṃha, to You, the author of creation and dissolution, homage, homage!
O Beloved of devotees, let there be homage to You; O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees, homage to You!

O Abode of Brahmā, homage be to you; O Lord of Brahmā, homage, homage! O You who have the form of Rudra, homage be to you; homage to you who delight in the deeds of Rudra! O Five Sacrifices, homage be to you; O All-Sacrifice, homage, homage!

O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, let there be salutation to you; O Lord Kṛṣṇa, obeisance, obeisance. O abode of Yoga, let there be salutation to you; O Lord of Yoga, obeisance, obeisance. O horse-faced one, let there be salutation to you; O wielder of the discus, obeisance, obeisance.
"O you who consist of the five elements, homage be to you; O wielder of the five weapons, salutations, salutations!
Vaiśampāyana said:
While Yudhiṣṭhira was thus offering praise with a voice faltering with devotion...
Taking him by the hand, Keśava, with a joyful heart, restrained him;
and having thus restrained Yudhiṣṭhira, who was bowed with devotion,
he proceeded to speak to that best of men, the son of Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
"O King, O bull among men, why do you praise me in this manner, as if I were someone else?
Yudhiṣṭhira replied:
"Stay, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and ask about the very dharmas as before.
O Blessed One, by your grace, though I remember them again and again, there is no peace for me, O Lord of Gods; my mind seems to dance."
"O Mādhava, you ought to explain this question of mine.
The Blessed One said:
"How are you to be worshipped on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight?"
Listen, O King, I shall tell you all that according to the truth.
The fruit [obtained] from worship on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight is my own fruit.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should then worship me on the twelfth day.
A devoted man should also feed Brahmins according to his means;
he shall go to me as Dakṣiṇāmūrti—of this there is no doubt.
Vaiśampāyana said:

"Or else, O King, honored by the planets and constellations, you shall attain the same world as the Moon (candrasālokya). When Keśava had spoken thus, the son of Dharma again questioned the Lord regarding the specific details of the time for giving and the ritual procedure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, what fruit has been declared for giving gifts during the equinoxes?
The Blessed One replied:

O King, listen to the fruit obtained from giving a gift during an eclipse of the sun or moon, at the equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses, at the *vyatīpāta* yoga, and at the solstices; O monarch, such a gift becomes inexhaustible.
"O King, they declare the equinox (*viṣuva*) to be between the two eyes;
on that day, O King, night and day are equal, and at the twilight of the equinox, O Monarch,
Brahmā, I, and Śaṅkara stand together once."
Because of the state of oneness among the actions, instruments, and effects,
that supreme state is fruitless for us who have become one. O King, that moment known as the Viṣuva is supremely meritorious.
That very first syllable is proclaimed as Brahman, the Supreme Brahman. At that moment, all—
the gods, the ancestors, the Rudras, the Vasus, and likewise the two Aśvins— were contemplating that supreme state.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and likewise the Brahmarṣis;
the planets beginning with the Sun, as well as the oceans and the rivers;
the Maruts, the Apsarases, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, and the Guhyakas.
O Indra among kings, these and others, having restrained their senses at the equinox,
observe fasts with great effort and remain intent upon meditation;
they likewise bestow food, cows, sesame seeds, land, and daughters in marriage.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, grant me a house, clothing, grain, a vehicle, and likewise a bed, as well as whatever else I have mentioned;
for such gifts are given especially to those learned in the Vedas during the equinoxes.
O Kaunteya, the exhaustion of that gift never occurs;
day by day, that merit increases, equal to ten million times that gift.
Whoever should perform my ablution, or that of Hara, on the equinox—
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of worshipping him according to the prescribed rule:
the sin committed over ten lifetimes is instantly destroyed for him,
and he obtains the fruit of ten performed horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*).
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*), able to assume any form at will and moving according to his pleasure,
he goes to my world or even to the world of Rudra,
being sung of as he pleases by the gods and *gandharvas* dwelling there.
For one thousand divine years and one hundred million [years], he rejoices;
then, having passed away from that time, he becomes the best of the twice-born in this world,
a knower of Brahman who has reached the further shore of even the four Vedas.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, or even on my own or Śaṅkara’s [auspicious day],
whoever should recite my *gāyatrī* or that of Śaṅkara,
accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets as well as the resonance of bronze bells;
If one should cause a sound to be made with devotion, hear now the fruit of that merit:
through the sounds of music, fire-oblations, recitations, and excellent noises,
even Rāhu becomes weak and the Moon becomes strong.
During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, if a gift is bestowed upon those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*),
O King, even if a man should be tainted by a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), that gift becomes equal to a thousandfold and attends upon the donor.
By that very act of giving, one becomes free from attachment at that very moment;
shining with the brilliance of the sun and moon in a resplendent celestial palace (*vimāna*),
one goes to the delightful city of Soma, being attended by hosts of *apsarases*.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O king of kings, for as long as the stars remain in the sky together with the moon, for that length of time he is honored in the world of Soma;
and when his time there has passed, he returns here to this world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Brahmin, one who knows the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas may become a lord of ten million in wealth;
but, O Blessed One, how is the Gāyatrī understood by men?"
"Or what, O God, is its fruit? Tell me, O Lord of the Suras.
The Blessed One said:
"On the twelfth lunar day, at the equinox, and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
During the solstice, during the Śravaṇa asterism, and likewise during the Vyatīpāta yoga;
upon seeing the Aśvattha tree, and also upon seeing me—
having recited my Gāyatrī or the eight-syllable mantra, O King.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The evil deeds accumulated by one would surely be destroyed; there is no doubt in this matter.
Is even the sight of the Aśvattha tree equal to the sight of you?"
"O Lord of Gods, tell me this, for my curiosity is great.
The Blessed One said:
"In the form of the Aśvattha tree, I protect the three worlds."
Where the *aśvattha* tree does not stand, there I am not established;
where I am established, O King, there indeed the *aśvattha* also stands. He who would worship this with devotion, he worships me directly.
He who would strike this tree out of anger would be striking me myself.
Therefore, one should circumambulate it and must not cut it down day by day. The completion of a vow is called a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); uprightness is said to be a sacred ford.
Service to the gods is a sacred ford, as is service to one's teacher;
service to the teacher is a sacred ford, and the retention of the knowledge of the sacred fords is likewise.
The nourishment of men is a sacred ford, and the life of the householder is called a sacred ford.
